News.title: More 7-year-old kids receiving disability benefits than 50-year-olds, data reveals – as calls grow to cut welfare bill
News.content:
BENEFITS BOOM More 7-year-old kids receiving disability benefits than 50-year-olds, data reveals – as calls grow to cut welfare bill







Next

MORE seven-year-olds are receiving disability benefits than 50-year-olds new figures have revealed.

A total of 69,799 seven-year-olds are now receiving disability support, while 66,670 50-year-olds are on similar benefits figures show amid growing calls to cut the welfare bill.

Parents of children eligible to claim Disability Living Allowance (DLA) do so on their behalf which critics say creates a “pipeline” to Universal Credit.



Many of the children who received DLA later go on to claim Universal Credit on medical grounds, often after an ADHD diagnosis or other mental health condition.



Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, branded this a “cash-for-labels pipeline to a lifetime on benefits”.

She added: “Thousands of children are being told they have something wrong with them and that they deserve benefits as compensation,” she said.

“It’s damaging for them and unaffordable for the taxpayer.”

The number of children who receive DLA is more than double what it was before the pandemic, as claims for ADHD and learning difficulties have also surged.

This total is expected to hit one million this year; it is currently at 915,000 – more than triple the 314,000 children recorded in 2010.

Before the pandemic, 37,690 seven-year-olds were receiving DLA handouts, making the new figures an 85 per cent increase.

The Telegraph reports that in some areas of the country, one in five children are in receipt of DLA, while the national average is now one in 10.



This follows a recent review that revealed the number of children officially diagnosed with ADHD has surged from less than 0.5 per cent to between three and four per cent over the same period.

Around one per cent of young people are thought to have autism, but recorded diagnosis rates have rocketed to more than four per cent.

Following the figures, a second report warned that wrong diagnoses risk children not getting the help they need and instead facing a future of benefits.

It added that defining a generation of youngsters by their conditions may lead them to believe they cannot achieve things they might otherwise manage.

Experts fear that while many youngsters have been overlooked for years, the country is now approaching a tipping point.



This comes as the Government predicts within five years spending on DLA will surpass £8billion.

The annual benefits bill is set to hit £409bn a year by 2030.

One recent report found Britain spent £1.6trillion on working-age benefits in the past 20 years — three times more than the investment in infrastructure.

This has put pressure on John Healey to cut the benefits bill at his budget in two weeks.

Labour has been blamed for fuelling the crisis by imposing punishing taxes on business, such as the National Insurance hike.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In response The Sun has this week launched a campaign to try to tackle the welfare bill, focused on young people who are not in education, employment or training.

The Department for Work and Pensions has been approached for comment.

News.title: Heart-stopping moment toddler plunges between train and platform after warning from staff
News.content:
Next

THIS is the heart-stopping moment a toddler plunges between a train and platform just seconds after railway staff warned his mum to hold his hand.

Shocking footage shows the woman struggling to board a carriage with two enormous suitcases as her young son trails dangerously behind.



Spotting the looming danger, a railway officer shouts “hold your child’s hand” and “mind the gap while boarding”.

But as the mum wrestles her luggage onto the train, the youngster suddenly vanishes into the narrow gap between the carriage and platform.





A quick-thinking officer immediately springs into action, crouching beside the train and desperately reaching down to rescue the trapped boy.

As the frantic effort unfolds, he is heard shouting: “Hurry! Pull! One, two, three. Watch the head. Slowly.”

The terrified youngster is then hauled back onto the platform, where his distressed mum rushes to comfort him.

The dramatic ordeal unfolded at a railway station in Chengdu, southwest China, on Monday, October 5.



Miraculously, the boy escaped serious injury after being checked over following the horrifying fall.

But the near-tragedy sparked a furious backlash online, with viewers blasting the mum for appearing more concerned with her luggage than her son’s safety.

One outraged viewer fumed: “This mum is really something. She’s carrying two suitcases and doesn’t even look back at her child. Can’t you put one suitcase and the child in the car first, and then take the other suitcase?



“I’m really fed up! There’s no excuse that can make me understand this parent. Their job is not done properly.”

Another warned: “First, never leave your child behind and they have to be your priority.”

A third blasted: “Luggage more precious than children.”

The terrifying incident echoes another nerve-wracking railway rescue in Argentina, where a heroic police officer snatched a toddler from the path of an oncoming freight train.

Heart-racing footage captured a three-year-old boy standing motionless on the tracks as a 29-wagon locomotive loaded with stone thundered towards him.



Despite the driver repeatedly blasting the horn, the youngster, wearing a red shirt, appeared frozen in place.

First Corporal Pablo Luna, who was patrolling nearby on his motorcycle, spotted the unfolding nightmare and sprinted towards the tracks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

With the colossal train bearing down on the child, the brave officer grabbed him by one arm and yanked him clear of the rails just seconds before disaster.

The remarkable rescue unfolded in Córdoba, where witnesses said Luna had raced towards the youngster without a moment’s hesitation.

News.title: Social media blocked for thousands of teenagers in major UK city ahead of under-16 ban
News.content:
Next

A UK city is trialling social media restrictions for thousands of 12 to 15- year-olds.

This comes ahead of the UK government’s social media ban for under-16s due to come into force in spring 2027.



Ahead of the ban, Bradford is trialling social media restrictions for six weeks.

Around 4,000 to 5,000 children across the city will either have their use of ten apps cut to two hours a day, along with a 9pm curfew, or will be allowed to carry on as usual but with their usage tracked.



Those with the restrictions on their phones will have access disabled to: TikTok, Snapchat, Instagram, Facebook, X, YouTube, Reddit, Twitch, Threads and Kick, along with their associated websites.

It will also disable access between 9pm and 7am each night.



Before the study, the children took part in a survey about their online activity, mental health, loneliness, exercise and sleep.

The survey will be repeated after the trial, in six weeks time.

Trial manager Dr John Pickavance explained: “We want to know if they are getting better sleep, will they be doing more physical activity, or will they just replace it with other forms of screen time – TV, video games, other things on the phone.”

Secondary school pupils in Bradford estimate that they spend an average of three hours and 20 minutes on social media on a school day but scientists suspect this is an underestimate.



To encourage pupils to stick to the rules, researchers are relying on vouchers rather than punishments.

Although participants can override the restrictions with the press of a button, the more they follow the rules, the more likely they are to win a £100 voucher on top of the £20 voucher they receive for participating.

News.title: My daughter, 12, died after drinking Twix milkshake made using dirty blender – I knew something was wrong after 2 sips
News.content:
Next

THE mum of a girl who died after drinking a milkshake made in an unwashed blender described how her daughter said something was wrong after just two sips.

Mia Shay St Hilaire, 12, suffered an extreme allergic reaction after drinking a Twix milkshake made in an unwashed blender from Pop Inn Cafe in London, August 2023.



Her mum, Chanel Spence, told Good Morning Britain hosts Susanna Reid and Ed Balls that Mia knew something was off after just “two sips”.

She told her aunt, who she was visiting: “This has nuts in”.



CCTV captured the moment then-operator Baris Yucel prepared the drink, using a blender that had been “cross-contaminated with hazelnut residue”.

Mia was put on life support so her heartbroken family could say goodbye before she died of anaphylaxis.



Host Ed asked Mia’s parents whether the youngster, who had a tree nut allergy, knew to check hygiene ratings when dining out.

They said it was something she was used to doing and had even visited the Bermondsey cafe previously.



However, the family were shocked to hear that allergy management didn’t fall under the same system as food hygiene ratings.

Chanel said: “When you see a five-star rating at a shop, you feel like, you know, you’re safe,” she said.

It prompted the parents to call for a separate rating system to allow customers to monitor how businesses manage allergy risks in the UK.

Dad Adrian St Hilaire said: “Had that been in place, we’d be looking at a different outcome and a totally different story.”

Reflecting on life since Mia’s death, Chanel said that the grief is still overwhelming.



“It doesn’t really change a thing, you know, she’s our every day,” she said.

The family’s solicitor Angela Bruno joined the parents on GMB and said that the cafe had faced scrutiny over its allergy management in 2020.

In spite of this, it was still awarded a five-star rating , before another inspection two years later was “missed”.



She said: “Mia passes away in 2023, and again they go in. Still no matrix, no allergy signs, other issues are raised with regard to contamination.”

According to the Food Standards Agency website, the restaurant received another five-star hygiene rating in 2024.

Former owner Yucel pleaded guilty to six offences in January 2024 at Croydon Magistrates Court.

This included not making allergen advice available to consumers, failing to manage allergen contamination and serving food that contained allergen ingredients that should not have been there.

He was fined £18,000 and given a 100-hour community order.



In a previous statement to PEOPLE, Rebecca Sudworth, Director of Food Policy at the Food Standards Agency, said: “We recently produced new guidance for businesses to make sure they understand their responsibilities to inform consumers about allergens, including the risk of cross-contact, and we are keeping this policy under review.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We also have free allergy training and practical tools that businesses can use.”

News.title: Eritreans facing BAN from entering Britain if country doesn’t accept more small boat migrants, Labour warns
News.content:
NO ENTRY Eritreans facing BAN from entering Britain if country doesn’t accept more small boat migrants, Labour warns







Next

BRITAIN has threatened to ban Eritreans from entering the country if the war-torn African country does not accept more migrants from small boats.

Eritrean diplomats could be stripped of their visas and face tough restrictions on their movements.



The crackdown comes as the African country topped the list of nationalities arriving in Britain by small boat in the 12 months to June.

They account for a staggering one in five arrivals.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood urged the Eritrean government to take back their nationals or face a hardline visa ban.



Ms Mahmood: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.

“I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate.”



Labour’s ultimatum comes after months of efforts by Britain to solve the migrant problem with the Eritrean government behind closed doors.

The warning comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew co-operation earlier this year.

Migrants arriving to Britain via small boat fell by 41 per cent compared to last year.

But a staggering 20,478 people have still crossed the Channel by small boat from France.



Labour has accused the Eritrean authorities of “abruptly” withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.

One migrant crossed the Channel every six minutes during the first week of October, new figures reveal.

An estimated 1,739 people made the journey to Britain in just seven days – an average of more than ten every hour.

News.title: Rogue mechanic who wrongly passed MOT of car that killed three young people in horror crash AVOIDS jail
News.content:
DEATH CRASH SHAME Rogue mechanic who wrongly passed MOT of car that killed three young people in horror crash AVOIDS jail







Next

A ROGUE mechanic who wrongly passed the MOT of a car that killed three young people in a crash has avoided jail.

Rafel Jeanne, who was driving at the time, and passengers Darcy Ross and Eve Smith, both 21, all died in the horror in St Mellons, Cardiff.



Two further passengers, Sophie Russon, 20, and Shane Loughlin, 32, were injured but survived.

The five friends were discovered around 46 hours after the Volkswagen Tiguan they were travelling in left the road and smashed into trees on a roundabout.



Neil Lewis admitted fraud by false representation after passing the car’s MOT – despite knowing it should have failed its safety inspection.

The garage worker was spared jail and was instead handed a community order for 12 months subject to probation requirements and will be required to complete 100 hours of unpaid community work.



It comes after Darcy’s family previously approached Lewis outside Cardiff Magistrates’ Court today with a framed photo of the young woman.

They shouted: “Darcy Ross, remember her name.”

The court heard the Volkswagen had previously been involved in a crash in Scotland in 2021.

It suffered damage to its nearside wing, the airbags had deployed, and the airbag and seatbelt warning lights were on.

But it was sold to a salvage company in Cardiff – and no work was carried out on the vehicle before it was sold at auction to a friend of Rafel Jeanne.



The Volkswagen failed an MOT on February 9, 2023, as there was an issue with the seatbelts.

Lewis subsequently conducted a re-test and passed the Volkswagen with some advisories.

Officers found messages on Lewis’ phone to the owner of the car saying: “You’ve got to sort the seatbelt and the airbag light.



“I’ve passed the car though.”

Prosecutor Francesca Parry said the seatbelts in the car had not been replaced since the car crash in Scotland.

She told the court that Lewis had authorised for the car to pass the MOT despite knowing about the issues.

The horror unfolded on March 4, 2023, as the friends made their way back from the night out.



The car is understood to have left the road on a slip road on the A48 as it approached a roundabout.

A major hunt for the group was sparked after they were reported missing but it took two days to find the wreckage.

Driver Rafel was the son of ex-QPR and Cardiff City player Leon Jeanne.

A court previously heard they had been drinking alcohol and inhaling laughing gas prior to the crash.



District Judge Charlotte Murphy told the court before Lewis’ sentencing that she wasn’t treating the crash as an aggravating feature.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But she said his decision to pass the car was a “dereliction of duty.”

Six police officers were charged with misconduct allegations in connection with the investigation but two have been cleared following an internal hearing.

News.title: David Amess’ daughter’s agony 5yrs on from MP terror murder…’Dad would have been heartbroken about Aunty Ann Widdecombe’
News.content:
MP MURDER David Amess’ daughter’s agony 5yrs on from MP terror murder…’Dad would have been heartbroken about Aunty Ann Widdecombe’







Next

KATIE Amess can acutely remember the last time she saw her dad, Sir David, before he was murdered by a terrorist as he carried out his constituency surgery five years ago today.

It was at Heathrow Airport in September 2021.



Katie, who was flying back home to LA, where she still lives, had been home to Southend-on-Sea, Essex, for her sister Alexandra’s wedding.

“Normally Dad and I would have been really upset and crying,” she recalled.



“But that time we were excited because I was due back shortly for my wedding.”

Sir David – who had been a Tory MP since 1983 when Margaret Thatcher was in power – was giddy with excitement.

“He jokingly called it ‘The Royal Wedding,’” remembered actress Katie, 41.

“He would take my arm and practise walking me down the aisle.

“I was marrying in the Crypt at the House of Commons, which I was allowed to do as the daughter of an MP, and he was so looking forward to that – he was so proud.”

The pair, who were incredibly close, had arranged parts of Katie’s wedding together.



Sir David had enjoyed picking out a suit and approved of the song he would be walking her down the aisle to – Pachelbel’s Canon.

Instead, he was to wear the suit, and mourners listened to that very same song, at his funeral in St Mary’s Church, Southend-on-Sea, on November 22, 2021.

“It was heartbreaking,” said Katie, who is speaking with the permission of her widowed mum Lady Julia, 72, who is unwell.



She told how her dad was so popular that after the funeral his casket was driven through the streets in a horse-drawn carriage while thousands of mourners gathered.

“So many people loved Dad,” she recalled.

“They all wanted to say thank you for serving us.”

A devout Catholic, he had a second mass at Westminster Cathedral, which was attended by then-Prime Minister Boris Johnson and then-Leader of the Opposition Keir Starmer, and where a tribute by the Pope was read out.

“It was extraordinary – but Dad was an extraordinary man,” said Katie.



Katie was asleep in LA when her dad was knifed to death by Islamic State fanatic Ali Harbi Ali.

He was two hours into meeting constituents in a church hall in Leigh-on-Sea when Ali – who had made an appointment with Sir David’s aide for noon – came in.

Ali, telling Sir David he wanted to “talk about foreign affairs”, quickly turned on him with a 12-inch carving knife.

Police were called, but the MP was pronounced dead at the scene and the knifeman arrested.



“I found out quickly about what had happened and flew back to the UK,” said Katie, who is still too traumatised to talk about the immediate aftermath.

At home, weeks from her wedding, she discovered her “energetic” Dad had organised lots of “secrets” for the big day.

“He’d planned a Eurovision singer and stilt walkers to surprise me on the day – it was very him,” she laughed.

“But it was absolutely heartbreaking going through all his notes and having to call people and explain.



“But everyone was so kind.

“They wouldn’t charge me.

“They all said he was wonderful to talk to.”

She said his constituents felt the same way too.



“He became an MP for Basildon, Essex, in 1983 and stayed there until 1997,” she explained.

“But he switched to Southend West in 1997 because Mum wanted to move.

“I asked him once if he wanted to be Prime Minister and he said: ‘No way!’

“He wasn’t the kind of politician who just climbed the greasy ladder.



“He was a constituency MP.

“He really cared about the people he represented.

“He would go to every shop opening, every fete, every street party he could.

“He would visit OAPs in their homes and went to see patients in hospital.

“He listened to people.



“I’ll never forget when someone was canvassing for him once and they knocked on the door of a man and he said: ‘I’ll never vote for the Tories! I’m voting for that David Amess anyway.’”

Recalling her childhood and her dad, Katie said: “He was fantastic.

“My parents had five children in seven years: my brother David, 42, and sisters Sarah, 39, Alexandra, 38, and Florence, 35.



“When we were younger he would regularly take us to waterparks, even though he couldn’t swim.

“It would terrify Mum.

“We had loads of animals too.

“Catholicism and animals were two of his big passions in life.

“He hated fox hunting and was against animal testing.”



It was his devotion to both which led to him becoming “best friends” with fellow long-serving Tory MP Ann Widdecombe.

Ann, 78, died in July this year at her home in Haytor, Devon after being struck multiple times with a hammer.

Joshua Kerry, 28, from Rotherham has been charged with her murder and preparing terrorist acts.

The Old Bailey has been told he is likely to contest the charges against him and a trial date has been set for next year.

“I called her Aunty Ann and she was my sister Alexandra’s godmother, so we were really close,” explained Katie.



“After Dad died, Aunty Ann supported the family, so we were all devastated when she died.

“Dad would have been heartbroken too.”

Katie didn’t attend Ali’s trial in the Old Bailey in March and April 2022, although she was pleased he was found guilty after just 18 minutes of deliberations and given a whole-life sentence, which means he will not be considered for parole and will never be released from prison.

“I didn’t need to and knew Dad wouldn’t have wanted me to go and be upset,” she said.

“He means nothing to me. He said he was fighting ‘for Syria’.



“But how was he doing that?

“He could have gone there and actually fought.

“Instead, he went armed to a church and attacked an unarmed 69-year-old man who would have greeted him with a smile and a ‘Hello’.

“It’s disgusting. He’s pathetic and embarrassing.

“He thought he was so innovative. He was a coward.



“That’s what I think about him – embarrassing.”

She is angry because Ali, then 26, from Kentish Town, North London, had been flagged as a terror risk before the attack.

He became known to the UK’s ‘Prevent’ anti-terror scheme in October 2014, but his case was closed in 2016 – despite Prevent staff meeting him for just one coffee at McDonald’s and suggesting “he seems to be a great person.”

A Prevent Learning Review into Ali’s case, commissioned by the Home Office and the Counter Terrorism Police and published in 2025, said the “hope” of addressing Ali’s vulnerabilities was missed because of a “breakdown in communications.”

Then-Security Minister Dan Jarvis said the review found “the rationale for certain decisions” in the monitoring of Ali was “not explicit”.



“The assessment in terms of the perpetrator’s vulnerabilities was problematic, and this ultimately led to questionable decision-making and sub-optimal handling of the case,” he said.

Katie, who rearranged her wedding but has since divorced, added: “There were supposed to be six planned follow-up sessions and they didn’t happen.

“He slipped through the system due to an ‘admin error’.

“As a result, my Dad died.

“I know we’ve had paper reviews but it isn’t enough as you can’t call witnesses and cross-examine.



“There’s been public inquiries for other serious terrorist incidents such as those in Nottingham and Southport – as there should be – so I just want the same for Dad.

“We’ve now accepted another review, the Robert Buckland Review, which has been set up to look into missed police opportunities and the current security setup for MPs in their constituencies.

“But it’s a compromise.

“I will not stop fighting for a public inquiry – Dad deserves it.

“All MPs, irrespective of party, deserve to be safe and to be able to do their job without fear of being killed.



“It shouldn’t take five years for our family to get this.”

A Home Office spokeswoman told The Sun: “Our thoughts remain with the friends and family of Sir David Amess grieving his horrific murder.

“There have already been several reviews into how this despicable attack could have been avoided, and we do not believe a public inquiry would unearth anything further.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Instead, the Home Secretary has commissioned a further review to identify improvements to security arrangements for MPs in their constituencies.

“We very much hope this will help give Sir David’s family the answers they deserve.”

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan live: Duke and Duchess of Sussex welcomed to Nottingham by cheering crowd
News.content:
One week after Harry and Meghan, along with their children Archie and Lilibet returned to the UK, Buckingham Palace issued an unprecedented statement to clarify their roles outside the monarchy.

In a firm letter issued on behalf of the King on September 8, it stated that the Sussexes' should not use their HRH styles, which are still in abeyance, and that they "do not represent the sovereign" while out making public appearances.

The letter added: "The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."

A royal source told the Mirror at the time in response: "Timing is everything. Harry and Meghan have only been in the country a matter of days but this important line has been drawn early, leaving no one in any doubt where his feelings lie on the matter. The King could not be clearer. You may have come back to the UK, but you are on your own."

Shortly after the letter was issued, a Sussex spokesperson issued a statement saying they were ‘surprised’ at the notice from the Palace. The statement read: "We were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance."

The spokesperson added that the publication of the letter had caught the couple off guard, and did not have enough time to clarify any points.

News.title: Istanbul floods chaos as at least two people dead with cars flipped and roads underwater
News.content:
Istanbul floods chaos as at least two people dead with cars flipped and roads underwater

Turkey's largest city has been battered by its heaviest rainfall since 1985, with the deluge killing at least two - including a teenager electrocuted while stepping into a puddle

View 4 Images Cars were swept away amid the deluge (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

At least two people have been killed after torrential downpours in Istanbul left entire neighbourhoods submerged with terrified residents and tourists rushed to safety.

‌



‌



The deluge on Wednesday night triggered landslides across Turkey's largest city and brought traffic to a halt, with dozens left stranded amid the chaos.

‌



Among those killed was a 14-year-old boy who was electrocuted after stepping into a puddle at a park in the Fatih district.

‌



The teenager was seen walking through the tourist hotspot of Balat before suddenly collapsing , CCTV footage verified by Al Jazeera showed .

View 4 Images An aerial view of roads submerged in Sariyer (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The boy was rushed to hospital unconscious but tragically later died, with an investigation into the incident underway.

‌



A second victim, a 34-year-old woman, died after slipping on a pavement in the Sariyer district and hitting her head, according to local reports.

Last night's downpour was the city's heaviest since 1985, with more rain forecast over the coming days.

A major rescue effort was launched to save dozens of people left stranded at their workplaces, while bystanders rallied together to help others.

‌



One woman who was swept across a street by the floodwaters was rescued by locals while another person trapped in a flooded basement was saved by firefighters.

View 4 Images The floods have killed at least two people (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Images showed damaged cars piled up along submerged streets after the vehicles were swept away by the deluge.

‌



According to the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IBB), almost 7,000 emergency reports were made as the heavy rain unleashed chaos across the city.

The governor's office said schools would be closed on both Thursday and Friday, adding that state employees with disabilities and mothers with young children would be placed on leave.

Residents were urged to stay at home and only travel unless absolutely necessary, while those living in basement apartments were told to leave their homes and spend the night elsewhere.

‌



The torrential rain also saw dozens of metro and tram services disrupted, and 43 flights attempting to land at Istanbul Airport were diverted to alternative airports.

View 4 Images Residents have been urged to stay at home (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Mayor Thodoris Tzoumas said up to 50 businesses and 20 homes had suffered damage.

‌



"The rain and winds continue," he said. "We are carrying out repairs to the main network, where we have some power outages.

"We had some trees fall and two cars have been swept away, while schools are closed. The phenomenon seems to be subsiding."

It comes as a severe storm battered large parts of Greece, with a 62-year-old hotel worker killed on the popular holiday island of Rhodes.

Article continues below

The island was battered by heavy rainfall on Wednesday, with Greek public broadcaster ERT reporting that more than 200mm fell in six and a half hours.

Authorities declared an emergency and urged residents and holidaymakers to restrict all but essential travel.

The warning read: "Due to severe weather conditions in the Regional Unit of #Rodos, limit your movement to the absolutely necessary".

News.title: Ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years over child sex abuse
News.content:
Ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years over child sex abuse

Ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson was convicted of sex offences relating to the abuse of two women when they were children between 1985 and 2008 - the judge said his sentence would be lengthy

View 4 Images Jeffrey Donaldson appeared in the dock at Newry Crown Court today (Image: Liam McBurney/PA Wire)

Former DUP leader and convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for child sex abuse.

Donaldson, 63, arrived at Newry Crown Court in a prison van and later appeared in the dock where judge Paul Ramsey handed down the sentence.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 sex offences, including one count of rape, relating to the abuse of two women when they were children. The offences were committed between 1985 and 2008.

Judge Ramsay said complainant A said she had been "traumatised" by the trial process. The judge said the woman said the impact of Jeffrey Donaldson’s abuse did not stop when the abuse ended, saying she grew up feeling “ashamed and dirty”.

View 4 Images Donaldson arrived at court in a prison van (Image: Getty Images)

The complainant said the last number of years had been a "living nightmare". The judge said complainant B said she prayed to God every day to let her die.

Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson had "doubled down on his denials" since his conviction. "There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort," he said.

He said Donaldson had experienced a "catastrophic descent into disgrace".

The former Lagan Valley MP has awaited his sentencing in Maghaberry Prison in County Antrim since the end of the trial. The two victims gave evidence against him earlier this year.

View 4 Images Donaldson was convicted of 18 sex offences (Image: Liam McBurney/PA Wire)

Complainant A said Donaldson engaged in inappropriate kissing and touching as well as an incident where he used a light to examine her genitals. Complainant B told the trial she had been raped as a child of primary school age by Donaldson and later sexually assaulted by him.

Donaldson denied the offences, but he was convicted on one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency. At a pre-sentence hearing last month, extracts from victim impact statements from the two women were read.

View 4 Images Donaldson has been stripped of his knighthood (Image: Liam McBurney/PA Wire)

Jeffrey Donaldson's barrister Kieran Vaughan KC said during that hearing that the former politician was a man of "previous good character" who "did achieve significant things". But he added: "These convictions obliterate all those achievements he has made in his life."

Donaldson has been stripped of his knighthood and removed from the Privy Council. His solicitor previously confirmed papers have been lodged for an appeal.

Jeffrey Donaldson "deserves every day of the lengthy prison service he has to serve", the Democratic Unionist Party has said. Donaldson, the former leader of the party, received a 15-year sentence at Newry Crown Court for a series of historical sex offences.

In a statement, the DUP said: "Today justice has been done with the sentencing of Jeffrey Donaldson for his vile and disgusting crimes against his victims. Our first thoughts are again with the innocent victims, who having suffered such evil, were re-traumatised through giving evidence at the trial.

"They deserve our compassion, support and respect. We hope they can find some measure of comfort and can look ahead to a new chapter in their lives." The party added: "Regardless of status or position every individual must be held accountable for their actions.

Article continues below

"He deserves every day of the lengthy prison sentence he has to serve following the guilty verdict for preying on innocent child victims."

News.title: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood threatens to ban all visas from African nation over migrant row
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood threatens to ban all visas from African nation over migrant row

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has warned the government of Eritrea that she is considering a complete visa ban because the oppressive regime has refused to take back failed asylum seekers

View 2 Images The Home Secretary has threatened action after a row over migrant returns escalated (Image: Dan Kitwood/PA Wire)

Shabana Mahmood has warned she will impose a complete ban on people from an East African nation coming to the UK as a row over migrant returns escalates.

‌



‌



VIPs and officials from Eritrea have been blocked from getting fast-track visas after their government refused to back down. Ms Mahmood says she is considering a complete visa ban if tensions are not resolved.

‌



Nearly two in 10 small boat arrivals were from Eritrea in the 12 months to June, Home Office figures show. Human rights groups highlight the country as one of the most repressive in the world, accusing the government of unlawfully killing and detaining its critics.

‌



Eritrea's diplomats have been banned from travelling more than 60 kilometres - 37 miles - outside of London without permission from the Foreign Office. Similar restrictions are in place for British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.

View 2 Images The government is locked in a diplomatic row with Eritrea in East Africa (Image: Getty Images)

Ms Mahmood said: "Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.

‌



"My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate.”

Three other countries that have faced similar threats - Angola, Nambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) - have since agreed migrant returns.

The face-off comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew returns co-operation earlier this year. The government is pushing for it to accept failed asylum seekers and foreign criminals.

‌



It has announced that the nation's preferential visa processing for VIPs and government officials has been scrapped. And the Home Office said there would be a total visa shutdown if the Eritrean government does not change course.

It accuses Eritrea of refusing to engage constructively. The number of arrivals from Eritrea has risen in recent years, and its nationals now account for the largest share of people crossing the Channel by small boat.

Latest data show 18% of small boat arrivals are Eritrean, followed by Sudanese (13%), Afghan (12%), Somali (12%) and Iranian nationals (11%).

‌



Eritrea is ruled by an authoritarian government led by Isaias Afwerki - who has been in charge since the country's last elections were held in 1993.

A 2025 report on the nation by Human Rights Watch details concerns about forced conscriptions, religious oppression and sexual violence by the armed forces.

It says: "The Eritrean government maintained an iron grip on its population at home and abroad. It continued to repress the population’s human rights, including freedom of opinion, religion, and expression, and forced some children and much of its adult population into indefinite military/national service."

Article continues below

The report goes on: "Arrests are frequently made without warrants or notification of charges, and many Eritreans, notably perceived dissidents, government critics, human rights defenders, religious leaders, and journalists, are subjected to enforced disappearance for years or even decades. Some are held in solitary confinement in undisclosed locations, while others are thought to have been killed or died in detention."

News.title: Pharmaceutical expert gives supplement warning to anyone taking magnesium
News.content:
Pharmaceutical expert gives supplement warning to anyone taking magnesium

Many people are taking supplements for sleep quality, anxiety symptoms, migraines and blood pressure

View Image Magnesium is an essential mineral involved in hundreds of processes in the body and many are taking it in the UK (Image: Getty)

A pharmaceutical expert has given an update for anyone taking magnesium - and said there are many types of medication which can have different impacts. There has been a massive surge in popularity of magnesium supplements across social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, where influencers and wellness creators market the mineral as a “miracle cure-all”

‌



‌



An essential mineral, magnesium is found naturally in food and comes with plenty of benefits. It helps our cells, organs and brain function, stabilises our moods, and maintains our muscles, nervous and immune systems. It also activates vitamin D – another immunity booster.

‌



The NHS recommends women aged between 19 and 64 get 270mg magnesium a day, and 300mg for men of the same age. Magnesium helps to regulate our metabolism and brain health and may also play a role in improving anxiety and depression.

‌



Writing on The Conversation website, Dipa Kamdar Associate Professor in Pharmacy Practice, Kingston University said there’s no shortage of influencers listing all the benefits that different types of magnesium supplements have – from boosting brain function to helping ease anxiety and improving sleep.

She said: “Magnesium is an essential mineral involved in hundreds of processes in the body. It helps muscles and nerves work properly, supports energy production and contributes to the maintenance of strong bones and teeth.

“Magnesium is also important for maintaining a healthy heart rhythm, regulating blood pressure and blood sugar levels. Many people don’t get enough from their diet, so supplements can be useful in some situations. But when you look closely at the research, there’s little evidence to suggest that any one type of magnesium supplement has unique benefits over another.”

‌



Magnesium Glycinate

Prof Kandar said: “One of the most talked about types of magnesium is magnesium glycinate, often promoted as the best option for sleep. This form combines magnesium with glycine, an amino acid that may improve sleep on its own.”

She said that evidence is that it helps improve sleep, but research shows it is no more effective for sleep than other magnesium forms. Main Benefit is that it is highly gentle on the stomach and easily absorbed.

Magnesium L-Threonate

It is claimed to boost memory, focus, and brain function. Prof Kandar said animal studies showed it increased brain magnesium levels. A human study using 2g daily found improvements in working memory, reaction speed, and mental performance compared to a placebo. She said human research is limited, and there is no proof it outperforms other forms for brain health.

‌



Magnesium Malate

Magnesium malate combines magnesium with malic acid, a compound involved in energy production within cells. Prof Kandar said correcting a deficiency improves muscle cramps and fatigue. Small studies in people with fibromyalgia showed reductions in pain and tiredness. But she said it lacks strong evidence showing it works better than other well-absorbed forms for the general population.

Magnesium Citrate & Magnesium Oxide

Commonly used to treat constipation by drawing water into the bowel and to reduce the frequency and severity of migraines. Prof Kandar said: “Both forms may also reduce the severity and frequency of migraines and are cost-effective options. However, the oxide form is absorbed less efficiently, so people may need higher doses to achieve the same effect as citrate, which may cause an upset stomach.”

She issued a warning about supplements and questioned if they are necessary: “Overall, across a range of clinical trials, magnesium has shown some benefits for sleep quality, anxiety symptoms, migraines and blood pressure. But there’s no strong evidence that one form is better than another.”

Article continues below

She said most evidence came from small pilot studies, animal research or supplement marketing – rather than large, well-designed human trials. “While magnesium is beneficial for our health, it’s worth asking whether supplements are even necessary. For most people, a varied and balanced diet is the best way to get magnesium.

Foods with naturally high levels of magnesium include leafy greens (such as spinach and kale), nuts and seeds, wholegrains and beans. These foods provide fibre, antioxidants and other nutrients that supplements cannot offer. They also reduce the risk of taking too much magnesium, which can cause diarrhoea or stomach upset.”

Reach the full article here.

News.title: Bridget Phillipson talks of 'absolutely crippling' pain and constant vomiting during periods
News.content:
Bridget Phillipson talks of 'absolutely crippling' pain and constant vomiting during periods

Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson said the UK has a 'system and a culture that’s built for men' and admitted more needs to be done to take women seriously

View 2 Images Former Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson said her monthly periods were 'debilitating' and caused her to take time off school (Image: Dig It with Jo Whiley and Zoe Ball/YouTube)

Bridget Phillipson said she suffered "absolutely crippling" pain and constant vomiting during her periods when she was younger.

‌



‌



The Minister for Women and Equalities said the UK has a "system and a culture that’s built for men" and admitted more needs to be done to take women seriously.

‌



She said there needs to be a "much bigger conversation" around women's experiences, including about the menopause, endometriosis and maternity care. She called for a whole society approach to better value women, saying men also must "step up".

‌



Speaking on the Dig It podcast with Jo Whiley and Zoe Ball, Ms Phillipson - the former Education Secretary - said her monthly periods were "debilitating" and caused her to take time off school.

She said: "For me, the pain was absolutely crippling every month, just absolutely crippling, and it was accompanied with really unfortunate vomiting, like constant vomiting, which kind of passed over time. But again, people just think you're being a bit melodramatic.

View 2 Images Labour chair Bridget Phillipson admitted women's voices were not valued enough (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



"Like, ‘well, it can't be that bad. It's just your period. It happens once a month’. It was really really debilitating. I came out the other side, and I was fine, but there are really dismissive attitudes even today.

She said her school was understanding but said it was "irritating" having to take a day or two off school every month. "If I could have been at school, I would be there, but if you physically can't get out of bed," she added.

In April, the Government launched a renewed Women’s Health Strategy to stop women being “ignored, gaslit, humiliated and disrespected”. Then Health Secretary Wes Streeting said the NHS is “failing women and girls on even the most basic measures of healthcare”.

‌



The strategy set out several pledges to improve women's experience in the NHS, including cutting waits for gynaecology care and a £1million menstrual education programme to ensure girls are better equipped to recognise the difference between healthy and unhealthy periods.

During the podcast with Ms Phillipson, concerns were raised about an overburdened NHS as well as a lack of understanding or research into women's health conditions.

Ms Phillipson admitted women's voicers were not valued enough. "We don’t take what women have to say seriously, whether that’s around menopause or endometriosis, or what we’ve seen more recently with some really appalling examples of maternal healthcare and the utterly shocking experiences that so many women have been through. We don’t listen to women. We don’t value what they have to say.

‌



"In shining a light on what needs to happen around the menopause, that also opens up a much bigger conversation I think about how we just don’t value women’s experiences and the things we all go through at different stages of our lives are seen as things we just have to put up with and just deal with in silence."

Asked if enough is being done to help women during the menopause, she said: "We’ve got a system and a culture that’s built for men and that doesn’t recognise women’s unique experiences and that’s what I’m determined to change."

She added that workplaces without the right support meant industries were losing "talented women right at the peak of their experience: She said: "I don’t want to see women stepping away from brilliant careers and jobs because they’re not being properly supported. That isn’t just damaging to that individual woman, that’s a tragedy for all of us.

Article continues below

"We lose out as a society where we don't value and recognise the contribution of women. Government’s got a role to play, all of us have a role to play, but actually I think we need men to step up as well and provide us with the support, not it always falling to us to have to campaign for the change that we want to see."

News.title: BBC in danger of losing two more huge sports rights with 69-year-old show at risk
News.content:
BBC in danger of losing two more huge sports rights with 69-year-old show at risk

The BBC could face further losses of rights to sporting events

View 3 Images The BBC could be in for yet another rude awakening (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

The BBC’s long-standing monopoly on top-tier sports broadcasting is facing a fresh challenge from talkSPORT. Fresh off securing live coverage for England’s upcoming cricket tour of South Africa, the commercial broadcaster is turning its sights toward two of the BBC's most prized properties: Formula One and home England cricket coverage.

‌



‌



With Test Match Special airing on the BBC since 1957 and live F1 coverage standard since 1994, talkSPORT's ambitious push - reported by The Telegraph - marks the latest threat to the corporation's sports line-up, following a string of recent rights losses ranging from the Commonwealth Games to the Boat Race.

‌



Liam Fisher, the head of talkSPORT, admitted that while football coverage remains the primary focus of the company, they are making a deliberate effort to tap into different audiences where they believe the returns will be substantial.

‌



He said: "Football still is our bread and butter... but we've definitely looked to extend it on the basic understanding that, even if football is your first, second and third sport, you are probably into something else as well.

BBC loses all rights to ANOTHER iconic sporting event they've shown since 1950 READ MORE :

"So our strategy has been to pick off the events where we believe there is an audience potential that sits well with what we're providing, we'll cherry pick what we think are the key sports and events that we think you might be interested in."

Fisher outlined the rationale behind talkSPORT's pursuit of F1, which has maintained an exclusive arrangement with BBC Radio for 32 years. He explained: "It's another brilliant set of rights. I wouldn't be doing my job if I wasn't actively exploring whether there's an opportunity.

‌



View 3 Images Jonathan Agnew has been a commentator for Test Match Special since 1991 (Image: Stu Forster/Getty Images)

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

"We think the audience goes quite well with the talkSPORT audience. We think there's an opportunity for us to deliver really good amplification for it as well." If the BBC loses the rights to the cricket coverage, it could mark the conclusion of its 69-year relationship with Test Match Special.

‌



Though this may not materialise after the England & Wales Cricket Board (ECB) suggested the possibility of having multiple radio broadcasters for its home series starting from 2029. Fisher claimed that, considering the BBC's cost-cutting efforts to save £500million, talkSPORT's move into the cricket sphere represents "good business."

He added: "It's something which we've been really keen on getting involved in more. Our tactic has been to just pick off some of the away series. I love cricket. We'd certainly love to do more in that space. And we believe, fundamentally, just as the Premier League have worked to have a couple of incumbents, it would work to the benefit of other organisations as well.

View 3 Images BBC Radio have had an exclusive deal with Formula One since 1992 (Image: Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Article continues below

"I think there is room to have two [audio] broadcasters delivering those rights. You're maximising probably the audience, you're maximising the money you're going to receive. And, ultimately, if what is being said about the BBC is to be believed, you are protecting; making sure that there is an audio platform willing to take the rights before the BBC potentially comes to you and says, 'Look, we just can't offer what we have historically.'

"I just think it makes good business sense from their point of view to have that, depending on where the BBC sort of ends up over the next couple of years. From the BBC's point of view I would say they'll always back themselves.

"Test Match Special has had a 60-plus years head start on whatever we do for home cricket. So they will always say, 'Look, we back the product that we have delivered really, really successfully for many, many years.'"

News.title: Man killed by tiger climbed two fences before suffering multiple injuries, inquest hears
News.content:
A man who was attacked by a tiger after climbing two fences to enter its enclosure at a wildlife park died of "multiple traumatic injuries", an inquest has heard.

William Chapman visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and entered the animal's pen.

The 24-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene and died of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction", the opening of his inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court heard.

Senior coroner Nicola Mundy said he had a history of mental illness, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had suffered previous bouts of psychosis. His family had raised concerns about his contact with Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS Trust, the hearing was told.

Chapman was under adult mental health services in Doncaster but was "highly functioning and independent with no care requirements", the inquest heard.

The self-employed online trader was born in Chichester, West Sussex, and living in Doncaster at the time of his death.

Coroner's officer Caitlin Brookes said his family had expressed "a number of concerns" in relation to his contact with mental health services, with the trust launching an investigation following his death.

On Wednesday, a trust spokesperson said it would "never comment on whether someone uses our services or does not use our services".

The BBC approached the trust for further comment.

News.title: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
News.content:
Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.

The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.

Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said restrictions to Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.

The Kremlin said Ukraine had "attempted a large-scale attack" on an oil refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.

According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris had caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.

Zelensky meanwhile said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.

He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal.

Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.

The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

After Starlink unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection on Tuesday, there were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame. But owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this, suggesting it was the Trump administration's doing. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing.

"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.

Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence told the BBC early on Thursday that Starshield services - the military-focused version of Starlink - had been restored.

They said officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances behind yesterday's restrictions".

News.title: Why Starlink internet is so important on the battlefield in Ukraine
News.content:
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.

For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.

Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.

But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.

The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless.

"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."

Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.

The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

News.title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.

From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.

Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.

Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.

The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

"Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.

She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".

The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.

The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.

The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.

Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said targeting Eritrea would have little impact.

"Eritrea is one of the major countries of origin for asylum seekers coming to the UK - we had roughly 7,000 asylum applications in the last year of data, roughly 8% of the total," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"Most Eritereans who come and claim asylum are not removable at all - the government would never be in negotiations to remove them because 84% are successful at initial decision; more will be successful on appeal."

She added that about 1,400 people were initially refused asylum, but that this number would reduce after appeals.

Many young Eritreans try to leave the country - which is a one-party state - to avoid military conscription, which can last for decades.

News.title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
News.content:
The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.

Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction.

It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week.

Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time.

Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will".

But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending".

The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August.

"It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said.

The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain".

Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.

The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.

News.title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
News.content:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".

It comes after Reform leader Nigel Farage vowed to root out "bad apples" from his party.

A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.

The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.

ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform â the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.

Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.

ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.

He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".

Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than 1% of British population can be non-white."

On a different day, Feeney, Solihull's deputy mayor, is joined by two other Reform candidates, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, who discuss speculation of a mosque being built in the local area.

"There's got to be a way of stopping them - like, go and buy some pork chops; we'll bury it in the ground," Campbell is heard saying in the film.

Whelan says "we'll take pictures of it", prompting Feeney to add: "I was gonna say, 'Unfortunately, this is a pig cemetery, mate'."

Discussing a female Reform candidate from Birmingham, Feeney is heard saying, "I didn't know where to look," before Whelan adds: "I'd have been sniffing that seat as soon as she got up."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons" and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

ITV reported that Whelan, who did not respond to the broadcaster's request for comment, would now be an independent councillor. The BBC has contacted him and Campbell for a response.

Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples".

Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".

"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.

Elsewhere in the film, Dean Miller, a councillor in the south London borough of Bromley, is shown campaigning for Reform in the Makerfield by-election.

"We've been ethnically cleansed out of London because you never used to get any blacks over in Bromley," he tells an ITV undercover reporter. "And now, you know, Bromley's like massive Nigerian communities there."

Miller says he is "not racist", before later adding: "The Muslim thing, that is going to be that thing that takes over everything and then everyone just has one religion. Because, apparently, King Charles is a [expletive] Muslim... I think that's [expletive] traitorous."

ITV reported that Miller would now sit as an independent councillor having resigned from Reform and had told them in a statement that he was heavily medicated due to a chronic pain condition when he made the comments.

The BBC has contacted him for comment.

In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".

Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."

The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

News.title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds
News.content:
BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.

Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.

BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.

Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.

Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.

For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.

A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.

News.title: Tiny critically endangered puddle frogs hatch at London Zoo
News.content:
Ben Tapley, curator of reptiles and amphibians at ZSL, which runs the central London zoo, said: "They may be tiny enough to sit on your fingertip, but their arrival represents a huge step forward for an amphibian facing an uncertain future."

ZSL said no other zoo or institution was known to keep the species.

It was only described by scientists in 2018. Fully grown, the frogs weigh less than 1.75g.

ZSL said almost nothing was known about them when they arrived, and keepers have since developed breeding techniques that are being shared with the CSIR-Forestry Research Institute of Ghana's breeding centre in Kumasi.

The aim is to build up a population in Ghana that could be released into the wild.

Ghanaian conservationist Caleb Ofori-Boateng, who helped identify the species, named it after his mother, Afia Birago.

"I named this frog after my mother so that her legacy would live on," he said.

"Thanks to this breeding programme, it will. Her name will be linked to a species we saved, not one we lost."

The births follow the zoo's success last November in breeding the Atewa slippery frog, another critically endangered species from the same forest, which had also never been bred in captivity before.

News.title: Meghan makes first official public appearance since moving back to UK
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex has made her first official public appearance since moving back to the UK, telling well-wishers "it's great to be back".

Meghan arrived at a youth charity in Nottingham alongside her husband, the Duke of Sussex, on Thursday morning. The pair, who are also expected to visit a food bank later, hugged and posed for selfies with the public.

The duchess spoke to a number of people in the crowd, telling one "we got lucky" as they chatted about the weather.

She has shared glimpses of her life back in the UK on social media, but this is the first time she has attended any public events since the family returned from California.

News.title: Poet says being dropped from Senedd royal visit over poem is 'concerning'
News.content:
Issa said the feedback received was that the poem had an "edge" and could "perhaps be softened."

"That's what I thought I'd done and obviously, it wasn't enough," she said.

Issa added it was "telling" that in the chamber where political issues are discussed "a poem that raises political issues is not welcome, that feels quite concerning".

The Welsh-Iraqi poet, filmmaker, and artist said she was inspired by Welsh poet Saunders Lewis' imagery of Wales as a vineyard, and developed that around the brief's request.

"The brief asked for something that celebrated members and their achievements, and something that served as a reminder of their commitment to the people of Wales.

"I don't know about you, but celebrating the achievements of members when they are just about to be sworn in feels a bit premature."

Instead, Issa decided to write something to remind the politicians of "their commitment".

"I wrote something that described Wales as a garden, and our Assembly Members as its gardeners."

Issa said that after submitting the first version she could have refused to make changes, but instead chose to compromise and try to find a halfway point.

A second version used "more abstract language", Issa said, but it was also rejected.

Based on the brief, Issa said it didn't sound like "they want a poem just about daffodils, and so it felt like a disservice to write something that was quite surface level".

"We've just faced a summer of wildfires. We're going into a season, no doubt, of floods. The proposed data centres, people have lots of concerns about that.

"There's so many things, and so it felt important for me to speak to those things."

Quoting John Lennon, Issa said: "'A poet's role is to try to express how people are feeling' and it felt like an important moment to do that."

News.title: UK temperatures to rise to 23C before autumn chill sets in
News.content:
Thursday will bring unusually high temperatures as warm air wafts across the south of the UK, while colder conditions dig into northern areas.

Afternoon highs in parts of eastern England are likely to be about 5-8C (9-14F) above typical mid-October values, probably peaking at 23C (73F).

It will be a different story further north and west with temperatures in much of Scotland and Northern Ireland sitting around the seasonal norm.

The two air masses are divided by a weather front which will bring outbreaks of rain. As that sinks southwards, chillier air will spread to all parts of the country bringing a colder feel to the weekend, though there will still be plenty of sunshine.

Frost and patchy fog are likely to develop in some locations.

News.title: PM launches brain cancer review after meeting 'inspirational' patient
News.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making a tearful TV appeal for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.

The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.

Burnham said: "He has spoken passionately about the need for change on brain cancer, and he's right: progress hasn't been good enough, here or anywhere else.

"Families facing this disease can't afford to wait."

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born athlete underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.

News.title: Warning to women after shortages of some HRT products in Northern Ireland
News.content:
Roisin Hillman, co-founder of Menopause Together, Northern Ireland's first menopause support charity, said some women forced to switch brands due to medication shortages had reported side effects like itchy skin or patches falling off.

She said that ongoing HRT patch shortages are deeply frustrating for women - and once they find a medication that works, it often falls in short supply.

"This is an issue going on for years," she said, advising women to request longer-term prescriptions from their GPs to stay ahead of supply gaps.

She also warned against sharing HRT with others.

"It is also really important that if you do have a shortage, and you can't get your normal HRT, to make sure you go back to your doctor," she said.

"Please do not share HRT with other women because what is prescribed to you may not suit someone else so it is very important that you go back to your GP."

Hillman said many women had "fear and anxiety" about shortages because "the HRT they are on is helping so many aspects of their life" and their mental health.

"If [a woman] is on HRT that works for her and then if she is not getting that HRT it can be really hard."

News.title: Dog that hunts invasive 'sea vomit' honoured as animal of the year
News.content:
"When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Sim.

"No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had."

Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed".

"She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said.

Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008.

It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream - and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK.

It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further.

Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients.

"These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained.

Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe.

News.title: Watch: BBC joins police on front line against car theft
News.content:
Vehicle thefts have risen by almost 50% in a decade, yet just 3% of offences resulted in a charge or summons last year, BBC analysis has found.

Organised crime groups are using increasingly sophisticated technology to steal cars to order, while police and manufacturers look to keep pace.

Criminals, the BBC has been told, are able to work out how to steal a car within weeks of a model being launched.

Investigations reporter NJ Convery has been out with police as they hunt for thieves.
