Sports.title: Former world champion boxer dies, aged 59, after heart attack at a bingo hall: Jorge 'Locomotora' Castro's daughter talks of dad's 'quick' death
Sports.content:
Former boxing world champion Jorge 'Locomotora' Castro has tragically passed away at the age of 59.

Castro, an Argentine great who won 130 of his 144 fights across a 20-year career, died on Wednesday after suffering a heart attack at a bingo hall.

Castro's daughter, Quimely, confirmed the cause of death and gave a heartbreaking account of his final moments in an interview with the Argentine media.

'My dad’s passing was natural,' she said. 'He had a heart attack. His chest started to hurt and he couldn’t take it.

'It was just a matter of 15 minutes, nothing more. The Scientific Police already took care of proving it was totally natural.

'He was with me and my mom. We had a routine outing with my mom. They’re very close friends; they haven’t been a couple for 15 years, but they’re very close friends. It was an outing the three of us did.'

Former boxing world champion Jorge 'Locomotora' Castro has passed away at the age of 59

Revealing what happened, Quimely added: 'We were fine and suddenly he told me, "I’m going to the bathroom".

'He went to the bathroom and when he came back he said, "My chest hurts a little." I told him, "That’s because you smoke like a savage." He told me, "It hurts a lot, daughter".

'That’s when we called the authorities at the place and it was like that, so fast, just like I’m telling it.

'They took him to a separate room, started doing CPR on him privately, and that was it.'

Castro, who turned professional in 1987, was a ruthless boxer, with 89 of his 130 victories coming via knockout.

He became WBA middleweight champion seven years after his professional debut following a split-decision victory over Reggie Johnson.

Castro had previously lost to Terry Norris in 1991 when fighting for the WBC light-middleweight belt.

Castro's most famous bout came in December 1994 when he completed an epic comeback victory over David Jackson, while he also faced legendary figures such as Roberto Duran and Roy Jones Jr during his career.

Outside of the ring, Castro was married six times and had 15 children and 14 grandchildren.

Sports.title: Vinicius Jr's nightmare 24 hours: Real Madrid star fumes at being subbed early by Jose Mourinho against Roma - after four-game ban for hair-pull rules him out of El Clasico
Sports.content:
Vinicius Jr's nightmare 24 hours: Real Madrid star fumes at being subbed early by Jose Mourinho against Roma - after four-game ban for hair-pull rules him out of El Clasico

Real Madrid star Vinicius Junior has endured a nightmare 24 hours after being hooked early against Roma - and being slapped with a four-match ban for a wild hair pull.

The winger was subbed by Jose Mourinho before the hour mark with Madrid 3-1 down at Roma in the Champions League - only to see his team-mates go on to thrive and win 4-3.

His frustrations were evident and he said: 'It’s only natural for me to be angry when I’m substituted, because I always want to play every minute, to be at my best and help the team, and today that wasn’t possible.'

He did acknowledge the positive impact of his replacement, 20-year-old Endrick, who scored his first goal of the season as Madrid completed a monumental comeback in the dying minutes.

The Brazilian will not have much of a chance to blow off steam, though, after he was hit with a ban for violent conduct after his outrageous hair pull during a recent 1-0 win over Villarreal.

And the Brazilian will miss the El Clasico against Barcelona next week as a result, with Real Madrid already playing catch-up in La Liga.

Vinicius Jr has been slapped with a four-match ban for this hair pull during Real Madrid's 1-0 win over Villarreal

He was also fuming after he was hooked early in Real Madrid's 4-3 comeback win over Roma

He was astonished when he heard the news on Wednesday night before Madrid's incredible 4-3 comeback win against Roma, saying afterwards: 'We've never had this [hair pulling] explained to us.

'Someone from La Liga and the referees' association always comes to explain the rules, but never this specific point. It was a red card for me, simple as that... I've never been violent towards another player. I get hit quite a lot, yet the cards end up going to me.'

Vini Jr was sent off with a direct red card after tugging the long locks of Villarreal's Nathan Saliba on Saturday.

And he was fuming at his dismissal, with referee Isidro Díaz de Mera noting: 'after being sent off and still on the field, he continued to protest my decision loudly, heading towards the area where I was with an aggressive attitude.'

The referee also noted that Vinicius 'had to be restrained by team-mates' before eventually leaving the field of play.

He even appeared to shove a La Liga official as he stormed off. Authorities condemned his 'aggressive attitude'.

Vinicius Jr later posted a brief apology on Instagram, writing: 'Sorry to my team and my fans'.

But he also posted a series of clips of flashpoints from other matches where he believes players should have been sent off, but were not.

That post came with the caption: 'And the one who always sees yellow and red is Vinicius. A disgrace.'

Mourinho was highly irritated at the fact that they found out of his ban a couple of hours before the Roma game.

He told AS: 'Is it normal for a player to find out two hours before a match that he is going to be suspended for four games? There is no need to answer me. Is that normal? Could they not have announced the decision now or tomorrow morning? Did they have to do it while we were on our way to the stadium?

He protested against his dismissal and was condemned for his 'aggressive attitude'

'"In Portuguese we say: the cat is hiding but its tail is showing. It seems to me that the cat is no longer hiding now. The cat is acting freely, and there are things happening without shame. It is acting freely.

'Two hours before a match, a player at a Spanish club who contributed three points towards strengthening the standing of Spanish football, I do not see that as normal. But I am starting to consider it normal, because the cat is no longer hiding. What is the question?

'At the very least, it shows a lack of respect. Playing in Athens on Wednesday evening, arriving in Madrid at five in the morning, then playing on Saturday in Valencia, during a week before the international break, does not seem to me to be innocent.

'I do not believe the usual excuses, such as that the reason is television (broadcasting rights). I do not believe that. I have grown too old for that. As for the Vinicius story, and him finding out two hours before the match that he had been given a four-match suspension, Real Madrid fans are not stupid.'

The ban will only apply to domestic competitions, so he will miss fixtures against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia. The next La Liga match he will be available for is against Celta Vigo on November 22.

Madrid, being a rather argumentative club in these circumstances, may still appeal the suspension according to the Spanish press.

Manager Jose Mourinho held his tongue in his post-match press conference, saying: 'I’m not going to speak because I want to be on the bench against Sevilla and Barcelona.'

In any case, he will be allowed to play against RB Leipzig and AEK Athens in the Champions League during the period of the ban.

His domestic absence is a blow but the No7 has not been at his prolific best this term, only scoring once and creating three assists in eight games.

'He is going to emerge,' Mourinho told TNT Sports in a display of confidence. 'It is just a question of when.'

Oddly enough, Vinicius thought he had scored his second goal of the season against Villarreal, but after the referee was called over to the monitor, he was sent off for the hair pull during the build-up and his effort was chalked off.

Madrid sit fourth in La Liga, six points behind Barcelona, who have made a perfect start.

They found their mojo at Roma in the Champions League, coming from 3-1 behind to win 4-3 late on as the Italian hosts paid tribute to their former manager Mourinho with a tifo, making him visibly emotional.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace's John Textor nightmare: BOBBY MANZI reveals the blazing rows with Steve Parish, his crumbling football empire and why Lyon can't stand him either
Sports.content:
When the full-time whistle went at Wembley and Crystal Palace had defied all the odds to win the FA Cup, John Textor leaned over a row of Royal Box seats to embrace Steve Parish.

After Eberechi Eze's goal won them the first trophy in their 120-year history, the image depicted an ownership group that was united and jubilant. In reality, their relationship was anything but.

On Thursday, Palace will reopen old wounds when they travel to Lyon for the Textor Derby. The disgraced former owner of both clubs will be nowhere to be seen and that's probably for the best, given the acrimony towards him in both France and south London.

Without his cross-Channel multi-club network, Palace may well have been playing in the Europa League last season. Instead they were demoted by virtue of no two clubs being able to play in the same UEFA competition and Nottingham Forest - now Public Enemy No1 in Croydon - took Palace's place. And the animosity extends beyond the supporters.

Textor arrived at Palace in August 2021, acquiring the largest minority stake in the club for £87.5million before increasing his shareholding to 43 per cent three years later. Yet, despite his attempts, Textor failed to convert his equity into control. On several occasions, he tried to purchase a majority stake but was consistently blocked.

That irked him. Chairman Parish, the club's ultimate decision-maker despite owning significantly less of it than Textor, angered him. Textor deemed Parish risk-averse, while Parish viewed Textor as a risk to the club. But Parish had the measure of him, using the Missouri-born former competitive skateboarder's capital to pay off debt during Covid, develop the academy site and strengthen the playing squad without giving him decision-making power.

Former Crystal Palace director John Textor (left) had regular slanging matches with fellow part-owner Steve Parish (right)

Textor's ownership of Lyon meant that Palace were kicked out of the Europa League last season, as no two teams in the same competition can have the same controlling partner

Meanwhile, Textor wanted Palace to be the cornerstone of his multi-club ownership group, Eagle Football, which owned Lyon, Brazilian top-flight side Botafogo and the now-defunct RWD Molenbeek of Belgium. Given that Textor has since lost all the clubs amid financial mismanagement, Parish's wariness has been vindicated.

Textor wanted Parish to prioritise the playing squad and was aggrieved by ring-fencing cash for Selhurst Park's new Main Stand. Some believe Textor never supported the development, with the issue often prompting bust-ups.

In fact, sources told Daily Mail Sport that Parish and Textor had regular slanging matches in the boardroom while employees were present. One source recalled occasions when Textor stormed out, explaining that the pair clashed over their respective self-righteousness.

Publicly, Parish and Textor mostly put on a united front, though Textor made some snide digs about the 'red Ferrari driving chairman' in an interview with talkSPORT. Behind the scenes, however, the pair never hid their dislike or the tension between them – and Textor eventually lost much of his interest in Palace after realising his sway was limited and he could not further his multi-club network ambitions.

The most disruptive period came during Textor's exit. He had been looking to sell for some time but the process was accelerated after the FA Cup win granted Palace entry into the Europa League for the following campaign, where the Lyon problem reared its head.

There was perhaps another reason for Textor's expediency. Lyon had problems of their own - the seven-times French champions were in the process of being kicked out of Ligue 1 by the French football authorities (DNCG).

But when Textor's money came in from selling his Palace stake to Woody Johnson, the former US Ambassador to the UK and owner of the NFL's New York Jets, they satisfied the DNCG's demands and were reinstated not just to the French top flight but also the Europa League.

So in the end, selling Palace and releasing them from the multi-club network resulted in Lyon taking their Europa League place. Palace were demoted to the Conference League - which they went on to win to again qualify for the Europa League - because Textor still had 'decisive influence' on the March 1, 2025 deadline for ownership conflicts to be resolved for the following season.

Palace fans had voiced their distrust of Textor long before the multi-club ownership issue hit them hard - with this banner in January 2023

Textor (centre) owned around 40 per cent of Palace from August 2021 to July 2025, when he sold his stake to New York Jets owner and former US Ambassador to the UK Woody Johnson

To this day, Textor is one of three parties Palace supporters blame for their expulsion, alongside Nottingham Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis and UEFA.

'F*** UEFA, f*** John Textor, f*** Marinakis' has become a staple chant at matches and will almost certainly be heard throughout the match at the Groupama Stadium on Thursday night.

Textor has both publicly and privately suggested that supporters are naive for blaming him. Of course, the Europa League demotion is the emotional source of their frustration. However, the Textor resentment originated in concerns over his ambition to put Eagle Football Holdings on the stock market and fears over whether he had suitable funding.

Having previously held stakes in four clubs, Textor now has none.

Palace and Lyon are under new management, Botafogo voted him off their board this summer a few months after the club were hit with a three-window transfer ban for non-payment of a transfer fee, and Molenbeek lost their Belgian football league licence in August over financial difficulties. At the top of it all, Eagle Football Holdings went into administration in March.

It should be said that Palace had not planned well enough for the possibility of playing European football. Had they done so, Textor's shares could have been placed in a blind trust before the deadline and the situation avoided. Whether Textor would have agreed to that while trying to sell up, though, is another matter.

Intriguingly, one Palace source defended Textor when speaking to Daily Mail Sport. The source argued that Textor was the driving force behind Palace appointing Oliver Glasner two years ago and that the investment he made helped to pay for the signings of Marc Guehi and Michael Olise, suggesting that none of Palace's three trophies in the last 18 months would have been possible without the American. That is an unpopular opinion among fans to say the least, though.

Even after his exit, there remained a tenuous link to the club. John Textor's son, Addison, was until this summer employed by Velocity Capital – an American private equity firm owned by minority Palace shareholder David Abrams. The firm invested more than £75m in leading football agency Unique Sports Group, which represents past and present Palace players Dean Henderson, Maxence Lacroix, Marc Guehi and Dwight McNeil.

Under Textor's ownership, Botafogo won the Copa Libertadores in 2024 but he was voted off the club's board in July this year

One source argued that Textor was the driving force behind Palace appointing Oliver Glasner, and as such none of Palace's three trophies in the last 18 months would have been possible

It was Textor who appointed now-Palace boss Pierre Sage as Lyon head coach in 2023. He led them to the French Cup final in his first season but was sacked the following January

Palace fans will use their trip to Lyon to lambast Textor once again and the home crowd is likely to join in. Although Lyon's involvement prevented Palace from competing in the Europa League, there is no bitterness between the two clubs – both equally disdain Textor.

Lyon endured persistent battles with the DNCG thanks to Textor building up debt, the provisional relegation last summer and being forced to sell key players because of their financial situation. Ironically, supporters also fumed over his decision to sack now-Palace boss Pierre Sage, a decision Textor admits he now regrets.

When Palace won the Conference League to qualify for the Europa League last season, they were almost destined to face Lyon.

This is the final chapter in their Textor debacle and, unless it's in their favourite chant, everyone at Palace will hope Thursday night is the last time he enters their thoughts.

Sports.title: Harry Maguire and Bruno Fernandes would be 'too busy doing podcasts' to pull up Lisandro Martinez for Man United rant, taunts Roy Keane - as Steven Bartlett is caught in crossfire
Sports.content:
Roy Keane has accused Manchester United's dressing room leaders of being too busy podcasting to enforce dressing room discipline. The Red Devils legend thinks Harry Maguire and Bruno Fernandes don't have the nerve to chastise Lisandro Martinez after his explosive outburst about the club. Martinez criticised the club's bosses and claimed they should have signed more players over the summer after their 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid on Tuesday night. For Keane it is symptomatic of a club culture where players air their grievances instead of working hard to improve – a mentality set by the senior players. 'Bruno, Maguire... they're probably busy doing podcasts, I can't imagine them pulling him (Martinez). Bruno's body language, he doesn't seem a happy lad at the moment. They're pulling nobody,' he told the Stick to Football podcast. 'This reflects where Manchester United are and where this dressing room is. Maguire gets left out of the England squad - he's all upset with that. Instead of rolling his sleeves up during the summer, "I'm going to go to New York and do a podcast for a few weeks". That's his mindset. Roy Keane has claimed Bruno Fernandes and Harry Maguire are 'too busy doing podcasts' to discipline Lisandro Martinez (YouTube: The Overlap) The duo both went on podcasts over the summer to talk about their grievances Martinez hit out at the club's hierarchy and hinted the squad was too weak in an explosive rant 'I made a mistake with Bruno (Fernandes) on this programme. Bruno goes on a podcast with (Steven Bartlett), this is the Man United captain, he goes on there, has a little dig at me, no problem, he's entitled to respond. 'That's the mindset of a Man United player, I'm going to start doing these little gigs instead of getting Man United competing at the very top. 'So this idea, when I see a player have a little b**** the last few days, I'd be more annoyed at Maguire and Bruno for getting things off their chests on podcasts. You get your priorities in place as a footballer. 'Back in our day it was more magazines than podcasts, but if a player went off and said something, even silly, he'd come in the dressing room, and lads would say: "What are you talking about?" You'd put him in his place in that sense - not a big bust-up. 'Man United is a circus. If you can, try and do your talking on the pitch. If you have to let off a bit of steam, ok, but try and do it on the back of some victories, or when you've won a league title or something like that. 'These players have done nothing for the last few years at Man United. Two years ago we were finishing 13th (15th) or whatever, getting knocked out by Grimsby, and they're coming up with all these comments.' The panel of Keane, Gary Neville, Steven Gerrard, Ian Wright, and Jill Scott agreed that Martinez calling for more signings could upset members of the dressing room. The Argentinian had said on Tuesday: 'I expect more (investment) 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night. Diary of a CEO host Steven Bartlett was caught in the crossfire of Keane's comments 'We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well.' And Neville hit back: 'What he says is right, they should have brought in more defenders. However, you can't say that as a player. 'If you say that publicly as a player, you're effectively saying that the players I'm playing with are not good enough. That's where the players have to pick him up. 'If you're Leny Yoro or Ayden Heaven, and you've got a little doubt about settling into the first-team, and you're a young player, you're thinking: "My World Cup-winning centre-back has said we should have brought more players in so I don't play", you're really feeling nervous and anxious.' Keane argued it was a matter of semantics: 'I'm sure we said it back in the day. Big clubs, new players help you improve. You'd say it in certain ways - "we need competition for places". '"We had a fantastic season last year" - there you go. That's where he's coming from. He actually thinks they had a fantastic season. Fine him two weeks' wages for saying that!' Martinez has not covered himself in glory as of late, scoring a comical own goal against Fulham and arguably being at fault for Dominic Solanke's goal in the 1-1 draw with Tottenham last weekend. Daily Mail Sport's Nathan Salt handed him a rating of five for his performance against Atletico, writing that it was an improvement on his Spurs showing but still with 'hairy moments'. Gary Neville hit out at martinez, asking how his comments would make young players feel The £120,000-per-week centre-back, whose contract expires in the summer, has acknowledged he spoke 'with anger and frustration' but refused to apologise for his blistering comments. He said: 'When I talk about wanting more, I’m talking about the ambition we must all have as part of this club. ‘To keep growing, to become stronger and to have everything we need to compete at the highest level. These are standards we must all hold ourselves to, starting with me.’ He added: ‘We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take Manchester United back to the top. I believe in my team-mates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward. ‘I’m convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment. My goal has been the same since day one, to win, to compete at the highest level and to give everything I have for this badge.’ The impact of Martinez’s initial statement is still likely to be felt through until Sunday’s trip to face Leeds United at Elland Road, while team-mate Amad Diallo is also in the spotlight after he added more fuel to the fire with a message on social media which read ‘f***ing disgrace, I have no words’, although it’s unclear what the Ivorian was referring to. Wayne Rooney had been unimpressed with Martinez voicing his dissatisfaction at the squad, saying: 'If you're Baleba or Tielemans, you're going to want to speak to Lisandro as it's disrespectful to them. Only Bruno can come out and say that. 'It looks like a player trying to look after himself. It's sad because you need players to stick together or something like that can rip the dressing-room apart.'

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo's international career likely to be OVER, says his sister - as she reveals talks over reconciliation have stalled after 'betrayal' and 'hurt' from Jorge Jesus
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo's international career likely to be OVER, says his sister - as she reveals talks over reconciliation have stalled after 'betrayal' and 'hurt' from Jorge Jesus

Cristiano Ronaldo's sister has hinted that the Portuguese superstar is unlikely to return to international football after he was suspended by his country following an explosive falling-out with boss Jorge Jesus.

Ronaldo, 41, caused controversy during the recent international break when he left Portugal's camp over what he claimed were 'broken promises' by Jesus.

That came after he was left on the bench during their 2-1 Nations League win over Norway, with the Portuguese Football Federation subsequently suspending the forward for his actions.

Ronaldo has since expressed a desire to return to the team, yet his sister, Elma Aveiro, poured cold water on that likelihood on Wednesday evening.

Speaking at a book launch event in Lisbon, which was ironically also attended by Jesus, Aveiro reflected on the saga and gave her thoughts on Ronaldo's international future.

'It's more likely a no than a yes,' she said. 'I think both [Cristiano and Jorge Jesus] are hurt; it was a situation they experienced, not me, I'm speaking for my brother.

Cristiano Ronaldo's decorated international career could be finished, his sister has claimed

Elma Aveiro said that 'it's more likely a no than a yes' when asked what happens next

'I think it's a situation that's stalled, we'll see what happens.'

When pressed on whether the pair could make up, she added: 'I don't know, it's very complicated. When we're betrayed, it's very difficult to go back to normal.'

Reflecting generally on what happened, Aveiro said: 'My feeling is one of sadness because the Portuguese people unfortunately forget what has already been done and think that things should be done differently now.

'I'm speechless, it's very difficult to see my brother go through this. He is one of the people who least deserve this.'

Ronaldo's sister's comments come after his mother, Dolores Aveiro, also hit out at the scenario, insisting that 'they are not valuing her son', before she added: 'He could have left through the front door and instead he left through the back door.'

Although Ronaldo fans are unlikely to enjoy hearing his sister's comments, back in the summer, one of his other siblings Katie said that he would retire from international football after the World Cup. The 41-year-old was forced to shut down those claims.

Ronaldo's main issue was his belief that a plan had been drawn up for him to come off the bench for 30 minutes in the aforementioned tie with Norway, but Jesus made him warm up without bringing him on because he 'didn't need Cristiano'.

Before Portugal's subsequent match against Denmark, the 41-year-old is understood to have agreed to an eight-point statement for Jesus to deliver at his press conference, aimed at quashing speculation that Ronaldo was demanding more playing time.

But Jesus veered off course, prompting Ronaldo to bail on the Portugal camp before releasing an extraordinary 1,996-word statement accusing the manager of twice backtracking on his word.

Despite apologising to his team-mates, Ronaldo now faces suspension while an investigation into his conduct takes place, and he could now miss the entire international break in November.

Ronaldo accused Portugal boss Jorge Jesus of backtracking on what he had promised

In a statement last week, the Portuguese FA said: ‘Disciplinary proceedings were initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo pursuant to a decision by the Non-Professional Section dated October 9, 2026, aimed at determining whether the events reported on October 7, 2026, warrant disciplinary action.

‘Without prejudice to the automatic preventive suspension to which he was subject prior to the initiation of proceedings, a non-automatic preventive suspension of the player was ordered, and the case was designated as urgent.

‘The case was referred to the FPF Disciplinary Investigation Committee on October 10, 2026, with the proceedings remaining confidential until the conclusion of the investigation.’

Sports.title: Lisandro Martinez's NON-APOLOGY: Ranting Man United star admits he 'spoke out of anger and frustration' but refuses to say sorry in 271-word statement
Sports.content:
Lisandro Martinez's NON-APOLOGY: Ranting Man United star admits he 'spoke out of anger and frustration' but refuses to say sorry in 271-word statement

Lisandro Martinez took to social media in a late bid to dilute his scathing comments 24 hours on from his blistering criticism of club bosses.

United’s players had Wednesday off after flying straight back from Spain following Tuesday’s Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid and Martinez’s bombshell television interview in which he accused the Old Trafford board and director of football Jason Wilcox of failing in the transfer market last summer.

United remained tight-lipped on what action – if any – was to be taken against the Argentina international ahead of a return to training, but it the defender took matters into his own hands by explaining – but crucially not apologising – what he meant.

‘When I talk about wanting more, I’m talking about the ambition we must all have as part of this club,’ Martinez said, in part of his statement.

‘To keep growing, to become stronger and to have everything we need to compete at the highest level. These are standards we must all hold ourselves to, starting with me.’

He added: ‘We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take Manchester United back to the top. I believe in my team-mates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward.

Lisandro Martinez has broken his silence after Tuesday night's extraordinary post-match rant

‘I’m convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment. My goal has been the same since day one, to win, to compete at the highest level and to give everything I have for this badge.’

The impact of Martinez’s initial statement is still likely to be felt through until Sunday’s trip to face Leeds United at Elland Road, while team-mate Amad Diallo is also in the spotlight after he added more fuel to the fire with a message on social media which read ‘f***ing disgrace, I have no words’, although it’s unclear what the Ivorian was referring to.

United will likely need to call on Martinez at Leeds with a number of injuries in defence. Luke Shaw, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui have been out of action, and Matthijs De Ligt only returned on the bench as an unused substitute in Madrid after nearly a year out with a back injury.

Martinez’s long-term future is more uncertain, however. He is out of contract at the end of June, although United can extend it by another year.

They are unlikely to let a 28-year-old World Cup winner leave as a free agent five years after his £57million move from Ajax, but could trigger the extension so they can demand a transfer fee for him.

Martinez took aim at the United hierarchy in the wake of a fourth defeat in nine games in Madrid when he was asked if the club have backed Michael Carrick enough. ‘I don't think so,’ he said. ‘He does his best. You can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager.

‘What about other areas? Tonight it is easy to say the coach and easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas.

‘I expect more (investment) 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.

‘I have to control myself a lot but sometimes is a reflection of the mirror of how is our club at the moment.’

Sports.title: Hiding under a flat cap, Pep Guardiola tried to be incognito but the ex-Man City manager's presence was felt on his return with demands his big moments are expunged entirely from history, writes JACK GAUGHAN
Sports.content:
Hiding under a flat cap, Pep Guardiola tried to be incognito but the ex-Man City manager's presence was felt on his return with demands his big moments are expunged entirely from history, writes JACK GAUGHAN

A returning hero at the Etihad, invited back for the night. Ali Benarbia, the mercurial midfielder, is considered a legend of a former Manchester City era as they won the First Division title in the early Noughties. He knows the second tier well etcetera, etcetera.

But then there was the other guy. The other guy didn’t do club media and interviews on the pitch but his presence fills an arena regardless.

Flat caps became a thing for Pep Guardiola when Mike Summerbee took him to tailors Williams & Gill on Chapel Street after taking over. He bought one for £75 and has in the past worn them as a tribute to the late life president Bernard Halford.

It was, at one stage, a symbol of Guardiola and Manchester. Less of a symbol when heading inside the place he called home for a decade on Wednesday. Instead, apparel to slightly conceal the identity of somebody who wanted to keep this return as low key as possible.

He emerged from the Chairman’s Lounge in the Colin Bell Stand nine minutes before kick off, taking a seat on the third row of the directors’ box behind Ferran Soriano and Khaldoon Al Mubarak, just as the club started playing a montage of great moments – Yaya Toure at Wembley, the Dennis Tueart bicycle kick, Bernardo Silva and Real Madrid – that stirred a fanbase visiting here for the first time since their world fell in.

Guardiola was sat alongside confidante Manel Estiarte in the seats he had spun on his heels and pointed towards hundreds of times when celebrating goals during a period of dominance that City’s fiercest critics want expunged entirely from history.

Pep Guardiola might have wanted to hide under his flat cap upon returning to the Etihad but his presence - a show of support - shouted loudly

Seated a few rows behind the current Man City hierarchy Guardiola was frequently locked in conversation with his old coaching assistant Manel Estiarte

He winced and he scratched the beard as Paris Saint-Germain ripped through the team he loves so dearly in a first half of glitteringly rapid dominance, with quickfire goals bearing some hallmarks of a few painful European nights on the Catalan’s watch.

This is a City side in its infancy and will need more nights against the very best in Europe, which PSG obviously are, before they look more comfortable in their new skin. Yet as it stands, those opportunities are likely to end once this season is over. A team destined for League Two cannot possibly compete with the vast riches of the Champions League kings.

The hierarchy, including chairman Al Mubarak, will have felt it important that Guardiola made the journey. As a show of support behind the club’s insistence of innocence heading into their appeal.

The 55-year-old had been in Abu Dhabi, where he is having a property built, last week and arrived in Manchester hours before this tie. He entered the main stand at a time when the congregated thousands were not waiting for the arrival of the coach carrying Enzo Maresca’s squad and clearly did not want to detract from those players or provide a distraction for his successor.

City didn’t make a song and dance about his attendance and that is how he’d rather it. Guardiola flashed up on the big screen once as some supporters inside this place must have been wrestling with how to feel and react to what has been a deluge dumped upon them over the past fortnight.

The volume dialled up once City found a foothold and started bossing the ball with more certainty, albeit three down by that point. It proves that watching this team play well, irrespective of what it ultimately may mean over the coming months, can provide some escapism for people who are suddenly having to morph into legal and financial experts – with an outside expectance for them to act as moral arbiters – around something that is supposed to be a hobby.

That will not stop until this whole thing ends. And even then it might not. Yet as City fought back, attacking with heart and gumption, there will remain performances to cherish for however long the fans’ purgatory lasts.

Sports.title: The secret behind Frank Lampard's Premier League turnaround? His lucky £880,000 watch! How superstitious boss rotated through £1m+ collection - and now has Coventry winning
Sports.content:
Frank Lampard has worn over £1million worth of watches on matchdays since Coventry's return to the Premier League, but the superstitious England legend may finally have found his lucky charm.

Coventry triumphed 4-1 over Newcastle to secure an emphatic second win of the campaign under Lampard on Monday night, having beaten Nottingham Forest 1-0 at the City Ground before the start of the three-week international break.

For the superstitious, Coventry’s sudden upturn in form could have something to do with the watch collection Lampard has flaunted since the start of the new season.

Against both Nottingham Forest and Newcastle, Lampard sported a new Patek Philippe Grand Complications timepiece worth a eye-watering £879,490.

Lampard’s latest luxury accessory, the Patek Philippe 5316/50P-001, features intricate complications housed in a platinum case and is by far the most expensive watch he has showcased since Coventry’s return to the Premier League, joining the ultra-rare grand complication timepieces in his collection.

At the start of the season, Lampard sported a Patek Philippe Nautilus Chronograph (Ref. 5980/1R), crafted from 18-carat rose gold and featuring a black gradient dial.

Frank Lampard may have finally have found his lucky charm with a new £880,000 watch

Lampard has been rotating watches this season and wore a new Patek Philippe timepiece during Coventry's last two victories against Nottingham Forest (left) and Newcastle (right)

Lampard wore a stainless-steel Patek Philippe in Coventry's defeats by Man City and Brighton

But the former England international ditched the £196,560 gold timepiece after Arsenal cruised to a 3-0 victory on the opening day, courtesy of goals from Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard.

In Coventry's next defeat against Hull on the Premier League's second weekend, Lampard wore a Patek Philippe Aquanaut Chronograph (Ref. 5968A), crafted from stainless steel and paired with a dark rubber strap.

That particular timepiece goes on the market for just £102,229, the cheapest from Lampard's lavish collection.

Against Manchester City and Brighton, in defeats of 1-0 and 5-0 respectively, the former Chelsea man wore a stainless-steel Patek Philippe Nautilus (Ref. 5711/1A), featuring the model’s iconic blue sunburst dial.

Although prices vary depending on the specific variant and its rarity, the watch is estimated to be worth more than £113,000, bringing the combined value of Lampard's four-watch collection to an estimated £1,290,000.

Whether or not rotating watches has become a key part of Lampard's matchday routine, the Coventry boss has previously opened up on his superstitious nature.

During his time managing Chelsea, Lampard superstitiously stuck to a rigid routine every morning, fearing that even the slightest change could affect results on matchdays.

‘It can be quite awkward,’ Lampard told Chelsea in 2019. ‘I walk the dog at a certain time on certain days and before training I will take her down to the local coffee shop, get my takeaway coffee and walk her at a certain time for a certain route. Nothing that exciting!

The manager began the season against Arsenal wearing a gold watch worth almost £200,000

He watched Coventry lose to Hull in August wearing a blue-strapped watch worth £102,000

'I walk the dog a lot and I find it is good for clearing the head and for that, I like going to the gym as well. That is another one of my superstitions. I have to do exactly the same amount of time on the bike, 50 minutes, or the exact same route that I run.

‘If I don’t do the routines I feel, ridiculously, like it might have an effect on results. But sometimes I do miss the dog walk for some reason.’

With a trip to winless Tottenham up next, Lampard may be reluctant to part with his new lucky timepiece as Coventry head to north London on Monday.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies.
