Sports.title: Formula 1 teams need decision ‘by mid-October’ on whether final races will go ahead | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 team bosses say they need to know by the middle of this month whether the series’ final two races will go ahead as planned.

Qatar and Abu Dhabi are due to hold the final two races of the season in November and December. However the war in Iran, which forced the cancellation of races in nearby Bahrain and Saudi Arabia six months ago, put those plans in jeopardy.

F1 has a back-up plan to hold an alternative event at Imola. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali previously said a decision would be made by mid-September. Teams say they need to know one way or the other soon.

“I believe Stefano was targeting to tell us in mid-October,” said Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu in Azerbaijan. “So, we all know what the situation is.

“I believe that Imola is getting ready in case we have to do it. I think the challenges are, for instance, things like European motorhome structure, etcetera. All those people who look after them, they have a winter job, so we need to find alternative people to do that.

“But I’m sure we all, as a family, community, will make sure if we have to do that, that will happen. But hopefully, as a baseline, we can go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. That would be really good.”

Drivers have pointed out the conditions could be very cold if the series races in Imola in December. However Audi team principal Mattia Binotto believes it would be no cooler than some other venues the series visits.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The main challenges are more organisation and logistics,” he said. “I would think, from a technical point, often we may say wintertime and snow tyres, but at the end, as a matter of fact, the average temperature in Imola in that time of the year is hotter than Las Vegas.

“So I don’t think that’s a true concern. It’s more from the organisation and the logistics, really. And again, mid-October, hopefully we may do the right decision.”

Domenicali told the Financial Times the “decision is done” but also admitted “Imola is the place that eventually, in case of a force majeure before a certain date, would be ready to host it.”

Sports.title: Formula 1 announces it will race in Rwanda from “early 2030s” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has announced it will return to race in Africa for the first time since 1993.

The series has agreed a 10-year deal to race in Rwanda, which has never previously held a round of the world championship. Unusually, no year for the inaugural race has been confirmed, with F1 saying only that it will “join the calendar in the early 2030s”.

A new circuit will be constructed in Bugesera, in the Eastern province of Rwanda. The track will be located 40 kilometres south of Rwanda’s capital Kigali, which hosted the FIA’s General Assembly and award ceremony in 2024.

F1 published an image of the planned RISE Motordrome circuit, which was created by Tilke Gmbh and Wurz Design, but gave no details of its specifications.

“Further details regarding the inaugural race date, circuit development milestones and race weekend plans will be announced in due course,” said F1.

According to Rwanda’s president Paul Kagame the race will be called the “Formula 1 African Grand Prix”.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali called the announcement “a landmark moment for Formula 1.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.”

F1 first raced in Africa in 1958, when Morocco’s Aib-Diab circuit held the final round of the season. However the series never returned to the northern African state.

The series found a longer-term home in South Africa, first at a track in East London, then at the popular Kyalami circuit near Johannesburg. South Africa held 23 grands prix, though the series faced growing criticism for holding events under the country’s racist apartheid regime, which led some teams to boycott the 1985 race.

Following a seven-year absence, F1 returned to a heavily revised Kyalami circuit for two races in the nineties.

By the time Rwanda hosts its first grand prix, up to 40 years may have passed since F1’s last race in Africa.

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley Puts Rematch Pressure on Daniel Dubois
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley believes Daniel Dubois faces the greater pressure in their rematch, with the champion needing to repeat his victory against a challenger who believes he has corrected the mistakes that cost him their first fight.

Dubois recovered from two early knockdowns to win. Wardley admits he became overconfident after that success, giving the champion an opportunity to recover. If Wardley avoids those mistakes, Dubois could face a different task this time.

“I think that for me, like again, it’s something Daniel’s gone through, but now he’s got three losses on his record,” Wardley told Fight Wire. “Two of those to Oleksandr Usyk, so you chalk them up a bit differently.”

Wardley argues that another defeat would put Dubois in a difficult position, while he views his own first loss as something he can repair.

“It just frees me up. It’s okay, we had a loss. Things didn’t go too great. Not the end of the world,” he said.

The pressure on Dubois goes beyond the number of defeats. He needs to demonstrate that his previous victory was repeatable, rather than a result that depended on Wardley getting careless after putting him down twice.

Wardley believes he has identified how he let that opportunity slip. Better decisions could leave Dubois with fewer chances to recover, although maintaining pressure without wasting energy or walking into punches will require more than determination.

“There’s a few adjustments to be made, a few things we need to capitalize on better, and then the fight’s ours,” Wardley said.

Dubois proved he could beat Wardley that night. Whether he can handle a more disciplined version remains unanswered. Wardley still has to deliver those improvements under fire, but the champion cannot assume the same openings will appear again.

Wardley also questioned Dubois’s conflicting comments about his punching power, suggesting some of his opponent’s remarks sound rehearsed.

“Especially when the camera comes out, some of the lines you can very much tell are forced, or they’ve at least been told to him to put in there,” he said.

The verbal sparring adds to Wardley’s portrayal of himself as the more relaxed fighter. Dubois’s harder task is showing that he has answers for the changes Wardley brings into the ring.

Sports.title: Edgar Berlanga Calls Sebastian Fundora A Cheat Code
Sports.content:
Edgar Berlanga can’t understand how Sebastian Fundora fits into the 154-pound division. Looking at a workout photo of the WBC champion, he compared Fundora to a video game character and suggested he should be making his money in the NBA.

Fundora’s long legs and arms dominate the picture. Berlanga fights two divisions above him at super middleweight, yet even he sounds taken aback by the sight of someone that tall competing at light middleweight.

How do they allow him to box at 154lb he’s a cheat code character from GTA WTF 🤣🤣🤣 listen he would have been a 200 million dollar NBA player. This is unacceptable he looks like a building https://t.co/AYW3y9aSuM — Edgar Berlanga Jr (@EdgarBerlangaJr) October 15, 2026

Berlanga isn’t the first fighter to reach for a video game comparison. After Fundora stopped Erickson Lubin in April 2022, Terence Crawford called him “a cheat code,” comparing him to a created Fight Night boxer with the height turned up in a smaller weight class.

It’s an understandable reaction. Finding sparring partners who can prepare an opponent for Fundora is difficult enough. Then comes the task of getting past those long arms and landing on a head that sits well above the usual target.

The odd thing is that Fundora often gives opponents a chance by coming to them. He likes fighting up close, throwing short punches rather than spending every round keeping shorter men at the end of his jab. They don’t always have to chase him to get their shots off.

That makes him entertaining, even if Berlanga thinks his dimensions look unfair. Fundora can make 154. The men across from him have to figure out the rest.

His WBC title defense against Ermal Hadribeaj this Saturday is a harder sell. Hadribeaj is the mandatory challenger, but most fans know little about him. They’re waiting to see Fundora against the bigger names in a division with plenty to offer.

Hadribeaj gets his chance to make himself known once the fight starts. Until then, Fundora’s unusual frame is likely to draw more conversation than the matchup itself.

Sports.title: Liam Paro Faces Long Wait For Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
Liam Paro booking another defense puts more distance between him and Ryan Garcia, though Garcia’s alternative choices present a far bigger hurdle. Matchups with Teofimo Lopez or Devin Haney carry massive commercial appeal, which could strand Paro well past his ideal timeline.

“We’re not going to sit on the sideline,” Paro told Fox Sports Australia.

Staying active is the smartest move Paro can make. Continuing to take bouts keeps him sharp instead of burning months chasing an opponent who sees little urgency to fight him.

Teofimo gives Garcia an established American audience. A return bout with Haney carries built-in personal drama. Paro holds a world championship belt, yet hardware alone might not outweigh the bigger paydays Garcia could chase instead.

The calendar for Ryan creates another headache. If Garcia sits out until May, that single appearance eats up the first half of 2027. Another high-profile date could easily swallow the remaining months, leaving Paro on the outside looking in despite handling his business in the ring.

Teofimo’s mandatory duty against Jack Catterall adds some problems, but it will not kill a potential Garcia meeting. The WBA might grant Teofimo an exception so he can keep the strap. Teofimo could also surrender the belt outright to lock down the more lucrative bout.

That situation does not assure Teofimo gets the nod. Still, Paro cannot count on sanctioning body politics to eliminate a popular name from contention.

Title dynamics bring further chaos. If Garcia meets Teofimo first, Paro must hope Garcia wins so the WBC unification prize remains intact. A Garcia loss instantly ruins that scenario before Paro ever secures a signed contract.

Paro holds the power to defend his title and keep his phone line open. He cannot dictate Garcia’s opponent, dictate fight results, or force Garcia to pursue undisputed status.

Taking another bout makes complete sense. Chasing Garcia is worth the ambition, but Paro must build an active calendar that keeps rolling even if Garcia never calls. Paro landing that fight in 2027 makes zero sense from Ryan’s financial perspective.

Ryan operates purely on box office scale. A return match with Devin Haney already has massive public heat, personal grudge, and built-in history that sells pay-per-view buys effortlessly. A fight with Teofimo Lopez brings two huge American fanbases together for an absolute blockbuster. Those two events generate monster gates. Paro simply cannot generate that kind of revenue in the United States.

On top of the financial gap, Paro presents a terrible risk profile for Ryan. Paro is a tough southpaw with an awkward style who makes life miserable inside the ring. Taking on that kind of stylistic headache for a fraction of the money Ryan can make elsewhere is bad business. Fighters in Ryan’s tax bracket do not volunteer for difficult nights unless huge checks back it up.

Then you have the calendar reality. Ryan is not fighting four times a year. If he takes a marquee date in the spring, that eats up the first half of 2027. A massive fall date takes care of the rest. Between Teofimo, Haney, or other lucrative names floating around, 2027 fills up instantly.

Paro holding a title belt does not move the needle for Ryan either. Ryan transcended the need for sanctioning body belts long ago because his name alone drives the promotion.

Sports.title: Carlos Adames Approval Leaves Meiirim Nursultanov Waiting
Sports.content:
Carlos Adames got the green light to take an interim bout before dealing with mandatory challenger Meiirim Nursultanov. The WBC approved a November 17 date above 160 pounds, but it includes a massive catch. If Adames loses, he loses his middleweight world title on the spot, even with the belt not officially on the line.

The WBC confirmed the ruling in an October 14 update. They left out the opponent, the venue, plus the exact weight limit. Because of that, nobody knows how tough this assignment will actually be.

Meiirim Nursultanov gets stuck waiting again. Holding the mandatory slot didn’t lock down his crack at the belt. Now he has to sit back, hoping Adames survives this detour so their scheduled clash can take place.

It puts Nursultanov in a weird spot. If Adames wins, Nursultanov still gets his shot at the active champion. If Adames stumbles, the title gets stripped, which leaves the top contender waiting on fresh orders for a vacant belt.

The WBC laid out clear terms. An Adames win routes him directly into the Nursultanov defense. Whoever walks away with the victory there has to face interim titlist Jesús Ramos Jr next.

There is a road map to clean up the division, but getting there takes three separate bouts. Every detour before the mandatory introduces the threat of an injury or an upset that blows up the entire schedule.

NEWS: Per sources, Carlos Adames’ @Zuffa_Boxing debut in a nontitle bout OK’d by the WBC is planned for November in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, where Zuffa is planning a show in November & one in December (obviously depends on status of the war & unrest in the region). #boxing — Dan Rafael (@DanRafael1) October 15, 2026

That vacant title rule also creates a bizarre setup for whoever steps into the ring on November 17. If the opponent beats the middleweight champ, Adames loses the belt, yet the winner walks away empty-handed without claiming it. Anyone signing that contract needs to realize what a victory actually delivers.

Adames lands the flexibility he wanted, while Nursultanov collects yet another promise about future dates. Until the promotion names a foe, nobody can tell if Adames is taking a dangerous test or just booking a tune-up above middleweight. Either way, Nursultanov stays on the sidelines waiting for his turn.

It sends a terrible message when a sanctioning body lets a champion put their mandatory obligations on ice just to chase an untitle bout above the weight class.

The whole point of a mandatory challenger is that you earn the number one spot through actual ring results, not politics. Nursultanov did the work, secured the position, and now he is forced to sit on the shelf watching the champion go hunt for bigger money elsewhere.

Nursultanov is not getting compensated while Adames takes this detour. Time away from the ring burns prime years, brings zero purse money, and creates ring rust. If Adames gets hurt on November 17, the layoff stretches out even longer. If Adames loses, Nursultanov does not even get the satisfaction or the profile boost of taking down the sitting champion. He gets stuck in a vacant title match that generates far less fanfare and a smaller check.

Sports.title: Sebastian Fundora Rules Out Saudi Arabia For Boots Fight
Sports.content:
Sebastian Fundora wants the winner of Jaron Ennis against Josh Kelly next, but the WBC junior middleweight champion insists Saudi Arabia will not host it. Fundora aims for spring 2027 to stage a unification bout, making it clear that facing Boots will not convince him to travel abroad to Riyadh.

That stance sets a firm condition on his future plans before his title defense against Ermal Hadribeaj on Saturday. Fundora expects Ennis to defeat Kelly, calling Boots the premier matchup at 154 pounds.

“I think the winner of Boots and Kelly should be the opponent for our next fight,” Fundora said to Ariel Helwani. “I think that’s early, early maybe springtime of next year, 2027.” Asked whether that reflected discussions or simply his preference, Fundora clarified: “That’s what I want. I think that’s what I’ll get as well.”

His preferred schedule remains a target rather than a signed contract, yet his refusal regarding Saudi Arabia sounded absolute.

“There’s a reason why I haven’t fought in Saudi Arabia,” Fundora said. “I wouldn’t feel comfortable, me being an American and everything like that.”

Asked directly if he would turn down an Ennis bout in the Gulf nation, Fundora confirmed he would walk away because that option feels unrealistic to him.

Securing an Ennis encounter would require common ground on location alongside purses. If promoters propose Saudi Arabia, Fundora makes it obvious that organizers must secure an alternate venue to get his signature.

He has not turned down an active offer to box Ennis. The scenario remains hypothetical right now, even while his desire to face the Ennis vs. Kelly victor is genuine.

Fundora must handle business against Hadribeaj first. Once Saturday concludes, his focus centers on collecting the remaining belts at 154 pounds in an arena he can accept. His stance puts him in a tricky spot financially. Crossing Riyadh off the list immediately shrinks the money pool, because nobody in the United States or the UK is writing those blank checks right now.

“My mother being a veteran and all the politics and that. It’s bigger than boxing. It’s way bigger than boxing,” said Fundora.

If PBC or another promoter has to finance an Ennis against Fundora unification on regular domestic pay-per-view, the numbers have to make sense organically, and that means significantly smaller paydays for both men.

Boots wants the belts, but he also wants to get paid like an elite fighter. If Fundora demands the bout take place in Vegas or Los Angeles, Ennis might look at the revenue split and decide the headache is not worth the discount, especially when other opportunities exist.

None of it matters if he looks past Saturday, either. Hadribeaj is not flying in just to collect a check and hand over the belt. If Fundora gets sloppy or gets caught while daydreaming about spring 2027, the whole discussion vanishes overnight. He will have priced himself out of an imaginary payday while holding empty hands.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois’ Odd Preparations For His World Title Fight On Saturday
Sports.content:
As the WBO world title fight between Champion Daniel Dubois and Challenger and former WBO Champion Fabio Wardley in The O2 Arena in London, England approaches, it is interesting to observe how both fighters are preparing during fight week.

Both Dubois and Wardley are taking part in the usual media engagements this week to promote their fight. Other than that, Wardley is more low-key in his preparations. However, Dubois is attracting much more attention in the pre-fight buildup not just because he is the reigning WBO Champion, but also due to his rather strange pre-fight preparations.

In this regard, he went on a walkabout in Brixton, London, England, at the beginning of this week with his WBO belt. While it is admirable that Dubois is seen with people, and welcoming photos to be taken with him and well-wishers, he gives the impression that he is an all-conquering hero rather than a fighter preparing to defend his world title against a dangerous opponent. It would surely have been better for Dubois to delay his meet and greet until after he had actually beaten Wardley in Saturday’s fight.

Yet, this is not the first time that Daniel Dubois has done something peculiar in the week leading up to a world title fight. Who can forget his baffling presence at a party in the afternoon of his heavyweight world title clash against Oleksandr Usyk on 19 July last year at Wembley Stadium, London, England? On that occasion, some argued that Dubois allowed his focus to wander by attending this party, when it should have been squarely on making last-minute preparations for his fight against Usyk. They had a valid point, as Dubois ended up losing this fight by knockout in the 5th Round, and his IBF title in the process.

This opens up the debate about whether Dubois is taking Wardley’s challenge too lightly. In the buildup to Dubois v Wardley II, the WBO Champion has gone on record saying that beating Fabio Wardley on Saturday night will be easy. However, Wardley is right to say that if this is the case, Dubois would not have been knocked down twice in the early Rounds in their world title fight on 09 May.

Confidence is one thing. But complacency is a different thing altogether, and Dubois should be wary that he does not fall into this trap. To his credit, Wardley says that he has learned from the mistakes he made in his first fight with Dubois, and will correct them on Saturday. The Ipswich fighter is even honest enough to admit the punches, which earned him his two knockdowns of Dubois in the pair’s first fight, did not land completely accurately. Wardley argues that if they had done so, they would have caused more damage. Further, the video footage from this fight seems to bear this out.

We shall see on Saturday night whether Dubois has prepared correctly for the challenges Fabio Wardley brings. Will it be Repeat or Revenge? One thing for sure is that Daniel Dubois would be foolish to underestimate Wardley, who, like Dubois, has beaten convincingly a former World Champion. Wardley did so when he beat former WBO Champion Joseph Parker by TKO in the 11th Round on 25 October 2025 for the WBO interim heavyweight title.

Time will tell who will be the victor on Saturday night. It should be one helluva fight.

Romer Cherubim

Freelance journalist

Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Needs Strong Finish To Saudi Contract
Sports.content:
Canelo Alvarez is eyeing a quick turnaround in February 2027 right after his October 31 meeting with Christian Mbilli. That timeline puts him on pace to wrap up his massive Saudi deal in just four months. How he performs down this final stretch will likely decide whether another giant contract follows.

“I want to fight quick, like in February,” Canelo said to Ring Magazine. “I have two fights left in Riyadh. So this one and another one.”

He wants February locked in, though nobody has named an opponent yet. Reports place his current four-fight package around $400 million, even if exact numbers stay private.

Canelo hasn’t said publicly that he wants an extension. Still, closing out the agreement forces the big question into the open: will the Saudis want to spend that kind of cash again?

His first two outings didn’t make a convincing pitch. William Scull left Canelo looking gun-shy. That bout really only existed to pick up the missing IBF belt rather than give fans an exciting matchup.

Against Terence Crawford, Canelo faded after round six. His sudden drop in punches looked like an aging fighter struggling with pace. Citing an injured elbow didn’t ease any doubts about his stamina.

Mbilli will push that gas tank immediately. Canelo needs an emphatic showing against a pressure fighter who won’t stop marching forward. Squeaking by with a disputed decision would damage his leverage, even if he leaves with his belts intact.

Assuming he clears Mbilli, February presents the next major hurdle. Hamzah Sheeraz brings strong British interest. David Benavidez or Osleys Iglesias would offer serious championship tests, though neither has received an official offer.

If Canelo dodges those challenges for an easier touch, the Saudis might start wondering what they are actually buying. Nobody knows how much control he holds over opponent selection anyway.

Dominating Mbilli before taking down elite competition would give Canelo real bargaining power. Another sluggish night marked by fading stamina could leave his next payday looking far smaller than what he is used to collecting.

If Riyadh Season is shelling out nine figures, they shouldn’t be subsidizing soft landings or vanity tours. Dropping rounds and gassing out against a 38-year-old blown-up welterweight like Crawford exposed the cliff Canelo is standing on. Pairing that with Scull in a dull performance showed zero return on entertainment value for the money spent.

Throwing him in with Benavidez or Ennis for the February finale would instantly force the issue.

Benavidez is the fight the public demanded for three years while Canelo priced himself out with absurd $150M to $200M demands. If Canelo wants another Saudi mega check, making him face the monster he avoided at 168 pounds is the only legitimate acid test left. He either proves he still possesses elite mettle or Benavidez completely takes the torch.

Jaron “Boots” Ennis would be pure tactical pressure. Boots would jump two weight classes, but his youth, hand speed, dynamic switch-hitting, and blistering volume would test Canelo’s fading stamina even worse than Crawford did down the stretch. Canelo cannot afford to stand flat-footed and rest against a guy throwing 70 punches a round.

IBF super middleweight champion Osleys Iglesias would be pure high risk, zero reward. The Cuban is a knockout artist who would likely batter this diminished version of Canelo, yet he doesn’t have the commercial profile to justify the Saudis burning their golden goose. There is no financial upside in letting an unknown derail the entire enterprise.

If Canelo rejects Benavidez or Ennis in February and insists on a soft touch like Edgar Berlanga 2 or John Ryder-level opposition, the Saudis have every reason to slam the checkbook shut. At this stage of his career, if he isn’t taking genuine risk into the ring, he isn’t worth the freight.

Sports.title: Anthony Olascuaga Faces Seven-Fight Challenger Yuberjen Martinez
Sports.content:
Anthony Olascuaga will defend his WBO flyweight title against seven-fight professional Yuberjen Martinez on November 14 at Dignity Health Sports Park in Carson, California. The unbeaten Colombian brings an Olympic silver medal and a perfect knockout record into a considerable jump in opposition.

Olascuaga (12-1, 9 KOs) makes his sixth title defense on the Diego Pacheco–Darius Fulghum undercard, with the event airing on DAZN and TNT Sports. The newly signed Matchroom fighter will also compete before his home Los Angeles crowd for the first time in his professional career.

Martinez (7-0, 7 KOs) gives the defense an interesting twist. His amateur pedigree separates him from the usual inexperienced challenger, but seven professional appearances leave plenty unanswered when the next opponent is an established world champion.

Stopping every opponent looks good on a poster. Doing it against the opposition Martinez has faced doesn’t establish that his power will have the same effect on Olascuaga. If the champion takes his punches and keeps coming, Martinez will need more than the finishing ability that has carried him through his professional fights.

That is where the scheduled 12-round distance becomes significant. Martinez’s Olympic success provides evidence of his boxing ability, but managing a world title fight requires decisions about pace, punch selection and energy that a short amateur contest cannot fully prepare him for.

Olascuaga has already been operating at championship level while Martinez has been building toward it. The challenger must show he can maintain his work when an experienced opponent forces him beyond the early success reflected in those seven stoppages.

The homecoming gives Olascuaga an opportunity to introduce himself to a local audience after defending his title in Japan. Matchroom gets a champion with Los Angeles roots on a card already headed by Pacheco.

Martinez gets the bigger opportunity: a chance to turn an accomplished amateur career and a brief professional run into a world championship. His medal makes him worth watching. This fight will tell us how far his professional boxing has progressed.

Ghana News.title: Sammy Gyamfi never BoG has not ceded forex role to us – GoldBod
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) has rejected suggestions that the Bank of Ghana (BoG) has transferred its foreign exchange market responsibilities to the Board, insisting that its role is limited to selling foreign currency earned from its gold operations and supporting supply to the domestic market.

The clarification follows reports after Tuesday’s sitting of Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC) which suggested that GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi’s explanation of the Board’s foreign exchange arrangements implied a transfer of the central bank’s mandate.

GoldBod said Mr Gyamfi was describing its Spot Foreign Exchange (FX) Sales framework, under which it sells US dollars to commercial banks in exchange for cedis, rather than taking over the Bank of Ghana’s broader regulatory functions.

According to GoldBod, the arrangement is consistent with Section 2(b) of the Ghana Gold Board Act, 2025 (Act 1140), which provides for the Board to supply foreign exchange to the country. The cedi proceeds from the sales are used to finance gold purchases through licensed aggregators.

The Board also said it sought guidance from the Bank of Ghana before implementing the framework and received authorisation to proceed.

The clarification is consistent with comments by Bank of Ghana Governor, Dr Johnson Asiama, who has dismissed suggestions that the central bank has relinquished its foreign exchange responsibilities.

He said the Bank remains ready to intervene when necessary to preserve market stability, while GoldBod supports foreign exchange intermediation and supply.

“We want to focus on reserve build-up while GoldBod supports with FX intermediation as well as some level of intervention for the market,” he said, adding that the Bank would enter the market if volatility threatened orderly trading conditions.

GoldBod stressed that authorisation to sell foreign exchange does not amount to a transfer of the central bank’s mandate.

Ghana News.title: High Court sets November 4 for ruling on Wontumi’s bail application
Ghana News.content:
The Accra High Court has set November 4, 2026, to deliver its ruling on a bail application filed by former New Patriotic Party (NPP) Ashanti Regional Chairman, Bernard Antwi Boasiako, popularly known as Chairman Wontumi.

The application seeks his release from custody pending an appeal against his conviction and 20-year prison sentence for illegal mining-related offences linked to a concession at Samreboi in the Western Region.

Mr Boasiako’s lawyers are seeking bail while the appeal process continues.

The application was initially scheduled for hearing on August 19 but was adjourned after Mr Boasiako and his lead counsel, Samuel Atta Akyea, failed to appear in court. The matter was subsequently rescheduled to today.

The Attorney-General has opposed the bail application, arguing that the former NPP regional chairman poses a flight risk.

The court is expected to determine whether Mr Boasiako should be released on bail pending the outcome of his appeal when it delivers its ruling on November 4.

Ghana News.title: Korle Bu appeals for more doctors, nurses as A&E Centre struggles under pressure
Ghana News.content:
Korle Bu Teaching Hospital

Management of the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital has appealed to the government for additional doctors and nurses to address persistent staffing shortages and ease pressure on its Accident and Emergency (A&E) Centre.

The hospital’s Chief Executive Officer, Dr Yakubu Seidu Adam, said the recruitment of more permanent medical personnel was critical to improving emergency care and strengthening services at the country’s leading referral facility.

Speaking during an engagement with Parliament’s Health Committee, Dr Adam disclosed that the hospital’s 64-bed Accident and Emergency Centre was struggling to cope with the growing number of accident victims and other emergency cases referred from different parts of the country.

He noted that the limited number of permanent medical staff was placing additional pressure on critical departments, particularly the A&E Centre and the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).

According to him, although the hospital has a significant number of doctors, a large proportion are medical trainees who leave after completing their training, creating challenges for the facility’s long-term staffing needs.

“This is a training institution. We have a number of doctors, but when we look at our numbers, most of them are not our staff. It’s a training institution; they come, we train them, and they go,” he said.

Dr Adam stressed that the hospital needed to recruit more medical officers who could provide sustained support for emergency and intensive care services, rather than relying heavily on doctors undergoing training.

He said management had already brought the staffing concerns to the attention of the hospital’s Director of Human Resources and the Minister of Health, but the meeting with Parliament’s Health Committee provided another opportunity to highlight the urgent need for additional personnel.

The Chief Executive Officer also called for more nurses to complement the efforts of existing medical staff and ensure patients receive timely and effective treatment.

The appeal comes as the hospital continues to face pressure on its emergency care services due to the volume of cases it handles from across the country.

Beyond addressing the shortage of personnel, management has also advocated the construction of a new facility to ease congestion and improve the hospital’s capacity to manage emergency cases.

The proposed intervention, alongside the recruitment of additional doctors and nurses, is expected to help strengthen emergency care delivery at the country’s premier referral hospital.

Ghana News.title: AFCON 2027Q: ‘I’m optimistic Black Stars can turn things around’ – Agyemang-Badu
Ghana News.content:
Former Ghana midfielder Emmanuel Agyemang-Badu is confident that the Black Stars can recover from their poor start and secure qualification for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON).

Ghana made a disastrous start to their Group C campaign, losing 2-0 away to Côte d’Ivoire before falling to a humiliating 4-2 defeat against The Gambia at the Accra Sports Stadium.

With zero points from their opening two matches, the team now sits at the bottom of Group C, with four matches left to play.

However, Agyemang-Badu, a key midfielder in Ghana’s historic 2009 FIFA U-20 World Cup-winning squad, believes the team can still bounce back when they face Somalia in a decisive double-header in November.

"I’m optimistic that the Black Stars might win their next games," Agyemang-Badu told Ahenfie Sports.

"Let’s give local players the chance they deserve," he added.

Agyemang-Badu’s comments come shortly after the Ghana Football Association (GFA) and head coach Carlos Queiroz mutually agreed to part ways following the disastrous start to the qualifiers.

A five-member committee has since been set up to interview candidates and recommend a permanent replacement.

In the meantime, an interim technical team is expected to lead the Black Stars in their upcoming fixtures against Somalia.

Ghana News.title: Digital innovation could widen Africa’s inequalities if people are left out – Sam Jonah
Ghana News.content:
Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has warned that digital innovation could widen inequality in Africa if its benefits are concentrated among people who already have access to technology, education and economic opportunities.

He said governments, universities and businesses must ensure that digital policies and platforms do not exclude people who lack reliable internet access, electricity or the resources to participate in the digital economy.

“Every digital policy, every new platform, must ask a simple question: who is left out?” he said.

Sir Sam was speaking at Methodist University Ghana’s international conference in Accra on Thursday, October 15, where he delivered the keynote address for the university’s 25th anniversary celebrations.

He argued that a child in Dansoman with a laptop and reliable internet access has substantially different opportunities from a child in a village without electricity.

“If digital innovation only serves the connected, it will not close our inequalities. It will widen them,” he said.

Sir Sam also called attention to barriers facing women in accessing credit, owning land and attaining senior positions in institutions across Africa.

Drawing on his experience as patron of the Executive Women Network in Accra, he said women had demonstrated what they could achieve when given opportunities.

“An economy that underuses half its talent is running on one leg,” he said.

He argued that inclusive development required businesses and institutions to open up access to finance, markets, technology and decision-making.

The business leader also called for greater respect for technical and vocational education, saying not every young person needed a university degree but every young person needed a skill.

He said Africa’s industrial development depended on technicians, artisans and engineers, and urged the continent to give practical skills greater recognition.

Sir Sam further emphasised mentorship, describing the opportunity to learn from experienced people as one of the most valuable contributions leaders could make to the next generation.

He said his own career had benefited from managers at Ashanti Goldfields who recognised his potential early on.

“The greatest gift we can give the next generation is not money. It is a chance,” he said.

His address called for digital innovation, education and economic development to be accompanied by deliberate efforts to ensure that opportunities reach people who are often excluded.

Ghana News.title: Galamsey is an economic, health and moral problem – Sam Jonah
Ghana News.content:
Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has described illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, as an economic, health and moral problem, warning that the pursuit of wealth without responsibility is damaging Ghana’s natural resources.

He said discussions about sustainability must confront the effects of illegal mining on rivers, forests and farmland.

“Rivers that fed our grandparents now run the colour of chocolate milk,” he said.

Sir Sam was delivering the keynote address at Methodist University Ghana’s international conference in Accra on Thursday, October 15, as the university marked its 25th anniversary.

Drawing on his career in the mining industry, he said mining companies and individuals must consider what they leave behind after extracting resources from the earth.

He posed the question of whether mining would leave communities with damaged land and polluted rivers or with lasting benefits such as schools, skills, roads and businesses.

“This is not only an environmental problem. It is an economic problem, a health problem and, in the end, a moral problem,” he said of galamsey.

Sir Sam said the principle of sustainability should also guide how public money and human talent are managed.

He criticised the use of borrowed funds for consumption instead of investment and pointed to abandoned public projects as examples of poor stewardship.

He argued that incomplete projects represent wasted resources, particularly when successive governments begin new projects instead of completing existing ones.

He also expressed concern about skilled young people who struggle to find opportunities after receiving an education, saying a sustainable Africa should provide conditions that allow its talent to contribute at home.

Sir Sam said digital tools could support efforts to improve environmental and public-sector accountability.

He cited satellite data as a means of tracking illegal mining, digital land registries as a way to reduce longstanding land disputes, and digital public procurement systems as a tool for showing citizens how public funds are spent.

“The technology exists. What we need is the will to use it, even when transparency is uncomfortable for the powerful,” he said.

He linked responsible resource management to ethical leadership, arguing that economic gain should not come at the expense of communities and future generations.

His address called for enterprise and innovation to be pursued alongside responsibility for the environment, public resources and society.

Ghana News.title: Africa must create AI technology instead of paying to use it – Sam Jonah
Ghana News.content:
Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has warned that Africa risks becoming a mere consumer of artificial intelligence and other digital technologies unless it invests in the skills and capacity needed to develop its own solutions.

He said the continent must avoid a situation in which it imports technology, exports its data and pays foreign companies to access the resulting products and services.

Delivering the keynote address at Methodist University Ghana’s international conference in Accra on Thursday, October 15, Sir Sam said Africa must learn from its history of exporting raw materials while buying back finished products.

“We must not do it again with data,” he said, referring to the risk of repeating that pattern in the digital economy.

The conference was held as the university marked its 25th anniversary under the theme “Excellence, Morality, and Service at 25: Advancing Digital Innovation, Equity, and Sustainability in a Transforming World”.

Sir Sam called on African universities to produce graduates who can develop digital technologies, rather than only use applications created elsewhere.

“Our universities must produce people who can write the code, not just use the app,” he said.

He argued that countries that had made significant progress had invested in building their own technical workforce.

He also urged entrepreneurs to focus on solving problems in African sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, logistics, energy and finance, particularly for people who remain underserved by formal systems.

According to him, Africa’s opportunities lie not simply in replicating products developed in places such as London and San Francisco, but in creating solutions suited to the continent’s needs.

Sir Sam cited mobile money as an example of innovation that emerged from a practical problem: millions of Africans had mobile phones but lacked access to bank accounts.

He said the development of mobile money demonstrated Africa’s capacity to create solutions that respond to local conditions.

He warned, however, that the next wave of technologies—including artificial intelligence, data and automation—could deepen the continent’s dependence on external providers if it failed to build local expertise.

Sir Sam also called for enterprise to be treated as a respected career path, arguing that Africa needed more young people who created businesses and jobs rather than focusing only on securing government employment.

He said the continent had the people, resources, and ideas needed to advance, but required the habits and investments that would turn its potential into prosperity.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Russia says Ukraine resumes attacks on oil refineries
World.content:
Ukraine president earlier said Kyiv was ‘done’ with energy ceasefire and strikes on Russian oil refineries would resume.

Russia says Ukraine has targeted an oil refinery in Ryazan, about 180 kilometres (110 miles) south of Moscow, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was “done” with an energy ceasefire unilaterally announced by United States President Donald Trump over the weekend.

“The Kyiv regime attempted a large-scale attack on an oil refinery in Ryazan,” Moscow’s defence ministry said in a statement on Thursday, adding that a “fire broke out after drone debris fell onto the refinery site.”

Ukraine’s president earlier told the British newspaper the Financial Times that strikes on Russian oil refineries would resume, and accused the US of weakening Ukraine’s position on the battlefield by allegedly withdrawing crucial intelligence sharing.

Trump on Sunday unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” that was not publicly confirmed, and Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Ukraine said it suspended attacks on Russian energy sites for several days after Trump’s announcement.

The US has pressured Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian refineries, claiming that a suspension of attacks and a deal to purchase 1.8 million tonnes of diesel from Russia would help reduce soaring fuel prices.

“This politically is not simple [in America], because everybody will want to ask how it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying – and you make . . . business with the guys with such aggression,” Zelenskyy told the FT.

Zelenskyy also alleged that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s satellite internet service was restricted, potentially leaving it more vulnerable to Russian attacks. The Ukrainian armed forces use SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield system for offensive and defensive operations.



In a post on X on Wednesday evening, SpaceX owner Elon Musk said that only the US military and Trump had the authority to limit Starshield’s usage and speed for clients.

In a separate post, he called for Zelenskyy to “go” as Ukraine’s leader.

“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote in a separate post on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”

Ukraine is heavily dependent on Western military aid in its fight against Russia, particularly from the US and Germany. However, Kyiv’s relations with Washington have been strained in recent weeks, with Trump calling on Saturday for Zelenskyy to be replaced.

Against this backdrop of tensions, Zelenskyy said he would be willing to pause strikes on Russian energy sites again, but only if the US supplied Ukraine with crucial Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy is due to meet European leaders in Brussels on Thursday as he pushes for tougher sanctions on Moscow and faster delivery of support from the European Union.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has called on EU leaders to “step up” their game to ensure Ukraine wins the war against Russia.

The EU has already pledged $50 billion in support for Ukraine next year. However, the sum falls far short of the $175 billion Kyiv plans to spend on its defences next year.

Trump has denied that the US has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

World.title: ‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel
World.content:
Balkan countries’ ties with Israel reflect domestic politics, defence deals and strategic interests rather than a united regional position.

Share ‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel on social media

Throughout Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Europe’s position has, to an extent, been aligned.

Outliers such as Spain and the Republic of Ireland have long been more vocal in condemning Israel, but overall, the shift from unconditional solidarity with Israel to concern over its conduct has taken hold in much of the continent.

Across the Balkans, divergent policies towards Israel reflect domestic calculations, transactional diplomacy, and unresolved identity politics rather than a shared vision for the Middle East, according to experts.

“The Balkan countries have almost no common positions at all, and so it’s not surprising their positions towards Israel and Gaza are all over the map,” Marko Prelec, analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Each country goes its own way.”

Prelec noted that while there is genuine revulsion towards Israeli policy in Gaza and sympathy for Palestinians – particularly among Bosnian Muslims – most countries in the region take their positions based on unrelated interests.

Florian Bieber, professor of Southeast European history and politics at Austria’s University of Graz, said regional consensus is nearly impossible.

“The position towards Israel is strongly shaped by domestic politics and also national narratives, which makes a regional or even a country-specific position unlikely,” Bieber told Al Jazeera.

Bosnia and Herzegovina: Differences from one entity to another

Nowhere is this fragmentation more evident than in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war in Gaza has deepened existing ethno-national divisions.



Bosniak political representatives and much of the public in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina have expressed strong solidarity with Palestinians, while leaders in Republika Srpska have been openly pro-Israel, and some Croat political figures have also adopted a more sympathetic tone towards Israel.

“Bosniak solidarity with Palestinians is often seen not just through an ideological lens, but also from the perspective of war and being a victim of Serb nationalist aggression, comparing the Palestinian experience with the Bosniak experience in the 1990s,” Bieber explained.

Conversely, leaders in the Serb-majority entity, Republika Srpska, led by former President Milorad Dodik, have openly embraced Israel.

Foreign policy analyst and journalist Bosko Jaksic told Al Jazeera that for Dodik, “The enemy of my enemy is my friend – Jews and Orthodox Serbs against Muslims. This religious and ethnic factor allows him to maintain an Israeli connection parallel to his closeness with Russia, while simultaneously performing a new American flip by glorifying [US President] Donald Trump.”

Prelec added that Bosnian Serb outreach to Israel and specifically Likud, the ruling Israeli party, represents “an attempt to find allies for its internationally unpopular flirtation with separatism, and an indirect way to strengthen ties with parts of the MAGA [Make America Great Again] movement and the Trump administration”.

Serbia: Arms sales and multi-vector balancing

In Serbia, the approach to Israel blends defence economics with foreign policy.

Despite historically friendly relations with Palestine and voting in favour of Palestinian membership in international bodies, Belgrade has exported ammunition and arms to Israel since October 2023.

The relationship has also moved beyond exports. In September, Serbia opened an Israeli-linked drone assembly plant, underlining the growing practical dimension of bilateral defence cooperation.

Vuk Vuksanovic, lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Serbia’s defence industry “has not been particularly picky when it comes to its customers, and the desire for profit has been one of the factors”.

However, he emphasised broader geopolitical ambitions.

“In the past three years, there has been a tilt towards Israel regarding security cooperation, while diplomatically Serbia tries to be cautious in multilateral institutions due to its ties with the wider Islamic world,” he said.

Vuksanovic noted that Belgrade views Israel as a partner to “acquire the protection of Israeli lobby groups and access to the Trump administration in the US”, especially as the Serbian government faces domestic political opposition.



Meanwhile, Jaksic warned of the international risks involved.

“Due to the significant increase in ammunition exports to Israel during the war in Gaza, Serbia risks being accused of complicity in genocide,” he said. “Beyond financial calculations, the Serbian president attempts to use closeness with his ideological, authoritarian, and nationalist ally, [Israeli Prime Minister] Benjamin Netanyahu, to get closer to Trump.”

Kosovo, Albania, and the Washington anchor

For Kosovo and Albania, foreign policy regarding Israel remains anchored to security alliances with Washington.

Under the 2020 Washington Agreement, Kosovo recognised Israel in exchange for Israeli recognition of Kosovo’s independence, subsequently opening its embassy in Jerusalem. Serbia, which had pledged in 2020 to move its embassy to Jerusalem, ultimately did not do so.

Pristina opened its Jerusalem embassy “defying the stance of the wider international community”, said Jaksic.

“Israel’s growing influence in the Western Balkans is evident,” he noted. “That includes investments, and in the case of Serbia, especially military cooperation. This absolutely does not exclude personal attempts to buy political impunity from American sanctions, or to ease diplomatic pressure.”

In neighbouring Albania, Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government has preserved warm political ties with Israel.

Driven partly by operational defence needs, Albania deepened cooperation with Israeli cybersecurity companies after cyberattacks, while aligning broader diplomacy with Washington and Brussels.

Executive rifts and ideological turnarounds

In Croatia, foreign policy on Gaza has been paralysed by a sharp executive rift between conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic and President Zoran Milanovic of the Social Democratic Party.

Plenkovic’s government has followed a cautious, mainstream European Union approach, while Milanovic has openly condemned Israel’s military conduct in Gaza, labelling it disproportionate and creating a public fracture in the country’s foreign policy leadership.

Further north in Slovenia, there are ideological shifts.

The previous centre-left government adopted firm measures against Israel – such as an arms embargo, a ban on imports from illegal settlements, and a ban on the entry of top officials like Netanyahu – as well as recognising Palestinian statehood.

Conservative forces under Prime Minister Janez Jansa have sought to reverse these policies.

“In Slovenia, we can see the classic left-right division where populist and far-right parties support Israel because of Netanyahu as a similar political actor,” said Bieber. “They recognise him as ideologically aligned, which helps reinforce their view of Islam as a threat, fitting their own narratives.”

Quiet alignment and strategic alliances

Smaller NATO members like Montenegro and North Macedonia have chosen a path of quiet alignment.

Both adhere to standard EU and NATO statements, calling for ceasefires and humanitarian aid while carefully avoiding high-profile bilateral disputes or bold independent diplomatic initiatives.



Further east, Romania and Bulgaria maintain a cautious tone that sometimes leans towards Israel. Grounded in historic bilateral relations and deep strategic defence partnerships with the United States, Bucharest and Sofia balance carefully worded statements at the United Nations with ongoing military and intelligence coordination.

Meanwhile, in Greece, consecutive governments in Athens have maintained a robust strategic military and energy partnership with Israel; Athens recently signed a $3.5bn missile deal with Israel. Originally forged alongside Cyprus to balance regional maritime rivalries in the Eastern Mediterranean, this alliance has held firm despite significant domestic public backlash and protests over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Ultimately, the disparate responses across the Balkans demonstrate that Middle Eastern policy in the region is rarely about the Middle East itself.

Whether driven by defence profits, constitutional rivalries, or the search for political backing in Washington, regional actors continue to view Israel almost exclusively through a transactional lens.

World.title: Could France trigger another Eurozone debt crisis?
World.content:
France is facing a growing crisis of confidence in its public finances.

Its borrowing costs have reached their highest level in more than two decades.

Investors now demand higher yields on French government bonds than on Italian or Greek ones.

With public debt nearing 120 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit above 5 percent, the government is under pressure to rein in spending.

But protesters are demanding more investment in education.

With parliament deeply divided and a presidential election approaching, agreeing on a solution is proving difficult.

The concern now is whether France’s troubles could spread across the Eurozone.

World.title: The irony of OpenAI crying foul over spying
World.content:
A company that owes much of its existence – and enormous valuation – to stealing other people’s work is now up in arms about people trying to steal from it.

Americans can rest easy – for the moment, at least. The fine folks at the Federal Bureau of Investigation have thwarted a major national security threat.

On October 9, the FBI arrested 35-year-old engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen employed at the California-based artificial intelligence company OpenAI, the maker of the chatbot ChatGPT, and a firm that describes its mission as ensuring that “artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity”.

A press release from the United States Department of Justice said that Alfozan was accused of installing a “surreptitious audio recording device” in an executive conference room at the OpenAI offices in San Francisco.

The statement quoted Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton’s assessment that “this serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative”. (For those who have not yet got the memo, US President Donald Trump recently decreed that the term “artificial intelligence” be changed to “super intelligence” or “SI.”)

FBI director Kash Patel concurred that “protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security”, and assured everyone that the FBI would continue doing its part “to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge”.

So much for the separation of corporation and state in the world’s self-appointed greatest democracy.

The covert device was reported to have been concealed in toilet paper and attached to the back of a television monitor. The Gizmodo website has noted with amusement that, despite being cast as a “sophisticated” spying apparatus, the device in question can in fact be easily ordered online “for the low low price of $13.99”.



If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in jail and a fine of $250,000.

Now, some of you may still be asking what the big deal is – and why the US government is acting like it’s 1950 and the Soviets are stealing our nuclear secrets.

The spectacle becomes all the more curious when we consider that the company up in arms over the alleged attempted theft of its technology owes much of its existence – and massive valuation – to stealing stuff from people.

The day before Alfozan’s arrest, USA Today and several other newspapers sued OpenAI in a Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement and the unauthorised use of hundreds of thousands of news articles and other materials to develop ChatGPT.

And back in July, various US media outlets including the New York Times and the New York Daily News requested that a federal judge impose sanctions on OpenAI for “hiding and destroying evidence showing how ChatGPT was trained on stolen journalism”, as attorney Steven Lieberman put it.

The moral of the story, perhaps, is that when OpenAI steals things it’s to “benefit all of humanity” – but when a 35-year-old Saudi engineer does it, it’s a national security crisis.

In case we were not already bored to tears hearing about national security, US Attorney General Todd Blanche took to X on Tuesday to preach that the “theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security”, necessitating continued “swift action … to protect American innovation and safeguard our nation”.

Of course, many Americans might wonder why “innovation” gets such special treatment when they themselves are so often on the receiving end of government abuse. The frequency with which US police officers murder unarmed Black people, for instance, would seem to indicate that there are far more literal threats to the nation’s security than a $14 device hidden in toilet paper.

But human security is of no interest to a corporatocracy increasingly dominated by AI, an industry that thrives on putting people out of jobs and that is deeply entwined in a number of sordid developments at home and abroad. Among them is mass surveillance, which combines AI-assisted violations of civil liberties and constitutional protections with good old police state “innovation”.

To that end, a bunch of US cops have taken advantage of new AI-powered technology, such as automated licence plate readers, to stalk their exes. Then there is the matter of the FBI and other government agencies buying up data en masse from tech companies in a bid to keep tabs, Big Brother-style, on everyone’s personal information at all times.



It makes you think twice about the sudden concern for “spying” in the Alfozan case.

As for threats to other people’s national security, OpenAI and like-minded tech companies that do business with the Pentagon have been complicit in recent US aggression – from Venezuela to Iran – as the US pursues its strategy for “Accelerating America’s Military AI Dominance” (concocted before Trump mandated the renaming of AI as SI).

Israel, too, has exploited OpenAI technology, among other US-made goodies, to conduct its contemporary apocalyptic exercises in the Middle East.
