In the fastidious arena of Nigerian democratic contestation, where political careers are routinely made or unmade at the stroke of an administrative pen, the electoral landscape of Ogun State has just witnessed a seismic reconfiguration.

The release of the Independent National Electoral Commission’s final candidates list for the upcoming February 6 poll did not merely refine the contest; it fundamentally altered the gravitational laws of the Gateway State.

With the dramatic administrative disqualification of the Peoples Democratic Party flagbearer, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu – whose campaign foundered upon the unyielding rocks of statutory compliance – the long-anticipated battle for Oke Mosan has dissolved into what looks unmistakably like a clear corridor for Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola, universally known as Yayi.

To observe the swift collapse of the opposition’s vanguard is to witness a classic lesson in political vanity. For over two decades, the Adebutu political machine operated under the comfortable delusion that inherited wealth and periodic electoral vanity projects could substitute for systemic party building and rigorous legislative stewardship.

His endless quest for the governorship had long assumed the tragicomic quality of Sisyphus rolling his boulder up the rocky heights of Olumo Rock, only to watch it inevitably slip from his grasp. Adebutu’s protracted struggle was defined less by ideological conviction than by an entrenched sense of elite entitlement – a belief that the governorship was a family birthright waiting to be claimed.

Yet, as the proverb wisely admonish: one does not gauge the readiness of meat merely by its outer appearance. While Adebutu spent years navigating internal party squabbles, procedural blunders, and endless litigation, he failed to erect a resilient, legally watertight institutional apparatus capable of surviving the basic rigours of electoral regulation.

His ultimate undoing by the fine print of the Electoral Act is not an act of political sabotage; it is the natural culmination of a long, chaotic campaign built upon shifting sand.

In stark, deliberate contrast stands Senator Olamilekan Adeola, whose trajectory reads like a masterclass in pragmatic political investment and calculated expansion.

Long before the INEC guidelines excised his chief antagonist from the ballot, Yayi had already redefined the parameters of representation across Ogun State.

Critics and political opponents once sought to tether him to a catalog of whispers, weaponising regional parochialism and dredges of past legislative disputes to question his lineage and motives. Yet, in politics as in life, performance is the ultimate antidote to prejudice.

Rather than engaging in the toxic mudslinging that so often characterises sub-national politics, Yayi adopted the philosophy of Niccolò Machiavelli, who observed that true authority is preserved through tangible virtue and visible beneficence. His systematically executed strategy was disarmingly simple: weaponise development.

Across the length and breadth of Ogun State – from the industrial hubs of Ado-Odo/Ota to the agricultural stretches of Yewa, through the historic precincts of Abeokuta and down to the coastal fringes of Ijebu – Yayi unleashed an infrastructural and human capital intervention of unprecedented proportions.

Transformers were planted in long-neglected rural corridors, primary health centres were rehabilitated, tertiary scholarships were distributed by the thousands, and massive road interventions were facilitated through legislative appropriations. He treated non-constituents with the same administrative urgency as his immediate constituency in Ogun West, effectively building a cross-zonal movement that transcended traditional senatorial fault lines. By the time the political establishment began to take stock of his ambitions, Yayi had entrenched himself in the daily livelihoods of the common folk.

Consequently, the lingering inquisitions regarding his past and the tired campaigns of calumny simply evaporated under the heat of his sheer productivity. The voter on the street of Sagamu or Ilaro is rarely persuaded by abstract political philosophy; they care deeply about illuminated streets, functional clinics, and economic empowerment.

Yayi provided all three in abundance. As the old Latin maxim goes, Res ipsa loquitur – the thing speaks for itself.

As the political machinery prepares for the February 6 election, the road to the executive house at Oke Mosan appears remarkably unobstructed. The opposition front lies in a state of irreversible fragmentation, reduced to post-mortem legal gambits that arrive far too late to sway an electorate that has already moved on.

The traditional fault lines that once split Ogun politics along rigid regional lines have been softened by Yayi’s broad-based, inclusive coalition, which seamlessly unites the political interests of the East, Central, and West.

Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola is not merely riding a wave of political good fortune following an opponent’s administrative error. He is harvesting the yield of years of deliberate, calculated, and generous political investment. When the voters turn out on February 6, they will not be participating in a tense, nail-biting thriller. Instead, they will be ratifying a process whose conclusion was written months ago in the concrete, asphalt, and human lives transformed by a politician who understood that the shortest path to power is paved with genuine service to the people.

Yes, Oke Mosan awaits its master builder.

*Somorin is a veteran journalist

World.title: N’Delta: Group Demands Equitable Distribution of Oil, Gas Pipeline Surveillance Contracts Among Stakeholders
World.content:
*Says Urhobo, Isoko, Ilaje, Opobo, Bakassi, Ibibio, Efik, Ogoni communities should demand fair share of contracts

As the debate for even distribution of oil and gas pipeline surveillance contracts in the Niger Delta region continues, the Initiator of “Guard Your Pipeline I Guard My Own Movement”, Fejiro Oliver, has urged the federal government to lay emphasis on the decentralisation of pipeline surveillance contracts which was originally driven by demands for fairness and equitable distribution of opportunities among oil-producing communities, rather than ethnic considerations.

He listed the Urhobo, Isoko, Ilaje, Opobo, Bakassi, Ibibio, Efik and Ogoni communities among those he believed should be demanding a fair share of the contracts.

He argued that the Eastern corridor, currently handled by PINL under Osahon Okunbo and, reportedly, the Olu of Warri, already provides opportunities for Edo and Itsekiri interests and should remain with them.

At a media briefing in Abuja, Fejiro stated that he sought to clarify his position amid renewed controversy over the allocation of pipeline surveillance contracts and allegations concerning the amounts paid to contractors.

He said the movement, which began in March, gained national attention and prompted the federal government, through the National Assembly, to convene what he described as an emergency town hall meeting to discuss the campaign’s demands.

He said his group, the United Niger Delta Congress, was invited to the meeting and participated despite concerns that the process might not produce meaningful results.

According to him, the central argument of the campaign was that Tantita Security Services and Maton Engineering should not exercise control over contracts worth about N2.1 trillion to protect pipelines passing through communities where other capable local contractors could perform the job.

He said the campaign drew part of its justification from the Petroleum Industry Act, which he argued supported a more equitable approach to opportunities in oil-producing areas.

Oliver also questioned the composition of the contractors initially engaged for the surveillance work, noting that two of the major contractors were associated with Ijaw interests, while PINL was led by Okunbo, whom he said was from Edo State with the Olu of Warri, an Itsekiri traditional ruler, serving as the company’s chairman.

He said his concern was that “communities across the Niger Delta should have a fair opportunity to participate in pipeline surveillance activities, rather than allowing contracts to remain concentrated in the hands of a few interests”.

The activist, however, said he was disturbed by recent media reports and social media discussions that, in his view, had distorted the original objectives of the campaign and turned the issue into a confrontation involving ethnic and commercial interests.

World.title: Don’t Interfere in 2027 Elections, Obidients Warn Wike
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja



The Obidient Movement has warned the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, against any attempt to influence the outcome of the 2027 general election.

This follows the former Rivers State governor’s declaration that he would lead President Bola Tinubu’s re-election campaign in Rivers State and the FCT.

The movement urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and security agencies to remain impartial and ensure that voters freely determine the outcome of the elections.

Wike had last Monday declared himself the field commander of Tinubu’s re-election campaign in the two territories, a move that has drawn criticism from the political group.

In a statement issued yesterday by its Media and Communications Directorate, the movement said taking charge of a political campaign did not give Wike control over voters or the electoral process.

“Wike must understand that coordinating a political campaign does not confer ownership of the electorate, control over voters, or authority over the electoral process,” the statement said.

The group insisted that Rivers State and the FCT belong to their people and not to any politician, political party, or influential political figure.

It challenged Wike to campaign for Tinubu based on the president’s performance rather than create the impression that political control over the two territories would determine the election outcome.

“If Wike believes the APC deserves victory, he should campaign for it and allow the people to decide. If he believes that Tinubu’s performance will earn him another term, he should present that record to Nigerians and submit himself to the verdict of the ballot box,” the movement said.

The group also called on INEC and security agencies to address concerns about the 2027 elections and demonstrate their independence from political interests.

It warned that any attempt by Wike, his associates or other political actors to manipulate the polls should attract legal consequences.

The movement further urged Nigerians to monitor the elections, document suspected irregularities and report credible evidence of malpractice through lawful channels.

It maintained that the credibility of the 2027 elections would depend on whether votes were freely cast and accurately counted, regardless of the political status of those involved.

The group concluded that neither Wike, Tinubu nor the All Progressives Congress (APC) should regard victory as guaranteed, insisting that the electorate must have the final say.

World.title: 1.5m Vote Target for Tinubu in Osun Unrealistic, Says Oyetola’s Former Spokesperson
World.content:
Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo



A former Chief Press Secretary to the immediate-past Governor of Osun State, Gboyega Oyetola, Ismail Omipidan, has questioned the feasibility of securing 1.5 million votes for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in Osun State in the 2027 general election, warning that the political strategy surrounding the target could undermine the All Progressives Congress (APC).

Omipidan also cautioned Tinubu and the APC national leadership against political arrangements that could alienate loyal party members, arguing that resentment within the party could weaken grassroots mobilisation ahead of the presidential election.

In an opinion article, he maintained that Osun State’s historical voting patterns did not support the projection of 1.5 million presidential votes, urging the president and the party leadership to adopt a strategy that reflects the state’s electoral history, political peculiarities, and the interests of its people.

He also expressed concern over the political implications of Governor Ademola Adeleke’s reported emergence as Osun State coordinator of Tinubu’s 2027 re-election campaign, warning that the arrangement could generate discontent among APC members if their established political structures were not adequately considered.

“In war, just like in politics, strategy is everything,” Omipidan wrote, arguing that a strategy driven by the ambitions of a few individuals could fail if it did not accommodate the interests of the wider party membership.

Omipidan said he first heard about the proposed 1.5 million-vote target less than 24 hours after the APC lost the August 15, 2026, governorship election in Osun State.

He added that the subsequent repetition of the target by the party’s National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Basiru, had heightened his concerns about the political calculations behind the proposal.

The APC lost the governorship election to Adeleke, who contested on the platform of the Accord Party.

According to Omipidan, the proposed target appeared inconsistent with Osun’s historical presidential election results, as the state had never recorded up to one million votes for a presidential candidate in previous elections.

Citing the 2011 presidential election, he said the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN) candidate polled 299,711 votes in Osun State, while the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) secured 188,409 votes, with registered voters standing at 1,342,289.

In 2015, he said the APC won the state with 383,603 votes against the PDP’s 249,929, while the number of registered voters was 1,407,107.

For the 2019 presidential election, Omipidan cited 347,634 votes for the APC and 337,377 for the PDP.

In the 2023 presidential election, he said the APC polled 342,941 votes in Osun, while the PDP secured 353,860.

He argued that the figures demonstrated the challenge of achieving the proposed 1.5 million votes, particularly without a substantial increase in voter participation.

“Historically, Osun State has never posted up to a million votes in any presidential election, and it will not happen next year, unless some persons just want to write figures,” he said.

Omipidan acknowledged that voter turnout in presidential elections could differ from that recorded during governorship elections but maintained that the distinction should inform the party’s electoral calculations.

He urged the APC leadership to establish realistic targets based on the state’s voting patterns and develop a mobilisation strategy capable of attracting voters across Osun State.

Omipidan expressed concern over the political arrangements being developed in Osun State to secure Tinubu’s re-election.

He specifically questioned the implications of Adeleke’s reported appointment as the president’s campaign coordinator in the state, arguing that the APC must ensure the arrangement did not undermine its existing structures.

While acknowledging the governor’s role in the emerging campaign arrangement, Omipidan maintained that the APC should be allowed to strengthen its organisational machinery and mobilise its members in support of Tinubu.

He warned that party members who felt sidelined could become less committed to the campaign, potentially weakening the grassroots mobilisation required to achieve the desired electoral outcome.

According to him, the presidency and the APC national leadership must pay attention to the concerns of party loyalists who have invested time and resources in building the party.

He also cautioned against political arrangements that could create unnecessary divisions between Tinubu and the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, a prominent APC figure in Osun State.

“President Tinubu and Oyetola must tread softly and cautiously,” he wrote, urging both leaders to consider the implications of the emerging political dynamics.

Omipidan suggested that those promoting the current arrangement could inadvertently create tension between the two leaders if the interests of the established APC structure were not adequately protected.

He argued that the party’s national leadership should not underestimate the feelings of members who might perceive the arrangement as favouring a few political actors at the expense of the wider party.

He maintained that the success of the president’s re-election campaign would depend partly on the ability of the APC to reconcile competing interests and ensure that its members remained actively involved in the mobilisation process.

Omipidan further argued that political strategies must reflect the peculiarities of the states in which they are deployed, noting that an approach that works in one part of the country might not necessarily produce the same results elsewhere.

He maintained that Osun’s political culture, voters’ expectations and prevailing interests should be considered in determining how the APC would pursue Tinubu’s re-election.

According to him, electoral mobilisation involves more than bringing prominent political figures together or announcing ambitious vote targets.

He argued that voters and party members are influenced by personal interests, political loyalties, emotions and expectations, which can shape their decisions at the polls.

Omipidan also drew on the Rational Choice Theory associated with economist and philosopher Adam Smith to explain how personal interests could influence voting decisions.

He said his earlier work applying the theory to electoral behaviour showed that voters’ decisions were influenced not only by candidates’ identities or party affiliations but also by their assessment of personal interests and potential benefits.

According to him, voters often consider available alternatives before deciding which candidate or political platform they believe will best serve their interests.

He argued that the theory offered a useful framework for understanding why political arrangements that appeared advantageous to party leaders might not automatically translate into widespread support among party members or voters.

He, therefore, called for greater engagement with stakeholders in Osun State to address concerns surrounding the emerging campaign arrangement before they developed into deeper divisions.

According to him, the APC needs to strengthen its structures in the state, address the concerns of aggrieved members and ensure that its campaign arrangements encourage rather than discourage grassroots participation.

World.title: IG Seeks Stronger Intelligence Gathering to Prevent Attacks on Schools
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare



The Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Rilwan Disu, yesterday called for stronger intelligence gathering, early-warning systems, and improved collaboration between schools and security agencies to prevent attacks on educational institutions across the country.

He stated that sustainable school protection requires a shift from reactive responses to preventive measures, stressing that safeguarding schools must be treated as a national security priority rather than the sole responsibility of school administrators or security agencies.

Disu also called for stronger police-community partnerships, improved emergency preparedness, and effective information-sharing among government, school authorities, parents, community leaders, and other stakeholders to address threats to educational institutions.

The IGP made the call while delivering the keynote address at the 7th annual summit of the Education Writers’ Association of Nigeria (EWAN) held in Lagos with the theme: ‘Schools Under Threat: From Reactive Responses to Sustainable Protection’.

Disu, who was represented by the Lagos State Commissioner of Police, Tijani Fatai, said the consequences of insecurity in schools extended beyond victims of attacks to include heightened anxiety among families, loss of public confidence, disruption of academic activities and the denial of educational opportunities to children.

According to him, a society cannot achieve its full potential when insecurity prevents children from accessing education or discourages teachers from performing their duties in safe and supportive environments.

“School safety must therefore be understood not merely as the responsibility of school administrators or security agencies, but as a national security priority and a collective obligation,” he said.

He noted that although immediate responses to security incidents, including rescuing victims, apprehending offenders and restoring safety, remained essential, greater attention must be given to identifying vulnerabilities and preventing the recurrence of attacks.

The police boss said the police would continue to strengthen intelligence-led operations, improve threat assessment and encourage the prompt reporting of credible security concerns.

The IGP urged school administrators, teachers, parents, students and community members to report suspicious developments through appropriate channels, adding that such information must be professionally assessed and acted upon where necessary.

He also emphasised the importance of trust between security agencies and communities, noting that effective partnerships depended on professional conduct, accountability and public confidence.

On emergency preparedness, Disu called on schools to establish appropriate safety arrangements and procedures that reflected their locations, sizes and levels of vulnerability.

He urged EWAN to sustain the conversation beyond the summit by developing practical recommendations, strengthening professional networks and maintaining engagement with institutions responsible for education and security.

“The future of our nation depends, in no small measure, on the opportunities we create for our children today. Protecting those opportunities is a responsibility we must all take seriously,” he said.

In his remarks, the Chairman of the occasion and former Vice-Chancellor, University of Lagos, Prof. Oluwatoyin Ogundipe, called for a unified national framework for school safety, urging federal, state and local governments to strengthen early-warning systems, improve security coordination and prioritise preventive measures to protect schools against attacks.

He said Nigeria must move beyond reactive responses to school attacks, including abductions of learners and teachers, to sustainable protection strategies that prevent threats, mitigate their impact and ensure continuity of education during crises.

Ogundipe, who is the chairman of the Governing Board of the National Universities Commission (NUC), said the recurring attacks on educational institutions in some parts of the country were not isolated incidents but a pattern threatening national development, disrupting learning and leaving affected communities traumatised.

According to him, protecting schools requires more than deploying security personnel after an attack, condemning incidents or providing temporary relief to affected communities.

“For too long, our responses have been largely reactive, mobilising security after an incident, issuing statements of condemnation, and providing temporary relief to affected communities. While these actions are necessary, they are not sufficient,” Ogundipe, who was represented by the Dean of Faculty of Education, Prof. Joseph Awoyinfa, stated

He urged stakeholders to build systems capable of identifying and addressing security threats before they escalate, stressing that effective school protection requires collaboration among security agencies, local communities, school authorities and the media.

He said journalists have a critical role to play in identifying emerging risks, amplifying community concerns, investigating security gaps and ensuring that vulnerabilities are addressed before they result in tragedies.

He also identified insecurity, weak governance in remote areas and socio-economic pressures as some of the underlying factors that made schools vulnerable to attacks.

Ogundipe advocated sustained investment in school infrastructure, surveillance systems, safe transportation and secure boarding facilities, with greater attention given to rural schools and institutions in conflict-prone areas.

Earlier in his remarks, the Chairman of the Education Writers’ Association of Nigeria (EWAN), Mojeed Alabi, urged journalists to intensify investigative and accountability reporting on school safety, warning that persistent attacks on educational institutions threaten the future of Nigerian children and national development.

Alabi said journalists must move beyond reporting school attacks after they occur to investigating security vulnerabilities, scrutinising funds allocated for school protection and tracking the implementation of government policies aimed at preventing attacks.

He said the protection of schools required coordinated action by government, security agencies, education authorities, communities and the media, stressing that journalism remained essential to exposing security lapses and holding public officials accountable.

“Children are not safe until every school is safe,” he said, adding that no parent should have to choose between a child’s education and safety, while no teacher should have to work under the threat of abduction

Alabi recalled the 2014 abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok, Borno State, and the subsequent Dapchi abduction, alongside other attacks on educational institutions, as evidence that insecurity in schools remained a persistent national challenge.

World.title: Shoga: Tinubu’s Revenue Reforms Creating Greater Fiscal Breathing Space
World.content:
Director-General of City Boy Movement, Hon. Oluwatosin Shoga, in this interview, defends President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, saying his government is correcting several years of structural distortions and laying a solid foundation for Nigeria’s emergence as a $1 trillion economy. He also speaks about Nigeria’s growing foreign reserves, proposed Gateway Deep Seaport and increased revenues to state and local governments. Folalumi Alaran brings excerpts.

States and local governments are now receiving higher allocations. What should Nigerians expect from them?

This is an important aspect of President Bola Tinubu’s reforms that deserves greater attention. By July 2026, monthly federation revenues available for distribution had risen to around N3 trillion. That means more resources are available to states and local governments for infrastructure and public services.

Governors and council chairmen must therefore take responsibility for delivering visible improvements in schools, healthcare, rural roads, water supply and agricultural development. It would be unfair to attribute every difficulty in local communities exclusively to the President when subnational governments now have greater resources and constitutional responsibilities.

President Tinubu is creating additional fiscal opportunities. States and local governments must demonstrate what they are doing with them. Citizens deserve accountability at every level.

How can the administration ensure that development reaches every geopolitical zone?

President Tinubu’s vision must be understood as a national development agenda. Every zone possesses economic advantages. The North-Central has agriculture, minerals and logistics; the North-East has livestock, agriculture and cross-border commerce; while the North-West has textiles, leather and food processing.

The South-East possesses formidable entrepreneurial and manufacturing capacity. The South-South offers petroleum, gas, petrochemicals and maritime industries, while the South-West remains strong in finance, manufacturing, technology and aviation.

The administration’s challenge is connecting these strengths through transportation, electricity, industrial infrastructure and digital development. A genuinely prosperous Nigeria cannot leave any geopolitical zone behind.

You are enthusiastic about President Tinubu’s economic achievements, yet millions of Nigerians are struggling. How do you reconcile this?

We must be fair to President Tinubu and honest about the condition of the economy he inherited. Nobody disputes that Nigerians have experienced hardship. Fuel prices increased, transportation became more expensive, food prices rose and household purchasing power suffered.

But the fundamental question is whether Nigeria could have continued indefinitely with the economic arrangements that created those problems.

President Tinubu inherited an economy burdened by unsustainable fuel subsidies, distorted foreign-exchange arrangements, weak government revenues, enormous debt-servicing obligations and infrastructure deficiencies. These were not problems created overnight, and they could not be solved through political convenience. What distinguishes President Tinubu is his willingness to confront challenges that had been postponed for years. Leadership sometimes demands taking difficult decisions today to prevent a much bigger crisis tomorrow.

The encouraging development is that the reforms are beginning to produce measurable results. Our responsibility now is to ensure those gains translate into jobs, affordable transportation, stronger businesses and improved living conditions.

What concrete evidence supports your claim that the economy is recovering?

The figures are increasingly speaking for themselves. Nigeria’s real Gross Domestic Product grew by 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 4.23 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025. That represents progress in an economy undergoing substantial structural adjustment.

We are seeing improvements in revenue mobilisation, foreign reserves, domestic refining and investment opportunities. Critics should acknowledge that these developments are occurring because the administration chose reform over the temporary comfort of maintaining an unsustainable system.

Of course, GDP growth alone is insufficient. But you cannot create sustainable prosperity without first building a productive and stable economy. President Tinubu is laying that foundation, and the next task is translating growth into employment, industrial expansion and stronger purchasing power.

Why does the Dangote Refinery feature so prominently in your assessment?

Because it illustrates the industrial transformation Nigeria desperately needs. For decades, we produced crude oil, exported it and spent enormous foreign exchange importing refined petroleum products. That was an economic contradiction which deprived Nigeria of industrial opportunities and employment. Today, the Dangote Petroleum Refinery is changing that narrative.

Seaborne petroleum-product shipments from Nigeria averaged approximately 561,000 barrels daily in the second quarter of 2026, with about 350,000 barrels going into exports. Consider what that means for a country previously heavily dependent on imported petroleum products. Beyond refining, the opportunities extend to shipping, storage, engineering, petrochemicals, transportation, logistics and thousands of associated businesses.

President Tinubu’s vision of economic diversification is about creating an environment where Nigeria increasingly processes what it produces and exports finished products rather than raw materials. That is how serious economies develop.

But Dangote Refinery is a private investment. Why should the administration receive credit?

Nobody is suggesting that government built or financed the refinery. Credit belongs to the entrepreneur who conceived and invested in it. However, no major industrial enterprise operates outside the policy environment created by government.

Crude supply arrangements, foreign-exchange policy, the naira-for-crude framework, regulatory decisions and infrastructure support all matter.

President Tinubu understands that government does not have to own every factory to drive industrialisation. Its responsibility is to create conditions that encourage investors to commit capital, expand production and generate employment. That partnership between government and private enterprise is precisely what Nigeria requires.

You have also highlighted the proposed Gateway Deep Seaport in Ogun State. Why is it particularly important?

Because it demonstrates the enormous investment opportunities that can emerge when government policies encourage productive partnerships. In September, Ogun State signed agreements with DP World for the proposed Gateway Deep Seaport and Blue Marine Special Economic Zone. The envisaged investment exceeds $7 billion, including a 10,000-hectare economic zone designed to accommodate manufacturing, logistics and export-oriented industries.

The proposed port is expected to have approximately four kilometres of berth and an 18-metre draft, with projections of more than 50,000 direct jobs at full development. These are substantial economic opportunities.

What President Tinubu’s administration is encouraging is a development model in which federal and state governments cooperate with credible international investors to expand Nigeria’s productive capacity. Of course, agreements must translate into construction and completed infrastructure. That is the next important responsibility.

There is also a separate Dangote-backed proposal around Olokola. How do the projects relate?

Publicly available information indicates that Dangote Industries is pursuing a proposed deep seaport and industrial development covering more than 10,000 hectares within the Olokola Free Trade Zone corridor. There is also the Gateway project involving Ogun State and DP World.

Whether these eventually become separate facilities or components of an integrated maritime development remains to be established. But look at the bigger picture. Ogun is already one of Nigeria’s strongest manufacturing centres. Providing modern maritime infrastructure along that coastline could fundamentally strengthen its industrial competitiveness. That is the kind of investment-led transformation President Tinubu wants across Nigeria.

How would a modern deep seaport benefit the national economy?

A seaport is not merely a place where vessels discharge cargo. It is an engine of economic development. Major ports attract industries, warehouses, logistics companies, financial institutions, shipping businesses and commercial activities.

Ogun already hosts significant investments in cement, pharmaceuticals, steel, food processing, packaging and consumer products. Many of those manufacturers currently depend on Lagos ports.

Modern maritime facilities in Ogun could reduce logistics costs, improve access to production inputs, expand exports and relieve pressure on Apapa and Tin Can ports. The important point is that President Tinubu’s economic agenda recognises infrastructure as a catalyst for production, competitiveness and employment. Nigeria cannot become an industrial powerhouse while manufacturers struggle with avoidable logistics bottlenecks.

How does the proposed maritime corridor connect with the administration’s $1 trillion economy ambition?

President Tinubu’s $1 trillion economy ambition is not merely a political slogan. It represents a vision of a more productive, diversified and competitive Nigeria. But such an economy cannot emerge without reliable infrastructure. We need modern ports, railways, roads, electricity, industrial estates and efficient financial systems.

Imagine Nigerian manufacturers exporting directly through modern maritime facilities, agricultural products from northern states reaching international markets and solid minerals being processed locally before export. That is how value is created.

The Gateway Inland Dry Port at Kajola, proposed Ijebu-Ode Inland Dry Port, Lagos-Ibadan railway, Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and Gateway International Agro-Cargo Airport could become important elements of an integrated logistics network. The administration’s ambition must be supported by this kind of productive infrastructure.

What difference would these investments make to agriculture and farmers outside Ogun State?

This is where the wider economic benefits become obvious. Nigeria produces cocoa, sesame, cashew, rubber, fruits and vegetables with substantial international demand. But inadequate storage, processing facilities, transportation and export infrastructure frequently limit farmers’ earnings.

Modern ports connected to warehouses, cold-storage facilities, processing centres and efficient transportation networks can open international markets to agricultural businesses. More importantly, we must stop exporting so much of our agricultural wealth in raw form. Why export raw cocoa or cashew when processing them locally creates additional jobs and income?

President Tinubu’s economic diversification agenda offers an opportunity to connect agriculture with manufacturing and international trade. That is how farmers across different geopolitical zones can participate in national prosperity.

Nigeria’s foreign reserves have reportedly exceeded $54 billion. Why is that significant?

It is one of the encouraging indicators of the administration’s economic management. External reserves exceeding $54 billion provide greater protection against international shocks, strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to meet external obligations and can improve investor confidence.

Stronger reserves also support efforts to achieve greater foreign-exchange stability. We should remember the difficult foreign-exchange conditions President Tinubu inherited. The administration has taken difficult decisions to address those distortions, and improving reserve levels are an encouraging development.

Naturally, the ordinary Nigerian wants to see a more stable naira, predictable prices and reduced business costs. That is precisely why these reforms must be sustained until macroeconomic improvements produce broader benefits.

What about Nigeria’s debt burden and the substantial cost of debt servicing?

Nobody is claiming that Nigeria’s debt challenges have disappeared. But we must recognise that stronger government revenues have improved the country’s fiscal position relative to the extremely difficult circumstances inherited by this administration. President Tinubu’s revenue reforms are creating greater fiscal breathing space.

The responsibility now is to sustain fiscal discipline and ensure borrowing increasingly supports productive investments. Nigeria needs resources for electricity, roads, education, healthcare, security and agriculture. The solution is not to abandon reforms but to consolidate revenue improvements, strengthen accountability and invest more strategically.

Critics argue that GDP growth, reserves and investment announcements mean little when Nigerians struggle to afford food. What is your take on this?

I understand those concerns, but we must distinguish between the hardship associated with correcting longstanding economic distortions and the long-term benefits of reform. President Tinubu did not create Nigeria’s structural economic weaknesses. He inherited them and demonstrated the courage to confront them.

The easy political option would have been to postpone difficult decisions and allow the problems to deepen. Instead, he chose a path intended to secure Nigeria’s economic future. We recognise that families need affordable food, young people need employment, businesses need electricity and farmers need access to markets.

That is why the reforms must continue to focus on food security, transportation costs, industrial expansion and job creation.

The President’s $1 trillion ambition is achievable, but its real value will be measured by improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians.

As Director-General of the City Boy Movement, why do you believe Nigerians should support the continuation of these reforms?

Because sustainable economic transformation requires consistency and political courage. President Tinubu has demonstrated his willingness to take difficult decisions in the national interest, even when those decisions carry immediate political costs.

At the City Boy Movement, we believe Nigeria must not return to the cycle of postponing essential reforms because they are politically uncomfortable. We support the President because we believe his economic programme offers a foundation for long-term stability, industrialisation and prosperity.

That does not mean denying hardship or suggesting that every challenge has been resolved. It means recognising the progress already made and supporting the continued implementation of policies capable of producing enduring results. The sacrifices Nigerians have made must not be wasted.

What concerns do you have about the implementation of major infrastructure projects?

Our support for these investments is accompanied by a strong expectation of delivery. Projects such as the Gateway Deep Seaport require transparent financing, environmental safeguards, proper engagement with host communities and effective road and rail connectivity.

Signing agreements is an important first step, but Nigerians ultimately want completed infrastructure. President Tinubu’s development vision must be matched by disciplined implementation from every participating institution. That responsibility extends to federal agencies, state governments and private investors.

What do you consider the greatest challenge facing President Tinubu now?

Consolidating the reforms and translating economic recovery into prosperity that Nigerians can experience. The President has taken courageous steps to address longstanding weaknesses. The task now is ensuring that improving indicators produce jobs, stronger businesses, food security and better public services.

Higher revenues must translate into infrastructure. Stronger reserves must support currency stability. Domestic refining must strengthen energy security, while modern ports must expand manufacturing and exports. Nigeria has the resources, population, entrepreneurial capacity and geographical advantages to become a $1 trillion economy. What we need is policy continuity, implementation, accountability and national commitment.

At the City Boy Movement, we believe President Tinubu has demonstrated the leadership and determination required to move Nigeria towards that ambition. The reforms are laying the foundation. The next phase must consolidate the gains and deliver prosperity. That is why we believe the President deserves the opportunity to complete the transformation he has begun.

World.title: Tinubu: I’m Ready to Renew Pact With Nigerians, Inaugurates 2027 Campaign Council
World.content:
• Says governance must not be grounded, as Nigeria needs fixing

•Shettima throws jabs at Atiku, Obi, says nation can’t be governed with borrowed statistics

• Yari: campaign for Tinubu will be performance driven

•Wike to APC Govs: don’t claim Tinubu’s victory if you failed to deliver your states

• Yilwatda: Tinubu’s reforms deserve continuity

•Rainbow coalition on course for Tinubu’s 2027 victory, senate maintains

• Sani tasks appointees on president’s election

•Atiku: inauguration of Tinubu’s campaign council in Aso Rock abuse of public office

• APC’s campaign council a Nebuchadnezzar coalition heading for the rocks, says MDPCO

•Soludo, Adeleke optimistic about Tinubu’s victory

Deji Elumoye, Chuks Okocha, Emmanuel Addeh, Adedayo Akinwale, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja and John Shiklam in Kaduna





President Bola Tinubu, yesterday, declares his readiness to renew covenant with Nigerians ahead of the official launch of his second term campaign, billed to kick off in Kaduna on October 24.

The president, who foreclosed the possibility of being present at all the campaign grounds nationwide, said the pressing needs of the country required his attention, stressing that governance must continue side-by-side electioneering.

Speaking while inaugurating the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council for the 2027 poll, he said while the council would lead the party’s mobilisation across the states and local government areas, he would make time to address Nigerians directly without accompanying the campaign to every location.

Tinubu said he agreed with party leaders, especially Governor Hope Uzodinma of Imo State, who advised him not to allow campaign activities to distract him from official duties.

Vice President Kashim Shettima, speaking at the occasion, threw jabs at former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, Peter Obi.

Shettima questioned both candidates’ economic interventions and their readiness to lead Nigeria.

He said the country’s size, population, and economic realities made it unsuitable for policies copied from other countries without proper adaptation to local realities.

In his acceptance speech, Director-General of APC Presidential Campaign Council (APC-PCC), Senator Abdulaziz Yari, said Tinubu’s achievements since May 2023 and his future plans would form the basis of the party’s campaign for the January 16, 2027 presidential poll.

Yari said the campaign would focus on communicating the administration’s record to Nigerians, particularly its impact on ordinary citizens, and its infrastructure projects.

Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, who is also a member of the APC campaign council, told coordinators of Tinubu’s 2027 re-election campaign not to claim victory if they failed to deliver their respective states.

Wike, though a member of Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), said every campaign official must be held accountable for their electoral performance.

Relatedly, the Senate, yesterday, declared that the rainbow coalition incorporated into the APC-PCC for Tinubu’s re-election in 2027 was on course, describing the initiative as an unprecedented political alliance aimed at promoting national unity and inclusive governance.

President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, and Senate Leader, Opeyemi Bamidele, made the remarks yesterday at plenary.

However, Atiku, yesterday, condemned the inauguration of Tinubu’s campaign council inside the Presidential Villa, Abuja, describing it as an abuse of public office and a troubling breach of public trust.

He said this in a statement by Director of Strategic Communication of African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC), Phrank Shaibu.

Nonetheless, Tinubu, at the inauguration of the APC-PCC in Abuja, said, “As I stand before you with a heart full of gratitude and spirit full of resolve, it is my honour to inaugurate the presidential campaign council of the All Progressives Congress for the 2027 General Election.

“I thank all of you for the last election, but no one gets credit for an incomplete assignment until you deliver the next election, until you deliver your electoral wards, until you deliver the votes.”

Tinubu acknowledged Uzodinma’s advice not to let the rigours of the election campaign distract him from his responsibilities of governance, said, “I hear you. I am in full agreement with your decision. Nigeria needs more attention now than ever before. The responsibility of this office does not pause.”

Uzodimma, in his speech, had assured the president that the governors and other party leaders would do their best to deliver the right message to Nigerians during the campaign.

On why he would not travel to every campaign ground, the president said the government had pressing financial obligations and needed to attract investors to support the country’s future.

According to him, “The job must go on. We have bills to pay. The American creditors cannot wait. We want those investors to come in, be here to stay, to invest for the future of our children.

“However, I will still make time to speak directly with Nigerians even as you lead the campaign in the states and local government areas.”

He charged the campaign council to take the party’s record, vision and agenda to Nigerians nationwide up to the ward level.

“Let the word go out from this hall to every corner of our nation. The APC is ready,” Tinubu said, adding that APC is renewing its commitment to Nigerians and the responsibilities entrusted to it as the governing party.

The president stated, “We have gathered not merely to inaugurate a council. We have gathered to renew a covenant, a covenant with the Nigerian people and the historic responsibility they have thrust to us as Nigeria’s governing party. We promise we will not let them down.”

He also warned all the 31 APC governors, as well as federal lawmakers and other party leaders against taking previous electoral efforts for granted, insisting that their performance in the 2027 election would determine whether they have fulfilled their assignment.

He stated, “No one gets credit for an incomplete assignment. So until you deliver the next election, until you deliver your wards, until you deliver the votes, before we can say thank you.”

Tinubu pledged to support legislative efforts to increase women’s representation in the National Assembly and state-level legislatures, describing women as key mobilisers and voters.

He said, “Women are the greatest mobilisers and voters. And from this hall, I assure you, the sponsorship of the bill.”

He urged women to work towards securing greater representation, while promising to support efforts to increase their numbers at both national and sub-national levels.

The president said, “The women deserve seats. Go and work for it, come to fruition. We will increase the number of women’s representation at both National Assembly and sub-national level. I assure you that.”

Tinubu, while commenting on security, gave an assurance that state police would become a reality, signalling his support for the proposed restructuring of policing in the country.

“On security, state police will be a reality,” he declared.

The president lauded the party leadership for conducting its congresses and strengthening its structures from the ward to the national level, describing APC as increasingly united.

He charged party members to remain determined in their efforts to build the country, recalling measures taken during his tenure as Lagos State governor to address the threat of flooding from the Atlantic Ocean.

“There is a limit, but there is no limit in daring. We dared the Atlantic Ocean, and the result is the Atlantic City in Lagos,” he said.

He commended Lagos State Governor Babajide Samwo-Olu and his Deputy, Obafemi Hamzat, for their contributions to the success he recorded during his term as governor of the state, especially in taming the encroachment by the Atlantic Ocean.

Speaking at the inauguration, Shettima threw political jabs at Atiku and Obi, questioning their economic interventions and readiness to lead Nigeria ahead of next year’s general election.

Criticising Obi’s reliance on foreign economic comparisons, Shettima said, “A country of over 250 million people cannot be governed through borrowed statistics and economic prescriptions detached from its peculiarities.”

According to him, policies that worked in Bangladesh could not simply be replicated in Nigeria without considering differences in population, economic structures, institutions and national circumstances.

He stated, “I respect Peter Obi. But he has gone beyond his mastery of philosophy to make an august claim about winning the 2023 presidential election without adducing a shred of evidence to buttress his assertion.

“Obi is the master of bogus statistics and incoherent economic prescriptions.”

Shettima compared the challenge of applying foreign policies to Nigeria to transferring a cloth meant for a smaller body onto a much bigger one.

He also faulted Atiku, who had several times in the past sought the presidency, saying political ambition must be matched by character, discipline and an understanding of the responsibilities attached to public office.

He was, however, quick to add that political opponents should be treated with respect, as they were fellow Nigerians and not enemies.

Shettima said, “For the rest of the duration of this campaign, we’ll discuss ideas, we’ll discuss policies, but we’ll treat all our opponents with respect and dignity. They are not our enemies. They are our brothers. They are our countrymen. They are our leaders.”

Shettima told the party leaders not to insult opponents in the course of the campaign, urging them, instead, to respond to criticism with evidence and reason.

He said, “We have the capacity to respond to all sorts of innuendos and outright lies that our political opponents are taking on. But we won’t fall into their traps. We’ll give them facts. We’ll give them statistics. We argue with reason, not with sentiments, not with exaggerated truth or fabricated lies.”

The vice president said the Tinubu administration over three years ago inherited an economy facing severe fiscal pressures and it had taken difficult decisions, including removing the petrol subsidy and addressing distortions in the foreign exchange market.

He explained that the reforms were necessary to address longstanding economic challenges, while acknowledging the responsibility to ensure that their benefits reached Nigerians.

“The next obligation is to turn these gains into jobs, meaningful earnings and meaningful planning,” Shettima stated, maintaining that the administration’s priority should be to protect the reforms, improve their implementation, and ensure that public resources deliver results for households and businesses.

He said, “We must protect the reforms, improve their execution, and carry their benefits from the treasury to the household.”

He said Tinubu deserved a second term because the government’s reform programme had gained momentum, which the country could not afford to squander.

“President Tinubu deserves a second term because the work has acquired momentum that Nigeria cannot afford to squander,” Shettima said.

Yari said Tinubu’s achievements in office and his future plans for the country would form the basis of the party’s 2027 campaign.

He stated, “As we start going around to royal fathers and clerics, this is the message I have been sending today: our campaign is going to be centred on what you have done and what you are going to do in the future.”

Yari commended the president for his achievements in infrastructure development and improving the lives of ordinary Nigerians, adding that his record has made the campaign team’s assignment easier.

He said, “You have touched the life of the ordinary man. You have been there in infrastructure, building the iron road as if the money is nothing.”

The former two-time governor of Zamfara State assured the president that members of the campaign council would work together to secure his re-election, describing the assignment as a collective responsibility.

“We are going to do it all honestly with the trust and, by God’s grace, we are going to deliver,” Yari said.

Wike, for his part, said securing a national victory for Tinubu would not excuse campaign coordinators who failed to mobilise sufficient votes in their assigned territories. He stressed that appointments and positions in the campaign council must translate into tangible electoral results.

The FCT minister said, “If you don’t deliver your state and the president wins, don’t say we have won. It is not a question of I am chairman of this, I am secretary of this, I am a member of this.”

The minister, who is the coordinator of Tinubu’s campaign in Rivers State and the FCT, said campaign officials must take personal responsibility for delivering their areas rather than rely on the overall outcome of the presidential election.

He illustrated the point with Lagos State, recalling a conversation with the Chief of Staff to the President.

“If you don’t win in Lagos, don’t say we have won,” Wike said.

The minister expressed confidence in his own assignment, saying Rivers and the FCT would deliver massive votes for Tinubu in the January 2027 presidential election.

Wike stated, “Simple, there is not too much work for me. It’s Rivers and FCT, and let me say and pledge, by the grace of God, Rivers and FCT will vote massively for Bola Tinubu. That is my job.

“Rivers and FCT, it is taken. I challenge any area council that can say they don’t see the presence of Mr President.

“For me, as an opposition party member, as the leader of the Peoples Democratic Party, there are not two leaders of the PDP. I’m the leader of the PDP, so I speak on behalf of the Peoples Democratic Party.”

Defending his support for Tinubu, Wike said being an opposition party member should not prevent politicians from acknowledging what they consider positive actions by the ruling party.

He said, “Democracy allows the opposition to be there to look at things that the ruling party has not concentrated on and say these are the issues you are not tackling. Democracy is not that if the ruling party is doing well, because you are in opposition, you say they are not doing well. That is not democracy.”

Anambra State Governor Charles Soludo and his Osun State counterpart, Ademola Adeleke, also expressed optimism about Tinubu’s re-election.

Soludo, a member and national leader of the opposition All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), disclosed that his party would campaign round the clock for Tinubu’s second term.

He told the president, “Count on us, the All Progressives Grand Alliance, 24/7. We are with you because we believe.”

The former Governor of Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) declared that the president’s return for a second term was already settled in the minds of his supporters.

He said, “We are talking about when you get into the second term. It is the acceleration in the transformation process — from stability and reform to shared prosperity.”

Soludo described Tinubu as a symbol of “the unity of Nigeria, the security of Nigeria and the shared prosperity of Nigeria”, saying those values informed APGA’s decision to back him.

He also defended the government’s economic reforms, acknowledging their difficulty but insisting they were necessary.

“The path you have chosen, that you have had the courage to take, is the difficult but necessary path,” he said.

Adeleke also declared that no one could stop the second term movement of Tinubu.

Adeleke of the opposition Accord Party said the president would emerge victorious during the January poll.

He stated, “I can see the victory in 2027. Nobody can stop this movement. I am going to lead. We will sing and dance all the way back to Aso Rock. Four years isn’t enough, that’s why I am here to throw my weight.

“Let us rise from all nooks and crannies to ensure his victory. Let us pray for Mr President and, by the grace of God, we shall be there.”

Yilwatda: Tinubu’s Reforms Deserve Continuity

APC National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, said the various reforms introduced by the Tinubu administration deserved continuity.

Yilwatda added that under Tinubu, the government had pursued major economic reforms that addressed longstanding structural challenges and established a stronger foundation for sustainable growth.

He spoke yesterday in Abuja during the inauguration of the Presidential Campaign Council of the party ahead of the 2027 general election.

He stressed that the inauguration marked the beginning of a coordinated and credible campaign to secure the re-election of Tinubu.

Yilwatda stated that the presence of party leaders reflected shared commitment and confidence in the party’s collective capacity to present a compelling vision for Nigeria’s future.

He charged the council to organise effectively, communicate the achievements and policies of the administration, and engage Nigerians with confidence.

Yilwatda stated, “Today, we begin an important assignment of bringing together the strength of our national structures, the experience of our leaders and the energy of our members to build a coordinated and credible campaign.

“We have made so much progress but must acknowledge where we have challenges while explaining the objectives, progress and continuing work of the administration.”

The chairman stated that the party must communicate its critical infrastructure investments in roads, power, gas projects, railways, ports, agricultural infrastructure, and digital connectivity, and explain how they translated into practical improvements in daily lives.

“This is the substance of our campaign: a clear record, an honest assessment of the challenges and a credible vision for the future,” he said.

Yilwatda assured party members at all levels that they mattered and that the party’s strength depended on their effectiveness.

He called for direction, coordination and clear responsibilities among governors, legislators and campaign officials.

Senate: Rainbow Coalition on Course for Tinubu’s 2027 Victory

Senate said the rainbow coalition incorporated into the APC Presidential Campaign Council was on course to deliver victory. It said the initiative was an unprecedented political alliance aimed at promoting national unity and inclusive governance.

The declaration came as the upper chamber called on the federal government to prioritise the completion of abandoned and ongoing road projects across the country before embarking on new ones.

It warned that the continued deterioration of critical highways was endangering lives, disrupting economic activities, and imposing additional hardship on Nigerians.

Akpabio and Bamidele made the remarks yesterday during plenary, shortly before the chamber adjourned proceedings to enable senators attending the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council at the Presidential Villa participate in the event.

Bamidele, who sought the indulgence of his colleagues to make what he described as a historic observation before moving the motion for adjournment, said the composition of the campaign council demonstrated the emergence of a broad political alliance cutting across party lines.

He cited the involvement of Soludo of APGA; Adeleke of Accord Party; Wike of PDP; and Senator Ibrahim Dankwambo of Gombe North as coordinators of different segments of the campaign council.

The senate leader said the arrangement represented an opportunity to deepen democratic engagement and promote a political campaign focused on ideas rather than partisan divisions.

He stated, “My point, Mr. President, is that in this country, in the best interests of the Nigerian people, a rainbow coalition, indeed, is on the move and very much on course.

“I think it is something that should not go unnoticed. We will proceed out of this chamber as members of the ruling party, accompanied by our colleagues, to go to the presidential campaign council. We look forward to a campaign that will really celebrate ideas and celebrate our democracy. I really congratulate you, Mr. President.”

Responding, Akpabio described the coalition as historic, stating that its composition reflects an effort to bring political interests together under a common platform ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

He said the arrangement went beyond infrastructure development, revenue allocation, and economic reforms to embrace national cohesion and unity of purpose.

Akpabio stated, “Let me also note, like you said, that this is historic and this is uncommon. This has never happened in the history of our democracy since 1999, that a sitting president will constitute his presidential campaign council with almost all the parties in Nigeria inclusive.

“So, this is not just an inclusive government in terms of infrastructure; it’s not just an inclusive government in terms of revenue allocation and allotments; it’s not just an inclusive government in terms of giant strides in reform. It’s also an inclusive government in terms of unity, unity of purpose in democracy.”

He said the composition of the campaign council suggested that Tinubu’s second-term agenda would place considerable emphasis on political cooperation.

The senate president said, “The coalition is evidence of the fact that President Tinubu’s second term is going to be a unity government, just like his campaign council is a unity campaign council made of almost all the political parties in the country.”

The political discussions came against the backdrop of mounting concerns over the condition of federal roads, with Senate urging the federal government to concentrate resources on completing existing projects while limiting new construction to essential interventions, including roads needed to reconnect communities cut off by flooding and provide access to underserved areas.

The resolution followed the adoption of a motion sponsored by Senator Tony Nwoye on the deplorable condition of the Ogbaru-Ndoni-Rivers Federal Highway, a strategic transport corridor linking communities in Anambra State to Ndoni in Rivers State.

Senate urged the Federal Roads Maintenance Agency (FERMA), South-East Development Commission, and the Federal Ministry of Works to undertake emergency palliative repairs on failed sections of the highway pending comprehensive rehabilitation and reconstruction.

It also called on the Ministry of Works to commence the immediate rehabilitation and reconstruction of the Ogbaru-Iyiowa-Odekpe-Atani-Ogwuikpele-Ndoni Federal Highway through a special intervention programme or another appropriate funding arrangement.

The lawmakers mandated Senate Committee on Works to inspect the highway, engage relevant stakeholders, and report back within four weeks. The committees on works and appropriations were also directed to ensure adequate budgetary provision for the project.

Sani Tasks Appointees on Tinubu’s 2027

Kaduna State Governor, Uba Sani, tasked political appointees in the state and at the federal level to deepen grassroots engagement and work towards delivering a resounding victory for Tinubu in 2027.

Speaking at a strategic meeting with the appointees at Government House, Kaduna, Sani charged them to mobilise for a successful presidential campaign flag-off scheduled for Kaduna on October 24.

He urged the appointees to “strengthen coordination of political activities, towards the success of the All Progressives Congress(APC) in the coming elections.”

According to the governor, “President Bola Tinubu has demonstrated an unprecedented commitment to Kaduna State through transformative investments in infrastructure, education and economic development.

“Such extraordinary commitment deserves more than expressions of gratitude; it demands collective responsibility to consolidate these gains and sustain the momentum of development.

“We must translate our appreciation into decisive political action. I charge every federal appointee and stakeholder to close ranks, deepen grassroots engagement and work towards delivering a resounding landslide victory for President Tinubu in 2027.”

Sani said Tinubu’s support for the Kaduna Light Rail, Abuja–Kaduna–Kano Highway, Kaduna–Birnin Gwari Road, Kaduna–Kano Rail Project and investments in federal tertiary institutions underscored the president’s commitment to the development of Kaduna State.

He emphasised that sustained collaboration between federal appointees and the state government was critical in translating the investments into lasting economic opportunities, improved security and better living conditions for the people.

Atiku: Inauguration of Tinubu’s Campaign Council in Aso Rock Abuse of Public Office

Atiku, yesterday, condemned the inauguration of Tinubu’s Presidential Campaign Council inside the Presidential Villa, Abuja, and described it as an abuse of public office and a worrying violation of public trust.

He stated that the seat of government belonged to all Nigerians and should not be used to host partisan political activities, particularly when alternative venues were available in Abuja.

Atiku, in a statement by Director of Strategic Communication of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential campaign, Phrank Shaibu, said the size of the APC campaign structure further reflected a president more concerned about political endorsements than accounting for the difficulties Nigerians had endured under his administration.

The statement said, “The Presidential Villa belongs to the Nigerian people. It is not a campaign venue or the private property of any political party. Using it for an APC political event is a gross breach of public trust and a troubling abuse of public office.”

Atiku questioned why the president chose to inaugurate the council at night within the Villa rather than use a conventional event venue. He said the decision raised questions about the administration’s commitment to separating state institutions from party politics.

Atiku stated, “Abuja has no shortage of halls and public spaces large enough to host a campaign gathering. Why, then, did Bola Tinubu choose to inaugurate his campaign council at night, behind the gates of the Presidential Villa?

“Nigerians may draw their own conclusions. But a president confident in his record should be willing to face the public in daylight and ask for another mandate.

“Tinubu cannot expect Nigerians to renew a mandate built on a promise of renewed hope when, for millions, that promise has given way to hardship and disappointment.”

Atiku also described Tinubu’s expanded campaign council as a “crowded confession of fear”.

He accused the president of assembling hundreds of politicians to shield himself from public anger over worsening economic hardship and insecurity.

MDPCO: Tinubu’s Campaign Council a Nebuchadnezzar Coalition Heading for the Rocks

The Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) dismissed the APC-PCC as a “Nebuchadnezzar Coalition” on a collision course with the will of the Nigerian people.

In a statement by Richard Ihediuwa, the campaign’s director of communications and strategies, the organisation described APC’s presidential campaign council as a haven of internationally discredited and politically inconsistent characters and corrupt politicians intoxicated by the arrogance of power, imperial ambition, and the dangerous illusion that political influence could substitute for public trust and democratic legitimacy.

The Makinde/Daura campaign council said, ‘’This Nebuchadnezzar Coalition is headed for the rocks as it cannot whitewash the failures of the Tinubu administration, nor rewrite the painful realities confronting citizens.

“It cannot manufacture public acceptance through a parade of ‘political predators’ and power drunk elites, who are mistaking political dominance for public acceptance.

‘’With the high confidence that President Tinubu reposes in this alliance of failed governors, yes-along legislators, and discredited politicians some of whom are fleeing from corruption investigations; even as his administration presides over an unprecedented economic crisis, worsening insecurity and a devastating collapse of public confidence, we see in the APC Presidential Campaign Council imminent political humiliation.”

The campaign council added, ‘’History is replete with the humiliation of those who mistake transitory power for permanence while reinforcing their illusions by surrounding themselves with compensated loyalists and sycophantic, who do not command the loyalty or followership of the people, rather than confront stark reality of failures.’’

World.title: December holidays 2026: School closing dates and public holidays
World.content:
Take a look at the dates you need to note for December holidays 2026 from the day schools close to the public holidays.

WHEN DOES SCHOOL CLOSE?

Public schools across South Africa officially close on 9 December. Educators stay on until 11 December. This is the long December school holidays. So, schools only reopen on 12 January 2027. The 2027 school year opens on 13 January. Private schools may differ from these dates, it would be best to check dates with the school directly.

PUBLIC HOLIDAYS



Wednesday 16 December: Day of Reconciliation

Friday 25 December: Christmas Day

Saturday 26 December: Day of Goodwill

1 January: New Year’s Day

Please note: Day of Goodwill falls on a Saturday. South African law only moves a public holiday to Monday when it falls on a Sunday. So, there is no extra day off. There is also a “bonus” public holiday this year on 4 November.

The declaration follows the formal gazetting and proclamation of 4 November 2026 as the election date by Minister of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs Velenkosini Hlabisa in August 2026. Ramaphosa first announced the election date on 30 April 2026, at the Birchwood Hotel in Boksburg, during discussions at the Extended Presidential Coordinating Council meeting.

At the time, he stated that as the local government elections were due in 2026, the date “should be held on a Wednesday, which is the middle of the week,” settling on 4 November 2026.

PLANNING YOUR LEAVE AHEAD OF TIME

You could take Thursday 17 and Friday 18 December off to give you five days off from 16 to 20 December or you could take Monday 14 and Tuesday 15 off to extend your weekend from 12 December. Christmas Day is on Friday the 25th and this will give you a long weekend. 1 January also falls on a Friday so you will also have a long weekend without using an leave.

It would be advisable to book your leave days in advance. The first full week after schools close become peak period with busier roads, flights and coastal accomodation. Book flights, accomodations and anythign else in advance if you are able to.

World.title: Want to go to Cape Town this December? Here’s how much it costs to get there
World.content:
Planning a Cape Town trip this December? Here's how much it cost you to get there. Image: canva

Cape Town is one of South Africa’s biggest December destinations, but getting to the Mother City is becoming an increasingly expensive part of the festive-season holiday.

For travellers from Johannesburg and Durban, flying remains the quickest option, while driving could work out cheaper for families and groups sharing a car.

Current December 2026 fares show that travellers could pay more than R3 000 for a one-way flight, depending on where they are travelling from and which airline they choose.



Johannesburg to Cape Town

There are five airlines competing on the Johannesburg-Cape Town route: SAA, FlySafair, LIFT, CemAir and Airlink.

A live fare comparison for Friday, 18 December 2026 shows a significant spread between the cheapest and most expensive options.

Johannesburg to Cape Town flight prices

Airline One-way fare on 18 December SAA R2 489 CemAir R2 909 LIFT R2 949 FlySafair R2 989 Airlink R3 359

SAA is currently the cheapest of the five for this particular date, while Airlink is the most expensive at R3 359.

The prices were checked on 15 October and are live fares rather than historical averages, meaning they can change as seats are sold.

Another current fare search found a R2 489 SAA one-way fare on 11 December, showing that prices can vary even within the same month.

Durban to Cape Town

World.title: Throwback: How Durban’s deadly floods led to an extraordinary act of bravery
World.content:
A man is led to safety as the rising floodwaters hit Tin Town on the Springfield Flats in 1917.Image: South African History Online

On 28 October 1917, more than 400 market gardeners from Springfield Flats (Tin Town) in Durban drowned when the uMngeni River burst its banks after heavy rain.

Six fishermen, later known as the Padavatan Six, saved 176 people from drowning. Led by Mariemuthoo Padavatan, they made five trips into the raging river in an oar-driven banana boat.

Their rescue remains one of South Africa’s largest civilian acts of bravery.



Tin Town

By 1917, more than 2 500 people lived in Tin Town, many of them former Indian indentured labourers.

Residents built wood and iron houses and grew vegetables along the riverbanks, selling their produce around Durban.

On the night of the disaster, heavy rain and debris blocked the Railway and Connaught bridges.



When the Railway Bridge’s pillars cracked, a wall of water swept away homes, people and livestock.

Padavatan, then 30, was checking his boats at Addington Beach when workers alerted him to the flooding.

He assembled five volunteers: Gangan Padavatan, Sabapathy Periyasamy Govender, Rangasamy Naidoo, 16-year-old Kuppusamy Naidoo and T. Veloo.



Despite Inspector Alexander’s warning against attempting a rescue, the six launched Veloo’s banana boat.

The rescue that saved 176 lives in Durban

Padavatan secured a rope around his waist and the boat’s prow, while another crew controlled it from the riverbank.

Four men rowed while two pulled survivors from the water. They faced strong currents, floating debris and frightened residents clinging to rooftops.



The fishermen rescued 30 to 40 people per trip, including a one-month-old baby.

After five trips, authorities stopped further attempts as darkness approached.

Aftermath

More than 400 people reportedly died, while many farmers lost their homes and livelihoods.



The fishermen donated money collected in their honour to a flood relief fund.

On 8 December 1917, Durban honoured the Padavatan Six with gold medals. Mariemuthoo Padavatan also received a gold walking stick and a watch.

The M. Padavatan Primary School in Chatsworth later took his name in recognition of his bravery.
