World.title: WATCH: Fikile Mbalula nearly collapses after ANC win at ConCourt
World.content:
African National Congress (ANC) secretary-general Fikile Mbalula nearly collapsed as he was overcome by emotions after the Constitutional Court ruled in favour regarding the candidate list dispute for the 4 November local government elections.

In September, the Electoral Court ruled against the ANC, and the party approached the Constitutional Court which has since ruled in its favour on Thursday, 15 October.

FIKILE MBALULA OVERCOME BY EMOTIONS AFTER ANC COURT VICTORY

The South African previously reported that the Constitutional Court ruling, handed down on Thursday, 15 October, follows the ANC’s appeal against an Electoral Court judgment that upheld the IEC’s decision to exclude the candidates from the ballot.



The ANC approached the apex court after failing to complete the final submission of its candidate lists for six municipalities before the deadline.

Addressing journalists following the court victory, an emotional Mbalula shed a tear and nearly collapsed saying the Constitution has spoken and it has spoken for the people of this country.

“Let me begin with thanks because this was never the work of one office, I thank the President of the ANC for his leadership through a hard month and for insisting that at every turn this movement takes the lawful route and no other. I thank the national officials of the movement who carried this matter with patience, which was not easy,” he said.

ANC VS IEC | “The Constitution has spoken, and it has spoken for the people of this country,” says ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula, who is emotional and brought to tears following the party’s victory in the Constitutional Court. pic.twitter.com/2zYc7pXGtc — SABC News (@SABCNews) October 15, 2026

Fikile Mbalula was overcome by emotions and nearly collapsed before he could finish responding to questions posed by journalists and had to be helped out of the court room, “I’m not feeling well,” he said.

[WATCH] Fikile Mbalula is overwhelmed with emotion, almost collapsing during a media briefing after the Constitutional Court ruled in favour of the ANC. #Newzroom405 pic.twitter.com/g9PgU9jSB1  October 15, 2026

IEC ORDERED TO INCLUDE FORMER RULING PARTY’S CANDIDATES ON BALLOTS

On Thursday, Constitutional Court Justice Rammaka Mathopo said the IEC’s decision to reject the ANC’s candidate lists in the six municipalities had been set aside.

“The first respondent, which is the IEC, is directed to do all things necessary to include the party lists and ward candidate nominations mentioned in paragraph four of this order, and the lists and nominations onto the ballot papers and all other relevant processes for the purposes of the 4 November 2026 local elections,” he said.

The ruling means the IEC must take the necessary steps to include the affected ANC candidates in the electoral process ahead of the upcoming local government elections.

World.title: Transfer update: Struggling Kaizer Chiefs graduate to Siwelele FC
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs academy graduate Happy Mashiane is poised to sign for Siwelele FC after searching for a new club since June.

The Tembisa-born left-back, now 28, trained with Stellenbosch FC for several weeks in July. Unfortunately, coach Gavin Hunt decided against signing him.

SIWELELE FC KEEN TO SIGN DISCARDED KAIZER CHIEFS GRADUATE HAPPY MASHIANE

After Mashiane had trained with the Bloemfontein-based club since September, the club’s new coach, Godfrey Mosoetsa, has revealed he is working on signing Mashiane.



“He started during the FIFA break. He has been training very well,” Mosoetsa told journalists at the Carling Knockout Cup Last 16 launch on Wednesday.

“There are just a couple of things that need to be sorted out administratively, and then we will take it from there. You cannot deny the fact that he is a very good player.

“He’s got PSL experience; he played for Kaizer Chiefs while he was still young. So he has much to offer,” added Mosoetsa.

EARLY PROFESSIONAL CAREER

Mashiane started his journey at Tembisa Black Pirates before moving to the Mamelodi Sundowns Academy and Future Through Football Academy.

In 2015, he moved to Kaizer Chiefs’ Naturena where he soon played in the DStv Diski Challenge (DDC) in 2018. The arrival of Ernst Middendorp in December 2018 was followed by Mashiane’s promotion to the senior team in January 2019, aged 19.

Mashiane would become a key player during Amakhosi’s FIFA transfer ban years. As one of former coach Gavin Hunt’s favourites, he Infamously suffered a red card in Kaizer Chiefs’ CAF Champions League final against Al Ahly.



He joined Siwelele FC on loan in the 2025/26 season. Following the conclusion of his loan spell, Kaizer Chiefs parted ways with Mashiane after a 12-year spell.

World.title: Buying a car in South Africa for Zimbabwe: The costs to know
World.content:
Buying a car in South Africa for use in Zimbabwe. Image: Pexels

Buying a car in South Africa for use in Zimbabwe may appear attractive to motorists looking for a particular model.

However, there are some factors and costs to consider before purchasing a car.

Zimbabweans importing vehicles must account for customs duties, taxes, transport, documentation and registration costs before putting their cars on the road.



Zimbabwe car imports: The 10-year rule

The Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA) prohibits the importation of second-hand vehicles that are 10 years old or older, subject to specific exemptions.

Under Statutory Instrument 54 of 2024, the restriction applies from the date of manufacture.

ZIMRA subsequently outlined exemptions for qualifying returning residents, diplomats, inherited vehicles and certain classic cars, among other categories.



Buyers should therefore confirm whether a vehicle qualifies for importation before paying a South African dealership or private seller.

ZIMRA duties and taxes add to the bill

Import duties and taxes can substantially increase the cost of buying a car in South Africa for use in Zimbabwe.

The amount payable depends on the vehicle’s classification, customs value, age and applicable tax rates.



ZIMRA also reserves the right to reassess a vehicle’s declared value if it does not reflect its bona fide open-market value.

This means buyers should not assume that the price stated on a sales invoice will automatically determine their final customs bill.

Importers should obtain a vehicle-specific assessment from ZIMRA or a qualified clearing agent before committing to a purchase.



Car transport and clearing costs from South Africa to Zimbabwe

Buyers must also budget for transporting the vehicle from South Africa to Zimbabwe, whether they drive it across the border or use a vehicle transporter.

ZIMRA lists several documents required when importing a vehicle, including the invoice or sale agreement, police clearance through the Southern African Regional Police Chiefs Cooperation Organisation (SARPCCO) for vehicles imported from within Southern Africa, export documentation, the vehicle registration book, and freight and insurance statements.

Any applicable clearing-agent charges, temporary storage fees and other administrative costs should also be confirmed in advance.



Is buying a car in South Africa cheaper?

The answer depends on the vehicle and the total landed cost in Zimbabwe.

A lower South African purchase price does not necessarily translate into savings once import duties, taxes, transport and registration are included.

Prospective buyers should compare the final cost of importing a specific vehicle with the price of an equivalent vehicle already available in Zimbabwe.



Before making a payment, they should also verify the vehicle’s year of manufacture, ownership documents and eligibility for importation.

Ultimately, the most useful comparison is not simply what a car costs in South Africa, but how much it costs to get it legally registered and ready for use in Zimbabwe.

World.title: Nelson Mandela statue the latest target of Glasgow’s famous traffic-cone prank [pics]
World.content:
A bronze statue of the anti-apartheid hero was unveiled on Friday, 9 October 2026. Image: Glasgow Tourist Board/ Facebook

Nelson Mandela has received many honours in his lifetime, but few are quite as Glaswegian as a traffic cone balanced on his head.

Just days after a new statue of the former South African president was unveiled in Glasgow, Scotland, the monument was given the city’s famous traffic-cone treatment.

The stunt is a nod to Glasgow’s long-running tradition of placing cones on the head of the Duke of Wellington statue outside the Gallery of Modern Art.



While some might view it as vandalism or an act of desecration, the cone is practically a rite of passage in the Scottish city.

In Glasgow, even a monument to one of the world’s most revered leaders isn’t exempt.

Mandela statue gets the Glasgow treatment

The new bronze statue stands in Nelson Mandela Place and was unveiled last Friday, 9 October. The date marked 33 years since Mandela received Glasgow’s Freedom of the City.



Created by artist Alan B Herriot, the monument was selected from five proposals displayed at Glasgow City Chambers last year.

Creating the structure reportedly cost around £180 000 (just under R4 million), raised entirely through donations and support rather than public funds.

Brian Filling, chair of the Nelson Mandela Scottish Memorial Foundation, said it would be a lasting tribute to Mandela and the struggle for freedom in South Africa.



“This will be a permanent memorial to Nelson Mandela and the struggle of the South African people and our solidarity, and that’s why Glasgow is important in that whole history,” he said.

The stunt follows Glasgow’s tradition of placing traffic cones on the Duke of Wellington statue. Image: Wikimedia

From the Duke of Wellington to Nelson Mandela

The Duke of Wellington statue has long been Glasgow’s most famous cone-topped landmark. The tradition even travelled across the Atlantic during Scotland’s 2026 World Cup campaign, when cones appeared on statues in Boston.

Scotland’s supporters made such an impression that Boston and Glasgow entered into a formal twinning agreement, announced by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu during the tournament.



Mandela’s ties to Glasgow run much deeper than a traffic-cone gag. The city became the first in the world to award him its Freedom of the City in 1981, while he was still imprisoned on Robben Island.

The anti-apartheid hero returned in 1993 to receive the honour in person, three decades before this latest monument joined the city’s collection of landmarks.

World.title: Correctional services commissioner encourages inmates writing matric
World.content:
DURBAN - Thousands of matriculants began writing their National Senior Certificate (NSC) examinations on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, inmates sitting their matric exams at Usethubeni School at Westville Correctional Centre received messages of support from National Commissioner of Correctional Services Makgothi Thobakgale.

The school was officially opened in 2013 to give young inmates, including those classified as juveniles, the opportunity to continue their education and write their matric examinations while incarcerated.

The correctional centre’s school has achieved a 100% matric pass rate, a record officials hope to maintain.

Thobakgale encouraged the inmates to remain focused on their studies, saying education could help them build a better future after their release from prison.

World.title: Emotional Mbalula collapses after ANC's ConCourt victory
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - ANC secretary-general Fikile Mbalula collapsed during a media briefing after the party won its legal battle with the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) over its candidate lists.

On Thursday, the Constitutional Court upheld the ANC’s appeal against the exclusion of 181 of its candidates from the local government elections. The ruling paves the way for the candidates to be included on the ballot for the November polls.

ANC members who were in court celebrated the victory, while an emotional Mbalula broke down in tears as he expressed relief at the ruling.

READ | ANC wins ConCourt battle over 181 candidates ahead of local elections

During a subsequent media briefing, Mbalula, who was visibly sweating, said he was not feeling well before slumping. He was assisted by ANC spokesperson Mahlengi Bhengu.

Reporters were asked to switch off their cameras as the incident unfolded.

Bhengu subsequently took over the briefing, telling reporters that Mbalula was receiving medical attention.

Reacting to the ruling earlier, Mbalula said the past month had been difficult for the party.

“I thank the national officials of the movement who carried this matter with patience. And patience was not easy,” he said.

World.title: NPA rejects claims Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma and husband face arrest
World.content:
DURBAN - The National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) has denied issuing arrest warrants for March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma and her husband, Xolani Zuma, following claims by the organisation that the couple could be arrested by Friday, 16 October.

The NPA was responding to a statement issued by March and March on Wednesday, alleging that the couple would be arrested on or before the date.

“The NPA wishes to categorically deny that any warrant of arrest was issued, and that it does not receive instructions from political parties, holders of public office, or anyone else on its prosecutorial function,” NPA spokesperson Kaizer Kganyago said in a statement.

READ | March and March demands tougher immigration enforcement

“The NPA encourages people and organisations to desist from making unfounded allegations or comments which may serve to misrepresent and undermine the criminal justice process,” Kganyago added.

KwaZulu-Natal police also dismissed the rumours.

In its statement, March and March alleged that the couple’s possible arrest was an attempt to “cause civil unrest and disrupt the upcoming 4 November local government elections”.

The statement further claimed that an executive committee meeting had been held to discuss whether the couple should be arrested before or during the elections.

March and March is among the organisations calling on undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.

World.title: Rural women hardest hit as hunger levels increases in food-rich SA
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Despite easing food inflation, hunger remains a persistent problem in South Africa, with 12% of households experiencing food insecurity, according to the latest Food Security Index.

Rural female-headed households are among the hardest hit, highlighting the growing struggle for vulnerable communities to put food on the table.

Stellenbosch University professor Dieter von Fintel says the research is important, particularly in a country that produces enough food to feed everyone.

“On a national level, we are secure,” he said.

“The real issue is what happens to specific vulnerable groups,” he added.

World.title: Alcohol policy should be part of election manifestos, organisation says
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - While political parties are making promises ahead of the local government elections, the South African Alcohol Policy Alliance (SAAPA) wants them to put alcohol-related harm at the centre of their campaigns.

Alongside pledges to create jobs, reduce poverty and improve service delivery, the organisation is calling for political parties to address South Africa’s drinking culture and the harm associated with alcohol consumption.

“South Africa is currently dealing with a lot that is connected to alcohol harm,” SAAPA’s Nomcebo Dlamini said.

“If political parties and the people we are letting into office are concerned about our communities, they need to be concerned about the issues that communities are dealing with,” she said.

World.title: ANC wins ConCourt battle over 181 candidates ahead of local elections
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The ANC has won its bid to have 181 candidates included on the ballot for the 4 November local government elections.

On Thursday, the Constitutional Court ordered the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) to take the necessary steps to include the party’s candidate lists and nominations on the ballot.

In a brief majority judgment delivered by Justice Rammaka Mathopo, the court granted the ANC leave to appeal the Electoral Court’s ruling last month and set aside its order.

The dispute centred on the ANC’s candidate list submissions for six municipalities.

The party challenged the IEC’s decision to exclude its candidates, arguing that it had met the submission deadline but that a technical problem with the commission’s online system had prevented its lists from being properly captured and processed.

Last month, the ANC approached the Electoral Court, arguing that the system failure had prevented the successful submission of its candidate lists. However, the court dismissed its appeal.

The dispute affected six municipalities across KwaZulu-Natal, the Free State and the Eastern Cape.

World.title: IEC approves more than 2.6 million special votes for local elections
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - More than 2.6 million special votes have been approved by the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) for the November local government elections.

According to the IEC, this represents a 131% increase compared with the 2021 elections. Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo says the commission is ready to manage the increased demand.

With fewer than 20 days remaining before the elections, plans are underway to deploy teams to visit about 670,000 voters at their homes. Approximately 1.9 million voters will cast their ballots at voting stations on 2 and 3 November.

“It shouldn’t have a disruptive effect,” Mamabolo said.

He said the increase showed that more people were participating in the electoral process and that the commission was making it easier for voters to cast their ballots.

“It does show that the participation envelope is increasing and the commission is making it easier for people to cast their ballots,” he said.

World.title: Prospect of Bolsonaro win looms large over Brazil's Indigenous
World.content:
MANAUS - Brazil's Amazonian Indigenous communities are watching with bated breath as presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro inches closer to power, recalling the damage wrought on the rainforest under his father Jair Bolsonaro.

The surname they share "represents everything bad for us," Inara Waty, leader of the Satere-Mawe people in the Amazonian city of Manaus, told AFP.

"It mainly means fear," she said, her eyes filling with tears as she recalled life under the last Bolsonaro administration.

Jair Bolsonaro governed the world's most biodiverse country between 2019 and 2022, a period marked by record levels of deforestation in the Amazon and backsliding in Indigenous rights.

His son, the favourite in the October 25 runoff against leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, says he would run a "Bolsonaro 2.0" presidency.

"The greatest way we addressed environmental issues was what we did during president Bolsonaro's administration," the senator said during an interview on the campaign trail.

The candidate believes his father, currently serving 27 years for coup-plotting, "fought" against a "radical environmental agenda."

He claims that extreme weather events that scientists attribute to man-made global warming are merely "cyclical."

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Optics tell it all: Why William Ruto looks tell of a desperate politician
World.content:
President William Ruto has taken on a worrying look of late – sweating profusely, eyes wild and blazing, teeth bared in a rictus smile, absolutely furious, panicking and shouting, and with no apparent control of what comes out of his mouth. Things fall apart, and this is the look and sound of a desperate man. And optics matter.

World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Kalonzo to Ruto: You have no numbers
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka speaks during launch of economic empowerment equipment distribution at Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos town on October 9, 2026. [John Muia, Standard]

The united opposition will deal President William Ruto a humiliating defeat in next year’s general election, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka has predicted.

Speaking Friday in his Ukambani backyard during an empowerment equipment handover ceremony hosted by Governor Wavinya Ndeti at the Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos, Kalonzo declared the opposition will defeat Ruto at the ballot ‘no matter what magic he (Ruto) deploys.

“Ruto has been cornered. We have heard him suggesting that they will import foreigners from neighboring countries to vote for him but even so, he will not secure the numbers. We in the united opposition have committed to produce a single candidate that will face Ruto at the ballot,” Kalonzo said.

Recognizing the need to consolidate his lower Eastern vote bloc, Kalonzo rallied the Akamba community to come out in huge numbers to register as voters in the upcoming voter listing initiative by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

“It is the time to redeem this country. The IEBC will as from next month undertake the final leg of voter registration and I urge all eligible voters to apply for national identity cards and register as voters,” he said, vowing he will defeat Ruto in Luo Nyanza.

Kalonzo called out Ruto over what he termed as the president’s habit of making empty promises to Kenyans. “The other day I heard Ruto promising thousands of dams across the country. He should come for benchmarking in Machakos. Retired President Mwai Kibaki and I secured African Development Bank (ADB) funding for the construction of Yatta Dam and now he has ten months left in office. When will he build?” he posed.

Former Attorney General Justin Muturi, who flanked Kalonzo, declared time was fast running out for the opposition to identify and name its presidential flag bearer for the next year’s general election.

The DP party leader, who has gone public declaring his choice of Kalonzo as the presidential ticket bearer for the opposition expressed his frustrations for the opposition’s dillydallying in naming its flag bearer.

“We (the opposition) are tired of singing one song for years that we will produce and name one person to face Ruto. When you see us here another day, do not entertain such kind of talk. Demand that it is Kalonzo for State House,” said Muturi.

During the ceremony, Governor Wavinya Ndeti unveiled assorted empowerment equipment targeting about 6000 beneficiaries across the county.

Addressing residents during the forum, Wavinya jeered at UDA-allied politicians who have been dishing out cash handouts to residents, terming it untenable.

“It is time to demonstrate to those who are approaching our people with cheap hand-outs that when the people of Machakos are given the tools to work, they produce real wealth. My commitment is that I will continue allocating resources to asset-based empowerment until every household in Machakos enjoys economic dignity,” Wavinya said.

World.title: Egypt, Tunisia discuss cooperation in Non-Banking Microfinance Regulation
World.content:
Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) is keen on strengthening cooperation with Arab and African countries prioritizing the exchange of expertise and knowledge-sharing, FRA Chairman Islam Azzam said. FRA chairman made the remarks during a meeting with Mahmoud Montasser Mansour executive director-general and founder of Tunisia’s Microfinance Control Authority and his accompanying delegation to discuss ways to enhance cooperation and exchange regulatory and supervisory expertise in non-banking finance.

The meeting was attended by FRA Assistant Chairman Rehab Taha.

The Tunisian delegation’s visit aimed to gain first-hand insight into Egypt’s legislative and regulatory frameworks governing financing for medium, small and micro enterprises, particularly given the relatively close timing of regulatory developments in the sector in both countries.

Azzam welcomed the Tunisian officials to Egypt, describing non-banking finance for enterprises as one of the key sectors supervised by the FRA, given its relevance to a broad segment of the population.He said the sector directly supports financial inclusion, one of the main objectives of Egypt Vision 2030 and the government’s plan to advance the national economy.It also has the potential to improve the livelihoods of vulnerable groups and contribute to sustainable economic and social development, he added.

Azzam said outstanding financing balances for medium, small and micro enterprises in Egypt exceeded 101 billion Egyptian pounds in the second quarter of this year, benefiting around 3.5 million people through approximately 4,400 outlets operated by licensed companies, associations and institutions nationwide.

He also said the FRA had recently placed especial emphasis on improving the financing experience for beneficiaries, especially microenterprise owners, by tightening assessments of borrowers’ repayment capacity to reduce defaults, ensuring transparent information and data protection, and encouraging providers to develop innovative products that meet customers’ needs.

The authority seeks to ensure that customers can effectively use available grievance and complaints mechanisms and to assess the actual impact of financing on their livelihoods and economic activities, he added.

Azzam pointed to recent regulatory decisions aimed at tightening oversight of debt collection practices to prevent abuses, strengthening customer identity verification, improving the FRA’s ability to detect risks early and reducing individual borrower defaults.

The measures also seek to improve the financial solvency of licensed financing providers and encourage the development of new products using financial technology to keep pace with market developments and changing customer circumstances.

The aim is to expand access to financing, particularly in poor and remote areas, alongside ongoing awareness campaigns conducted in cooperation with various government entities, he said.For his part, Mansour reviewed the development of Tunisia’s microfinance sector since its regulation in 1999, initially covering associations, followed by a restructuring of the sector in 2011 that brought commercial microfinance institutions under regulatory supervision.

He also outlined the authority’s role since 2012 in regulating pricing and monitoring financing costs, as well as measures introduced last year, including reviews of the prices of certain products offered by seven licensed microfinance companies and 289 licensed microcredit associations.

Mansour said more than 856,000 clients currently benefit from microfinance in Tunisia.

Last year, financing worth around 2.7 billion Tunisian dinars, equivalent to 47.1 billion Egyptian pounds, was extended through more than 524,000 financing transactions, reflecting the sector’s continued expansion.The meeting also addressed the development of financial products and diversification of financing instruments, as well as the two countries’ experiences in digital transformation, financial technology applications and the use of artificial intelligence in supervisory tools.

Participants also discussed modern approaches to risk management, compliance and consumer protection to improve the efficiency of activities overseen by both authorities.

World.title: IMF, World Bank launch global roadmap to combat online financial fraud
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank unveiled a global roadmap to fight online financial fraud as increasingly sophisticated scams undermine confidence in digital finance.

The “Bangkok Blueprint” developed in coordination with the Bank of Thailand and released during the institutions’ annual meetings on Wednesday in Bangkok sets out 12 policy considerations to help countries identify vulnerabilities and develop comprehensive and coordinated responses, Thai central bank chief Vitai Ratanakorn said.

“The framework calls for a whole-of-ecosystem response, stronger cross-border cooperation, and sharing practical experience to inform evolving global standard setting,” Vitai said during the report launch, adding that it drew experiences from Hong Kong, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. Asia accounted for 67 per cent of global fraud losses in 2024, he said.

Scam operations have been proliferating across South-east Asia in recent years, particularly in border regions adjacent to Thailand, which has become a transit hub for human trafficking linked to scam compounds.

The initiative comes as Thailand’s efforts to crack down on scam operations have uncovered sophisticated ways in which proceeds of cyber fraud become a major part of broader illicit financial flow, Vitai said.

World.title: WHO confirms Egypt as first country to retain Hepatitis C gold status
World.content:
Egypt has become the first country in the world to retain the World Health Organization’s (WHO) gold-tier status on the path to eliminating hepatitis C, following a review of its national prevention, testing and treatment programmes.

The WHO confirmed the recognition on Wednesday after assessing Egypt’s progress between 2023 and 2025. The assessment was approved by the organization’s regional validation committee in July 2026.

Egypt first achieved gold-tier status in 2023 after reducing hepatitis C prevalence from around 10 percent to less than 0.38 percent in just over a decade.

The achievement follows Egypt’s nationwide 100 Million Healthy Lives campaign, which screened more than 60 million people and provided treatment to over 4.5 million hepatitis C patients.

According to the WHO, Egypt has since moved from large-scale screening campaigns to a permanent healthcare system that provides routine hepatitis C testing, diagnosis and treatment.

The country has also expanded hepatitis services through primary healthcare and universal health insurance while improving disease surveillance, laboratory standards and blood safety measures.

These efforts are supported by a national plan to sustain progress towards eliminating viral hepatitis, including measures covering 2025–2030.

The WHO said that it had provided technical support to Egypt throughout its hepatitis C programme, helping improve prevention, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring.

World.title: FM, Thai deputy PM discuss trade, investment cooperation
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, to discuss strengthening economic, trade and investment cooperation between the two countries.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of a dinner hosted by Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul for heads of delegations attending the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group.

The two ministers stressed the importance of expanding bilateral trade and investment, exchanging expertise in economic and financial reforms, and attracting further investment.They also discussed strengthening cooperation through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), building on the cooperation agreement signed between Egypt and the regional bloc in 2016.

Both sides expressed their commitment to expanding economic partnerships and advancing mutual interests.

World.title: At least 28 children killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
World.content:
Lahore, Pakistan —

Twenty-eight children and a teacher were killed and dozens injured when the roof of a school in northern Pakistan collapsed on Thursday morning, authorities said.

Heavy rainfall had caused the roof of the two-story building in the city of Peshawar to collapse, Bilal Ahmed of the local rescue services told CNN. Some children were still trapped in the rubble and rescuers were working to reach them, he said.

Forty-seven children were injured, Asim Khan, spokesperson for the Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, told CNN. Video from the scene obtained by CNN showed ambulances rushing through narrow streets and crowds gathered outside the school building.

Local residents were among the first people to reach the scene, and rescue workers arrived within minutes, The Associated Press reported citing eyewitnesses.

Building collapses are a common problem in Pakistan. Construction standards in the country are often poorly enforced, and many structures are built with substandard materials.

The collapse comes just weeks after a fire tore through a hospital in the capital Islamabad, killing at least 14 newborns and sparking widespread anger and multiple arrests.

The fire was confined to a third-floor nursery but officials said it spread so quickly that staff were able to rescue only one baby from among the 15 being cared for there.

An inquiry found that the nursery had no fire alarm or sprinkler system and that the hospital lacked detailed procedures and training for responding to fires and other emergencies.

In July, a roof collapse at a tutoring center under construction in Pakistan’s eastern city of Lahore killed at least 14 schoolchildren, police and rescue officials said at the time.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: Two cargo ships sunk in Strait of Hormuz as Iran ramps up attacks in run-up to midterms
World.content:
Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the heightened danger to shipping as Iran steps up attacks in an attempt to regain control over the critical waterway.

The Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck on Tuesday while passing through the strait, catching fire and later sinking, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. All crew members were safely evacuated.

Videos verified by CNN show black smoke rising from the ship as it takes on water, while later footage and satellite images show cargo scattered in the water and a small oil slick. Iranian state media Press TV reported that the ship had “hit a sea mine on an unauthorized route” – which experts cast doubt on, saying a drone attack was more likely.

The merchant vessel Cape Dao, registered under Antigua and Barbuda, also sank, according to data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on Wednesday – after it was first hit by projectile on September 23. One Indian crew member was killed.

While many vessels have been hit in the Strait of Hormuz this year, these are only the second and third to have sunk in the Middle East since the Iran war began in February, according to IMO data. Attacks have ramped up significantly since the end of September, once again reducing the amount of oil transiting out of the Middle East and raising oil prices around the world.

A satellite image shows floating containers and an oil slick in the Strait of Hormuz after the GFS Pride sank. European Space Agency/Sentinel 2

That’s been a consistent headache for US President Donald Trump as the midterm elections approach, with gas prices, tariffs, and other factors driving up the cost of living top of mind for many voters.

Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which monitors shipping incidents, shows just how high the risk is. Nine attacks in or near the Strait of Hormuz have been reported since Monday, including a drone strike on a tanker.

Only 4.147 million barrels of oil successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday – less than a quarter of pre-war levels, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler. And the seven-day average of oil flow through Hormuz has dropped sharply since early October, Kpler’s data shows.

“The sinking of Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE marks a dangerous escalation after weeks of near-daily attacks on commercial shipping. Iran claims a naval mine; but a drone strike is more likely,” said former US Navy officer Charlie Brown, also a senior adviser for United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit that tracks and reports on Iranian sanctions violations.

Small boats visit the site where shipping containers float in the water after Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank near the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. Reuters

“Many ask what response will the US Navy mount to Iran’s escalating attacks on global shipping,” he added. “But the real question is what response will other nations take? How long will the world tolerate this threat to shipping, seafarers and freedom of navigation?”

The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports to maintain economic pressure on Iran. To some extent, it’s worked: Iran’s economy is in tatters, and in recent months it clearly lost its leverage over the strait, with the amount of oil flowing from other Gulf nations through the waterway increasing to near-normal levels.

That’s partly thanks to a complex operation involving US-military-escorted “dark” transits across the strait at night, with tankers turning off their transponders to avoid detection.

That rise in oil flow is why Iran is now ramping up its attacks and threats, hoping to wrestle back the leverage it once had over the strait – especially as American voters head to the polls.

The Trump administration has tried to lower prices in other ways, including a controversial deal announced last week to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country’s diesel. But this has been met with bipartisan criticism – and there’s no guarantee it will bring any substantial relief, with analysts warning that diesel could climb near all-time highs by November.

World.title: Zelensky says Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian refineries, as frustration with Trump mounts
World.content:
Ukraine will resume strikes on Russia’s oil refineries President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in a fiery interview where he lamented what he said was a “dangerous” withdrawal of US intelligence sharing and access to the Starlink satellite internet service.

“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the FT in London.

The comments by Zelensky are the latest that publicly lay bare the growing frustration he has with President Donald Trump, deepening the already fractious relationship between the two leaders.

Trump announced a controversial deal last week to buy Russian diesel and he has heaped pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Moscow’s refineries as he works to bring down energy costs ahead of the midterm elections.

Then on Wednesday, Ukraine said Starlink had restricted some military internet services, disrupting key operations, deepening alarm in both Kyiv and among European allies.

According to the FT, Zelensky condemned Trump’s willingness to strike business deals with Moscow as well as the US president’s apparent admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

He also said Ukrainian military officials were told by their US counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence”.

Zelensky’s warning that strikes on Russian refineries will resume came after another interview where he voiced anger over Trump’s fuel deal with Moscow.

When asked by British media personality Piers Morgan if he had been “betrayed” by the Trump administration, Zelensky answered, “Yes,” describing the agreement as a “simple victory” for the Kremlin.

“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” the Ukrainian president told Morgan on Wednesday during his YouTube talk show, “Piers Morgan Uncensored.”

Last week, Trump wrote on social media that Russia’s President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply markets with his country’s diesel fuel as the US president works to bring down energy costs ahead of the midterm elections. That move drew bipartisan criticism and sparked anger among European allies.

On Monday, Russian forces launched fresh attacks on Ukraine just hours after the US president stated an “energy ceasefire” had come into effect – a measure that neither Moscow nor Kyiv had publicly confirmed.

In a clip shared on X from the interview with Morgan, the Ukrainian president said: “This is our country, our body, our home, our children… That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”

“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side,” said Zelensky. “This is not the right side of history.”

“Russia wants him (Trump) to be weak,” he added. “They don’t care about elections in the United States.”

Both Russian and Ukrainian troops have intensified aerial attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure in recent weeks, as movements on the battlefield remain relatively stagnant.

The Trump administration had warned Ukraine and allies in Europe that the US could suspend intelligence sharing and European purchases of US weapons for Kyiv if it did not halt deep strikes on Russian energy facilities.

Information sharing is invaluable to Ukrainian defense efforts against Russian ballistic missile attacks by giving the locations of missile launchers along with data on where the strikes are being directed, and when.

In the days that followed, Trump administration officials, including the president, insisted such intelligence sharing continued. But what explained the lack of missile warnings?

When asked by Kyiv for an explanation, US officials blamed the weather. But Ukrainian officials suspected it was deliberate. “America says it was a failure,” a European official told CNN. “But it can’t be the truth.”

“This will give Russians a real leverage on a frontline at the time when we effectively stopped their advances, and de-occupy the territories,” a Ukrainian official told CNN.

‘People will die’

That information deficit has been compounded by Elon Musk’s Starlink curbing some internet services in Ukraine, according to local officials. Ukrainian authorities said they were caught off-guard by restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, called Starshield.

Zelensky claimed Russian forces were trying to capitalize on the Starshield disruption by unleashing heavy strikes overnight, telling Morgan that Ukrainian forces use the satellite system to defend against Moscow’s jet-powered Shahed drones.

“It’s a big mistake,” he said during the interview on Wednesday. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses… People will die,” Zelensky said. “My message (to Musk) is absolutely clear. I hope it’s a mistake, a huge technical problem. We’re asking (him) to switch on (the service).”

Musk on Wednesday said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government and that any limits on its speed or usage are up to the US military and president. He added that Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX and is limited to civilian or defensive activities.

Musk said Starlink “cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

CNN has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.

Zelensky has spent the past week trying to shore up support among European leaders. On Wednesday, he met Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles over two separate meetings in London – just as he Kremlin fired drones and ballistic miles that left more than 600,000 people in Ukraine without power, according to Zelensky.

World.title: Exclusive: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, sources say
World.content:
The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter.

Using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a notable escalation, even though there are doubts over how effective it would be in accomplishing any of Trump’s stated strategic objectives or tipping the balance of the war, multiple sources familiar with internal military planning discussions about potentially deploying the weapon said.

Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war — as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the upcoming midterm elections and there is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of US bombing.

While the US military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against outstanding Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that incorporates those plans in a way that could actually end the war — something only the president has the power to do.

For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could act as a “definitive” end to the war, at least from a messaging point of view, aware of how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans.

While some administration figures have characterized the war as essentially won, Trump has been more guarded in recent remarks, stopping short of declaring victory and saying the US still has unfinished business in the country.

Behind the scenes, Trump has also cast doubt on some outside allies who have encouraged him to simply bring US troops home and move on. Doing so, Trump has argued, would look like defeat.

Over the course of the last several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterms, several advisers said privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before Election Day.

Trump has ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure” and the potential use of a MOAB, one of the sources told CNN. The same source said the phrasing used was that this attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” indicating the administration could launch the additional strikes, attempt to declare victory and quickly pull everyone out.

A second source told CNN that military plans for striking Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, also explicitly call for using the MOAB. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe, where the US and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program, even after pausing full combat operations earlier this year, and Trump continues to emphasize that his goal is to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon.

Doubts MOAB would be effective

Another US official noted that when the military plans, it develops a menu of options for policymakers that range from the high-end to low-end. Higher-end targets, including those that are located deep underground, require bigger bombs, and the MOAB is the biggest, the official added.

But there are questions around whether the MOAB would be an effective munition to use against Iran’s nuclear facilities and other sites that are located deep underground. While the GPS-guided bomb is capable of destroying an area equivalent to nine city blocks, it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough under the surface to destroy the suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe, which is believed to be fortified by layers of granite, and other remaining Iranian nuclear sites, sources said.

The GBU-43/B, also known as the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, detonates during a test at Eglain Air Force Base, Florida, on November 21, 2003. US Air Force/Handout/Reuters

What to know about the MOAB bomb Called the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB bomb

Nicknamed the “mother of all bombs”

Is America’s most powerful non-nuclear bomb

Weighs 21,600 lbs.

“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a third source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”

If used, the MOAB would have devastating effects on the area that it impacts but likely only at the surface level, the sources noted. And the bomb’s massive blast radius would almost certainly raise concerns about the prospect of civilian casualties — particularly if it is used to target Iranian infrastructure targets located near populated areas and in close proximity to non-military sites.

Still, Trump could opt to use the MOAB as a psychological weapon at a time when the Iranian regime appears dug in and unwilling to bend to his diplomatic demands. While US officials warn that deploying it is unlikely to force Iran’s capitulation or achieve a strategic military victory — it could provide Trump with an additional option, short of restarting full combat operations, to alter the conflict’s current status quo.

“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level … you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the third source familiar with recent planning discussions added.

Many within the administration as well as outside analysts agree that the only way to decisively defeat Iran would be through a major operation involving ground troops, a commitment that could potentially cost thousands of American lives. The Pentagon considers all scenarios, so those plans exist, but as of now no one in the administration is arguing for such drastic action.

Trump has indicated he has little interest in putting US boots on the ground in Iran but his desire to end the conflict as soon as possible presents a political dilemma for a president who is keenly aware of how unpopular the war has become yet has been unable to secure a diplomatic agreement that would bring it to a close.

Top Trump administration officials and military planners have been focused, for weeks, on finding an off-ramp that gives Trump a “symbolic” win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, CNN has reported.

A fourth source familiar with the Pentagon’s recent planning discussions on Iran told CNN that military officials had developed some options that would amount to a “fireworks show,” with the goal of providing Trump an off-ramp from the conflict even if those strikes fail to accomplish his stated goals for starting the war in the first place.

And despite Trump’s recent pledge to hold off on launching additional strikes before the midterms, the US military already appears to be preparing for potential Iranian retaliation should the president give the go-order.

The next turnover of US troops deployed to CENTCOM is also expected to take place within the next few weeks, according to a fifth source, a US official who acknowledged it is possible some of the personnel who rotate out of the region, may not be replaced by fresh service members.

Asked about the plans, a White House official told CNN that they do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.”

In response to CNN’s request for comment, a Pentagon official said: “The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”

MOAB developed for ‘psychological operations’

Developed during the Iraq War, the MOAB is an air blast-type warhead that explodes before hitting the ground to project a massive explosion from all sides.

During the final stages of testing in 2003, military officials told CNN the MOAB was mainly conceived as a weapon employed for “psychological operations.”

Military officials said then they hoped such a huge blast would rattle Iraqi troops and pressure them into surrendering or not even fighting.

As originally conceived, the MOAB was to be used against large formations of troops and equipment or hardened above-ground bunkers. The target set has been expanded to include targets buried under softer surfaces, such as caves or tunnels.

Trump was the first US president to deploy the MOAB, during his first term when he authorized the military to use its most powerful non-nuclear bomb on ISIS positions in Afghanistan in 2017.

That strike targeted a network of fortified underground tunnels that ISIS had been using to stage attacks on government forces — killing 36 ISIS fighters, Afghan officials said. The blast destroyed three underground tunnels as well as weapons and ammunition, but no civilians were hurt, Afghan and US officials added at the time.

At the time, the bombing marked a dramatic change in attitude for Trump, who advocated an isolationist, “America first” foreign policy during his first election campaign.

Following the 2017 strike, US military officials were pressed on whether the 21,600-pound bomb was necessary for that particular target and would likely face similar questions if the munition is deployed against Iran.

World.title: Liberia: The Jury Debate — “A Corrupt Jury Is Worse Than No Jury.” But What About a Judge Who Has Already Spoken?
World.content:
MONROVIA — When Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. rose to open the Supreme Court’s October Term on Monday, he did not deliver a routine ceremonial charge. He delivered an indictment of the jury system itself.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Jury manipulation, he told the courtroom at the Temple of Justice, was eroding the administration of justice in civil and criminal matters alike. He pointed to reported tampering in Nimba, Grand Gedeh, Bomi and Margibi counties, in cases ranging from rape to drug trafficking. Then he turned to the most politically charged trial in the country: the US$6.2 million economic sabotage case against former Finance Minister Samuel D. Tweah Jr. and others. The post-trial inquiry conducted by Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika, the Chief Justice said, had established “gross jury tampering.”



“A corrupt jury is worse than no jury at all,” he declared, calling on the Legislature, the Liberian National Bar Association, the Law Reform Commission and the Liberian people to consider abolishing trial by jury.

The remarks have set off a wave of reaction in law offices, on radio talk shows and across social media. But beneath the larger argument over whether Liberia should keep its juries lies a narrower and more urgent question, one with direct consequences for the Tweah case: by publicly characterizing findings that are now under appeal, has the Chief Justice compromised the appearance of his impartiality — and should he step aside if the matter reaches his bench?

A verdict under appeal

On May 8, a 15-member jury returned a split verdict, acquitting Tweah and one co-defendant while convicting three others of theft and criminal facilitation. Judge Feika later set the verdict aside following an inquiry into alleged juror misconduct and ordered a new trial.

Defence lawyers have appealed that decision. Tweah himself has said he will not join the appeal; his co-defendants have signed on.

At the heart of the challenge is a question of proof. The inquiry reportedly established that jurors had mobile phones in their possession. The defence argues that this falls short of showing the phones were used to influence jurors or interfere with the verdict.

The distinction matters. Possessing a prohibited device, communicating with outsiders and actually corrupting a verdict are separate factual and legal questions. Evidence of the first does not automatically establish the second or the third. The defence has also questioned the identities and voting records of the jurors found with phones — a claim that will have to be tested against the official jury record and the inquiry’s findings.

These are precisely the issues an appellate bench must decide independently, weighing the evidence, the law and the reasons Judge Feika gave for vacating the verdict. That is why the Chief Justice’s words carry such weight. Spoken by the head of the Judiciary from the Supreme Court bench, “gross jury tampering” does not sound like commentary. It sounds like a finding.

The Chief Justice’s own standard

Gbeisay has been here before — on the other side of the argument, and in this very case.

In January 2025, sitting as Chamber Justice, he ordered the then-presiding trial judge in the Tweah prosecution to recuse himself over remarks the prosecution said were prejudicial. The Supreme Court, he said at the time, was appalled by the judge’s statements. He went further, laying down a test: a judge’s perceived bias, real or implied, is sufficient grounds for recusal, and where a judge’s words and actions lead a party reasonably to believe it will not receive a fair trial, the judge should step aside for the sake of transparency and justice. Judges, he reminded the bench, must not only be impartial but must also appear to be impartial.

By that measure, the defendants now challenging Judge Feika’s ruling may argue they have reasonable grounds to doubt that the Chief Justice can approach their appeal with an open mind.

The Judiciary itself drew a similar line only months ago. In May, responding to reports that the Chief Justice had ordered an investigation into alleged jury tampering in the Tweah case, the Judiciary issued a strong denial. Its statement stressed that the Chief Justice does not interfere in criminal proceedings or initiate inquiries into jury deliberations in cases pending before the courts. Monday’s remarks sit uneasily alongside that assurance.

What the canons say

Liberia’s own judicial standards offer a starting point. Judicial Canon Ten, published on the Judiciary’s official website, requires a judge to be temperate, attentive and impartial, and diligent in ascertaining the facts. Canon Eleven, which deals with avoiding impropriety, restricts judicial commentary on current news and matters of general public interest. Both reflect a long-standing principle: public confidence in the courts depends on judicial restraint.

Other jurisdictions are more explicit. Rule 2.10(A) of the American Bar Association’s Model Code of Judicial Conduct bars judges from public statements that “might reasonably be expected to affect the outcome or impair the fairness” of a pending or impending case. The American rule is not binding in Liberia, but it illustrates a standard widely shared across common-law systems, from which Liberia’s own jurisprudence descends.

None of this suggests a judge may not speak out against jury tampering. Protecting the integrity of trials is a core judicial duty. The concern is narrower: whether the head of the Judiciary can characterize the findings in a specific, contested case in definitive terms and then sit in judgment on those same findings.

A bench running short

The question is complicated by arithmetic. The two female Associate Justices on the Supreme Court have already recused themselves from the matter. Should the Chief Justice follow, the Court would face pressing questions about the composition of the bench and whether it can muster a quorum.

The Judiciary Law anticipates such situations. Section 2.7 governs the disqualification of Supreme Court justices, while Section 2.8 provides for reconstituting a quorum through ad hoc appointments when more than two justices cannot sit on a pending case. How those provisions apply will depend on the actual recusal orders and the procedural posture of the appeal.

But practical difficulty cannot settle a question of principle. The law provides a route to constitute a bench; the need to fill seats cannot by itself determine whether a particular justice should occupy one.

The larger debate

The Chief Justice’s scepticism about juries is not new. At his confirmation hearing, he argued that Liberia was the only country in West Africa where jury trials were mandatory and called for the Constitution to be revisited on the issue. Other judges have voiced similar views. Civil Law Court Judge Kennedy Peabody has argued for abolishing jury trials to curb corruption, and in August, opening the criminal courts’ term, Judge Banwon described the jury as the most vulnerable link in the justice chain and proposed a national conversation on its future.

Yet abolition is no simple reform. Trial by jury is a fundamental right under Article 21(h) of the 1986 Constitution, which guarantees an accused person a speedy, public and impartial trial by a jury of the vicinity unless the right is expressly waived. Removing it would require a constitutional amendment, not a policy decision by the courts.

Critics also warn about what would replace juries. A lawyer who spoke to FrontPageAfrica on condition of anonymity, citing fear of retribution, argued that shifting verdicts entirely to judges, without confronting allegations of corruption on the bench, could further erode public trust. Remove the jury, the argument runs, and the judge becomes the sole gatekeeper of guilt and innocence.

Meanwhile, defendants are not abandoning juries. In the Saudi rice diversion case now before Criminal Court “C”, former officials have demanded a full 15-member panel — the same strategy used in the Tweah trial. And the Supreme Court is still weighing a separate dispute over the dissolution of the jury in the Capitol arson trial. The jury question, in other words, is before the Court in more ways than one.

The question that remains

The Chief Justice may sincerely believe that jury tampering threatens Liberia’s justice system, and he may be right. But judicial impartiality is measured not only by the absence of actual bias; it also depends on whether a reasonable observer could doubt a judge’s ability to weigh a disputed matter afresh.

Recusal is not a punishment, nor an admission of bias. It is a safeguard — for the parties, for the integrity of the proceedings and for the credibility of the Court.

Liberia can investigate jury tampering rigorously and debate the future of the jury system openly. What it cannot afford is a Supreme Court ruling on the Tweah appeal that half the country believes was decided on Monday morning, in the Chief Justice’s opening address.

The issue is not whether jury tampering should be condemned. It is whether the man who has publicly condemned it in this case can now judge it. That question deserves a clear answer — grounded in Liberia’s judicial canons, its law on disqualification and the constitutional promise of impartial justice.
