World.title: Liberia: Global Study Shows Most African Workers ‘Struggling’; the Cost is Paid by Teachers, Healthcare Workers Who Hold the Economy Together
World.content:
Elaine Duowai teaches at Euphemia Barclay Elementary School in Bensonville, where low pay, missing pupils and limited resources shape the school day. Photo: New Narratives

Summary:

A global study found nearly three in every four workers in Sub-Saharan Africa are “struggling,” not “thriving.” In Liberia, that struggle is visible in classrooms and clinics where public servants work through low pay, stress, and poor conditions.

Teachers and midwives interviewed for this story described low take-home pay, delayed payroll placement, overcrowded classrooms, understaffed clinics, and salary bureaucracy that leaves many exhausted and others walking away.

Economists and labor advocates warn the cost hurts everyone: weak classrooms and clinics mean weaker learning, poorer health, lower productivity, and a future workforce Liberia may not be preparing.

By Tetee Gebro and Joyclyn Wea, health and gender correspondents with New Narratives

BENSONVILLE, Montserrado County – Before sunrise, Elaine Duowai prepares lesson notes in a house where electricity is not reliable. By morning, she is walking to Euphemia Barclay Elementary School, where some pupils are already missing from the rows of benches before the day begins.



Some stay home because families cannot afford transport, food, or school materials. Others are sent to help parents sell or work on nearby farms. Duowai teaches the children who come. She worries about the ones who do not.

“Sometimes I look at the empty benches and feel weak,” Duowai said. “The children are not lazy. Their families are just struggling.”

The work is also hard inside the classroom: too few materials, absent pupils, children carrying adult burdens, and teachers expected to supply patience when the system supplies little else.

Then there is the pay. After one trip to central Monrovia to correct a salary problem, Duowai said she was told she needed money she did not have to open a new bank account. She returned to school with the problem unresolved and her strength nearly gone. Her husband, also a teacher, died in 2024. She is still fighting bureaucracy to access his benefits. She makes soap at night to feed her family and then gets up at sunrise to begin the school day.

Hers is the face of a wider warning for Liberia. In the latest State of the Global Workplace: 2026 Report produced by U.S. based polling company Gallup, nearly three in every four workers in Sub-Saharan Africa are “struggling” rather than “thriving.” The annual employee study, based on more than 141,000 employed respondents worldwide, also found high daily stress across the region.

Larwuo B. Walker, a registered nurse and midwife, works at Johnsonville Public Clinic, where staffing shortages stretch workers across long shifts

In Liberia, that finding shows up in public schools and clinics where workers continue to report for duty while low pay, delayed payroll placement, crowded facilities and weak systems drain the very people expected to keep the country moving. Interviews with teachers, midwives and economists describe a labor crisis that is not only about salaries, but about morale, working conditions and the cost of asking essential workers to survive on purpose alone. Especially when the country’s lawmakers take home as much as $US15,000 a month, more than most lawmakers in wealthy countries.

Duowai is clear about why the issue matters: the classroom is where Liberia’s future nurses, doctors, accountants, farmers, engineers and public officials begin. If the government forgets the classroom, she said, it forgets the people who will one day run the country.

Mary W. Mulbah-Nyumah, president of the National Teachers Association of Liberia, said the Gallup finding sounds familiar. She says low pay and repeated administrative frustration are weakening teachers before they even reach the classroom.

Nyumah taught in Liberia’s public school system for two decades before leading the association. She remembers years when teachers received salaries only twice a year, and only for one month at a time. She survived by trading, relying on food support and taking extra work. She says that old pattern has not fully ended; it has only changed form.

Today, some teachers still wait years to be placed on the payroll. Others are paid but say what reaches them after deductions cannot cover transport, rent, food, children’s needs and the small classroom expenses they often absorb themselves. In schools with too few books, desks or teaching materials, the emotional cost builds alongside the financial one.

Nyumah said the country is relying on teachers’ sacrifice to keep schools open. If too many leave, children lose more than lessons. They lose time, preparation, and the chance to move into adulthood with the skills needed to escape the poverty their parents are fighting.

Public-sector pay in Liberia has long lagged the cost of living. Successive governments have promised to address the problem. The Boakai administration has pointed to payroll verification, a promised $US150 gross monthly salary floor, and civil-service testing as steps toward cleaning up the payroll and reducing “no-show” jobs awarded in corrupt deals. Some of that is happening.

The Civil Service Agency said it integrated 3,406 essential workers in education, MCSS, and health into the national payroll in 2025, including 2,148 teachers and technical workers and 1,050 health workers. But the government’s own 2025 budget said fully absorbing all volunteer workers would cost about $US15 million, far more than the $US2.6 million allocated that year to begin the process.

Nearly two years into the administration, workers interviewed for this story said the reform is still uneven.

Maxim Bleeten and Augustus Walker, public relations officers at the ministries of education and health, did not respond to requests for comment by the deadline.

Jerry Barclay, assistant coordinator and instructor in the Department of Economics at the University of Liberia, said wages are among the strongest signals a government sends to its workforce. When workers are underpaid, unpaid or emotionally exhausted, he said, absenteeism rises, errors increase, service quality falls and productivity declines.

A weak health sector means sick workers may not recover quickly enough to return to farms, offices or classrooms. A weak education sector sends less-prepared students into the labor force. When schools and clinics struggle, Barclay says, agriculture, finance and other parts of the economy eventually feel it.

Duowai writes on a classroom board at Euphemia Barclay Elementary School. Teachers interviewed for this story described low pay as one burden among many, including limited materials and pupils kept home by poverty. Photo: New Narratives

At Johnsonville Public Clinic, Larwuo B. Walker, a registered nurse and midwife, sees the same pressure from the health side. Six midwives cover shifts that stretch from morning into night for a community of thousands. On some nights, she says, midwives sleep in chairs because there are not enough people to cover the work. Some women arrive in critical condition after delaying care because they were afraid or could not afford to come. Unnecessary birth injuries to mothers and babies that result in lifelong hardships often follow.

Walker holds a Bachelor of Science in Midwifery, but her monthly take-home pay is less than $US200. She has stayed in the clinic because she knows she is often all the stands between patients’ life and death.

Barclay said that is the breaking point policymakers often miss. Purpose can keep people in service for a time, but it cannot pay transport fare, rent, school fees or market prices. When a worker’s income stays fixed while prices rise – as they are now – living standards fall. Eventually, he says, productivity falls too.

Barclay said Liberia should treat spending on teachers and health workers as an economic investment, not only a social cost. If the government says it cannot afford better support for them, he said, it should also count the cost of weak schools, exhausted clinics and skilled workers leaving essential sectors for jobs that offer more dignity.

Nyumah said the teachers’ association will keep pushing salary complaints, payroll delays and volunteer-teacher cases to the ministries. Until then, teacher Douwai will prepare soap at night, wake before daylight, and walk back to school where her students, and the country’s future, depend on her.

World.title: Liberia: Snowe, Konneh Reject Gbeisay’s Call to Abolish Jury Trials, Urge Constitutional Reform
World.content:
MONROVIA – Two Liberian senators have publicly rejected the Chief Justice’s call to abolish jury trials, arguing that the answer to allegations of compromised jurors is a stronger jury system rather than no jury at all.

Senator Snowe, a senior member of the Senate and former Speaker of the House of Representatives, and Senator Konneh, who chairs the Senate Committee on Public Accounts, issued separate statements responding to Chief Justice Gbeisay. The Chief Justice made his appeal at the opening of the October Term of Court, citing concerns that jurors have been bribed or otherwise compromised in criminal cases.

Neither senator brushed aside those concerns. Both acknowledged that bribery, intimidation and interference are real threats to justice. But they said ending jury trials would punish the public for the misconduct of a few.



A Right Beyond the Reach of Ordinary Law

Senator Konneh framed the dispute first as a legal one. “Before it is a policy question, it is a constitutional question,” he said.

Both men pointed to the 1986 Constitution, which guarantees due process and trial by jury. Snowe cited Article 20(a), which protects due process and jury trial subject to constitutional exceptions, and Article 21(h), which covers the right to a speedy, public and impartial jury trial in the cases it addresses. That article also lets an accused person waive the right under set conditions.

Senator Konneh argued that neither an ordinary statute nor a directive from the judiciary can lawfully strip a citizen of a constitutionally protected right. The only route, he said, runs through Articles 91 and 92.

Under Article 91, an amendment needs the approval of two-thirds of the membership of both houses of the Legislature. It must then be ratified by two-thirds of registered voters voting in a national referendum held at least one year after the legislative vote. Article 92 sets further requirements on publishing and voting on proposed amendments.

The senators also drew a line between an accused person choosing to give up a jury and the State taking the option away from everyone.

Judges Can Be Bribed Too

The senators’ sharpest objection was that abolition would not cure the underlying disease. “Removing juries from the courtroom would not remove corruption from the courtroom,” Konneh said. He warned that judges are also vulnerable to bribery, intimidation and political pressure, and that placing a verdict in the hands of one judicial officer could hand manipulators a single target. “Corruption follows power. Wherever verdicts are decided, corrupt actors will attempt to influence that process,” he said.

Senator Snowe extended the point beyond the bench. Improper influence can reach prosecutors, investigators, court staff and witnesses, he said, and weakness at any stage of a case can undermine its outcome. He urged the country to examine the whole chain of criminal justice, from how crimes are investigated and evidence is kept to how witnesses are protected and cases are prosecuted.

Senator Snowe stressed that corruption “demands investigation, accountability, and institutional repair,” but that its existence “does not, by itself, justify withdrawing a fundamental right from the Liberian people.” He added that he is not a lawyer, and said his legislative experience and constitutional duties require him to weigh the matter independently.

Caution on Reading Acquittals

Senator Snowe also warned against treating every not-guilty verdict as proof of a bought jury. Referring to the proceedings involving former Finance Minister Samuel Tweah and Abdullah Kamara, he said verdicts, misconduct allegations, later court rulings and the evidence in each case must be judged on their own terms.

An acquittal, he said, can reflect thin evidence, unreliable testimony or a prosecution that failed to prove guilt. Where there is credible evidence of interference, he said, it should be investigated through lawful procedures, not inferred from public unhappiness with an outcome.

What the Senators Want Instead

Both men offered reform agendas, though with different emphases.

Senator Konneh called for:

– Mandatory sequestration and anonymity for jurors in serious criminal cases

– Meaningful compensation and protection for people who serve

– Tougher penalties for jury tampering

– A transparent, professionally managed selection system

He also asked the Chief Justice to submit a comprehensive Jury Reform Act to the Legislature.

Senator Snowe’s list was broader. He wants the existing Office of Jury Management strengthened, better education for jurors, and a review of how jurors are paid. He called for jury selection that is transparent and auditable, with screening for conflicts of interest, bias and improper relationships, while keeping both prosecution and defence able to challenge unsuitable candidates.

He said jurors should receive adequate allowances, timely payment, transportation, meals and safe accommodation where needed, so that citizens are not left out of pocket for performing a public duty. He also proposed channels for reporting threats or improper approaches, with safeguards for jurors’ identities and communications where justified, balanced against the accused’s right to challenge bias.

On accountability, Senator Snowe said investigators should pursue not only jurors who take bribes but also anyone who offers money, arranges improper contact or threatens jurors. He asked for a review of existing offences and penalties to see whether new legislation is needed.

Use the Laws Already on the Books

Senator Snowe argued that Liberia has not yet exhausted its existing tools. He noted that the Office of Jury Management was created through the 2013 legislative reform, which he said he supported. The office is responsible for jury selection, managing the central jury pool and educating prospective and sitting jurors. He urged authorities to assess how well it is performing and where it falls short, instead of bypassing it.

He also cited provisions in the Judiciary Law that bar jurors from accepting bribes or rewards meant to influence their duties, and said enforcement of those provisions should be examined before lawmakers consider new ones.

“Passing another law will achieve little unless the responsible institutions have the resources, independence, and commitment to enforce it,” he said. He called for stronger criminal investigations, better evidence collection, effective witness protection and improved prosecution and legal representation. He also proposed a costed implementation plan with clearly assigned responsibilities and regular reports to the relevant legislative committees. Oversight, he said, should cover spending, trial delays, protection arrangements and the handling of misconduct complaints, while respecting judicial independence and the confidentiality of jury deliberations.

Public Hearings Urged

Both senators asked for wider consultation. Snowe proposed public hearings bringing together the Judiciary, the Ministry of Justice, the Liberian National Bar Association, jury administrators, civil society groups and citizens who have served as jurors. Such hearings, he said, should establish what is failing, which reforms have already been tried and which can realistically be funded and carried out.

He also urged lawmakers to accept their own share of responsibility for giving the justice system the legal framework and resources it needs.

Senator Konneh said hearings would help identify practical ways to curb jury interference without moving immediately to eliminate jury trials. He did not rule out abolition forever. “If reform ultimately fails, the constitutional amendment process exists for exactly that reason,” he said. “But abolition cannot be our first answer.”

Juries as a Check on State Power

Beyond the mechanics of verdicts, the senators described the jury as a matter of citizenship. Konneh called it a way for ordinary people to take part directly in justice and to check the use of State power. He said Liberia’s history makes safeguards against concentrated, unchecked authority especially important.

Senator Snowe said the country must show it can punish corruption and strengthen accountability while staying faithful to its constitutional commitments. He said he is ready to work with the Chief Justice and fellow lawmakers on reforms that protect citizens, deter misconduct and improve the delivery of justice.

The senators were careful to say they are not dismissing the Chief Justice’s alarm. Their quarrel is with his proposed cure. As the debate continues, the question for Liberia’s justice system is whether the flaws he identified can be fixed while the right to a jury trial is preserved. For Snowe and Konneh, the answer is yes, and it starts with repairing the system rather than abolishing the right it exists to protect.

World.title: What Does Liberia’s ICJ Climate Vote Mean Ahead of COP31?
World.content:
A COP31 preparatory press conference in Istanbul, Türkiye, ahead of the November climate summit. UNFCCC/Yasin Okan Guven/Flickr.

When Liberia joins other countries at the United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, in November, it will be asking for many of the things climate-vulnerable countries have demanded for years: more climate finance, support for adapting to a changing climate, action on loss and damage and greater accountability from countries that have contributed most to global warming.

By Aria Deemie

But months before the 31st Conference of the Parties, Liberia found itself on the opposite side of a major international climate vote.



On May 20, Liberia was the only African country among eight nations that voted against a United Nations General Assembly resolution welcoming the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion on climate change. The resolution received 141 votes in favor, eight against and 28 abstentions.

A voting tally displayed during a United Nations General Assembly session. Photo credit: Observer Research Foundation.

The vote was surprising because Liberia is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change, while contributing very little to the greenhouse gas emissions responsible for global warming. The government later said the vote was an error.

So, what exactly was Liberia voting against, why did the vote matter, and what does it mean for a country preparing to demand stronger international action on climate change?

The International Court of Justice is the United Nations’ highest court, established to resolve legal disputes between sovereign countries. In July 2025, it issued an advisory opinion on climate change after being asked by the United Nations General Assembly to clarify the obligations countries have under international law to protect the climate system.

The Court said countries have obligations under international law to protect the climate and environment from human-caused greenhouse gas emissions. Countries that breach those obligations may face legal responsibility, including an obligation to prevent the harm from continuing, ensure it does not happen again and provide full reparation for harm caused.

The opinion was important because it strengthened the legal basis for arguments around climate responsibility and accountability. It does not operate like a normal court judgment ordering a particular country to take a particular action, but its findings can influence governments, negotiations and climate-related legal cases.

The United Nations General Assembly resolution adopted in May did not create the Court’s opinion. Vanuatu, a small Pacific island nation on the frontlines of the climate crisis, led a cross-regional “Core Group” of like-minded countries to author the draft text. They introduced the resolution to welcome and operationalize the International Court of Justice’s landmark 2025 advisory opinion. By the time it was put to a vote on May 20, 2026, Vanuatu’s initiative had attracted 90 co-sponsoring countries before passing with an overwhelming majority of 141 votes.

The United Nations General Assembly welcomed the Court’s findings and called on countries to take them into account.

This is why Liberia’s vote drew attention. For a country like Liberia, climate change is not simply an international debate. It is already affecting people’s lives.

An aerial view of a community in Liberia affected by flooding during the country’s recent rainy season. Photo credit: WFP/Mamadou Jallow.

Farmers are dealing with changing rainfall patterns, extreme heat and crop losses. Communities are increasingly exposed to flooding , while the country continues to face major gaps in the systems needed to forecast and respond to extreme weather.

Liberia’s contribution to global emissions is very small, yet the country is among those that need international support to adapt to climate change.

That has made climate justice an important part of Liberia’s international climate position.

“It was a complete contradiction to what we stand for,” said Ezekiel Nyanfor, Programs Coordinator and Climate Justice and Humanitarian Inspirator at ActionAid Liberia.

Nyanfor said Liberia has a moral obligation to protect the environment for present and future generations, but is also among countries with very low readiness to respond to climate change. He described the vote as a misalignment with Liberia’s principles, national policies and national priorities.

Nyanfor was among the civil society representatives who met with officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Environmental Protection Agency on July 3 to seek an explanation for the vote.

During the meeting, government officials said the negative vote had been cast in error . They said Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti had instructed that Liberia’s vote be withdrawn and replaced with an affirmative vote supporting the Court’s advisory opinion. Government officials also said administrative measures had been taken to prevent similar incidents in the future.

Civil Society representatives welcomed the clarification but called on the government to issue a public statement formally clarifying the circumstances surrounding the vote.

In August, Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti publicly said at a Ministry of Information Culture Affairs and Tourism press briefing that Liberia had officially written to correct its position and that the correction was registered. She said Liberia’s position was consistent with its membership in the African Group and its climate priorities at the United Nations.

The official United Nations voting record for Resolution 80/263, however, still lists Liberia as having voted “No” on May 20.

But civil society representatives did not consider the matter settled. They called for a fuller public explanation of what had happened, how the error occurred and what corrective measures had been taken. Three months after the meeting, they said that fuller clarification had still not been provided.

“An explanation is different from accountability and institutional learning,” said Dayugar Johnson, Chairman of the Management Team of the NGO Coalition, who also attended the meeting.

In an interview with this reporter, Johnson said civil society wants to know how the error occurred, what position Liberia had intended to communicate before the vote, who was responsible for communicating that position and what safeguards are now in place to prevent a similar incident.

For the civil society representatives who attended the meeting, the issue is therefore not simply that the government said the vote was an error. It is that the government has yet to publicly clarify in detail how the error occurred and what corrective steps were taken.

The original vote remains part of the official voting record, but a delegation can communicate a correction to its voting intention after a vote. United Nations guidance says such corrections should be addressed directly to the Secretariat after voting has concluded. The United Nations Delegates Handbook also says a footnote can be added to the verbatim record to reflect how a Member State intended to vote.

This means a government can clarify its intended position without changing the original tally of votes cast.

This is not the first time Liberia has had to explain an unexpected vote at the United Nations.

In December 2023, Liberia voted against a United Nations General Assembly resolution calling for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire in Gaza. The resolution passed with 153 countries voting in favor, 10 against and 23 abstaining.

The administration of former President George Weah subsequently said Liberian diplomats had voted without the President’s backing, and the Foreign Ministry requested that the vote be reversed and registered in favor of the ceasefire.

The Gaza vote and the climate vote concerning the International Court of Justice concern very different issues and happened under different administrations. But both resulted in Liberia later saying that a vote recorded at the United Nations did not reflect the position the government intended to take.

The two episodes also highlight the importance of how Liberia communicates and verifies its positions before important international votes.

For climate advocates, that issue is particularly important as Liberia prepares for the 31st Conference of the Parties.

Liberia will be going to the climate talks with several competing interests to navigate. The country needs more support for adaptation and loss and damage, while also pursuing opportunities through carbon markets and forest finance.

Those opportunities could provide resources for a country facing significant climate and development challenges. But they also raise questions about whether the benefits reach the communities that depend on Liberia’s forests and other natural resources and how those communities are protected.

“Liberia’s preparation for the 31st Conference of the Parties offers an opportunity to reinforce our position on climate justice,” Nyanfor said.

He pointed to preparations involving young people, who are expected to engage government on their priorities ahead of the climate conference.

He also said President Joseph Boakai’s recent international statements have helped reposition Liberia on climate justice. In his address at the United Nations, the President said climate responsibility must be paired with climate justice and called on developed countries to meet their financial obligations to vulnerable countries, including through the operationalization of the loss and damage fund.

For Nyanfor, those statements demonstrate that Liberia is again publicly positioning itself as a voice for climate justice.

But he said the government still needs to fulfil the commitment made during the civil society-government meeting by informing Liberians about the corrective action taken after the Court vote.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Meets New U.S. Chargé d’Affaires, Pledges Stronger Liberia-U.S. Ties
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has received newly accredited United States Chargé d’Affaires Kristin Gilmore, with both sides expressing commitment to strengthening bilateral relations through investment, trade, public health, and security cooperation.

By J.H. Webster [email protected]

The October 14, 2026, courtesy meeting marked Gilmore’s first engagement with President Boakai since the United States Government announced her appointment, as Liberia and the United States seek to deepen their longstanding diplomatic and economic partnership.



Welcoming the U.S. diplomat, President Boakai reaffirmed his government’s commitment to maintaining peace and stability while creating an enabling environment for investment and expanding bilateral cooperation for the mutual benefit of both countries.

The engagement comes amid continued diplomatic consultations between Monrovia and Washington on shared priorities, economic development, public health, and international security.

During the meeting, Gilmore expressed enthusiasm about returning to Liberia, where she previously served from 2007 to 2009, and commended the country’s progress in democratic governance and its growing role in international affairs.

“Mr. President, I want to say that it is great to be back in Liberia. I worked here before from 2007 to 2009, so it really is an honor and a privilege to come back and to see how far Liberia has come in terms of democratic governance and also Liberia’s role on the world stage,” Madam Gilmore said.

She added: “It’s very impressive. I actually have an even deeper connection to Liberia. My mother, back in the 1960s, was confirmed at an air base in California by the Episcopal Bishop to Liberia, Dilworth Houston Brown, at that time. And so my mom, before I came this time, took out her prayer book and showed me that the Episcopal Bishop to Liberia had been the one to give her her first communion.”

Gilmore described her return as a privilege and expressed her desire to work with the Liberian Government to strengthen cooperation between the two countries.

“I’m very excited at the prospect to seek out new commercial opportunities, to look for U.S. investment, to look for U.S. companies to come to Liberia to participate in your arrest agenda and to deepen our economic collaboration together,” she said.

The U.S. diplomat also highlighted public health, security, and the development of collaborative teams as areas of potential cooperation between Liberia and the United States.

Charge’ D’Affaires added: “I look forward to working on public health together, and I’m also looking forward to building teams, including through Liberians, to U.S. The Foreign Minister and I have discussed a little bit of that, and I really welcome your thoughts as well. We can together to build peace strength, Liberia Security Council together.”

Gilmore was accompanied to the meeting by Deputy Chief of Mission Robert Newsome, Ms. Tiffany Miller, and Mr. Jullion Cooper.

U.S.-Liberia Diplomatic Engagement Continues

Before meeting President Boakai, Gilmore had engaged Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti on October 8, 2026, to discuss shared priorities and Liberia’s engagement at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

According to the U.S. Embassy in Liberia, Gilmore also thanked the Foreign Minister for Liberia’s endorsement of the Proliferation Security Initiative, a framework aimed at strengthening international cooperation against the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.

“She also thanked Minister Beysolow Nyanti for Liberia’s endorsement of the Proliferation Security Initiative. The United States values Liberia as a strong partner and looks forward to working closely together,” the U.S. Embassy posted on its Facebook page on October 10, 2026.

Liberia and the United States maintain longstanding diplomatic relations covering political cooperation, economic development, public health, and international security. Both countries have continued to pursue opportunities to attract investment, expand commercial partnerships, and support Liberia’s development agenda.

Gilmore’s engagement with President Boakai signals the continuation of diplomatic efforts to build on that relationship, with investment, public health, and security cooperation emerging as key areas for further collaboration.

World.title: Liberia: Beijing 12345 Hotline Urges African Countries to Adopt Chinese Public Service Model
World.content:
BEIJING, China — Authorities operating Beijing’s 12345 Citizens Service Hotline are encouraging African countries, including Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria, to adapt China’s public service model to strengthen government accountability, improve service delivery and enhance citizen engagement.

By J.H. Webster Clayeh | [email protected]

The call was made by Feng Yingyi, Deputy Director of the Beijing Municipal Citizens Service Hotline Center, during a visit by participants of the Second Session of the China International Press Communication Center.



Feng said China is willing to share its experience with African countries and other developing nations interested in improving the way governments response to public concerns.

“In the past years we have received guests from abroad most especially from the African countries who are more interesting in our Beijing models. We are very much willing to share our success stories,” Madam Feng told journalists.

“We also hope that all countries can adapt this model to their own conditions and learn properly from these practices because we have the Chinese characteristics model. We hope that these countries can develop their own model, their own characteristics so that we can all be successful,” she stated.

A MODEL FOR AFRICAN GOVERNMENTS

The Beijing 12345 hotline provides a centralized platform through which residents can submit complaints, make inquiries and offer suggestions to government authorities.

With Beijing’s population estimated at 21.8 million, the system enables residents to communicate their concerns to relevant government departments while allowing authorities to coordinate responses and monitor cases.

For African countries such as Liberia, Sierra Leone and Mali, the model could offer lessons in establishing integrated citizen service centers that connect people to ministries, local authorities and public agencies through telephone services, digital platforms and in-person assistance.

Such systems can also help governments establish clear deadlines for resolving complaints, track cases transparently and use public feedback to identify recurring problems and improve policies.

Madam Feng called on developing countries to study Beijing’s experience while adapting the system to their respective national circumstances.

THE CHALLENGES FACING THE HOTLINE

Despite its reported achievements, Beijing’s 12345 hotline continues to face challenges associated with heavy workloads, complicated complaints, interdepartmental coordination, service quality and the long-term resolution of public problems.

According to figures cited in the center’s 2025 annual report, the hotline handled 25.802 million requests from the public and businesses in 2025, representing a 6.6 percent increase from 2024.

The report put the resolution rate at 97.3 percent and the satisfaction rate at 97.7 percent.These figures highlight the scale of the operation and the demands placed on the system as Beijing continues to address the concerns of residents and businesses.

Madam Feng said the city’s size, population and complex urban challenges require authorities to continually improve public service delivery. She acknowledged that the challenges confronting the hotline change as the city develops and public expectations increase.

“We have higher rates and higher standards for future governments. So, for the challenges, we have different stages when it comes to development. But we are trying our best to continue to overcome more challenges back to another and then we set our new higher goals for us,” Madam Feng said.

HOW THE 12345 HOTLINE OPERATES

The Beijing 12345 Citizens Service Hotline originated in 1987 as the Mayor’s Hotline. In January 2019, it was renamed the Beijing Citizen Service Hotline Center and developed into a central platform for handling public complaints and supporting urban governance reforms.

The system operates on a people-centered approach built around rapid response, efficient processing, timely feedback and proactive governance. According to information provided by the center, the hotline has handled approximately 200 million requests from residents and businesses over more than seven years.

The center’s reported resolution and satisfaction rates have remained high, reflecting its central role in Beijing’s approach to public administration. In 2025 alone, the hotline processed 25.802 million requests, averaging more than 70,000 cases daily.

To manage the workload, the center operates 750 workstations staffed by more than 1,700 operators working in shifts to provide round-the-clock services. Its mission is captured in the phrase, “When the people call, we respond,” while its service commitment is expressed through the slogan, “Let You Hear Our Smile.”

The operational framework is designed to ensure that citizens’ concerns are received, assigned to the appropriate departments, addressed and followed up. The hotline consequently serves as a link between residents’ everyday experiences and the broader machinery of municipal administration.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TRANSFORMS PUBLIC SERVICE

The visit also provided journalists with an opportunity to learn about the digital transformation of Beijing’s 12345 hotline and the growing role of artificial intelligence in public service delivery.

In line with the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints, whose annual theme is “Digital Intelligence Era and People’s City,” Beijing has upgraded its “Visit 12345” program.

The initiative includes the “12345 Hotline Digital Intelligence Innovation Lab,” which showcases developments in digital technology and artificial intelligence through interactive demonstrations and practical applications. The transformation focuses on four major areas: intelligent customer service, intelligent agent systems, intelligent workplace operations and the intelligent hub.

These innovations are intended to improve efficiency, strengthen coordination among government departments and help authorities respond more accurately to public needs.

Technology has helped transform the hotline from a traditional telephone-based complaint service into an integrated, data-driven public service and governance platform.

Through digital communication systems, big data, artificial intelligence and interconnected government information systems, the hotline can receive complaints, transfer cases to responsible departments, monitor progress, analyze recurring problems and provide feedback to citizens.

The approach supports Beijing’s Swift Response to Public Complaints reform, which emphasizes addressing citizens’ needs and resolving problems more efficiently.

TECHNOLOGY AND THE HUMAN TOUCH

Feng said the growing demands on government made technological innovation increasingly important in improving public service delivery. “Now with Science and Technological advancements, our artificial intelligence with our technological model, it is guaranteed that our services are fast running,” she said.

She added: “By the technology we can use these to analyze, to make judgment in an accurate way to identify potential risks and timely and accurate support to decision makers.”

One major area of development involves using large artificial intelligence models to improve communication between residents and the hotline.

The technology can facilitate dialogue between people and AI, automatically collect information about requests, generate work orders and direct cases to the appropriate government departments.

Through the Jingtong App, residents can access the quick-response public complaints service and use the 12345 intelligent agent. The system allows users to submit requests through an interactive process similar to a telephone conversation. It also supports text-based submissions, multilingual consultations and the uploading of photographs and videos.

These features give residents additional ways to explain their concerns, provide supporting evidence and communicate with government authorities.

MULTILINGUAL SERVICES EXPAND ACCESS

Beijing’s 12345 hotline also provides multilingual services to improve access for foreign residents and users who do not speak Chinese. According to a Beijing municipal government report published on October 11, 2026, the hotline provides services in eight foreign languages in addition to Chinese.

However, the official Beijing government website’s multilingual hotline page lists 10 languages, including Portuguese and Italian, suggesting a discrepancy between the two published sources. The multilingual arrangements reflect the importance of making public services accessible to people from different linguistic backgrounds.

For African countries considering similar systems, Beijing’s experience offers examples of how centralized complaint-handling platforms, digital technologies and multilingual communication can be incorporated into public administration.

While Feng expressed Beijing’s willingness to share its experience, she emphasized that countries should adapt the approach to their own circumstances and develop systems reflecting their national characteristics.

World.title: Liberia: Amelia Queen Cassell Turns Birthday into Hope for Chief Compound School Pupils Gbarnga Struggling to Find Chairs
World.content:
The Bong County Land Administrator also emphasized the importance of individuals taking practical steps to address community challenges instead of relying exclusively on government institutions. She expressed hope that her intervention would encourage other prominent citizens, businesspeople and organizations to identify pressing needs within their communities and contribute toward addressing them

GBARNGA, Bong County — For hundreds of children attending Chief Compound Community Public School in the heart of Gbarnga, the struggle to secure a comfortable place to sit has become an unfortunate part of their daily educational experience. While some pupils manage with broken chairs and damaged benches, others have been forced to sit on bricks or classroom floors, a situation that has recently brought the government institution under public scrutiny.

But amid growing concerns about the deteriorating learning conditions, Bong County Land Administrator Madam Amelia Queen Cassell has offered a measure of relief, donating 40 armchairs to the institution as part of activities commemorating her birthday.

The gesture, which also included the distribution of traditional lappers to elderly women selling vegetables and greens at the Gbarnga Sunday Market, marked a departure from conventional birthday celebrations, as Cassell chose to direct attention toward vulnerable residents and schoolchildren confronting everyday difficulties.



Her intervention comes at a time when Chief Compound Community Public School has been attracting attention over the shortage of classroom furniture, a problem that has continued to undermine efforts by teachers and administrators to provide a conducive learning environment.

Located in Gbarnga, the administrative headquarters of Bong County, the school occupies a position that makes its difficulties particularly troubling. The city is home to county authorities, educational administrators, lawmakers’ local offices and other influential stakeholders whose responsibilities include promoting development and improving public services.

Yet, within this same urban setting, children attending one of the city’s government schools continue to struggle with something as basic as finding a proper chair during classroom instruction.

With an enrollment reportedly exceeding 1,500 pupils, the institution has experienced increasing pressure on its limited furniture, leaving administrators to manage overcrowded classrooms with insufficient desks and chairs.

Recent reports about conditions at the school have drawn attention to pupils sitting on bricks, damaged benches and classroom floors while attempting to follow lessons. Some students reportedly carry chairs from

their homes, while others rely on makeshift seating arrangements that provide little comfort during lengthy instructional periods.

The situation has also raised concerns about educational inequality, particularly for children from low-income households whose parents are unable to purchase chairs for their use.

Although the 40 armchairs cannot accommodate the school’s entire student population, they represent immediate assistance to children who might otherwise continue attending classes without suitable seating

Reports that some pupils have stayed away from school because of the furniture shortage have added urgency to calls for intervention, with residents questioning how such conditions can persist in the heart of a city where many of the county’s decision-makers are based.

It is against this background that Cassell’s birthday donation has taken on significance beyond the number of chairs presented. Although the 40 armchairs cannot accommodate the school’s entire student population, they represent immediate assistance to children who might otherwise continue attending classes without suitable seating.

Cassell said her decision to support the school was motivated by a desire to make her birthday meaningful through service to others. According to her, the occasion presented an opportunity to reflect on the needs of people within her community and provide assistance where it could make a difference.

She explained that children should be encouraged to pursue their education under conditions that promote concentration, dignity and academic achievement.

The Bong County Land Administrator also emphasized the importance of individuals taking practical steps to address community challenges instead of relying exclusively on government institutions. She expressed hope that her intervention would encourage other prominent citizens, businesspeople and organizations to identify pressing needs within their communities and contribute toward addressing them.

For Chief Compound Community Public School Principal Moses Plator, the donation represents a welcome response to an issue that has remained a serious concern for the institution. Plator expressed appreciation to Cassell for recognizing the plight of the students and making their welfare part of her birthday activities.

He noted that the school’s administration has continued to face difficulties providing adequate seating for its growing population, describing the shortage as a challenge that affects both students and teachers.

The principal said the donation demonstrates that meaningful assistance to public schools does not always require large-scale projects, but can begin with individuals identifying specific problems and responding according to their abilities.

Plator said, “We want to sincerely appreciate Madam Amelia Queen Cassell for this important gesture toward our school. The fact that she decided to remember our students while celebrating her birthday means a great deal to us. We have been experiencing serious challenges with classroom furniture, and anyone who understands the situation at Chief Compound Public School will appreciate the importance of these 40 armchairs. They will provide some relief to our children and help create better conditions for learning. We are grateful that she has recognized education as something deserving of her personal attention and support.”

Plator explained that the institution’s furniture shortage has become increasingly difficult to manage because of the number of children seeking education at the school.

He said the challenge extends beyond the physical discomfort experienced by pupils, noting that inadequate seating can interfere with classroom organization and make it difficult for teachers to maintain an effective instructional environment.

According to him, a child who spends several hours sitting on an uncomfortable surface may struggle to concentrate fully on lessons, while teachers must devote additional attention to managing seating arrangements instead of focusing entirely on instruction.

He stressed that the donation should serve as a reminder to county authorities, educational stakeholders and other concerned citizens that improving public education requires consistent attention to the basic needs of students.

The principal further observed that the school’s location in central Gbarnga should make it easier for concerned individuals and institutions to witness its difficulties firsthand.

He expressed hope that the recent public attention surrounding the furniture shortage, together with Cassell’s intervention, would encourage broader efforts to improve conditions at the institution.

“Our school is situated right here in Gbarnga, the capital of Bong County, where government officials, education authorities and many prominent citizens are carrying out their responsibilities every day. Yet, we are still struggling to provide enough chairs for our children. Madam Cassell has taken an important step, and we appreciate her for that. However, the need remains enormous, and we are appealing to other well-meaning individuals to follow her example. We want a situation where every child who comes to Chief Compound Public School can enter the classroom and find a proper place to sit and learn. Education is everybody’s responsibility, and we believe that with collective support, these challenges can be addressed,” Plator said in a second proposed quotation requiring verification.

Beyond the school compound, Cassell extended her birthday outreach to elderly women at the Gbarnga Sunday Market, where she distributed several pieces of traditional lappers.

The beneficiaries included women who depend on selling greens, vegetables and other locally produced agricultural commodities to generate income for their households.

Cassell acknowledged the difficult circumstances under which many elderly market women operate, noting that some spend long hours at the market despite their advanced ages and limited financial resources.

She said their contributions to family welfare and the local economy deserve greater recognition and support. The women welcomed the assistance and expressed appreciation for being included in the birthday activities.

They described the gesture as a demonstration of concern for ordinary people whose daily struggles often receive limited public attention. Meanwhile, the challenges confronting Chief Compound Community Public School remain far from resolved.

World.title: Liberia: Agriculture Minister Unveils US$370 Million Investment Portfolio in Rome, Rallies Global Investors to Boost Food Production
World.content:
Rome, Italy– Agriculture Minister Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah has unveiled a US$370 million agricultural investment portfolio at the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Hand-in-Hand Investment Forum in Rome, rallying international investors, development finance institutions and agribusiness leaders to support Liberia’s drive to boost domestic food production, reduce import dependence and create thousands of jobs.

By Augustus D.R [email protected]

Minister Nuetah, accompanied by a high-level Liberian delegation, is attending the 2026 World Food Forum, being held from October 8–16 at FAO headquarters under the theme, “Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow.”



The gathering brings together government leaders, investors and development partners to advance agricultural investment, innovation and global food security.

Presenting Liberia’s investment opportunities on Wednesday, October 14, under the theme, “Liberia: From Import Dependence to Food Self-Sufficiency,” Minister Nuetah outlined four priority investment areas: US$243 million for rice, US$70 million for cocoa, US$32 million for cassava and US$25 million for maize.

“Liberia should not remain a country with abundant agricultural potential that depends heavily on imported food. We must turn our land and natural agricultural endowment into food, wealth, employment and prosperity,” the Minister declared.

Rice accounts for the largest share of the proposed investments, reflecting the Government’s determination to reduce import dependence. Domestic production currently meets only 35 to 40 percent of national demand, while rice imports exceeded US$75 million during the first half of 2026.

With more than 600,000 hectares of potentially irrigable land, Minister Nuetah highlighted opportunities to invest in irrigation, mechanized production, modern milling facilities, and market development.

“Our ambition is not simply to grow more rice. It is to build a competitive domestic industry that serves not just Liberian consumers but continental Africa and the rest of the world,” he emphasized.

The Minister also highlighted opportunities in cassava processing for industrial starch and animal feed, cocoa production and value addition, and maize cultivation to support Liberia’s poultry and livestock industries.

The four investment opportunities are projected to benefit about 23,900 people directly and 119,700 indirectly, creating jobs, expanding markets, and improving livelihoods, particularly for smallholder farmers, women, and young people.

With agriculture contributing approximately 29 to 34 percent of Liberia’s GDP and employing more than 60 percent of the workforce, Minister Nuetah stressed the importance of private investment in unlocking the sector’s largely untapped potential.

He assured prospective investors of the Government’s commitment to facilitating investment through One-Stop-Shop services, investment incentives, agro-industrial processing zones and duty-free provisions for eligible agricultural machinery and inputs.

“Capital does not move on ambition alone. Investors need credible information, sound project preparation, clear implementation arrangements and a supportive policy environment.

The Government of Liberia(GoL) is committed to providing these,” he stated.

Concluding his investment presentation, Minister Nuetah invited international investors, financial institutions and development partners to engage directly with the Liberian delegation and explore opportunities to transform the proposals into concrete investments.

“Let us move from agricultural potential to productive investment. From import dependence to food self-sufficiency. And from underused resources to a prosperous, resilient and inclusive agricultural economy,” he urged.

The Minister thanked FAO for providing a platform to connect Liberia’s agricultural priorities with international financing, expertise, and commercial partnerships.

In a related engagement earlier in the day, Minister Nuetah participated in a high-level panel discussion titled “From Bean to Bar: Ensuring Chocolate’s Value Reaches Cocoa Farmers,” alongside senior representatives of the Democratic Republic of Congo, European Investment Bank, African Development Bank and global chocolate manufacturer Ferrero.

The discussion examined how cocoa-producing countries can secure greater benefits from the global chocolate industry through improved farmer incomes, stronger market access, sustainable production and increased investment in processing and value addition.

For Liberia, the engagement highlighted the country’s growing potential as an emerging cocoa producer in West Africa and the importance of attracting private investment in processing, aggregation, storage, and marketing to strengthen competitiveness in international markets.

The discussion also reinforced Liberia’s US$70 million cocoa investment proposal, which seeks to expand production, promote value addition and improve market opportunities for more than 40,000 smallholder cocoa farmers.

World.title: Kasempa Council qualifies for ZDSP capital grant
World.content:
Kasempa Town Council has qualified for a second capital grant from the Zambia Devolution Support Program (ZDSP), paving the way for a modern market, improved waste management and extended street lighting projects in the district.

Council Public Relations Officer, Mukosela Kasalwe, disclosed that the local authority qualified under Disbursement-Linked Result (DLR) 9.1 after increasing its local revenue by five percent, the second critical criterion for the grant.

Mr Kasalwe said this in an interview with the media in Kasempa today.

“The funds will be used to construct a modern market in the Central Business District, procure a skip truck and waste bins, and extend streetlights to Mukinge Hospital,” he added.

Mr Kasalwe said the grant would translate into more infrastructure and socio-economic development for Kasempa District.

He further disclosed that the grant would also support other projects aimed at improving the welfare of Kasempa residents.

“The council qualified for its first grant of K18 million under DLR 2.1. The performance-based grant is available to local authorities that meet minimum set standards and is intended to strengthen institutional capacity in implementing decentralisation,

“Projects funded under the first grant include a water reticulation system at Nselauke Market, solar street lights in the Central Business District, and the procurement of a tractor and trailer,” he added.

Mr Kasalwe said the latest qualification followed a rigorous and transparent assessment by the ZDSP, which recognised its transparency, commitment to duty and tireless efforts.

“Kasempa Town Council celebrates this milestone with you, our esteemed members of the public, as it will enable the Council to serve you even better,” he added.

World.title: Councils urged to align their programmes towards Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development Permanent Secretary for Administration, Gabriel Pollen, has called on all local authorities across the country to align their developmental programmes with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Speaking during the installation of Choma Mayor, Honest Mweemba, Dr Pollen said local authorities should leverage their economic potential and identify programmes that can actualise the Grow Zambia Agenda for the benefit of the local people.

He said local authorities should utilise the enhanced Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to implement projects that create jobs, promote investment and stimulate local production to improve household livelihoods.

“The council has a critical responsibility to translate national development policies into services that people can see and experience,” he said.

Dr Pollen further called for enhanced cooperation among councils, government institutions and Members of Parliament to ensure development reaches both rural and urban communities.

Earlier, during a courtesy call on Southern Province Permanent Secretary, Gift Monde, Dr Pollen emphasised the need for the province to explore ways of harnessing its contribution to the presidential target of one billion dollars in beef exports.

He said Southern Province, being a cattle hub, could establish an aggregation centre for bulking and value addition in Choma to serve as a transit centre for exports.

Meanwhile, Mr Monde said the province had already begun engaging stakeholders on the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

“Since the President’s policy direction, as a province, we have already held two meetings and planned another meeting with chiefs in the province to ensure full participation of everyone,” he explained.

And Choma Mayor Honest Mweemba has pledged to work with the people of Choma to achieve the President’s vision of economic growth through the responsible and accountable use of public resources.

“Our vision is to grow the economy of Choma, as espoused in the Grow Zambia Agenda, attract investment, see youths employed and ensure that opportunities reach all corners of the district,” he said.

Mr Mweemba said he would prioritise the improvement of road infrastructure and the provision of clean and safe water for the people of Choma.

He also called on residents to unite in fostering the growth of Choma and support efforts to make the town a city by 2031.

Meanwhile, outgoing Mayor, Javen Simoloka, noted that the enhanced Constituency Development Fund (CDF) had facilitated the provision of health and education infrastructure over the past five years.

“The enhanced Constituency Development Fund has been instrumental in advancing rural development,” he said.

The installation of Choma Mayor Honest Mweemba marks the beginning of his five-year mandate.

World.title: Health workers urged to uphold professional and ethical conduct
World.content:
Minister of Health, Roma Chilengi, has warned health workers against using mobile phones and social media at the expense of providing healthcare to patients.

Professor Chilengi says health workers, especially nurses, must uphold professional ethics and conduct themselves in a manner that promotes public confidence in the healthcare system.

In a speech read for him by Serenje District Commissioner, Ellen Mibenge, during the 8th Central Province Combined Graduation Ceremony for nurses and midwives at Malcom Moffat College of Education in Serenje, Professor Chilengi reminded the graduates of their responsibility to serve patients with dedication and professionalism.

“Always remember that you are trained to care for and nurture people from all walks of life without segregation,” he said.

Professor Chilengi said the public expected nurses to perform their duties diligently while maintaining appropriate ethical conduct and attitudes.

He warned that the government would not tolerate negative attitudes towards patients, stressing that nurses found wanting would be disciplined accordingly.

Meanwhile, Nursing and Midwifery Council of Zambia Director of Practice and Compliance, David Mbewe, said the council developed guidelines on the professional use of mobile phones and social media among nurses and midwives.

Mr Mbewe said the guidelines were intended to protect patient confidentiality, maintain professional boundaries and promote ethical communication among healthcare practitioners.

And Zambia Union of Nurses and Midwives Organisation (ZUNMO) Deputy General Secretary for Finance and Administration, Ernest Semulo, said the organisation would work with the Ministry of Health to ensure that more graduates were considered for employment during this year’s health workers’ recruitment.

A total of 414 nurses and midwives graduated from Kabwe College of Nursing, Chitambo College of Nursing, Chisomo College of Health Sciences, Serenje College of Nursing and Midwifery, and Mkushi College of Applied Science.

The graduation ceremony was held under the theme, “Caring for Individuals, Empowering Families and Transforming Communities through Excellence in Nursing and Midwifery.”

World.title: Great Lakes defence experts meet in Lusaka
World.content:
The Fourth annual meeting of the Specialised Committee of Defence Experts on the Great Lakes Region has been convened in Lusaka to address regional security challenges and evaluate defence mechanisms.

During the opening of the three day meeting of Ministers of Defence, Zambia Army Commander, Geoffrey Zyeele tasked the Great Lakes Region member states to strengthen implementation of regional security and humanitarian initiatives to address persistent conflicts and emerging threats.

Lieutenant General Zyeele emphasised on peace, security and regional cooperation among defence experts from the Great Lakes Region.

“The ICGLR outlines a structured, multi – level approach to regional security, integrating technical expertise, military leadership and strategic policy guidance to foster collective action and peace in the Great Lakes Region,” Lieutenant General Zyeele said.

He also highlighted some of the critical security threats currently impacting the Great Lakes Region and surrounding areas.

Lieutenant General Zyeele said that the ongoing conflict in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains a primary concern.

He further said that the war in Sudan has resulted in a massive humanitarian crisis, prompting high – level consultations by ICGLR held last month.

“Security instability persists in South Sudan due to localised violence and intercommunal clashes, while the Central African Republic requires continued diplomatic attention.

ICGLR Deputy Executive Secretary Amb Yasir Mohammed says that the Great Lakes Region continues to face complex and interconnected security challenges to the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and the ICGLR continues to be concerned about these atrocities committed against civilians.

Mr Mohammed added that the ICGLR is working to provide impartial verification and confidence building measures.

“Your deliberations will consolidate member states’ security updates, review humanitarian challenges and provide recommendations to guide the Chiefs of Defence Forces and Ministers of Defence,” Mr Mohammed said.

ICGLR Specialised Committee of Defence Experts Chairperson Emmanuel Kasenga says that the specialised experts meeting will also focus on the situation in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Brigadier General Kasenga added that a report will be done and forwarded to all the leaders of the member states.

“In order for us to put into practice a surveillance system in the Eastern side of DRC, this situation will be our focus of examination during this meeting, your combined intelligence and expertise will help us come up with a report that will be distributed to member countries,” he said.

World.title: BOXING: Kanyanta rallies support for Zambia’s IBA trip
World.content:
Retired boxing star Kennedy Kanyanta has appealed to government and the corporate world to help Zambia participate in this month’s International Boxing Association (IBA) Africa Elite Men’s and Women’s Championship in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The Zambia Boxing Federation (ZBF) is struggling to raise K1.2 million needed for Team Zambia to travel to Kinshasa for the championship slated for October 19 to November 1.

Zambia is expected to field 14 boxers – seven men and seven women – at the continental showpiece.

Kanyanta, who is now a boxing coach and 2002 Commonwealth Games gold medallist, said Zambia, as a powerhouse in African boxing, cannot afford to miss the tournament.

“It is very important that Zambia participates in the IBA tournament coming up in DR Congo. That is where our prowess could be shown as a nation,” Kanyanta said.

“As a powerhouse in African boxing we need to continue exposing our boxers to international competitions.”

The former national boxing coach said international exposure is critical for the development of local pugilists and technical benches.

“Such tournaments help coaches to assess areas of improvement for our boxers. The other important thing is that the IBA tournament will help to upgrade the standards of our boxers as they are exposed to such international games. Exposure is very important to the boxers,” he said.

National Coach Charles Kangwa has drawn his provisional squad from Green Buffaloes, Green Eagles, Red Arrows and Exodus boxing stables.

At his peak, Kanyanta won bronze at the 2007 All Africa Games and the African Boxing Union (ABU) bantamweight title.

PROVISIONAL SQUAD

Men: Mengo Mwale, Emmanuel Katema, Albert Ngulube, Andrew Chilata, Gabriel Mukuka, Gerald Kabinda, Elias Banda, Nene Mahonga and Jonathan Mwiinga.

Women: Catherine Mwape, Felistus Nkandu, Maureen Tembo, Joana Bwalya, Chipo Kapempe, Violet Moonga and Patricia Bwalya.

World.title: Farmers Face Market Uncertainty As Treasury Freezes FRA Funding For Next Season
World.content:
Small-scale farmers face uncertainty over where they will sell their maize and soya beans next year. The Government will not release any Treasury money to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) for the coming farming season, after overspending on this year’s strategic reserve purchases.

Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane confirmed that the Government bought more maize than it had budgeted for. He said purchases exceeded the initial target of 500,000 metric tonnes.

“Yes, it is true that the amount of money spent to acquire the strategic food reserves is much more than what we had in the budget. Arising from the fact that we bought more,” Dr Musokotwane said.

The decision means the agency, for years the dependable buyer of last resort for smallholder farmers, will go into the next marketing season without fresh funding from the Treasury.

Go Back to the Land Zambia executive director Cyprian Chimwendo Phiri described the announcement as a big setback for farmers who rely on the FRA to buy their crops.

“The announcement by the minister of finance that government will not release any treasury funds to the Food Reserve Agency for next year’s farming season is a sad development for small-scale farmers who depend on FRA for the sale of their produce,” Mr Phiri said.

He said the freeze raised concerns about what lies ahead for farmers under the Grow Zambia Agenda, which President Hakainde Hichilema unveiled on October 9. The five-year programme aims to double the size of the economy, create jobs and improve living standards.

Mr Phiri said the agenda held real promise for rural producers, but only if they had somewhere to sell what they grow.

“The Grow Zambia Agenda is a great opportunity for small-scale farmers to enhance and improve their livelihoods with a predictable market,” he said.

He said reliable markets were essential if small-scale farmers were to benefit from the country’s agricultural opportunities.

The overspend followed a record season. Zambia harvested about 4.9 million tonnes of maize in the 2025/2026 farming season, a historic high that left strategic stocks at record levels. Dr Musokotwane has cited those reserves as a key reason the country is better prepared for the El Niño threat that led the Treasury to cut its growth forecasts for 2027 and 2028.

The cost of building those reserves has drawn concern from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). IMF resident representative Reginald Darius flagged fiscal slippages arising from spending beyond budget allocations, singling out FRA maize purchases alongside shortfalls in revenue collection.

Mr Darius called for corrective measures. He said reforms at the FRA should help the agency stay focused on its strategic mandate and avoid spending that could undermine fiscal discipline.

The funding freeze lands as the Government finalises a new US$1.5 billion Extended Credit Facility with the IMF. That programme awaits approval by the Fund’s executive board in December.

Opposition voices seized on the decision. Leadership Movement (LM) president Dr Richard Silumbe described the suspension of FRA funding as a total betrayal of farmers by the Government.

He questioned how the Grow Zambia target of producing 10 million tonnes of maize a year by 2031 could be met without a properly funded agency.

“Mr Hichilema wants to increase maize production by 10 million tonnes of maize, but how will he achieve that if FRA is not empowered?” Dr Silumbe said.

He said Zambians should brace for harder times, pointing to the high cost of fuel, electricity and fertilisers.

The FRA question goes to the heart of the agenda’s agricultural ambitions. The national targets include 10 million tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans and one million tonnes of wheat a year by 2031, all of which depend on farmers having confidence that their harvests will find buyers.

For now, the Treasury’s position is settled. The FRA will receive no fresh Treasury allocation for the next season, and farmers preparing their fields for the coming rains must plan without the certainty of the agency’s purchases.

World.title: Zambia Cuts Growth Forecasts As El Niño And Gulf War Cloud Outlook
World.content:
Zambia lowered its economic growth forecasts for 2027 and 2028 to 4.9 percent and 5.0 percent. The previous projections were 6 percent and 7.5 percent. Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane cited the threat El Niño poses to agriculture and the prolonged impact of the Gulf war.

Dr Musokotwane announced the downgrade in Bangkok, Thailand, where he is attending this week’s annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group.

The weather threat is serious. Global forecasters predict that this year’s El Niño will peak at an intensity never observed in the modern era, compounding man-made climate change. Some countries are already grappling with drought, while others face severe disruptions to monsoon rains that are damaging crops.

Zambia knows the cost of such an event. The El Niño-driven drought of 2024 forced a declaration of a national disaster after the staple maize crop was destroyed. It also caused prolonged electricity outages as the drought choked the hydro-power dams.

The minister said the country is better prepared this time. Strategic maize stocks stand at a record level following this year’s bumper harvest, and the country has added substantial solar power capacity.

The figures support that confidence. Zambia recorded a historic maize harvest of about 4.9 million tonnes in the 2025/2026 farming season. Installed solar capacity rose from 178MW in 2024 to 1,027.5MW, beating the 2026 target of 1,000MW. Total installed generation capacity climbed to 4,722.3MW from 3,777MW in 2024.

Those record maize stocks came at a price. Dr Musokotwane confirmed that the Government had exceeded its initial purchase target of 500,000 metric tonnes and overspent its budget for the strategic reserve.

“Yes, it is true that the amount of money spent to acquire the strategic food reserves is much more than what we had in the budget. Arising from the fact that we bought more,” he said.

As a result, the Government will not release any Treasury money to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) for the next farming season. Go Back to the Land Zambia executive director Cyprian Chimwendo Phiri described the decision as a setback for small-scale farmers who depend on the agency to buy their produce.

The downgrade came alongside a staff-level agreement with the IMF on a new US$1.5 billion, 36-month Extended Credit Facility (ECF). The programme is subject to approval by the IMF executive board in December.

The new arrangement follows the completion in January of the previous IMF programme. That programme was approved in August 2022 and provided about US$1.7 billion. The successor is expected to address budgetary and balance-of-payments needs, preserve debt sustainability and support more diversified, private sector-led growth.

The IMF expects real GDP growth of 5.6 percent in 2026, down from the 5.8 percent it projected in January. Agriculture, mining and exports are expected to support that growth.

Copper remains the backbone of the economy. The metal contributes about nine percent of GDP, generates 72 percent of export earnings and accounts for nearly half of government revenue.

IMF resident representative Reginald Darius said Zambia is better positioned to withstand shocks associated with El Niño and other global developments. He cited improved agricultural performance, higher foreign exchange reserves and progress in power generation, and said the programme offers flexibility to respond to severe shocks.

Mr Darius also raised concern over fiscal slippages, pointing to spending above budget allocations, particularly FRA maize purchases, and to shortfalls in revenue collection. He called for corrective measures and stronger oversight of state-owned enterprises. He said reforms at the FRA should keep the agency focused on its strategic mandate.

The Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD) urged the Government to make sure the new programme protects spending on education, healthcare, social protection, agriculture and productive infrastructure. It also cautioned against new debt that could undo the gains made through restructuring.

“Macroeconomic stability is necessary, but it is not the final development outcome. The task now is to convert it into one,” CTPD head of advocacy and campaigns Natalie Kaunda said.

In Bangkok, Dr Musokotwane also urged the World Bank Group to sustain concessional financing for Africa. He called for continued international support ahead of the IDA22 replenishment.

The IMF executive board’s decision in December on the US$1.5 billion programme is the next step that will shape how the economy navigates the lower growth path now projected for 2027 and 2028.
