World.title: Mundubile, Makebi Zulu And 16 Others Ask High Court For Constitutional Bail
World.content:
Opposition leaders Mr Brian Mundubile and Mr Makebi Zulu, together with 16 others facing treason and terrorism-related charges, applied to the Lusaka High Court for constitutional bail. They contend that their continued detention without trial violates their constitutional rights. The focus on Mundubile highlights the serious nature of these allegations.

The applicants include former Anglican bishop Rt Rev Trevor Mwamba. In an affidavit supporting the application, they say they have been deprived of their liberty while the State continues to investigate the allegations against them.

Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu were the presidential candidate and running mate of the opposition Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance in the August general election. Their application now places the question of pre-trial detention squarely before the High Court, emphasizing the implications for Mr Mundubile’s political future.

The applicants made clear they are not challenging the State’s right to investigate. Their complaint is with what that investigation is being used to justify.

“We don’t dispute that the State is entitled to conduct criminal investigations, but what is in dispute is the proposition that the incompleteness of an investigation constitutes a sufficient constitutional basis for prolonged detention without judicial proceedings,” the applicants stated.

They said the law guarantees them the right to be brought before a court without undue delay. If they are not tried within a reasonable time, the law entitles them to be released unconditionally or on reasonable conditions.

The applicants pointed to the position of the prosecution itself to support their case.

“We have been deprived of our liberty while the State continues to gather the evidence which, according to the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions), is required before the case can properly be taken to court,” they stated.

The affidavit cites a September 14 statement attributed to Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri, which said investigations into the treason allegations were still ongoing. The applicants used that statement to question the continued detention of those facing terrorism-related charges.

The application also describes the circumstances of some of the arrests. The applicants said Mr Ezra Tolopo, Mr Dickson Tembo and Mr Victor Muzyamba were apprehended at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on August 1, 2026. They were then held at unknown locations for more than nine days.

The conditions of detention have also come into question. Reports earlier this week alleged that Zambia Correctional Service officers at Mukobeko Maximum Prison in Kabwe turned away food brought by relatives for political detainees, among them Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu. The allegation drew public condemnation from commentators, who said that even condemned prisoners are entitled to food taken to them by their families.

The applicants contend that their detention has continued without any judicial determination authorising it. They told the court they are ready to answer the charges before a competent court.

Their case rests on a distinction between investigation and incarceration. In their view, the State may take as long as it needs to build its case, but it cannot keep accused persons in custody indefinitely while it does so.

The application asks the High Court to weigh the State’s interest in completing its investigations against the accused persons’ constitutional right to liberty and to a trial within a reasonable time.

The case involves some of the most prominent figures in opposition politics, including the alliance’s presidential ticket and a former senior Anglican cleric. Its outcome will set out how the courts treat prolonged detention in high-profile security cases.

The High Court is expected to hear the bail application, with the State yet to file its response to the applicants’ affidavit.

World.title: Africa: New TB Vaccines Could Save Millions, but Africa Must Prepare Now
World.content:
interview

More than a century after the BCG vaccine was licensed, new tuberculosis vaccines could arrive in 2029. Gavi says the groundwork has to start now.

TB remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases, causing around 1.2 million deaths every year - equivalent to roughly one death every 26 seconds. Africa still records the highest rates of cases and deaths of any region. The burden remains substantial despite progress in diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

For more than 100 years, the only licensed defence has been the Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.

But now, a new generation of vaccines could offer a major breakthrough in the fight against the disease, potentially saving 7.3 million lives between 2030 and 2050, according to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. The opportunity, however, will depend on more than scientific progress. This will include ensuring that vaccines reach the countries and communities that need them most, which will require early planning, sufficient manufacturing capacity, sustainable financing and equitable access.

The next-generation TB vaccines will potentially become available from 2029. Gavi is urging governments and global health partners to prepare now, before the first products are approved.

Closing the gaps in TB prevention

Africa has made significant progress in expanding access to diagnosis, treatment and prevention. However, significant gaps remain, with many people diagnosed late or not at all, while others struggle to access treatment.

Emily Kobayashi, Director of Vaccine Programmes at Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, said these gaps allow TB to continue spreading within communities, particularly among people living in poverty, overcrowded environments and areas with fragile health systems.

"Too many people with TB are diagnosed too late, or not at all, and others fail to access treatment," she said.

Closing those gaps, Kobayashi said, will take both stronger delivery of proven interventions and new tools. She said that the existing BCG vaccine remains vital in protecting infants and young children against severe forms of TB. However, it has limited impact on pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults, who account for most TB transmission.

"New vaccine candidates are being developed specifically to address this gap," she said. "If successful, they could represent the first major breakthrough in TB prevention in more than a century."

She said that the vaccines could offer a real opportunity to dramatically reduce transmission, save millions of lives and accelerate progress towards ending one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases.

Next-generation vaccines, if proven safe and effective, could complement existing prevention, diagnosis and treatment efforts by reducing the number of people who develop infectious TB.

"Next-generation TB vaccines can help to further bend the curve, meaningfully reducing the number of people getting sick with TB," she said. "In practical terms, it means millions of families being spared the devastating consequences of TB, with fewer parents, teenagers and breadwinners becoming seriously ill or dying from a disease that remains one of the world's leading infectious killers."

GAVI Emily Kobayashi, Director of Vaccine Programmes at Gavi.

For countries with a high TB burden, she said, a successful vaccine could also reduce pressure on health systems, lower treatment costs and boost economic productivity by helping adolescents and adults stay healthy during their most productive years. However, Kobayashi cautioned that the ultimate impact would depend on the characteristics of the vaccines approved and how quickly countries could introduce them.

She said the projected 7.3 million lives saved highlights why new TB vaccines are considered one of the most significant public health opportunities in decades.

Preparing for demand and securing supply

For Africa, where TB continues to cause significant illness and death, the question is not only whether new vaccines will work, but whether they will be accessible and affordable when they become available.

Kobayashi said that figure shows where the new vaccines must be prioritised. "The greatest health impact will come from reaching the communities where the disease continues to cause the most illness and death," she said.

That is why Gavi's focus from the outset has been on readiness. If a vaccine is successfully developed and approved, the countries carrying the heaviest burden need to be able to access and introduce it as quickly as possible. "Working with governments and partners," she said, "we want those most affected by TB to benefit first."

Gavi's Early Market Shaping Roadmap for Novel TB Vaccines suggests demand could average 86 million vaccination courses a year, with high-burden countries needing substantial supplies during the initial rollout.

The roadmap estimates that global demand could average 86 million vaccination courses annually. The vaccines could also generate up to US$135 billion in economic benefits for low- and middle-income countries, according to Gavi analysis.

One of the principal risks, said Kobayashi, is uncertainty over future demand. Manufacturers must be confident that sufficient demand will exist to justify investing in production capacity before a vaccine receives regulatory approval.

Manufacturers need confidence that there will be sufficient demand for the vaccine to justify investments in production capacity before a vaccine is licensed. Without that confidence, there is a risk that supply may not increase quickly enough to roll out the vaccine broadly after the evidence comes from the ongoing trials. That is why early planning is so important, she said. Working with countries, manufacturers and partners to describe future demand and likely introduction timelines, which she said can help reduce uncertainty and encourage investments that then support adequate supply.

Between now and 2029, Kobayashi said, several things must happen in parallel.

First, vaccine candidates must successfully complete clinical trials and demonstrate that they are safe and effective. At the same time, country governments, manufacturers and global health partners need to prepare for widespread access to the vaccine. This includes understanding future demand for the vaccine, planning how it will be delivered to communities, assessing manufacturing needs, developing policy recommendations and ensuring financing is available the moment a vaccine is licensed.

Simi Vijay/WHO Low funding, COVID-19 curtail tuberculosis fight in Africa.

"The key lesson from previous vaccine introductions is that preparation cannot start after approval," she said. "It needs to begin well in advance."

Kobayashi pointed to the malaria vaccine rollout as an example of how early coordination among partners can support rapid scale-up, with preparations taking place while vaccines were still undergoing trials. It resulted in one of the fastest rollouts in Gavi's history.

For African countries, this means considering how potential vaccines would be integrated into existing immunisation and TB programmes, which populations should be prioritised and what resources would be needed to deliver doses effectively.

Beyond preventing illness and death, next-generation TB vaccines could also contribute to efforts to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR), including drug-resistant TB.

Drug-resistant TB is one of the most challenging forms of the disease because it is difficult, lengthy and expensive to treat. It can take a significant toll on individuals and families, often requiring prolonged treatment and time away from work or school. By preventing TB disease in the first place, she said, vaccines can reduce the number of people requiring treatment and help limit opportunities for drug resistance to develop or spread.

Kobayashi said that is why vaccination is increasingly recognised as an important part of the broader response to AMR alongside diagnosis, treatment and infection control. Vaccines can help reduce reliance on antibiotics and contribute to long-term efforts to combat AMR.

Making sure access is equitable

The risk with any new vaccine is that it reaches wealthier or lower-risk populations first. Gavi said its focus is on the countries with the highest TB burden, most of which are low- and middle-income.

Drawing on more than two decades of experience supporting vaccine introductions and shaping vaccine markets, she said the goal is "to help ensure that public health need drives access." If a new vaccine becomes available, she added, the countries hardest hit "should be among the first to benefit."

Why now?

Kobayashi said the urgency of preparing for new TB vaccines was underscored by the continuing toll of the disease, which claims around 1.2 million lives globally each year. Africa bears a disproportionate share of the burden, with the region continuing to face high rates of TB cases and deaths despite progress in prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

At the same time, she said, the world was closer than it had been in decades to developing a new vaccine that could protect the communities most affected by TB and responsible for much of its transmission.

"This combination of urgent need and scientific progress makes now the moment to start preparing," said Kobayashi.

She warned that the decisions made before the vaccines become available, including forecasting demand, planning delivery strategies and ensuring adequate supply, would help determine how rapidly people will benefit from these vaccines and how much impact they can ultimately have on reducing the global burden of TB.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 15, 2026
World.content:
Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case Linked to First Patient

Kenya has confirmed a second Ebola case, 10 days after a 40-year-old man died from the virus following travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) through Uganda. The new patient, a 39-year-old close relative of the first victim, was already in quarantine when he developed symptoms. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Health officials said that both cases are linked, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Authorities have traced 128 contacts of the first patient, 113 of whom are in quarantine. Efforts to find the remaining contacts continue. Kenya has maintained that travel, trade and public gatherings remain unrestricted. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Mauritius Imposes Curfew After Violent Protests

Mauritius has imposed an overnight curfew following violent protests over water shortages and the rising cost of living, marking the island's worst unrest in decades. Demonstrations escalated after a woman was shot and injured by police at a roadblock. The circumstances of the shooting were not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody. Protesters burned tyres, blocked roads and vandalised police stations and public infrastructure, prompting school and public transport closures. Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam warned that those responsible would face consequences. Police reported some overnight incidents and arrests. Analysts warn that unrest could return if water shortages persist until the rainy season in December.

Sudan's War Deepens Humanitarian and Food Crisis

Fighting between Sudan's Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season. The conflict, which began in April 2023, has displaced more than 12.4 million people and left an estimated 24.6 million facing acute food insecurity. Aid organisations warn that hundreds of thousands of young children are suffering severe malnutrition. Drought, flooding, fuel shortages and declining fertiliser supplies are worsening food production and prices. The UN's 2026 humanitarian response plan, requiring US$2.9 billion, is only 41% funded. Observers also warn that continued arms supplies and drone attacks are prolonging the conflict and increasing civilian casualties.

Amnesty Warns of Continued Abuses in Mali Despite Wagner's Replacement

Amnesty International has warned that serious human rights abuses against civilians in Mali continue despite the Russian-backed Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group in supporting Malian military operations. The organisation documented seven incidents between 2023 and 2025 in which 34 civilians were allegedly deliberately killed, alongside torture, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, looting and destruction of property. Members of Fulani, Tuareg and Arab communities along the Mauritanian border were among those most affected. Amnesty also cited allegations of abuses by Africa Corps members, including a July 2026 raid in Bombori in which six people were reportedly shot dead and three others executed. It called for independent investigations to hold accountable those suspected of war crimes and for greater protection for civilians.

DR Congo Cholera Cases Surge Amid Ebola Outbreak

The World Health Organisation has said that from January 2025 to the end of September 2026, there were more than 125,000 suspected cases of cholera and 3,644 suspected deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In 2026, there were more than 51,400 suspected cases and 1,487 deaths in 21 provinces. Most of the cases were in South Kivu, North Kivu, and Haut-Katanga, which together made up almost 60% of the cases. Response efforts are being hampered by a lack of clean water and toilets, as well as by safety concerns and problems getting to remote communities. Health authorities are expanding water chlorination, household disinfection and vaccination preparations, including a planned cross-border campaign with the Republic of Congo. The crisis comes as the DR Congo continues to battle Ebola, with neighbouring Kenya recently confirming a second case linked to the outbreak.

Close 

Foot-and-Mouth Restrictions Push Up Meat Prices in Namibia

Foot-and-mouth disease restrictions in Namibia are causing meat shortages and price increases at butcheries and restaurants as limits on livestock sales and slaughtering disrupt supplies. Butchers report rising costs for meat trimmings and cheaper cuts traditionally used to make mince and sausages, forcing some businesses to switch to more expensive cuts and raise prices. Restaurants have also increased prices for selected dishes, including rump, sirloin and T-bone steaks. Others are absorbing higher supplier costs to avoid passing them on to customers. Some small businesses say they cannot obtain livestock at all, threatening their ability to operate. The disease has spread to 17 farms in the ||Kharas region. Positive cases have also been reported in the Zambezi region.

World.title: Independent wrestling promotion bringing the sport to New Jersey town for first time in over a decade
World.content:
Independent professional wrestling is one of the last true sports where sports fans can get into an event, meet up-and-coming superstars, see a great show and leave with your shirt on your back. Tickets to shows are usually cheap, promotions – for the most part – try to keep the entertainment family friendly and you might leave with a smile on your face.

That’s what it’s all about, right?

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Titan Championship Wrestling, a New Jersey-based wrestling promotion, has made that formula work for several years. On Saturday, the company is bringing the sport back to Spotswood, New Jersey – a town in the central part of the state that hasn’t seen wrestling come through in nearly 11 years. The company will hold Resurrection and feature some of the biggest names on the scene.

"This is a great experience for the people of Spotswood or any kind of professional wrestling fan in the area," Titan Championship Wrestling co-promoter Charles DeLutri told OutKick Dropkick in a recent interview. "Wrestling has not been in that area for almost 11 years, and we're happy to bring you not only an unbelievable event, but at the same time, a portion of what we actually do here at Titan Championship Wrestling.

"We bring in any kind of sort of entertainment aspect to between the comedy style, the strong style, and the entertaining style to where that it's a fully rounded family experience for anybody to attend."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Former WWE superstar Jay Tha Gawd (formerly known as JTG), Joey Janela and Michael Fain are just some of the names set to appear at the event.

DeLutri said he’s known Janela for a long time and has worked with him closely during different points in the business. Jay Tha Gawd has been making a new name for himself on the indie scene as well, appearing in several events in the area recently.

Fain is the TCW heavyweight champion, who DeLutri thinks is someone to watch out for on the scene.

"Michael Fain has to be one of the biggest up-and-comers out there," he said. "Michael Fain has been grinding with us since almost day one of Titan Championship Wrestling. And what he's done toward that, he's taken that title toward that, it's evolved to a faction called the TBA which was him and his organization tour that he's now called the king of the titans, and he uses that name well."

World.title: 'Heartbroken' Washington state superintendent says no consequences for girls who protested transgender runner
World.content:
For one question, Camas School District superintendent John Anzalone chose not to answer as an administrator, but rather a father.

He has been navigating what may be the most contentious, controversial sports story in the country right now and understands the angst it has caused numerous teenagers.

That angst came to a head Tuesday when about a dozen runners from the Camas High School girls cross country team walked off the starting line when the gun went off in their race against Battle Ground, a fellow Washington state school. Why? They were protesting their male teammate competing against the females.

WASHINGTON GIRLS WALK OFF CROSS COUNTRY MEET IN PROTEST OF MALE ATHLETE, PARENTS REVEAL HOW IT CAME TO THIS

Last month, a Camas sophomore switched to the girls team midseason after finishing 76th in a boys race. He has since won a varsity meet and placed second in two others. Unsurprisingly, this has ballooned into a national story with teammates and opponents staging protests. Anzalone didn't take a side on the issue, but he empathizes with the students' plight.

"It's always hard to see when students are upset, let alone our families. And I know this issue has polarized our country for a long time, and this has probably added to that, right," Anzalone said. "And so, as a dad, it's always hard to see your own kids or any kids in the middle of something like this. And that's probably been the most heartbreaking for me, is to see certain students really kind of in the middle of this, right? They're kids. So that's been challenging, and that's always gonna be hard."

It's hard to know exactly how Anzalone or anyone involved with the school feels about the biological male competing in these meets after starting the year with the boys. They have been either neutral (Anzalone) or mute (the coaching staff) when asked about the topic. But at a meet in Arlington, Washington, last Saturday, numerous parents made their disapproval clear. And increasingly, the athletes are doing the same.

This isn't an easy thing to do. Despite most of the country supporting the separation of biological males and females in sports, the vocal minority can be vicious. A parent last week told me he didn't want to talk because "I don't want my house burned down," while one girl who protested last month said some of her friends stopped acknowledging her.

DAD BANNED FROM SCHOOL GROUNDS AFTER PROTESTING TRANS RUNNER COMPETING AGAINST HIS DAUGHTER

But Anzalone wanted to make clear that there will not be consequences for the Camas girls who walked off the line Tuesday.

"The girls are entitled to handle this however is best for them, and I was at the meet and it was peacefully done. And of course, we'll support whatever they want to do," Anzalone said. "I felt that this wasn't just about supporting and protecting (the male runner). This was really about supporting and providing that space for the girls who did walk off to do so and not feel any repercussions. And of course, some of them looked very sad. I think some of them were very conflicted. But they're also teenagers. They're still children."

Next on the Camas cross country schedule is the Greater St. Helen's League district meet on Oct. 21. A parent of one of the Camas runners who protested Tuesday said she isn't sure how the girls will proceed. But the district meet allows for only seven varsity runners from each team, meaning the male runner will very likely displace one of his female teammates.

Anzalone said there will be no action taken to prevent such a scenario.

WASHINGTON OFFICIALS WON'T BUDGE ON TRANS ATHLETE POLICY AFTER GIRL FILES SCOTUS APPEAL FOR ALLEGED ASSAULT

"As long as WIAA policy allows (the biological male) to run, and she's eligible to run, she'll continue running. Nothing's changed," Anzalone said. "We don't make political stances as a school district. We just won't, and we can't. And so, as long as the policy stands, we're going to follow the policy."

The male runner's midseason switch violated no rules. Under Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA) policy, students are permitted to compete on teams consistent with their gender identity. This could change soon, though. On the November 3 ballot in Washington is Initiative 638, which would require students in K-12 sports to compete on teams corresponding to their biological sex. A spokesperson for Let's Go Washington — the group behind the initiative — said the measure would take effect 30 days after the November 3 election (although delays in certifying the results could push back that timeline.)

Cross country season would be over by then, but I-638 would prevent similar situations from arising in the future.

Anzalone said Camas would comply with whatever rules are in place.

"I'm at a point where I have to stand by policy and by law," he said. "And like I said earlier, if those change or go in a different direction, we'll follow that."

The Camas School District issued its own statement on the matter Wednesday.

"Camas School District recognizes that students and community members hold differing views about athletic eligibility and have the right to express those views peacefully. Our responsibility is to ensure that school-sponsored events remain safe and respectful for all participants, staff, and spectators.

As a Washington public school district and member of the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA), Camas follows applicable state law and WIAA eligibility rules. RCW 28A.642 prohibits discrimination in public schools based on gender identity and gender expression, and current WIAA rules permit students to participate in athletics consistent with their gender identity. The district does not set these eligibility standards independently.

World.title: This sparsely populated red state quietly climbed to the top of America's financial rankings
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Of the 50 U.S. states, 24 don't have enough money to cover their bills. Meanwhile, one under-the-radar red state stands apart from the rest, according to a new analysis of state finances.

North Dakota ranked No. 1 in Truth in Accounting's 2026 Financial State of the States report, ending fiscal year 2025 with $21 billion more than it needed to pay the state's bills. That financial cushion gave North Dakota the highest "Taxpayer Surplus" in the country at $72,300.

The taxpayer surplus figure does not mean that the state's residents receive that amount of money back in their pockets at the end of the year — rather, it represents each taxpayer's share of the state's surplus under the group's methodology.

The divide between the states with surplus versus those with burden matters, especially when the economy weakens. States with stronger balance sheets have more room to weather downturns, maintain public services and meet retirement obligations, while states carrying large unfunded debts can face tougher choices over taxes, spending and borrowing when revenues fall.

THINK YOUR STATE IS EXPENSIVE? NEW DATA REVEALS WHERE AMERICANS FACE THE HIGHEST COST-OF-LIVING

North Dakota's financial position was bolstered by its Legacy Fund, a state investment fund built with oil tax revenue.

Although oil, gas and coal tax revenues declined amid lower energy prices, strong investment earnings and federal grant revenue helped offset the drop, according to the report.

North Dakota was followed in the rankings by Alaska, Wyoming, Utah and Tennessee. The five states all had taxpayer surpluses ranging from $11,400 in Tennessee to topping out in North Dakota with $72,300. Those handful of states' financial position stands in sharp contrast to nearly half the country.

The report found that 24 states did not have enough available assets to cover their financial obligations.

New Jersey ranked last, with a $162.3 billion shortfall. Truth in Accounting translates that gap into a $45,800 "Taxpayer Burden," the highest in the country. Connecticut ranked 49th, followed by Illinois, Massachusetts and California.

The bottom five states had taxpayer burdens ranging from $16,000 in California to $45,800 in New Jersey.

THE RED STATES CHARGING AHEAD WITH AMERICA'S WEALTH AS RIVALS WATCH BILLIONS SLIP AWAY

Long-term retirement obligations are a major source of pressure on state finances.

Across the country, states had $775 billion in unfunded pension liabilities and $490 billion in unfunded retiree health care obligations in fiscal 2025, according to the report.

Despite those shortfalls, most states improved financially in 2025. Strong investment returns boosted pension assets and helped reduce unfunded pension obligations, though Truth in Accounting cautioned that those gains can reverse when markets fall.

AN OVERLOOKED RED STATE QUIETLY BUILT ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST COMPETITIVE TAX SYSTEMS

World.title: Best foods for reducing dangerous belly fat and protecting heart health
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Incorporating a few nutritious staples into the diet can help reduce belly fat and, in turn, lead to underlying health benefits.

A surplus of fat around the stomach area can be an indication of visceral fat, which lies deep inside the abdomen and is linked to multiple health issues.

Overweight individuals with excess fat around their midsections tend to be at greater risk for heart attacks and strokes, Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist based in New York City, told Fox News Digital.

WANT TO DODGE THE FLU THIS YEAR? EAT THESE SECRET-WEAPON IMMUNITY-BOOSTING FOODS

Genetics certainly contribute to obesity, Aziz acknowledged, but people can change their "genetic destiny" by making healthy choices such as eating a balanced diet and exercising regularly.

Here are Aziz's recommendations for foods that can help beat belly fat and facilitate a healthier lifestyle.

1. Lean protein

Sources of lean protein such as chicken breasts and eggs are low in calories but still satisfying.

Some studies have shown that following high-protein diets can help burn extra calories, Aziz said, but consuming too much protein can increase the risk of kidney stones, heart attacks and strokes.

CLICK HERE TO 

"In general, red meats, such as beef, pork and lamb, have more saturated fat than skinless chicken, fish and plant proteins," according to the American Heart Association. "Saturated fats can raise your blood cholesterol and increase your risk of heart disease."

Edamame, tempeh and tofu are great meat-free options that still pack a lot of protein, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine.

2. Fruits and vegetables

Those trying to lose belly fat should load up their plates with vegetables that are low in calories and full of fiber, Aziz said.

Lettuce and salads are usually smart choices, and adding lean protein and healthy fats can make for a well-rounded, satisfying meal.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Aziz also recommends eating anti-inflammatory fruits that are low in sugar, such as berries.

Harvard Medical School lists apples, citrus fruits and stone fruits (like cherries and peaches) as other anti-inflammatory options, highlighting their vitamin C and fiber content.

3. Healthy fats

"Fat is a very important factor in making us lose weight," Aziz told Fox News Digital. "For decades, we were told to avoid fats and to follow a low-fat diet, but many fats are good for us."

He recommends eating a bit of fat with each meal in order to feel more satisfied while eating less. Monounsaturated fats can promote a feeling of fullness and are found in foods like olive oil, avocados, walnuts, butter and cheese.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Hydration is important, too, and Aziz recommends that those trying to lose belly fat drink lots of water, adding that they can also incorporate green tea and coffee into their diets, in moderation, as caffeine can help boost metabolism.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Avoiding refined carbohydrates and sugar will help, too, Aziz said, as they can raise cholesterol and don't keep people feeling full for very long.

World.title: Most dramatic moments from Rep Mike Lawler's fiery debate against Dem Cait Conley in battle for House control
World.content:

Tensions flared on the debate stage Wednesday night, where Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat military veteran Cait Conley to represent their suburban New York district in Congress.

Lawler is vying for a third term representing the Empire State's 17th Congressional District.

One of the few swing seats left in Congress, the race could prove decisive for which party controls the House of Representatives for the latter half of President Donald Trump's term.

Below are some of the most dramatic moments during their one-hour head-to-head on PIX11 News:

HOW ONE NYC SUBURB COULD DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE HOUSE

Lawler calls out moderator for 'focus on gangbanger' shot by ICE

While the debate was filled with the two political rivals criticizing each other, one tense moment came when Lawler turned his ire on moderator Dan Mannarino.

Mannarino had asked both Conley and Lawler what should be done to rein in Immigration and U.S. Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who run afoul of their own guidelines, invoking the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant in the Bronx by federal officers while the man's five-year-old was in the car.

Lawler pointed to the man's rap sheet and accused Democrat state leaders of creating the situation with their sanctuary policies and Gov. Kathy Hochul's recent bail reforms. He also accused Conley of supporting those policies.

The moderator began, "Mr. Lawler, I just want to follow up. The question was, how do you ensure if ICE agents do not follow through objectives, and what's the discipline —"

"I understand the question," Lawler said amid the cross-talk.

PROTESTS ERUPT IN THE BRONX AFTER ICE AGENT SHOOTS MAN DURING IMMIGRATION OPERATION

"But you didn't answer the question," Mannarino said.

"I understand the question. But here's the problem, Danny," Lawler shot back. "You guys want to focus on a gangbanger who has put people in harm's way? I want to make sure that our communities are safe."

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF MURDERING COLLEGE STUDENT DIALS INTO HEARING FROM HOSPITAL BED

Lawler and Conley clash over Sheridan Gorman's killer

The GOP incumbent notably used the immigration standoff to pivot to the case of Sheridan Gorman, a teen from his district who was shot and killed near her college campus in Chicago earlier this year. The accused is an illegal immigrant who was previously arrested for shoplifting but was never turned over to ICE due to Chicago's sanctuary policies.

Conley called Gorman's death an "atrocious crime," while Lawler repeatedly said over her, "It was preventable."

SHERIDAN GORMAN’S MOM SCORCHES DEM LAWMAKERS SHE SAYS REFUSED TO HEAR FAMILIES OF SLAIN AMERICANS

"Can I finish?" an irate Conley shot back. "It was an atrocious crime committed in Chicago. And that man should have been deported. And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent criminals."

Lawler then pointed out, however, that the man would only have been deported if the sanctuary laws were not in place — laws he has repeatedly accused Conley of supporting along with her fellow Democrats.

"This is important," Lawler began as the moderator tried to regain control. "If you think he should have been deported when he was arrested for shoplifting, he should have been turned over to ICE. Under the new law that you support, he will not be turned over to ICE and he will be released under cashless bail."

"Mr. Lawler, there's not a cross-examination round, so thank you," the moderator said.

Conley quipped at her GOP rival, "If you wanted to be the moderator, you should have volunteered."

Conley accuses Lawler of 'mansplaining' on sexual assault

At another point, the candidates were asked whether there should be a federal definition or law for consent to help stop sexual assault.

Conley took the moment to attack Lawler for being allied with Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, a fellow House Republican who has been accused of domestic violence by his wife. Miller has denied the allegations.

Lawler said their matter was "tragic' and should be dealt with in family court without blaming either side. He then accused Conley of taking money from former New York Gov. World.title: Rubio push on Greenland delivers a huge diplomatic win for US against China
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

China seeks to replace the United States as the leading global superpower and key to its strategy is securing critical sea lanes. The country that can control the fate of sea lanes will have leverage over markets and the kind of system on which global trade will rely, access to limited natural resources and a significant ability to project power far from its shores. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been planning and executing a diplomatic sweep from Panama to Greenland, and now Iceland, to box out China, protect its access and interests and establish an American advantage over the long term.

About 40 years ago, President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Reykjavík, Iceland, and initiated the start of the thaw of Cold War tensions. Rubio returned to the site of the meeting where Reagan refused to surrender his vision of a space-based missile shield to the Soviets and reminded the world that the High North still matters for American power and interests.

Standing side by side with Iceland’s foreign minister, Rubio noted that the location remains a "critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behavior and deterring our adversaries." When a reporter asked him if the United States may expand its military footprint there, he didn’t commit to plans but emphasized that doing so would require Icelandic consent. The negotiations will continue, and, though he didn’t mention Russia or China by name, those are the nations now posing acute threats to the United States and its allies.

TRUMP'S GREENLAND OBSESSION ISN’T RANDOM. HERE’S WHAT’S AT STAKE

The Reykjavík visit follows the recently secured landmark deal with the Kingdom of Denmark. This deal ensures that the United States can prevent the Chinese from establishing its habitual scheme in the Arctic. Critics of the deal have said that the negotiations between Washington and Copenhagen were "much ado about nothing," considering that China isn’t (yet) in Greenland.

This misses the point. As the ice melts, Arctic shipping routes are becoming increasingly navigable, creating new sea lanes (and thus choke points) that will shape global shipping and military posturing for decades to come. The agreement gives Washington the authority to block non-NATO commercial and military presence in Greenland, a direct role in screening and accelerating foreign investment in critical sectors, overflight, missile defense access and unrestricted undersea access across Greenland’s territorial waters.

TRUMP DECLARES VICTORY IN HISTORIC DEAL WITH GREENLAND AS HE SECURES 'PERMANENT' US MILITARY RIGHTS

Critically, the deal honors Greenland’s sovereignty, a non-negotiable issue for Denmark, while remaining in force in perpetuity, regardless of if Greenland were to ever become independent. In doing so, the deal clarifies where the 1951 treaty was silent. Dismissing the deal, perhaps due to a desire to deny the Trump administration credit, also shortchanges the Danes’ very real concessions and diplomatic skill. Furthermore, the deal came just in time for NATO, whose steadfast solidarity is key as Russia ramps up its campaign of terror attacks across the alliance to collapse support for Ukraine.

For years, both the Chinese and Panamanian governments denied China was taking over the Panama Canal. But the president said that the Chinese had illegally stationed soldiers to operate the canal, and a Chinese-owned company was illegally charging for passage to the disadvantage of the United States, which has paid billions to maintain the canal, of which 72% of all vessels (according to the U.S. government) are transiting to or from an American port.

CHINA’S INFLUENCE MACHINE: FEDERAL RECORDS EXPOSE BEIJING’S PUSH TO SWAY AMERICA

For years, the U.S. was asleep at the wheel, allowing China’s incremental, commercial expansion to dominate the canal. After Rubio’s discussions with the Panamanians, a Panamanian court ruled that the contract to operate the container terminals at the canal’s Pacific and Atlantic entrances violated the constitution, and it ended the contract.

Some have praised President Donald Trump’s "Art of the Deal" for these diplomatic successes. That is, making maximalist demands, including threats of aggression against trusted allies in the hopes of getting a deal somewhere short of the opening threat, but close to it. But that is the wrong lesson to learn here.

TRUMP’S GREENLAND DEAL SET FOR SIGNING AFTER MONTHS-LONG FIGHT OVER US CONTROL

Trump’s threats to seize Greenland by force did not help the United States achieve this deal with the Danes, who have been good allies. Instead, it created panic across NATO, which undermined the administration’s efforts to update and strengthen the alliance. Progress toward the deal only began once Trump stopped making threats in response to the blowback.

On Jan. 21, in the lead-up to the Davos World Economic Forum, Trump’s threats contributed to a sharp decline in financial markets. Polling showed 91% of U.S. voters opposed taking Greenland by military force, and Congress was decisively against it, too.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

As articulated by Rubio, the Trump administration believes the security of the United States remains linked to Europe’s and that the U.S. must make sure that NATO is strong so that it can continue to be a "deterrent against hostility" which makes "our nations and our continents safer from foreign threats and more secure for our people."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The threats were a distraction; foresight and effective diplomacy are the real story. And, on that front, Rubio won for the president and the country with significant gains over the Chinese and the Russians.

World.title: Trump touts booming economy at Montana rally, but supporters feel the pinch
World.content:
KALISPELL, Mont. — On a day when the U.S. inflation rate was shown to have climbed 3.7% over the past year, President Donald Trump said at a rally in Montana on Wednesday, “We have very little inflation.”

Trump touted a booming economy as he campaigned for Republican candidates on the final leg of a Western campaign swing, three weeks before the midterm elections.

Poverty is down and incomes are up, he told the crowd. More than $22 trillion is flowing into the country and with that record-setting level of investment, “they’re building plants all over Montana, and they’re building plants all over …”

“Everyone, we’re all having a good time,” he said.

Yet the economic resurgence he described isn’t the reality that many people say they are living.

People arrive before Trump at a campaign rally at Majestic Valley Arena, in Kalispell, Mont., Wednesday. Ross D. Franklin / AP

In interviews before Trump appeared onstage, some of the supporters who came to see him said they’re feeling squeezed by grocery, housing and fuel costs.

Moneen Ahlquist, an 84-year-old homemaker who lives in Missoula, said that she is careful to combine errands in one trip so that she can keep her car in the garage and save on gas.

“We shop at grocery stores where we can pump our gas and get a few cents off,” she said.

Megan Gurhlke, 44, who works on a dairy farm, said that three of her four family members work full time and yet, “We can’t afford stuff because the prices are so bad.”

“I represent the majority of our country,” she said. “We barely make ends meet, but we push to do it.”

If there’s encouraging news for Trump in the face of such sentiments, it’s that his supporters don’t believe he’s at fault. Some echoed Trump’s contention that former President Joe Biden is to blame for high prices. Others said that they’re prepared to be patient and wait for Trump’s policies to fully kick in and make life more affordable.

“Right now, they [prices] are getting worse,” said Gary Hanson, 67, a hardware store owner in Kalispell. “It’s going to take a long time to turn everything around and that’s what Trump is looking at.”

As she stood in line to see the president, Jennifer Piperakis, 53, mentioned that filling her truck with diesel fuel costs her $200.

“Gas prices are outrageous,” she said. Still, she said, “I love President Trump. I love what he’s doing for veterans. He’s not about himself. He’s about trying to help. My husband is a veteran. Biden didn’t do anything for him.”

Elections often hinge on the economy. Polling suggests that voters’ unhappiness with economic conditions could cost the Republicans their slim congressional majority.

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., speaks before Trump at a campaign rally at Majestic Valley Arena, in Kalispell, Mont., Wednesday. Ross D. Franklin / AP

Trump’s message as he campaigns across the country is that people aren’t hurting; they’re thriving. In his speech Wednesday, he cited stock market gains that are boosting retirement savings. He nodded to high fuel costs but predicted that they’ll drop once the Iran war ends.

Defending the tariffs he’s imposed on foreign countries, he said that they’ve produced considerable wealth.

“We’re richer now,” he said. “We’re making more money now there than we ever — and we have more jobs than ever before. Remember that.”

As for inflation, he said “we don’t have inflation.”

World.title: Suspicious white powder sent to election offices in 3 states
World.content:
Secretaries of state’s offices in Ohio, Louisiana and Oklahoma were sent packages this week with mysterious powders, just weeks before the offices are set to oversee the midterm elections.

Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it.

The national groups representing secretaries of state and state election directors expressed concern about the suspicious letters in a letter Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement.

“Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities,” the statement added.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose on Wednesday echoed the sentiment that election officials should “never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties,” adding that his office was working with state and federal law enforcement following the mailing targeting it.

“Fortunately, delivery of the letter was preempted by investigators at the U.S. Postal Service, who are dealing with similar mailings sent to election officials in multiple states,” LaRose said, while thanking the Postal Service.

Ohio is one of a few states facing tight elections in just a few weeks.

The election bodies of Oklahoma and Louisiana, facing fewer contested elections, were threatened Tuesday, when each state announced it had received packages with suspicious powders.

“We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections. Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections,” Oklahoma State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax said in a statement.

Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams said in an email Wednesday that an employee in the office’s Election Division opened a package containing a white powder and was taken uninjured to the emergency room “as a precaution.” Williams added that law enforcement did not find evidence of “harmful substances.”

“Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Williams said.

Louisiana State Police said in a statement that it responded to reports of a white powdery substance found in a package at the secretary of state’s office.

“LSP is working with the FBI to identify the substance, which was successfully recovered and submitted for testing at the FBI’s crime lab. No employees have reported injuries or adverse health effects related to the incident,” state police spokesperson Jacob Pucheu said in an emailed statement.

NBC affiliate KTAL of Shreveport reported Tuesday that the Baton Rouge building was evacuated.

The FBI declined in an email to confirm specific instances or locations. The agency said in a statement that it and the Postal Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the FBI’s national press office said.

It is not the first time that states’ election officials have faced threats near an election. In 2024, at least 20 states were targeted with letters containing suspicious powders. In one instance in Utah, a mailing with a suspicious powder was intercepted, with a letter signed by a so-called United States Traitor Elimination Army.

The mailings prompted several agencies, including the Justice Department, to release guidance about protecting personnel against hazardous materials.

World.title: DOJ threatens legal action against California over alleged noncitizen voters
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizen individuals on their voter rolls.

Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter on Tuesday sent letters to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan with a list of names of possible noncitizens identified by the federal government. The letters demand they review the list by noon on Thursday.

“Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote in the letters, which was obtained by NBC News.

McCotter wrote that the DOJ provided a password-protected thumb drive with a list of individuals the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the 2026 election. He asked that county election officials “segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots” until their citizenship status was determined.

“This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement. “It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.”

Reuters first reported on the letters.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said the federal government has no authority supporting its demands.

“They can send the letter,” he said. “California doesn’t have to do anything about it.”

Federal law prohibits systemic list maintenance within 90 days of a federal election. At this point, less than three weeks out from Election Day, the only changes to the voter rolls can come from individualized information, like notification from the Social Security Administration that someone has died.

A DOJ spokesperson said the department is asking California to sequester ballots, not change their voter list.

In a statement Wednesday, Logan said his office had not accessed the thumb drive the DOJ provided “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” He added, “We do not consider the device a secure medium.”

“Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office,” Logan said in the statement. “Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”

Weber said in a statement Wednesday that the DOJ did not provide a list of purported noncitizens to her office and that the administration lacked the legal authority for its request.

“The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said in the statement. “California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed — as always — to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election.”

All registered voters in California receive mail-in ballots, which started going out on Oct. 5.

The legal threats came amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizen individuals. Trump has long made unfounded claims that voting is marred by widespread fraud.

Election officials in several states — including Georgia, Connecticut, Nevada and Washington state — say they have received federal subpoenas in recent months for election records.

Some officials said they fear these actions were designed to set up possible legal challenges after the midterm elections.

“What we have seen is some groundwork laid out for postelection challenges,” said Stuart Holmes, the director of elections in Washington state. “Whether that’s the seizure of voting equipment, ballots themselves, tabulation equipment ... we’re preparing for any and all eventualities in that case.”

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said officials in his state are also preparing for potential challenges to this November’s results. He added that he viewed the administration’s moves as “an effort to dissuade people from participating in the elections.”

“You have a president who’s trying to choose the voter base rather than the voters choosing the elected, and that’s not how our democracy works,” he said in an interview. “It’s the people control our elections, and when you try to take that control out, you do it through intimidation, you do it through threats, and you do it by trying to dissuade people from participating.”

Levitt agreed with the election officials’ conclusions.

“Are they laying the groundwork to say that voting was fraudulent? Of course they are, 100% they are,” he said, referring to the Trump administration. “Is the boy who cried wolf going to cry wolf? Yes, that’s what the boy who cried wolf does.”

Since Trump took office, his administration has brought over 100 cases involving allegations of voting by noncitizens. More than 154 million people voted in the 2024 election, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

During the second Trump administration, the DOJ has sought voter registration data from every state in the country. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing.

World.title: ‘We’re done’: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries as anger mounts with Trump
World.content:
Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of betraying Kyiv with the “dangerous” withdrawal of support critical to its defense against Russia.

Ukraine held off on attacks for three days after President Donald Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, but accused Russia of repeatedly attacking its power grid. Zelenskyy voiced mounting frustration over the Kremlin’s failure to abide by the truce, and what he sees as U.S. attempts to pressure Kyiv after gaps in intelligence sharing on Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink internet service.

Satellite internet functionality while in motion via Starshield — the military version of the SpaceX service — had been restored Thursday morning, according to a source in Ukraine’s defense ministry, speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the topic.

In an interview with the Financial Times, published early Thursday, Zelenskyy indicated his patience had already been exhausted.

“The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.

Zelenskyy acknowledged Wednesday that he felt betrayed by what was happening with the U.S. Sergei Supinsky / AFP via Getty Images

Hours later a fire was reported at an oil refinery in the western Ryazan region, Gov. Pavel Malkov said. The Russian defense ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”

Ukraine has been reeling from a sudden shift from Trump, who struck a diesel deal with Russia in an apparent bid to relieve pressure at the pump ahead of the Midterm elections. He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil facilities and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as leader.

Trump’s “energy ceasefire” appeared to take both sides by surprise. He has blamed the Ukrainian campaign for fueling a rise in energy prices, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.

The moves caused frustration and confusion in Ukraine and Europe, intensifying concerns over how much of an ally the U.S. remained in the fight against Russia.

Ukrainian attacks on oil facilities have sparked fuel shortages inside Russia. AFP via Getty Images

That worry was exacerbated Wednesday when Kyiv said it was facing the slowing down of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite terminals, disrupting battlefield missions and its ability to intercept Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities.

Ukraine was swarmed by Russian drones on Wednesday, and since midnight on Thursday more than 850 had filled Ukraine’s skies, Zelenskyy said. “And this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted,” he said, referring to the Starlink slowdown.

Musk, a staunch ally of Trump, wrote on social media that decisions on restricting the use of Starshield, the military version of his company’s satellite system, were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.

Overnight, Musk said it was “time for Zelenskyy to go.”

The defense ministry source said Kyiv was still seeking clarification on the reasons for Wednesday’s throttling of the technology, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communication, drone operations and air defense.

Ukrainian officials said Starlink Starlink was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months. Evgeniy Maloletka / AP

It came amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. has stopped or limited the sharing of critical military intelligence with Ukraine, after Zelenskyy said several ballistic strikes on Kyiv did not come with the usual advance warning from its partners.

Coming only days Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves were likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

Ukraine was concerned that the chain of events amounted to an effort to pile pressure on Kyiv and backtrack on years of U.S. promises to help fend off the Russian invasion, one of the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukraine relies heavily on U.S. intelligence and the Starshield satellite network to defend itself against Russian drone and missile attacks and to target Russian forces with its own drones. A reduction in intelligence assistance or satellite access could seriously undermine Ukraine’s battlefield prospects just as winter sets in, according to military experts.

Ukrainian military officials were told by their U.S. counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence,” Zelenskyy said, according to FT, although it was subsequently presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch.

The withdrawal of the intelligence and simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet were “dangerous” for Ukraine at a time when Russia is intensifying its strikes, he told the newspaper, adding that fighting without the U.S. would be “very difficult.”

In a separate interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s actions.

The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on Zelenskyy’s accusations and the renewed Ukrainian strikes.

World.title: Harry and Meghan make first joint appearance since returning to U.K.
World.content:
LONDON — Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, were making their first royal-style public appearance together on Thursday since they returned to the United Kingdom with their two children.

Harry, 42, and Meghan, 45, were visiting three charities in Nottingham, as they look to rebuild their image in Britain six years after walking away from royal life.

Nottingham, a city in central England known as the setting for the famous “Robin Hood” legend, holds a special place in the couple’s history as the place where they made their first joint public appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.

“It’s almost a full circle moment because it looks very much like a royal engagement,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said.

The events on Thursday began with a visit to the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity in Nottingham that Harry has visited before, including just last year. They will also visit the region’s biggest food bank, Himmah, and Epic Partners, which offers disadvantaged young people mentoring programs, sports and education.

Noting that the couple will be visiting a charity Harry has a “long history with,” Nash said they were certain to “get a warm reception” given their “long connection with it.”

But they have not always received such a warm welcome since their return to the U.K. with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5.

The couple remains locked in a public row with Buckingham Palace about their status and their lack of publicly funded police protection.

A letter sent on behalf of King Charles III to senior government and military officials confirmed Harry and Meghan remain nonworking members of the royal family. A spokesperson for the couple told NBC News they were “surprised” by the letter, though they accepted that status when they left Britain for a quieter life in Montecito, an affluent coastal enclave in Santa Barbara.

Their relationship with the royal family has been strained in the years since, with the couple leveling explosive allegations of racism and bullying in their Netflix documentary “Harry & Meghan” and in Harry’s memoir, “Spare.”

News of their return to the U.K. sent shockwaves through the British media, and the couple have faced other complications as they settle back into British life.

Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet in England, in a video posted by Meghan to Instagram last month. @meghan / via Instagram

“It was a bit of a bumpy road for Harry and Meghan,” Nash said. “They had to had to move their children from their school after just two days, but I’m told they’re settling in well now and Archie and Lili are very happy at their new school.”

The couple’s royal-style visit to Nottingham will renew questions about their security.

With or without it, Nash said, “this is them dipping their toe back in the water” and “nothing’s stopping them.”

“They don’t need the palace’s permission to do this,” she said.

World.title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
World.content:
For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.

Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

Sens. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., and Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn. Getty

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.

I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened. -Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.

Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”

Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.

Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the first nine months of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.

The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”

Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began.

Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.”

“They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”
