World.title: Pakistan school collapse kills almost 30 students and a teacher
World.content:
Islamabad — Almost 30 students and a teacher were killed Thursday when the roof of a private school collapsed in the Pakistani city of Peshawar, local officials said.

The bodies of 17 children were brought to Lady Reading Hospital in the city following the incident, in addition to the body of a female teacher, Mohammad Asim, a spokesperson for the hospital told CBS News, adding that some survivors were also admitted in critical condition.

At least 29 people were killed in total after the collapse at the Al-Khair Education Center in Peshawar's southwest Dir district, according to Asim and other local officials.

The cause of the disaster remained unconfirmed, but a witness told CBS News the building appeared "not suitable" for use as a school, and a local police official said there was ongoing construction on the roof that could have overweighted the structure.

"We have taken out at least 45 children," district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan said, according to the Reuters news agency.

Residents gather during a search operation after a roof collapsed at a school in Peshawar, Pakistan, Oct. 15, 2026. Abdul MAJEED/AFP/Getty

Mahwish Zaman, a teacher who was injured in the collapse, told the Associated Press after regaining consciousness in her hospital bed that the school had about 1,200 students enrolled, and she was in her class when the roof collapsed. She described it as feeling as if the sky had fallen.

Zahir Hussain, who lives a couple of blocks from the school, told CBS News he was walking to work when he saw people running out onto the street.

"I rushed to the spot and the school with others to see what had happened," he said. "Apparently first-period classes had just started … The building was overcrowded. The lesson had barely begun" when the collapse occurred.

He said the school was in a relatively small residential building on a narrow street, and that it catered mainly to children from low-income families. Signage on the outside of the building indicated that there were classes for both boys and girls.

"The parents and families were in unbearable pain. The street was extremely narrow, which made it difficult for rescue teams to reach the site quickly," he told CBS News.

"The building was not suitable for use as a school at all. It is a very tragic incident, seeing dead innocent children's bodies left me silent, and it was extremely painful," Hussain said, calling it a "heavy tragedy for parents and the entire Dir colony."

"It was a weak building structure," Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said, according to Reuters. "Its roof was overweight with construction on a weak structure that caused the collapse."

World.title: Exclusive video shows Cornell University Faculty Senate meeting
World.content:
Exclusive video offers insight into Wednesday's high-stakes meeting at Cornell University.

The school's president, Michael Kotlikoff, faced questions from faculty Wednesday over the handling of sexual assault allegations as the faculty considers a resolution of no confidence in the school's administration.

This comes nearly two years after a student reported being gang-raped at a fraternity house. Earlier this month, the university announced former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will lead what they call a "comprehensive independent review" of its handling of sexual misconduct claims, including the 2024 case.

Additionally, on Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced sweeping changes, saying Cornell will work with New York State Police on an arrangement to bring in independent experts to investigate sexual assault allegations.

At Wednesday's meeting, faculty debated whether they have confidence in the university's leadership to address sexual assaults.

The meeting was closed to reporters and the university said no cameras were allowed because it would inhibit the debate, but CBS News New York investigative reporter Mahsa Saeidi obtained access through a source.

Part of the video shows a speaker questioning the university president about the outside investigation.

"President Kotlikoff, can you name all of the different kinds of assaults, both sexual and otherwise, on men, women and children that the outside investigators will be examining, and how far will they go back in time in their investigations?" one speaker asks.

"That is a board review. I don't dictate that review. It's an open review. It does have a very broad mandate. I don't know how far back they're going to go, frankly, but I will say that we're open to anything they ask," Kotlikoff says.

Additional video shows a separate exchange.

"We've seen this administration suppress our academic freedom, as well as our students' voices over the past few years," another speaker says.

"What academic speech has been restricted?" Kotlikoff asks the speaker.

"Since 2023, the administration has punished over 80 students for nonviolent speech," the speaker replies.

Another meeting will take place on Oct. 28. After that, faculty members will have about one week to submit their vote on the no-confidence resolution.

Some faculty members told CBS News New York that the 2024 case is just the tip of the iceberg, saying other students and former students have shared their own experiences of sexual assault and they've been too afraid to report what happened.

All seven men who have been accused in that 2024 case have denied the allegations.

World.title: DOJ tells California to review whether noncitizens got mail ballots
World.content:
Washington — The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming November election despite not being U.S. citizens, according to a letter reviewed by CBS News.

In the Oct. 13 letter, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter imposed a 48-hour deadline to review the list of names, which were provided on a password-protected thumb drive, to determine the citizenship status of each individual.

"For individuals whom you cannot independently confirm citizenship status, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals' vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined," McCotter wrote.

"If individuals on the list have not yet been sent a vote-by-mail ballot, take all immediate and reasonable steps to not provide a ballot to those individuals until we confirm their citizenship status," he added.

In a statement, California Secretary of State Shirley Weber confirmed that her office received a letter from the Justice Department, but said the federal government "did not provide the list [of alleged noncitizens] to our office."

"The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said.

Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder/county clerk of Los Angeles County, confirmed he had received the letter but said the records were on a USB drive that his office had not yet accessed.

"The letter included a USB drive purportedly containing the referenced records, along with a handwritten note providing a password. We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols," Logan said in a statement. "We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records."

He added: "Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching."

Similar letters were also mailed out to other counties in the state, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The move comes after Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July told California's secretary of state that the government believed there were noncitizens listed on its voter rolls.

Reuters was the first to report on the letter.

McCotter's demands represent the latest effort by the Trump administration to press blue states on whether they have people who are unlawfully registered to vote on their rolls.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

Since President Trump took office, the department has criminally charged more than 100 people with voter fraud-related crimes.

The crackdown comes as the president has continued to allege, without evidence, that the 2020 election was stolen due to voter fraud.

Experts have repeatedly found across multiple studies that the incidents of voter fraud are minimal and have not been numerous enough to impact the outcome of an election.

A data analysis published last month by Reuters found that states may have added more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens to voter rolls since 2000 because of software glitches and clerical errors that came about during the processing of driver's licenses and state IDs.

That figure is small relative to the number of registered voters. In the 2024 election, Census data showed there were about 174 million people registered to vote.

World.title: Fossil overlooked for 100 years ID'd as new dinosaur species
World.content:
London — A previously unknown species of dinosaur — a "long-clawed predator the size of a tiger" and a cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex — has been identified from a fossil originally found 100 years ago, but which remained hidden away in a British museum until recently.

The species has been named Invictibellatrix amberina, and it belongs to a group of two-legged carnivores known as megaraptorans according to an article published in the Royal Society Open Science research journal.

Megaraptorans were closely related to the group of dinosaurs T. rex originated from, the tyrannosaurs. Unlike T. rex, however, scientists say Invictibellatrix did not attack prey with its mouth, but with its long arms and giant curved claws.

Researchers believe the dinosaur would have been between 10 and 13 feet long and almost 5 feet tall. Its body would have had feathers, and it would have hunted smaller dinosaurs, lizards and mammals.

An artists' rendition depicts the newly identified dinosaur species Invictibellatrix amberina. Sergey Krasovskiy and Pedro Salas/Royal Society Open Science

The fossil that led to the discovery sat in a drawer at the Natural History Museum in London for nearly 100 years, having first been obtained by the vaunted institution in 1924.

Dr. Cassius Morrison of University College London, the lead author of the article that announced the discovery, called it a "real mystery that the fossil was overlooked for so long."

Morrison wrote that while Invictibellatrix "was not the apex predator of its time," it would have been a formidable threat to humans if they had coexisted with the species — even "more dangerous than a T. rex."

"We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight," he said. "They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small."

The fossil itself is a chunk of the back of a skull. It was one of 1,000 specimens originally discovered by Reginald Walter Tooley on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England, and it was then acquired by the Natural History Museum.

Photos show the fossilized portion of a braincase that belonged to an Invictibellatrix amberina, found in 1924 on the U.K.'s Isle of Wight, and identified a century later by a team of researchers at University College London. Royal Society Open Science

Invictibellatrix lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 120 million years ago, and is one of the smallest and earliest known members of the megaraptoran group.

To understand Invictibellatrix, researchers first took a CT scan of the fossil to create a 3D model of that part of its skull. The results were compared with the skulls of other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs, such as tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and raptors. A number of unique features led researchers to conclude they had discovered a new species.

Invictibellatrix is Latin for "unconquered female warrior" and amberina refers to the amber found in the rocks where the fossil was discovered. The researchers said by naming the dinosaur Invictibellatrix, they wanted to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in the face of such odds."

World.title: Mystery of Amelia Earhart's plane could be solved in days
World.content:
A group of American researchers believes it may be days away from finding what remains of the missing plane of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart off a remote island in the South Pacific.

An expedition team led by Steve Schultz from Purdue University and Richard Pettigrew from the Archaeological Legacy Institute on Wednesday began the painstaking search for what could be Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.



"We're looking at the land, we're looking for artifacts that might relate to Amelia Earhart," Pettigrew told CBS News on Wednesday.

"We're still very much in the data-gathering phase," Schultz added.

Members of the expedition are searching a lagoon off the coast of Nikumaroro. They are focused on inspecting what is known as the Taraia Object, a visual anomaly that has been visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938 but was first noticed in satellite imagery in 2020. That satellite imagery is what inspired the new expedition.

Stormy weather hindered their efforts on Wednesday, but expedition members said they expect to have a definitive answer on the object in the coming days.

U.S. researchers search for Amelia Earhart's plane on Nikumaroro in October 2026. Purdue University

The search area is so remote, it took the 17-member expedition team five days at sea to reach it.

However, the team is confident it will be able to say in just a matter of days whether they have found Earhart's plane.



"Our next step is complete analysis of the data that we gathered and then to begin using a hydraulic dredge to remove sediment from the bottom," Pettigrew said.

Earhart went missing on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first person to fly around the equator. Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished 22,000 miles into their expedition.

Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, which is located about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. It's about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, which, according to researchers, was the final destination of Earhart and Noonan's journey around the equator.

Their disappearance has become one of the world's greatest mysteries.

"We're the only people who have put together a plan to do something like that," Pettigrew said. "So it's entirely new."

World.title: Why AI could end the price tag as we know it
World.content:
The humble price tag has long served as a common measure of value for consumers. Now, experts warn that artificial intelligence could allow retailers to charge people different prices based on their personal data.

Lindsay Owens, CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a nonprofit think tank focused on economic policy, said AI threatens to upend universal prices for consumers. That could overturn norms that have been in place since the 1860s, when pioneering retailer John Wanamaker introduced fixed prices in his Philadelphia department store.

"The posted price has been paramount for consumers, and I do think the price tag is at risk of extinction," Owens, a consumer protection expert and author of "Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet," told CBS News. "Predictability is really essential if you're on a budget, and knowing how much something is going to cost from one week to the next is part of what the posted price offered."

A price tag just for you

AI-enabled pricing builds on so-called dynamic pricing, which companies have used for decades to adjust prices in response to shifting patterns of supply and demand, weather, time of day and other factors.

Firms aren't stopping there, however. Today, retailers are starting to test new ways of pricing goods based on who you are, where you live and myriad other insights gleaned from AI — an approach known informally as personalized or "surveillance" pricing, Owens said. AI also gives companies a powerful new tool to continually analyze vast amounts of disparate data to gain insights into consumer behavior.

"These technologies may empower firms to collect, process and analyze vast amounts of consumer data, leading to more granular, dynamic, and individualized pricing than previously observed," analysts with economic consulting firm Cornerstone Research said in a 2025 report.

The upshot: Retailers could use AI to tap the vast amounts of consumer data they already collect to set prices not on a product's value, but rather on the maximum amount they believe an individual shopper is willing to pay, Owens said.

Currently, this Uber-style pricing typically fluctuates based on, say, the number of drivers and passenger demand in a given market. But with AI, companies could also harness your consumer profile to set what amounts to a personalized price, Owens said. The result could amount to a form of AI-enabled haggling, in which consumers face perpetually shifting prices based on factors largely invisible to them.

"Technology is allowing companies to stop setting prices for products and start setting prices for you," she said.

A sign of prices to come?

In December, Groundwork Collaborative and Consumer Reports reported on a trial by grocery-shopping platform Instacart that used AI to simultaneously show customers different prices for the same goods from the same store. The pilot built on Instacart's 2022 purchase of Eversight, a software platform designed to enable AI pricing.

The AI-enabled tech ran experiments by setting different prices for different consumers and collecting insights into how people respond, including when they proceed with a purchase and when they walk away. The investigation found that grocery baskets containing identical items cost up to 23% more for some shoppers. That could translate into a swing of about $1,200 per year for a family of four, Groundwork and Consumer Reports concluded.

Instacart disputes the report's findings, telling CBS News that the $1,200 price gap among some shoppers reflects an "atypical" grocery basket with the greatest possible price difference for every item. The company also said it doesn't use consumers' personal data, including federally protected characteristics such as race or gender, to set prices.

In December, however, Instacart said it would stop using AI to let retailers charge customers different prices for identical items on its platform.

According to Owens, other companies have begun experimenting with using AI to charge consumers individualized prices based on their personal data, such as their online browsing habits, income level, ZIP code or family structure.

In separate Groundwork research released this month, the group said that Walmart had applied for patents on technology that would allow the retailer to compile comprehensive shopper profiles and use them to set individualized prices. The tech, such as electronic shelf labels, could be used to charge consumers a "different price than the customer in front of them in the checkout line," Owens and her co-author wrote.

One patent application indicates that Walmart has already developed technology to adjust prices based on items in a shopper's cart, according to Groundwork. "If a customer has tuna fish, they may be offered a different price for mayonnaise," the group claimed.

Walmart denies developing tools that would allow it to use customers' personal data or other factors to adjust prices.

"Walmart does not and will not use an individual customer's personal information, income, shopping history, urgency or willingness to pay to set an individualized price," Dan Bartlett, Walmart's executive vice president of corporate affairs, said in a public letter to Owens this month in response to her research. "We do not engage in dynamic pricing, raising prices in response to a hot afternoon or an approaching snowstorm, for example."

Jay Zagorsky, a senior lecturer at Boston University's Questrom School of Business, has also warned about the potential risks of using AI for personalized pricing, noting that businesses are unlikely to disclose such practices for fear of facing consumer backlash.

"Nothing positive is gained by a merchant stating they are doing this," he told CBS News, while expressing his belief that retailers are developing the tools to set individualized pricing. "The days when the price you saw stayed fixed for a relatively long period of time appear to have passed."

World.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
World.content:
Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce

toggle caption i Alberto Pezzali/AP

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.

The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.

A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.

Zelenskyy complains about U.S. behavior in recent days

The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.

Sponsor Message

Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.

The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.

Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.

Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.

Sponsor Message

"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."

He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."

Starlink speed limits affect Ukraine's ability to defend itself

In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.

He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."

Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."

The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.

Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.

The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians

Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.

Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."

Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.

"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."

Sponsor Message

Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.

Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

World.title: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training
World.content:
Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training

Eyder Peralta/NPR

They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.

"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.

"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.

Sponsor Message

"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."

The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.

As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."

Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.

World.title: Essential items to stock in your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
World.content:
Essential items to stock in your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season

Andee Tagle/NPR

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. 

Is your household ready if you get hit with a stomach bug tomorrow? Sniffles on Saturday? The flu in a month or two?

Life Kit How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season Listen · 20:57 20:57

In the United States, cold and flu season occurs in the fall and winter, starting in October and stretching all the way through May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The combination of dropping temperatures and drier climates makes us more susceptible to common respiratory viruses like the common cold, the flu, RSV or COVID-19, and "back-to-back illnesses," says pediatrician Mona Amin .

Get ready now by creating a cold and flu prep kit. "Have things readily available so that you're not scrambling or depending on someone else to run to the drugstore for you when you become sick," says pharmacist Alisha Reed . That includes fever and pain relievers, hydration supplements and monitoring tools to help manage symptoms.

Sponsor Message

Many viruses and fevers can be managed at home, says Amin. And the common cold and the flu are viral infections, so they can't be treated by prescription antibiotics anyway.

Below, you'll find a list of items for the whole family, recommended by Amin and Reed. Put the products in one designated place, like a shelf in your medicine cabinet or a handy "sick day" box.

You'll also want to take preventative measures like disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, getting vaccinated and washing your hands. But remember, says Reed, no prevention strategy is foolproof.

What to include in your cold and flu prep kit

Over-the-counter medications

When you're dealing with cough, congestion, sore throat, fever, fatigue or other common cold and flu symptoms, you may be tempted to reach for a medication that hits multiple symptoms.

But those meds often include extra unnecessary ingredients that can sometimes put you at risk of accidentally overmedicating yourself, says Reed. Instead, opt for medications that target individual symptoms.

These items all come with a price tag, of course. So if you don't have something like a flexible spending account to help cover costs, consider purchasing your personal sick day must-haves to start, then building from there as you're able.

Sponsor Message

Reed and Amin suggest these medications:

Pain relievers. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help relieve pain and discomfort from headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation, says Reed.



For kids: Don't use children's ibuprofen for children under 6 months old; naproxen is only approved for children 12 years and older.

Fever reducer. Medications like acetaminophen and ibuprofen can safely reduce body temperature, though acetaminophen is usually the better choice for fevers .



For kids: Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow this dosing chart when using children's acetaminophen.

Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow when using children's acetaminophen. For pregnant people: Acetaminophen is the recommended OTC pain reliever for pregnant people , according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.

Antihistamine. Yes, the same thing you take for spring allergies! Colds and allergies have similar symptoms like sneezing, runny noses and watery eyes, which is why they can both be treated by a histamine-blocking medication that can help dry up your sinuses.



For kids: Some OTC allergy medicines are approved for children as young as 6 months, but not all — and some have more side effects than others, says Amin. Check in with your care provider first if you have questions.

Decongestant. Pseudoephedrine pills or nasal spray can relieve a stuffy nose or sinus pressure by restricting blood vessels and opening airways in your nasal passages.



For kids: Pills are not recommended for kids under 4 and medicated sprays are not recommended for kids under 6.

Cough suppressant for a dry cough. Dextromethorphan — often referred to as "DM" on the cough syrup box — can temporarily suppress the signal in the brain that triggers your cough reflex, says Reed.



For kids: Not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Cough expectorant for a congested cough. Guaifenesin may help relieve chest congestion by thinning mucus in your airways, says Reed. But before you buy, try just staying hydrated first. "Water is a natural expectorant," she says.



Sponsor Message

For kids: Cough medicine is not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Read the label on the box or bottle of OTC products carefully to make sure that what you're taking isn't expired and will treat the ailment it's intended for. And always stick to the recommended dosage and usage to avoid unnecessary risks or side effects, says Reed.

Honey

Honey is a great sick day remedy for all ages, but is especially helpful for small children not yet old enough for cough medicine, says Amin. "Honey is an anti-inflammatory that also helps with coating the throat, which can help with that cough trigger that children will have."

Note: honey isn't safe for children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.

Thermometer

This is a basic, must-have tool to check your temperature on those days you suspect you or your little one are running a fever, says Amin.

Rectal thermometers are preferred for children 3 and under; oral and digital infrared thermometers are both fine choices for anyone older than that. (But oral thermometers are usually more accurate.)

Nasal saline treatment

The dryness of winter can dehydrate your nasal passages and make it easier for viruses to attach and replicate in your nose and throat.

One easy solution is to irrigate your nose with a saline spray or rinse, says Amin. This can be both preventative by helping to keep the mucous membranes in your nose moist, as well as symptom-relieving by loosening thick mucus if you have a cold.

Research even suggests that using saline drops at the first sign of a cold can reduce symptoms in small children by up to two days .

Other comfort items

Chest rub. Vapor rubs containing combinations of camphor, eucalyptus and menthol oils may provide some relief for nighttime cough and cold symptoms when applied to the chest and neck.

Sponsor Message

Use with caution, says Amin. Though a lot of families use this homeopathic remedy, there's not a lot of research supporting its effectiveness, and it can be harmful if used improperly. Vicks VapoRub, for example, should be applied only to the chest and throat and never heated up. And be sure to check age restrictions before using any products on children — baby and child chest rubs will be formulated with gentler ingredients.

Disposable vomit bags. These are useful to have, easy to store and a great replacement for sitting by the toilet if the stomach flu should hit your house this year, says Amin.

Humidifier. A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which can help loosen mucus stuck in your sinuses. Reed suggests using a cool-mist humidifier when sick, which can help ease stuffiness during a cold.

Pedialyte, apple juice, water, Gatorade. Diarrhea or vomiting, common symptoms of the flu or COVID-19, can sometimes lead to dehydration. Make sure to have a few favorite drinks handy that can help replace those lost liquids for you or your little one, Amin says.

When to call your doctor

As long as your symptoms are improving — and responding to treatment — many viruses can be dealt with from the comfort of your home.

However, if you're seeing these concerning symptoms, reach out to your doctor.



A fever in infants younger than 3 months; above 102 F for children; 103 F for adults; or any high fevers that last longer than 1-2 days and/or don't respond to fever-reducing medicine.

Shortness of breath or erratic breathing

Extreme thirst, inability to drink liquids, trouble urinating or producing tears, dark urine, severe or persistent vomiting

Confusion, disorientation, extreme irritability or weakness

These aren't the only signs to look for, so when in doubt, reach out, says Reed. "Don't be afraid to call your doctor or talk to a pharmacist about what's going on. It doesn't hurt to double check," she says.

Sponsor Message

This digital story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and

World.title: For some Christians, Hegseth's plan for public execution fits a biblical mandate
World.content:
For some Christians, Hegseth's plan for public execution fits a biblical mandate

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

It is not clear if the public execution of the man behind the Fort Hood attack will be livestreamed, as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said it would be late last week. When asked about it on Tuesday, President Trump said, "We're looking at it," and Vice President JD Vance has stated that he would not watch it, raising doubts about whether it would happen. But whether or not the public execution proceeds, some religious scholars worry that damage has already been done.

"I think one of the most worrisome parts of this development is that … it pushes the boundaries of what's acceptable," said Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religion at the University of North Florida who specializes in the religious right and Christian Reconstruction. "Just saying it out loud moves the boundary."

Sponsor Message

The last time the U.S. government conducted a high-profile public execution was 90 years ago. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth suggested that livestreaming Nidal Hasan's death by firing squad would deter future, similar attacks. Hasan, a former U.S. army major and violent Islamist extremist, killed 13 people and injured 32 in a 2009 attack at Fort Hood. His execution is set for Dec. 3.

"We'll make sure that people are able to … watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that … there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in an interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.

For Ingersoll and some other religious scholars, Hegseth's promotion of an idea that has largely fallen out of favor with the American public ties in closely with his religious background. Hegseth affiliates with the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, or CREC, whose leader identifies as a Christian Nationalist, envisions a theonomous America where women are denied the right to vote and has defended the institution of slavery.

"These are extreme ideas and these are extreme leaders, and I don't have a better way of phrasing it than to just note that Pete Hegseth is a religious extremist," said Matthew Taylor, a visiting scholar at the Center on Faith and Justice at Georgetown University. "He holds ideas that are far outside the mainstream. He is trying to implement those ideas within the U.S. military structure within the Pentagon."

Sponsor Message

Near "unanimous endorsement" of the death penalty in the CREC

Hegseth's announcement of a livestreamed execution elicited reactions of disgust and condemnation from some faith leaders and politicians. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who serves Catholics in the U.S. military, issued a statement of disapproval on the proposal and instructed any Catholics who may be assigned to the firing squad to request an excusal. Taylor said he believes Hegseth's idea represents "an outlier position within American Christianity," including, he said, within right-wing Christianity.

But Ingersoll said that within Hegseth's church, it is not an outlier.

"The religious community from which Hegseth comes is very comfortable, shall we say, with the death penalty. There's a pretty much unanimous endorsement of it," Ingersoll said. "The crimes discussed in the Hebrew Bible or the Old Testament that carried the death penalty are understood by them to still carry the death penalty. So execution, and even public execution, is very much a part of the way they see the punishment for crime in general."

But some are also asking whether Hasan's religion may partly account for a public proposal that is, to many Americans, abhorrent.

"The question is, why is he being punished differently than everyone before him?," said Joshua Salaam, president of the Association of Muslim Chaplains. "And the answer that most people from my community will say is it has something to do with his religious beliefs, his religious identity."

Indeed, Ingersoll said that the CREC goal to enact Christian governance, and Hegseth's own apparent animus toward Islam, are key factors in this discussion.

"I think he sees himself as engaged in a battle on behalf of God against the infidels," she said.

A new "crusade" from the Pentagon

When Hegseth was nominated to head the Pentagon, his tattoos drew national attention. At the time, he had tattoos of the Jerusalem Cross and of the phrase "Deus Vult" on his body. At some point later, he also added another tattoo in Arabic script of a word that means "infidel." Taylor said all this, plus his authorship of a book titled American Crusade, point to a clear worldview.

Sponsor Message

"Hegseth is, for lack of a better term, obsessed with the Crusades," Taylor said.

Within the context of the CREC's goals, this history of civilizational conflict between Western Christendom and Islam holds particular importance, said Ingersoll.

"There is an idealization of the Christendom of the medieval period," she said. "Because that was a Christian society, it was the theocratic kind of world that they wanted built. So, much of the viewpoint that seems medieval, actually is."

Today, Ingersoll said, a term often used to describe this project is "dominionism." It is a concept that extends beyond the CREC to other strands within the Christian nationalist movement. It holds that Christians have a Biblical mandate to assert their version of religious governance over every aspect of society. In the U.S., concern over the growth in Christian Nationalism over the last decade has largely centered on the fundamental conflict between dominionism and American principles of inclusive democracy.

Perhaps among the most concerning aspects of the discussion around a livestreamed execution, said Taylor, is the possibility that Hegseth may be instrumentalizing the U.S. military in pursuit of his personal religious goals.

"What Hegseth is trying to do is consolidate the military around a particular ideology – an ideology of Christian nationalism, an ideology of Christian supremacy, an ideology of Western supremacy, that also has racial undertones and patriarchal and misogynistic undertones and anti-LGBTQ undertones," he said.

NPR reached out to the Pentagon for comment, but did not hear back by the publishing deadline.

Normalizing an extreme idea

But the idea of reviving public executions has, in fact, been openly discussed in more mainstream rightwing circles, beyond the CREC. In a 2024 podcast, the late hard-right activist Charlie Kirk argued in favor of it, saying, "It should be public, it should be quick, it should be televised." Kirk even suggested that large corporations might underwrite the televising of executions to raise money for public coffers.

Sponsor Message

"Part of what is underneath Christian nationalism and the coalitions that Christian nationalists have made with … the 'tech bros' and the 'podcast bros' and that whole world is this interest in being transgressive," Ingersoll explained.

The name of the podcast where Kirk floated these ideas was "Thoughtcrime."

Even if a livestreamed execution of Hasan does not take place, Taylor said the proposal serves as a warning sign of how someone in a position as powerful as Hegseth's can reorient government and society toward what he calls extremist goals.

"Somebody like Hegseth presents an opportunity for them to test some of these ideas, to enact them on a more shortened timeline, and to create precedence within American culture, within the U.S. military, for the ultimate vision that they hope for," Taylor said.

Amidst all the discussion, Salaam said it is important also to reflect on the potential damage that public executions do to the moral fiber of the country.

"It does something to all of us to have to watch something like that publicly," he said. "This is not normal for us to promote something like that for our children, for men and women and community members to watch this."

World.title: These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices
World.content:
These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices

toggle caption i Megan Varner/Getty Images

📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App

Some key voters say deep frustration and disappointment with President Trump are motivating their election plans just weeks before Election Day.

NPR observed two online focus groups Tuesday night with 12 Georgians who voted for President Biden in 2020 and then supported Trump in 2024.

Almost every voter — 11 out of 12 — said they were disappointed with the overall job Trump has been doing. And 10 said they regret voting for him.

"I've been disappointed," said Charles P., 43, who identified as a Democrat. (The voters participated under the condition their last names would not be used.)

Sponsor Message

"I just don't feel like there's any positive to this administration at all," he continued. "Inflation has only gotten worse, there've been more wars. The tariffs haven't done anything. It seems like we have more enemies now than ever. I just don't see anything positive with his tenure."

Richard A., a 56-year-old Republican, said he's been out of work for 10 months and there is a long list of problems he sees with the direction of the country under Trump.

"Food crisis, starting the war with Iran, inflation," he said. "ICE immigration has just torn families apart, has caused deaths. ... It just seems like everything has gone downhill."

The comments align with Trump's faltering approval rating and a darkening midterm outlook for Republicans. Trump has picked up his campaign travel in recent days, touting his record and arguing for the GOP to retain control in Washington.

These focus groups with swing voters are conducted every month in battleground states across the country. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR partners with them each month as part of the Swing Voter Project.

Focus groups are not scientifically significant like polls, but they do provide insight into what voters are thinking. And in this case, they provide some insight into how voters are deciding who they are supporting this fall.

Sponsor Message

Swinging to Democrats

Rich Thau, president of Engagious, moderates these focus groups. He said for the first time this year, a majority of swing voters said Trump was going to influence their midterm decisions.

"In previous months, when we asked people whether President Trump would influence how they vote, they would say things like, 'Well, I'm looking mainly at the candidates themselves,' or 'I'm looking at the overall sort of environment in the country,'" Thau said.

"This month, seven out of 12 said that he would influence them to vote for Democrats. And that was new."

Karla S., a 49-year-old Democrat, was one of those seven.

"I did vote Republican for 2024," she said. "I made up my mind. I've been so disappointed that I'm just going to go straight and just do Democrat, Democrat, Democrat. Because I'm so disappointed with how this administration has been doing."

Cedric, a 41-year-old independent, said he won't be voting for any politicians that are closely aligned with Trump.

"I think we're not going in the right direction, so I don't want to vote for a candidate that's not going to stand up to him or they're going to go along with his policies," he said. "I'm looking for something different."

Ten out of the 12 participants said they plan on voting for Georgia incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Some voters said they wanted to keep him in office specifically because he wouldn't be aligned with Trump.

Restoring order

Thau said some voters felt that if Democrats take control of Congress, it could provide some needed stability to the country — and the economy, in particular.

"There was some sense that Democrats could restore some semblance of order, and that they'd be able to control a bit of what the president is trying to do or has been doing, to the point where that might restore some of their confidence in the economy," he said.

Sponsor Message

That's what Thomas M., a 65-year-old independent voter, said is his expectation of a Democratic-run Congress.

"I think there would be more controls placed on Trump with people who are not afraid to stand up to him," he said.

In contrast, if Republicans retain power, Thau said "some respondents told us they thought that the president would have even more control over what goes on because Republicans are afraid to stand up to him."

Jennifer W., a 43-year-old Republican, said she worries "Trump would have free rein."

World.title: School roof collapse kills at least 29, injures more than 3 dozen in Pakistan
World.content:
School roof collapse kills at least 29, injures more than 3 dozen in Pakistan

toggle caption i Maaz Awan/AP

PESHAWAR, Pakistan — The roof of a private school collapsed in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday, killing at least 28 children and a female teacher and injuring more than 50 other people, a hospital spokesman said, as rescuers searched the rubble for anyone still trapped. Six girls were among the dead.

Several children were also trapped under the rubble in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, said Bilal Faizi, a spokesman for the emergency services.

A hospital spokesman, Mohammad Asim, also confirmed the casualties, saying some of the injured were in critical condition. All the children killed or injured were age 13 or younger, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded.

Sponsor Message

Hours later, rescue officials said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews were clearing the debris. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Gov. Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause of the collapse. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children.

Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said that the three-story school had an estimated 1,200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She told The Associated Press that she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital.

toggle caption i Maaz Awan/AP

According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighborhood in central Peshawar. Rescue workers arrived within minutes of being alerted, according to accounts from the scene.

A resident, Samiullah Khan, said that he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom to drink water.

A resident, Mohammad Khan, said rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived.

Sponsor Message

The cause of the collapse was under investigation. Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school's owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak.

The provincial government said that the school occupied a three-story building and that a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse.

The provincial government spokeswoman, Samar Haroon Bilour, said that the government directed hospital officials to provide prompt medical care to the injured children and praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety.

In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements.

"The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow," Zardari said.

He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies.

In July, a roof collapsed at a tutoring center under construction in Lahore, killing four schoolchildren.

Building collapses are common in Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs.

World.title: Aboard an icebreaker, a writer got a closer look at the Arctic's 'Sea Change'
World.content:
Aboard an icebreaker, a writer got a closer look at the Arctic's 'Sea Change'

toggle caption i Crown

As polar ice melts in the Arctic, shipping lanes are opening up, making the region a new zone of superpower competition. Writer Rana Foroohar got an up-close look aboard the USS Healy, a Coast Guard icebreaker. She says that traversing the North Pole by ship — once a "largely conceptual" route — is now becoming a "real possibility" for two or three weeks a year.

"If you are taking one of these Arctic routes, you can save as much as 40% of the time it would take you to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and depending on the price of oil, that's a heck of a lot of money," she says. "China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest."

Sponsor Message

In her new book, Sea Change: America's New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, Foroohar makes the case that the "High North" may become as critical to world shipping as the Suez or Panama canals. But she also notes that beneath the Arctic waters are large deposits of oil, natural gas and rare earth minerals, as well as underwater cables, which carry a large part of the world's intercontinental information flow.

"Undersea cables have become a real touchstone in wars and conflicts around the world," she says. "So you are seeing a race to lay down new cable, and who can get there fastest, and then who can potentially commercialize and even militarize areas where those cables have been laid."

Foroohar describes the Arctic Circle as one of the few areas of the globe where countries and companies can still "hunt" for territory and "duke it out potentially with rivals." And she predicts more conflict in the coming decades as the region continues to warm.

"There is going to be more commerce done through this area. There is gonna be greater military interest in the area, and all of that matters because it really is in America's backyard," she says. "I just think that everything in the High North is going to be higher priority for America in the future."

Sponsor Message

Interview highlights

Penguin Random House

On increased international interest in the Arctic

China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest. And that's very interesting because it starts to dovetail with something that's happening in U.S. policy, which is more of a sense of we need to protect what's close to home. And so if you look at things that way, then you have the U.S. and China coming into much closer geographic conflict. Whether or not it would ever be a hot conflict, I hope not, but certainly competition in that area.

On the debate over rights to resources in international waters

There's some debate over that. There is something called the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which governs maritime activities, including those in the Arctic. It has ... rules about where you can mine, how you can mine, who gets what. But the U.S. never signed on to that convention. Various presidents from Clinton to Bush [to] Obama did support it, but key Republican senators opposed it, basically on ideological grounds, the notion that no international body should have sovereign right over what the U.S. does. ... And so it makes it much more of a free-for-all as to who gets what in the Arctic. And then you throw in the fact that Russians and Chinese don't always play by the U.N. rules either.

On how Arctic power struggles are part of a larger global trend

It's kind of part and parcel of a bigger collapse of international rule and a pendulum shift from globalization to something that is much more about regionalization and spheres of power ... and influence, which is exactly what's happening in the Arctic, which to me is so interesting, not only just for itself, but because it's a mirror into what's happening in other parts of the world. Some of the same conflicts over territory and mineral rights and ports that you see in the Arctic now are also happening in Latin America or West Africa or parts of the South China Sea. So it's a bit of a bellwether for geostrategy more broadly. …

Sponsor Message

And then there's this — kind of largely theoretical up until now, but becoming more realistic — trans-polar route where right now it might be a couple of weeks that you could consider going right across the pole, but if global warming continues the way it seems to be going in the next decade or two, that could turn into a month, two months, three months. And so who's going to control that area? This is what's up for stake now.

On what it's like to be onboard an Arctic icebreaker

You begin to feel and hear the ice as it is being broken by the ship. And I remember being down on the mess hall, which is a couple floors down from the waterline, and I was sitting eating my lunch and you begin to hear this shhhhhh kind of sound, like something traveling through sound, and then it becomes squeaky, like fingers on chalkboard, and you can kind of feel vibration and it gets louder and louder and you're like, "Wow, there are only 12 inches of reinforced steel between me and death." That's very sobering.

On the region's changing climate

I actually touched base with some of those scientists several months after we had come off of the Healy, and they were starting to go through that data and look at it. And there is some real scientific data showing that these areas are changing. They are warming. They are becoming different than they have been in the past. And that affects all kinds of things. It affects the kind of fish that could live there. It affects wind and wave patterns that you might get, which could in turn affect things like the Canadian boreal forest fires that I experience in my home in Brooklyn, New York. You would think that has nothing to do with the Arctic, but it actually has everything to do with what's happening in the High North.

Sponsor Message

Therese Madden and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For nearly a year, U.S. President Donald Trump has been trying to persuade voters not to get riled up over rising prices.

Trump has brushed off concerns about affordability as a "con job by Democrats," insisted consumer prices had fallen during his term when they'd actually risen, and repeatedly claimed the costs of gas and diesel — up sharply after he launched the war against Iran — would start falling soon.

Numerous polls suggest voters aren't buying Trump's sales pitch, with respondents giving him low marks on the cost of living.

On average, more than 70 per cent of American respondents in recent polls disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation, according to Silver Bulletin, which aggregates public polling.

The latest inflation data won't make things any better for Trump and his Republican Party as they try to maintain control of U.S. Congress in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, less than three weeks from now.

The consumer price index was up 3.7 per cent in September compared with the previous year, driven largely by increases in the prices of fuel and clothing, the U.S. Department of Labour reported on Wednesday.

WATCH | Affordability is top issue on voters' minds ahead of U.S. midterms: Inflation top of mind for voters ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:04 U.S. President Donald Trump’s approval ratings have dipped to around 30 per cent ahead of the midterm elections, according to recent polls, as affordability continues to be a top voter issue.

Polling indicates that the economy is the top issue for voters across the U.S. heading into the midterms, says Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling Center in Boston.

Drill down further into the data, and he says it's the cost of living — rather than jobs or taxes — underlying those concerns about the economy.

'Everyday expenses'

"It looks like it's just everyday expenses that are beginning to pile up and people are concerned about being able to afford," Kimball told CBC News.

"It's hard to imagine in the next three weeks there'll be a solution to the gas price or the other costs of living associated with that," he said.

Trump flew to Wasilla, Alaska, Tuesday to hold a campaign rally at a hockey rink. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

The political impact can be mapped out through Trump's recent travels across the U.S. as he tries to boost Republicans' chances of winning U.S. Senate seats.

In the past two weeks, Trump has flown to a series of previously reliably red states, including Alaska, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, all of which he won by double digits in the 2024 presidential election.

Tim Malloy, polling analyst with the Quinnipiac University Poll in Hamden, Conn., describes Trump's travels as "a last mad dash" to try to shore up Republican candidates who should not have been in jeopardy during the midterms but are now at risk of losing largely because of cost of living issues.

"What Hail Mary pass or home run can you hit at this point if you're the Republicans? I don't know. It's really, really late in the day," Malloy told CBC News.

He says gas prices are the predominant concern showing up in polling and voters are pinning the blame on Trump.

"All of that is tied into the fact that the president said the war would be over very quickly," Malloy said. "The president has not lived up to the promise he made to Americans, and they're kind of fed up and the midterms are coming."

Outside a supermarket in Martinsburg, W.Va., Juliana Kaiser said she's started baking her own bread, making soup stocks and limiting her driving to save costs. She says rising prices will be a factor she keeps in mind when voting in the upcoming U.S. midterms. (Jonathan Austin/CBC)

In the staunchly Republican community of Martinsburg, W.Va., on Wednesday, people told CBC News that they're feeling the price pinch.

"It's hard to even do grocery shopping anymore. I've had to really survive off of food pantries," said Christalyn Levy, a cashier in a local thrift store. "Literally I pay my rent, and I have nothing left."

Outside a nearby supermarket, Juliana Kaiser said she now tries to cut costs by baking her own bread and reducing her gas consumption.

"I've definitely limited the amount of travelling that we do, and I try to condense my [shopping] trips into all one big loop," she said, adding that rising prices will be on her mind when she votes in the midterms.

World.title: Uncertainty is the point: The growing drone campaign stalking NATO’s skies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As concerns rise about a Russian strike on NATO territory, the alliance’s top commander spelled out the consequences of any direct attack, promising Monday that “we will fight.”

But countries belonging to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) are already contending with a menace that is much harder to fight and is increasingly stalking their skies with impunity.

Suspected Russian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace on its eastern flank, in countries like Romania and Poland, and the organization's jets have scrambled multiple times to head off a possible attack.

But there are also hundreds and hundreds of ambiguous drones that have been increasingly spotted over sensitive sites — military bases, nuclear power plants and airports — in NATO countries as far west as Germany , Belgium and France , causing disruptions at airports and exposing gaps in defence.

It has the hallmarks of a deliberate campaign to stoke fear and uncertainty — and the problem appears to be growing.

German authorities, for instance, have clocked more than 1,000 suspicious drone-related incidents since January 2025, CBC News has learned. That's about 1.5 incidents a day on average over “critical infrastructure, military facilities and defence companies,” according to the country's Federal Criminal Police Office.

Meanwhile, there were 261 overall drone-related disruptions at German airports or in its airspace between January and August, an 80 per cent year-over-year increase, according to a report obtained by CBC News from the country's air traffic control authority.

The mysterious drones repeatedly spotted across Europe are difficult to detect and intercept and, as a result, hard to attribute. But taken together, the pattern that emerges strongly suggests they are one element of a Russian hybrid campaign, say defence experts.

Ulrike Franke is a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. (CBC)

“There is an increase in the absolute number,” said Ulrike Franke, one of Europe’s foremost drone experts, in an interview from Paris.

“And I'm comfortable to say that it is very likely, if not certainly, linked to Russian aggression towards Europe, and the war that Russia is waging against Ukraine and the war it sees itself in against the West."

Hybrid warfare

Mysterious drone-related incidents have occurred over Europe for years, prompting accusations of a below-the-radar “hybrid warfare,” meaning non-conventional means of undermining an adversary, staying below the threshold of an open war. But such incidents spiked in number last fall and now again appear to be on the rise.

Norway has seen more than 300 occurrences so far this year, leading to six airport interruptions, a spokesperson told CBC News. In the U.K., drone incidents near military bases have reportedly doubled over the past year . And in Belgium, there were 150 incidents over sensitive sites, per one media report .

On Sept. 12, a suspected drone sighting again interrupted flights at Brussels Airport. A week later, another diverted 19 flights from Luxembourg Airport, affecting nearly 2,000 passengers. Four days later, Berlin’s main airport was shut down after a drone was spotted over its north runway.

“It's hybrid warfare,” Elio Di Rupo, a member of the European Parliament and its security defence committee, and a former Belgian prime minister, said in an interview.

“It’s not only the drone war, but cyber attacks. And all together, it’s a real war, but we don’t see nobody, except indeed the drones.”

Elio Di Rupo spoke with CBC News in Mons, Belgium, about what he says is a new kind of war. (David Iacoluccio/CBC)

Exact numbers are hard to come by, making it a challenge to connect the dots across Europe.

CBC reached out to 11 national air traffic authorities, several EU organizations, research institutes and think-tanks as well as NATO.

NATO refused a request for a tally, referring CBC News to national authorities instead, which have various mechanisms to track data. European Union organizations were also unable to provide data, pointing out that defence is a national domain.

In one snapshot, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) reported 144 suspicious drones flew over sensitive sites with “substantial impunity" in a dozen NATO countries over 18 months ending in February.

The report adds they were likely launched from a Russian “shadow fleet” — tankers and other vessels that the country uses to clandestinely evade sanctions and export oil.

Russia has repeatedly rejected all such accusations.

This photo taken in October 2025 off the coast of France shows the tanker Boracay from Russia's so-called 'shadow fleet' suspected of being involved in drone flights over Denmark. (Damien Meyer/AFP/Getty Images)

The authors of the IISS report point out their argument is not that every drone sighting was Russian, but that the overall pattern “cannot be adequately explained” by other means such as human error or hobby drones deployed incorrectly.

It also says that even having a large number of benign drones is, "if anything, analytically consistent with Russian operational design: engineering an environment of ambiguity," where real incursions are hard to distinguish from others.

Franke agrees it’s the pattern that speaks to Russia’s involvement: the type of drones, the time of day, their movements.

She also concurs that the uncertainty is the point.

“Russia benefits from our hysteria, and it benefits from the fact that of course there are going to be drone sightings, no matter what,” she said.

“This is the kind of genius of these hybrid attacks that it is so difficult to attribute, that there will be false positives… and [they] work so well, and are so difficult to deal with in open, democratic societies.”

Turning point

A turning point came on Aug. 4, with the discovery of a custom-built drone carrying explosives near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, which is used as a hub for support sent to Ukraine.

A Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane stands at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5. (Getty Images)

German investigations concluded that the drone was hard evidence pointing to Russian involvement. The information the drone made possible has also reportedly since been key to mapping other escalating hybrid operations and connecting them to Russian intelligence.

The foiled Leipzig attack was the furthest into NATO territory such a dangerous attempt has been made since Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

“It tells us that Russia is definitely targeting countries and companies that are supporting Ukraine," said Michelle Haas, an associate fellow in the Europe in the World programme at Egmont Royal Institute for International Relations in Brussels.

"And one of the main goals is to get into our minds and make us believe that the cost of supporting Ukraine is too high."

Michelle Haas is a PhD researcher at the Ghent Institute for International and European Studies. (David Iacolucci/CBC)

The Leipzig incident also focused European attention and forced a co-ordinated response that included diplomatic and economic measures against Russia. Other EU countries and NATO allies including Canada issued statements of support for Germany and admonitions of Russia.

"Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia, but it is part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the time, hinting at Russia’s culpability in the bigger picture.

Initially reluctant to explicitly point the finger at Russia out of concern about escalation, European leaders now appear to be increasingly willing to do so. How to deter and repel future similar attacks, however, is still an open question.

Von der Leyen acknowledged such incidents may well be “the new normal" in Europe. Still, Haas said, they must be taken “very seriously."

Critical infrastructure should be protected better, she said. And European leaders must also prepare the public for more attacks without causing alarm, while being “very clear that there is something happening.”

“It’s also a question about: how do we make sure we don’t let this polarize us or destabilize us? Because that’s also part of the goal.”
