World.title: Starlink restrictions may hamper Ukraine's war effort. Can the country adapt?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, then- Ukrainian vice-prime minister Mykhailo Fedorov went on what was then known as Twitter to publicly plead with Elon Musk to activate his company SpaceX's Starlink satellites for use in the country.

Soon after, Musk posted, "Starlink service is now active in Ukraine. More terminals en route."

Since then, Starlink and the military-grade version known as Starshield have been integral to Ukraine's war effort against Russia. Indeed, in February, Musk appeared to acquiesce to a request from Fedorov , who most recently served as Ukraine's defence minister, to block Russia's access to Starlink.

But now, according to Ukrainian officials, its military has lost some access to the system.

It's not clear why the restrictions have been imposed. On Wednesday, Musk, in a post on X, said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits would have been ordered by the U.S military and ultimately the president, he said.

He added that usage of Starlink "is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."

So far, there has been no response from the U.S. government. But the restrictions come as U.S. President Donald Trump has criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacking Russian refineri es, which he blames for the high cost of oil.

Here's a look at how the Ukrainian military has used Starlink, and what impact these restrictions could have on its capabilities.

How does Ukraine's military use Starlink?

Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites with roughly 13 million subscribers. Its low Earth orbit satellites around the planet deliver faster connections than traditional counterparts.

Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has since restricted Starlink for certain military uses, instead developing Starshield, a more secure network, for government and military purposes.

Ukraine has used the technology for both offensive and defensive operations, with the military using thousands of terminals connected t o the system, according to the New York Times.

A September 2022 photo shows an antenna of the Starlink satellite-based broadband system donated by Elon Musk, in Izyum, Ukraine. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)

The network is used for long-range drone missions, interceptor air defence systems and front-line logistics, according to a recent social media post from Serhii Beskrestnov, defence tech adviser to Zelenskyy.

He said the system has been key for Ukraine’s aerial defence and helped intercept the drones that Moscow has unleashed on cities in the country in recent months.

"It's just an incredibly capable communication system that has proven very valuable to the Ukrainians," said Thomas Withington, a military sciences associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, in an interview with CBC News.

He said the military has tended to use it primarily for tactical and operational communications. For example, if a deployed unit near the front line needs to communicate back with commanders hundreds of kilometres away, "Starlink provides an excellent way of doing that," Withington said.

He added that Starlink is also beneficial in that its system is very difficult to jam or use electronic warfare against.

Renard Sexton, an associate political science professor at Emory University and managing director of the Empirical Studies of Conflict, said that Starlink was crucial to the Ukrainians' ability to push back against Russia's initial invasion in 2022.

Sexton added that his research has found that in certain moments when Starlink was less accessible, the Ukrainian offence suffered much more than its defence.

What restrictions have been imposed?

Earlier this week, SpaceX started to interrupt the functioning of its military-grade terminals when they are moving at high speed, Ukrainian officials said.

According to Beskrestnov, the Zelenskyy adviser, that included imposing a speed limit on Starlink terminals mounted on drones.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on Wednesday that a decision to restrict access to Starlink would have been made by the U.S government and military. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

The limit has disrupted operations, including making the slower-flying attack drones easier targets for R ussian defences, he said.

The speed cutoff has also hampered Ukraine's ability to conduct strikes on Russian targets inside Ukraine, Reuters reported.

By late Wednesday, drone operators were reporting improved data connections, Zelenskyy said. But Fedorov posted on X that removing the speed limit entirely was "now critical for Ukraine’s defence."

How could the restrictions impact Ukraine's military effort?

There could be quite a significant impact on the Ukrainian army's operational level communications and its use of drones, said Withington.

"Depriving that capability through a stalling deprivation is quite serious," he said.

But the Ukrainians are incredibly innovative, Sexton said, and a restriction that might have hurt them two years ago likely hurts them a lot less no w due to their ability to adapt.

WATCH | Russia strikes Ukraine hours after Trump claims 'energy ceasefire': Russia strikes Ukraine hours after Trump’s claim of an 'energy ceasefire' | Duration closed caption 2:18 Just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump proclaimed a Ukraine-Russia 'energy ceasefire,' Russia struck a Kharkiv suburb, killing at least three people and placing doubt such a truce could be negotiated.

"They're less likely to be relying fully on that as their only option for a given scenario," he said. "So I think there's more redundancy."

Withingt on agreed, saying that while the restriction is a ser ious inconvenience, the Ukrainians, together with their European allies, would be able to engineer workaround solutions that reduce its severity.

"It can't be done ... tomorrow, but it probably could be done in a matter of months, if not shorter."

That could include using existing capacity in both government- and private-sector-provided satellite communications in Europe, as well as looking at other systems, he said.

However, Sexton said while the Ukrainians could adapt to a short-term Starlink restriction, he cautioned that a prolonged or complete inability to ac cess it "wo uld be a big issue for them."

"There's no question. They don't have any way to replace it in the short run."

Sexton said he wouldn't go so far to say that it would turn the tide of the war, as at this point the conflict seems to have calcified, with both sides having difficulties making significant progress.

But he said that a long restriction could mean that any prospect of a future counteroffensive, or any prospect of holding out forever, would certainly become more difficult for Ukraine.

World.title: Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour, fire-and-brimstone documentary Musk — about tech oligarch and the world's richest man Elon Musk — is not uplifting. Instead, it is one of the most depressing and terrifying pieces of public media since An Inconvenient Truth alerted a largely unaware public to its imminent annihilation by climate change.

Unlike An Inconvenient Truth, Gibney's Musk does not appear to offer a hopeful final message about how we might get out of this mess. Instead, we get an outline of how, in Gibney's view, Musk rose from upstart entrepreneur to political arriviste who orchestrated the dismantling of USAID , then attempted to create a baby farm and commune to survive a supposed civil war . That is all before, we are to believe, he supposedly upended all of Western democracy.

Sitting for an interview this September ahead of the film's showing at the Toronto International Film Festival, Gibney was not too surprised by the dour perception: he had spent the previous few days fielding defamation lawsuit threats from a similarly unhappy Musk, after all . That is along with Musk's descriptions of Gibney as "a shill for the far left," "horrible human" and, simply, a "douche."

Gibney also acknowledged the foreboding length: it was only after they finished their original two-hour feature that Musk allied himself with U.S. President Donald Trump. At that point, he said, HBO executives told Gibney they needed to expand the work, using it as a "building block for a much more epic drama … For this figure, who has so much influence on the future of the planet, it's deserving of that three hours and 45 minutes."

WATCH | Musk documentary trailer:

That relationship proved fraught on its own. The film hits North American theatres Oct. 16, but — at the time of the interview — Gibney was nervous. The international rights-holder, Universal, hadn't confirmed whether it would even distribute the film outside North America, given the potential of political pressure.

At the same time, he said Paramount's acquisition of HBO parent company Warner — with Paramount controlled by the Trump-friendly David Ellison — had him "concerned in the back of [his] mind" that the documentary's streaming release could be scuppered entirely.

Since that interview, Gibney has said international theatrical release plans are now being discussed; the documentary is slated for an early 2027 streaming release, though no specific date has been given. When, or if, audiences do see it, he hopes the reception isn't quite so bleak.

"It's not a funeral; it's a warning. But things are pretty dark. We're going to be lowered into the earth if we're not careful," the director said, even while recognizing the sheer inescapability of dread his film tends to elicit. "You know, and the film ends with the planet Earth exploding and Musk escaping on his spaceship. So that's about as pessimistic as it gets."

A question of objectivity

Though he started the project as an avowed Musk fan — a Tesla solar panel system-owner and all — by the time he began working on it in earnest, he says, any benefit of the doubt he had extended to his subject had evaporated. When he reached out to interview Musk himself, he said he was stonewalled.

Director Alex Gibney poses for portrait photographs for the film Musk during the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy, in September 2026. (Scott A Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)

Outreach to those around Musk was similarly stymied: close business associates uniformly refused to speak without his permission. The workaround was to instead give Musk a voice of his own.

An AI-avatar, using Musk's own statements, narrates much of the documentary. Much of what it says, like the real Musk's statements about the "hit piece" Gibney came out with , is overtly critical of the documentary's framing.

The result is a somewhat bifurcated, but overwhelmingly negative picture of a man Gibney asserts is at the centre of modern politics' downfall.

There is the charting of Musk's early history as a self-described "founder" at Paypal and Tesla — including interviews ranging from journalists covering him at the time to his former wife, Justine Musk — that characterize his public persona as an engineer and genius as little more than a PR-crafted lie.

"There is a kind of generalised notion in modern societies that if you're rich, you must be very smart — you must be a genius," Gibney says, sharing the central thesis of the documentary. "But maybe you're just ruthless. And maybe you can be very rich and very powerful — and also, to some extent, unhinged."

And then there is Musk's time at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and, in Gibney's telling, his role as an architect of the dismantling of the U.S. federal government.

The film includes accusations from former MAGA influencer Ashley St. Clair, the mother to one of Musk's children, who speaks about cryptic text messages Musk sent her ahead of the 2024 U.S. presidential election that saw Trump re-elected — messages that include references to an "anomaly in the Matrix" created by "ten thousand lasers in space."

Gibney then asks her whether she thinks that was a reference to SpaceX satellites. She responds: "I don't know where else he has lasers."

"I should point out that the remarks about the 'anomaly in the Matrix' and lasers from space didn't come from a critic of Musk. It didn't come from me; they came from Elon Musk himself," Gibney said.

That is despite a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions, claiming the exchange reinforces a disproven conspiracy theory that Musk used his internet provider, Starlink, to interfere with voting machines in swing states.

"That seems a legitimate thing to put in a film," Gibney said. "I don't say in the film that's what he did. I say that's been said."

WATCH | Musk steps down as advisor to Donald Trump: Elon Musk steps down as top adviser to Trump | Duration closed caption 8:25 Elon Musk is leaving his special government role as a top adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump. His departure, announced Wednesday, marks the end of a turbulent chapter that included thousands of layoffs and the removal of government agencies. Musk says he still plans to act as a consultant despite his decision to step down.

Similarly when pressed, Gibney defended the decision of including an AI-generated avatar in a documentary critical of an AI proponent: "We used some AI tools, but they're being used by — they're guided by human hands," he said. He explained that the idea was for it to serve as a sort of "agent provocateur" that foments a negative reaction to AI proliferation by forcing audiences to witness it.

When asked whether he hopes or theorizes that the film could affect people's votes ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterms, he has a simple response: "I do."

Because to Gibney, Musk's accumulation of power isn't just a failure on Musk's part. When "a reckless tech billionaire takes effective control of the federal government, and attempts to destroy it for personal aggrandisement," he says, Americans themselves bear responsibility.

"We did. We let him take it, because we didn't demand that our representatives hold him to account," he said.

"You know, 'Oh, I like my Tesla, so he must be a good guy.' Well, you may like your Tesla, but what if he's not a good guy, right?"

World.title: How much pain do I need to be in for health-care professionals to see past their biases and help me?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person is the experience of Gabriel Badejo, who lives in Toronto. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ .

Imagine you’re walking down the street and someone falls in front of you — an elderly woman with a walker. Do you stop to help her? What about a man in a suit? What about a teenager in a hoodie?

I'd like to think most of us would help all three. But if we're honest, our biases would determine how quickly we respond. Or if we respond at all.

I was born with sickle cell disease, an inherited blood disorder that causes red blood cells to become hard, sticky and misshapen into a crescent or sickle shape that blocks blood flow. It results in episodes of extreme pain. One woman with sickle cell said the pain of a sickle cell crisis is much worse than labour contractions .

Sickle cell disease, a debilitating and life-threatening genetic blood disorder, disproportionately affects Black people and those of South Asian and Middle Eastern descent.

I have had too many of these sickle cell crises to count. But when I seek care, I am often dismissed for reasons I struggle to understand. It’s something I explored in my documentary on CBC, The Sickling.

When I was 18, I felt a sickle cell crisis coming on and within 15 minutes, I went from moving normally to being barely able to stand. On the way to the hospital in Toronto, my pain went from a seven out of 10 to a 10.

While waiting to be seen in the emergency room, I was in so much pain that I wasn’t able to sit. The nurses said there were no beds available, so one of my friends put a jacket on the floor for me to lie on. I was on the floor screaming, writhing in pain, without any pain meds for hours.

I was in a position where I couldn’t help myself, and being told to wait by the people who could help was deeply isolating.

I remember trying my best to hold back tears while asking myself: Why don’t the staff want to help me? What makes me a low priority?

Does something about me suggest I’m not actually sick and just looking for drugs? Is it because I'm Black? Do they lack understanding about how to treat sickle cell crises? Are there that many patients in a worse condition than me? Are they unaware of the treatments for a sickle cell crisis?

Even if any of that is true, shouldn't seeing someone in that much pain break through someone’s assumptions?

WATCH | My childhood with sickle cell disease: A lifetime of pain: growing up with sickle cell disease | Duration closed caption 2:19 Filmmaker Gabriel Badejo was diagnosed with sickle cell disease early in life. He learned quickly that the simple joys other kids took for granted could send him to the hospital. Watch The sickling on CBC Gem.

For most of my life, I had numerous pain episodes each year, with at least two sending me to the hospital every year. With so many visits, I began testing ways to present myself, hoping that my care might improve.

Maybe I shouldn't wear a hoodie. Maybe I should dress like I had just come from work. Maybe I should bring my prescriptions and someone to advocate on my behalf. If that person isn't also Black, maybe they will listen. But nothing changed.

Then in 2018, I had the worst episode of sickle cell of my adult life. With all my experience dealing with pain crises, even I was shocked at how bad it was. It felt like my time was coming.

I called 911 and the ambulance rushed me to the nearest hospital. Even after being dropped off by paramedics, the hospital staff told me I was a drug seeker.

What more has to happen for that magic threshold to be met and for my situation to receive the care it warrants?

WATCH | Not receiving the care I need: The hospital labelled me as a drug seeker | Duration closed caption 2:41 Then in 2018, Badejo had the worst episode of sickle cell of his adult life. Even after being dropped off by paramedics, hospital staff labelled him as a drug seeker and delayed providing pain relief. Watch The Sickling on CBC Gem.

An opportunity I never dared to dream of

That particular experience had a significant impact on me.

What’s worse is the feeling that if this is happening to me, it’s also happening to others with sickle cell.

Health-care workers can't keep dismissing , doubting or accusing us of putting on an act to get drugs when we need help.

It was during that hospital visit that I decided to make The Sickling. I wanted to do something that might make things better for whoever came after me.

Then my own story took a turn. I was invited to participate in a stem cell transplant trial to cure my disease, an opportunity I’d never dared to dream of.

Sickle cell has historically received far less research funding than other genetic diseases, such as cystic fibrosis or hemophilia. But an estimated eight million people are living with sickle cell around the world . Most will never have access to the treatment I received.

Throughout the process of making The Sickling, I discovered that the first person to be cured of sickle cell, through a bone marrow transplant, was an eight-year-old in 1983. The transplant was actually meant to treat her leukemia, but it cured both diseases. Nearly four decades later, I began my transplant trial at Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto.

I couldn’t help but wonder, if this was discovered long ago, why is my procedure a medical trial? Why couldn't I have done this when I was eight?

In 2021, Badejo was offered access to a stem-cell transplant trial, launching years of treatment and healing. (Gabriel Badejo)

When do we decide to care?

When I think about the example of the person on the sidewalk, perhaps the question isn't whether we would help someone who falls. Maybe the question is, how far are we willing to let them fall before we decide they’re worth helping?

I don't expect anyone to suddenly lose every bias they have. I have them, too.

But I do think we can check ourselves. We can notice when our assumptions shape how we treat someone. We can ask why we believe one person's pain faster than another's. We can speak up when we see someone being dismissed. We shouldn't need to see someone hit rock bottom before we decide to care.

Watch The Sickling on CBC and the CBC Docs YouTube channel.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: The 'leap second' could disappear. How a minor time adjustment became a major problem
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth.

On Thursday, an international timekeeping body in France is expected to do away with leap seconds and let the clocks slip until they're out of alignment by a full hour, which could take centuries or even millennia.

The precise atomic time we use to track our days — developed in the 1950s and measured by tracking the natural vibrations of atoms — is slightly out of sync with solar time, which is based on the position of the sun in the sky relative to a specific location on Earth, because the planet's rotation has been gradually slowing.

The leap second was introduced in 1972 as a way to correct the discrepancy. Ten seconds were added immediately, says Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre.

Since then, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, which tracks the difference between the solar day and atomic time, has monitored the discrepancy to determine when an extra second is needed.

When that threshold is reached, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures adds a second at either the end of December or the end of June. Leap seconds have been added 27 times, most recently in 2016.

Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre, says leap seconds are becoming increasingly difficult to manage as more systems rely on precise timekeeping. (National Research Council Canada)

If we didn't make those tiny adjustments, nothing would perceptibly change in our lifetimes. But eventually, Beattie says, "you might get the brightest part of the day at midnight and the darkest part of day at noon."

The concept is similar to leap years, whereby a day is added to the end of February every four years to keep the Gregorian calendar aligned with the seasons because the Earth's orbit around the sun takes about 365¼ days.

Without leap years, our hottest months would eventually fall during what is now winter, and the colder months during summer, Beattie says.

What's the problem?

But the time has come when leap seconds seem to be causing more trouble than they're worth.

"The basic global agreement is that we want to do away with these abrupt leap seconds," Beattie said.

That's because the small adjustment can be a headache for tech and telecommunications companies and infrastructure that relies on precise timekeeping.

WATCH | Potential issues with the trend toward permanent Daylight time: Sleep experts say permanent daylight time could negatively impact kids | Duration closed caption 2:07 Manitoba clocks won't spring forward or fall back anymore, after the province announced it's doing away with the twice-a-year time change. But some experts say choosing daylight time rather than standard time could cause health issues and will be more of a burden for school-aged teens.

Companies also have different ways of implementing leap seconds, such as changing their clock rates to stretch the extra second over several hours or an entire day.

Beattie says that variation among networks creates a risk of system failures.

The leap second was blamed for Reddit and LinkedIn crashes in 2012, for example, and brief outages at Cloudflare in 2016.

"The problem is that the needs for timing and network synchronicity are just going up and up, they're ever increasing," Beattie said. "And so the risks are just increasing along with them, because all you need is for some system to not implement it properly and then you could have a cascade effect that could cause quite significant problems."

Negative seconds?

There's another complicating twist.

Over the last six years or so, the Earth's rotation has actually sped up, raising the possibility that a "negative leap second" — in which a second would be taken away — could be needed in the future.

Tech giant Meta said in 2022 that a negative leap second could have a "devastating effect" on software, adding, " In any case, every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures."

The proposed fix, which would take effect in May 2027, is instead to let those extra seconds add up to 3,600 — a full hour — before adjusting the clocks, pushing the issue many generations down the road.

Not everyone is impressed by this approach.

Paul Delaney, a York University physics and astronomy professor emeritus, says he was "surprised" to hear the proposal.

"It is a problem for an increasingly computerized, AI-oriented economy, and that's obviously what we have," he said. "But that said, gosh, don't we still hire computer programmers to sort these sorts of things out? Some part of me says that we're throwing in the towel and saying, 'Oh, it's too difficult to do, and what the heck, it is just a second.'"

'Not a perfect system'

Samantha Lawler, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Regina, says many factors affect the Earth's rotation speed, but it has tended to slow over time, in part because of the moon's effect on Earth's tides.

But complex variables, including climate change and glacial melting, can cause changes in that trend.

She says there is no perfect system for our clocks to account for these shifts and "we'll be fine" without leap seconds.

"This is a real human problem that we've been struggling with forever, as long as we've been watching the stars move across the sky and tracking when the sun rises and sets, and trying to get the patterns right," Lawler said.

"It's always going to be a little bit wrong, and I think we just have to accept that."

World.title: School roof collapses in Pakistan, killing at least 28 children and teacher
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The roof of a private school collapsed in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar on Thursday, killing at least 28 children and a teacher and injuring more than 50 other people, authorities and a hospital official said.

All of the children killed or injured at Al-Khair school were aged 13 or younger, Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim said. Some of the injured were in critical condition, he said.he hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded.

Hours later, rescue officials said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews were clearing the debris.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Gov. Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause of the collapse. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children.

As if the sky had fallen: teacher

Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said that the three-storey school had an estimated 1,200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She told The Associated Press that she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital.

An infographic indicates the location of Peshawar in northwestern Pakistan. (Mehmet Yaren Bozgun/Anadolu/Getty Images)

According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighbourhood in central Peshawar.

A resident, Samiullah Khan, said that he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom to drink water.

Building owner arrested, police say

A resident, Mohammad Khan, said rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived.

The cause of the collapse was under investigation. Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school's owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak.

The provincial government said that the school occupied a three-storey building and that a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse.

The provincial government spokeswoman, Samar Haroon Bilour, said that the government directed hospital officials to provide prompt medical care to the injured children and praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety.

In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements.

"The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow," Zardari said.

He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies.

In July, a roof collapsed at a tutoring centre under construction in Lahore, killing four schoolchildren.

Building collapses are common in Pakistan , where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs.
