World.title: Sheinbaum signs decree blocking violent and hostile content from minors’ social media feeds: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📱 Sheinbaum signs decree to curb harmful online content for minors: Social media sites and online forums will be barred from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, self-harm, eating disorders, cyberbullying and illegal conduct. Platforms must also verify users’ ages, classify content by age group and offer parental supervision tools. The decree, drawn up after an Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, takes effect one month after its publication in the government’s official gazette today.

🚓 Sheinbaum orders CNDH probe into alleged police torture in Guadalajara: The president said the National Human Rights Commission must conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations that Jalisco police tortured people detained at Sunday’s water contamination protest. “How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

⚖️ Sheinbaum defers to judges on ex-INM chief Garduño’s exoneration: Asked about Francisco Garduño’s exoneration over the 2023 Ciudad Juárez detention center fire that killed 40 migrants, the president said, “It’s what the judges determined.” Lawyers for the victims will challenge the ruling.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum signed a decree that will bar social media sites and other online forums from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, sexual exploitation or violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, cyber-bullying and illegal conduct in general.

The government drew up the decree after a fatal Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, that was allegedly perpetrated by twin 18-year-old brothers who authorities say were exposed to violent content and extremist ideology online.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to allegations that Jalisco state police tortured people who were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday during a protest against contaminated water. One woman said that police beat her and stepped on her bare feet, causing fractures.

Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said Tuesday that all 39 people detained during Sunday’s protest had been released. He said that police used excessive force and made “unjust arrests.”

He also said that “serious mistakes that must be investigated and sanctioned” were made.

“… No one should have been exposed to violence,” Lemus said.

Sheinbaum signs ‘safe digital environments’ decree

Presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde told reporters that she and other officials met with representatives of social media and other tech companies to discuss the “decree to guarantee safe digital environments for girls, boys and adolescents,” which was presented by the government last Friday.

“Far from demonstrating resistance, they perfectly understood the need for an instrument of this nature,” she said.

Alcalde said that the decree will be published in the government’s official gazette today and take effect one month later.

The decree will oblige social media sites to detect and “immediately” remove “accounts and content that promote or generate violent conduct,” she said.

📲 SHEINBAUM FIRMA DECRETO PARA QUE PLATAFORMAS DIGITALES EVITEN DIFUNDIR CONTENIDOS VIOLENTOS La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum da un mes a las plataformas digitales para avanzar en la regulación de contenidos que inciten a la violencia, contra niñas, niños y adolescentes. ⚠️ Advirtió que, si las medidas no funcionan, se promoverá una reforma legal que establecería SANCIONES. Aclaró que no se trata de censura, sino de garantizar espacios digitales seguros. 📱🫡🫡 — Isabel Uribe (@Isa_Uribe) October 14, 2026

Alcalde said that social media sites will also have to “classify content” by its appropriateness for different age groups, verify the age of their users and “establish supervision tools” for mothers, fathers and legal guardians of minors.

Before signing the decree, Sheinbaum noted that social media and “digital platform” companies agreed with the government’s initiative.

“The only thing they asked for was a month to prepare their platforms so that this is a reality,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the government’s Digital Transformation and Communications Agency will monitor social media sites to ensure that companies are complying with the decree.

“If we see they aren’t complying, we would move onto a law which would involve sanctions for the platforms,” she said.

Sheinbaum orders investigation into allegations of police torture in Guadalajara

Regarding allegations that police tortured people who were detained during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday, Sheinbaum said that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) has to conduct a “very thorough investigation.”

“Yesterday I was asked about the issue of torture in Jalisco. … What happened in Jalisco can’t be allowed,” she said.

“… In addition to the use of streams of water and tear gas [against protesters], the issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” Sheinbaum said.

“A police force cannot torture anyone,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the CNDH investigation should examine “who gave the order” to torture detainees and interview “the victims.”

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

“… We, who came from the fight against [government] repression, cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum responds to exoneration of former INM chief

A reporter asked the president her opinion about the exoneration of former National Migration Institute (INM) chief Francisco Garduño, who faced a charge of improper exercise of public service in connection with a 2023 fire in an INM detention center in Ciudad Juárez that killed 40 migrants.

“It’s what the judges determined,” Sheinbaum responded.

Garduño, head of the INM between 2019 and 2025, was exonerated at a court hearing in Ciudad Juárez on Tuesday. Lawyers for the victims said they will challenge the decision.

Sheinbaum said that “a very thorough investigation” that examined “the responsibilities of each person” in connection with the fire was carried out. She then reiterated that the exoneration of Garduño was a decision made by “judges.”

According to authorities, the fire started when two detained migrants set a mattress alight to protest poor conditions in the INM detention center. Those two men survived the blaze and face homicide charges.

The Federal Attorney General’s Office began criminal proceedings against Garduño in April 2023, alleging that he failed to fulfill his duty to “supervise, protect and provide security to the people and facilities” under his control.

In September 2025, the former INM chief issued an apology to victims and relatives of the deceased.

There were “human rights violations that never should have happened” due to “omissions by personnel of the [INM],” he said at the time.

The Associated Press reported that Garduño “called for ‘those responsible’ to be punished and for reparations to be made without recognizing his own responsibility in the tragedy.”

To date, no one has been convicted of criminal wrongdoing in connection with the deadly fire.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Helping out after hurricanes, planning for Día de Muertos
World.content:
By the time you read this, Puerto Vallarta will be recovering from its third consecutive hurricane in the last few weeks. First came Polo, then Rachel, and now Simón — a Category 3 storm currently making its way up the Pacific coast. Luckily, the storms’ eyes stayed offshore, sparing the city the worst impacts. Still, our malecón and beachside resorts have taken a beating from intense tidal surges and waves; many neighborhoods have flooded, and we haven’t been able to safely enjoy the beach since Sept. 23, when the first red flags were raised.

Needless to say, many residents — myself included — are feeling a bit of a hurricane hangover these days and are thinking less about going out on the town and more about helping our communities recover.

So instead of entertainment listings, this week’s events roundup highlights a few volunteer opportunities and organizations that provide disaster relief and organize cleanup efforts after major storms and throughout the year. Whether you live in Puerto Vallarta permanently, seasonally, or just vacation here from time to time, there are ways you can help residents recover through these groups.

We’ve also thrown in what we know so far about Día de Muertos happenings. Even though we’ve been thrashed around by storms lately, this is still Mexico, so the celebrations will go on come hurricanes or high water.

Disaster relief, cleanup and community support organizations

Vallarta Cares

Vallarta Cares is a local charity that mobilizes food, water, hygiene and medical supply distribution to communities affected by natural disasters, including hurricanes, floods and other emergencies. The organization also operates a year-round soup kitchen that serves hundreds of meals daily, provides weekly medical services, including free dental services, and organizes medical brigades throughout the year.

Vallarta Cares was also recently awarded first place in the interior of Jalisco category for the 2026 Premio a la Generosidad Jalisco. You can inquire about volunteer opportunities and make a donation through its website.

Limpia Tu Mar

Limpia Tu Mar organizes trash cleanups along Vallarta’s beaches, rivers and at sea. Since its inception in 2017, the group’s cleanup brigades have removed more than 900 kilograms (1,984 pounds) of plastic, 125 kilograms (275 pounds) of styrofoam, 350 kilograms (771 pounds) of glass and 5,000 kilograms (11,023 pounds) of general garbage from the sea. Each week, volunteers set sail on boats from Puerto Vallarta to remove floating trash from the ocean.

Limpia Tu Mar also hosts one of Mexico’s largest environmental awareness events, the annual International Trash Fishing Tournament. This year’s tournament is coming up Oct. 18, and registration is still open if you want to participate or help sponsor the event. With all the recent storms washing tons of trash and debris into the bay, we could use all the help we can get to clean it up.

Local collection centers and cleanup brigades

If you are in Puerto Vallarta during hurricane season (June through November), local collection centers (centros de acopio) are often set up at community centers, fire stations and churches on short notice to organize relief efforts. Joining local community and business groups on social media is one of the fastest ways to find pop-up volunteering needs immediately following a storm.

One such brigade I join regularly is the Banderas Bay Project, started by local real estate agent Luis Salazar, which organizes monthly trash pickups around Boca de Tomatlán, one of the harder-hit areas from the recent storms.

Planning for Día de Muertos

Día de Muertos — Mexico’s annual celebration honoring departed souls — is around the corner, and that means Puerto Vallarta will again be pulling out all the stops.

This year, the city is participating in the statewide Festival de Las Almas (Festival of the Souls), featuring more than 350 free events across 11 municipalities in Jalisco from Oct. 24 through Nov. 2.

In Vallarta, the city is planning 28 free events and experiences Oct. 31 through Nov. 2 along the historic center, Los Arcos, Muelle de Los Muertos, Isla del Cuale, and, of course, the Malecón, which will again feature a monumental Catrina. The giant beauty has adorned the Malecón for the past several years, each time designed by a different Mexican artist. According to the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Board, this year she will be adorned with waves, whales, manta rays and bougainvillea.

If you do plan on heading downtown for the festivities, I recommend going early before the crowds get too big. Last year, we waited until after dark to go see the Catrina and were stuck in traffic for more than an hour trying to drive from the Marina to the Malecón.

Concierto de Día de Muertos

The Vallarta Symphony Orchestra will perform with the choirs of Puerto Vallarta and the University of Brasília for special Día de Muertos concerts on Oct. 30 at the Iglesia Reina de la Paz in Marina Vallarta at 9 p.m., and on Oct. 31 at the Haramara Auditorium at Universidad Tecnológica de Bahía de Banderas in Nayarit at 7 p.m. Tickets can be purchased from IAMPV.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: US congressional candidate says Mexico is where he gets healthcare as high costs dominate midterm debate
World.content:
Bobby Pulido, a singer and Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’s 15th District, recently said that he does not have health insurance and has had to go to Mexico to receive medical care.

Pulido, who is running against Republican Mónica De La Cruz, made the unexpected remark to Council President and CEO Javier Palomerez during a virtual discussion on Monday with the U.S. Hispanic Business Council.

“I’m going to start off by telling you that I don’t have health insurance, Javier. And I’m embarrassed to tell you that I’ve had to go to Mexico for my health care,” Pulido said, as cited by news outlet Border Report, reportedly the only journalism outlet that accessed the meeting.

Pulido, 52, whose full name is José Roberto Pulido Jr., lives in Edinburg, a border city located in southern Texas. According to Border Report, he also owns a home in Mexico.

During the conversation, Pulido contrasted U.S. President Trump’s reported plans to boost military spending with the difficulties U.S. residents face in obtaining affordable medical care.

“I live in the richest country in the world. Now the president wants to give a million and a half trillion dollars for our military budget when we cannot provide affordable health care to our people,” he said.

Pulido’s statements did not describe what specific illness, procedure or medical emergency has brought him to seek care in Mexico. Nor does the information shared by Border Report specify which Mexican city he visits for treatment, how much he pays or the reasons why he lacks insurance in the United States.

However, this isn’t the first time Pulido has publicly shared that he has traveled to Mexico for healthcare. On Sept. 27, he told Univisión he sought medical services in Mexico due to high costs in the U.S., while questioning the power of insurance companies in that country.

Before turning to politics, Pulido had a renowned career as a Tejano singer, with a fan base spanning Mexico and the U.S. Over the course of a three-decade career, he won two Latin Grammy Awards for Best Tejano Music Album — one of which he won in November 2025.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The MND Peso Index™ for October: Is the peso approaching its fair value?
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily.

The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued, undervalued or fairly valued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas.

Since we published the September index, the peso has been on quite a ride.

Between Sept. 2, the date on which we collected prices for the September index, and Oct. 6, the date on which we collected prices for this index, the peso depreciated 5.5%, trading at 16.98 to the dollar on the former date and 17.97 to the greenback on the latter date.

The peso’s depreciation was the decisive factor behind our first undervaluation finding for the currency since we launched the MND Peso Index™ in May.

Our headline finding for October 2026 indicates that the peso was undervalued against the dollar by 0.7%, a swing of 6.5 percentage points compared to the 5.8% overvaluation we determined in September.

For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May.

What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in October 2026?

In October 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, undervalued the Mexican peso by 0.7%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Oct. 6, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.84 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 17.97 pesos per dollar on Oct. 6.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 17.97 to the US dollar — was undervalued by 0.7% in early October.

In the table above, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (i.e., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the undervalued assessment for the peso.

Why did the peso go from overvalued to undervalued in just one month?

In contrast to September, the MND Peso Rate for October (17.84) is lower than the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected (17.97).

As a result, the peso has gone from being overvalued against the dollar in early September, per the MND Peso Index™ methodology, to being undervalued against the dollar in early October.

The shift was primarily driven by the significant weakening of the peso, as mentioned in the introduction to this article.

The peso depreciated 99 centavos from 16.98 to the US dollar on Sept. 2 to 17.97 to the dollar on Oct. 6, per the Banxico FIX rates for those dates. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s Sept. 16 interest rate hike and increased investor risk aversion are among the factors behind the peso’s recent depreciation. The Fed’s hike narrows the gap between U.S. and Mexican interest rates, making peso carry trades less attractive to investors.

The MND Peso Rate declined 12 centavos from 17.96 in September to 17.84 in October, reinforcing the shift toward undervaluation. Had the MND Peso Rate increased by 1 centavo, rather than declined by 12, it would have been exactly the same as the Banxico FIX rate, indicating that the peso was trading at fair value under the index’s methodology.

In any case, the difference between the Oct. 6 Banxico FIX rate and the MND Peso Rate in October was just 13 centavos. Hence, the undervaluation assessment for the peso is minimal, indicating that it was trading close to fair value on Oct. 6.

The slight variation in the MND Peso Rate is due to month-over-month changes in the implied rates for some individual goods and services. The implied rates that changed due to price fluctuations are highlighted in the table above.

6 months of the MND Peso Index™

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June, 2.4% in early August and 5.8% in early September. That’s right — there were five consecutive overvalued assessments for the peso before this month’s determination that the currency was slightly undervalued in early October.

The difference between this month’s undervalued assessment for the peso and the highest overvalued assessment — that in early September — is 6.5 percentage points.

So far in 2026, the peso has depreciated around 2% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Oct. 13 was 18.38. If the Banxico FIX rate was 18.38 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Oct. 6, the undervaluation assessment for the peso would have been 2.9%.

* Price sources: Mexico prices were collected from the websites and apps of Walmart México, Costco México, AutoZone México, Telmex, Cinépolis, Petco México, McDonald’s, Starbucks, Netflix, Spotify and Microsoft. Dallas prices were collected from their U.S. equivalents. The Banxico FIX rate of 17.97 published on Oct. 6, 2026, was used as the official exchange rate reference.

World.title: Horn of Africa 2026: Why It Matters and Who Backs Whom
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Horn of Africa · Pillar Guide

Key Facts The region Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti and Somalia, home to about 160 million people, with Sudan and Yemen across the borders and the water.

Why it matters The Bab el-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea and the Suez Canal to the Indian Ocean and the trade routes of Asia.

Why now Ethiopia and Eritrea cut ties on 1 October 2026, and Ethiopian troops reached the Eritrean border at Zalambessa by 13 October.

Who backs whom The UAE is close to Ethiopia and to Sudan’s RSF. Egypt, Eritrea and Saudi Arabia favour Sudan’s army, and Egypt courts Somalia and Eritrea.

Foreign bases Djibouti hosts bases for the United States, China, France, Japan and Italy, a rare cluster of rival armies in one small country.

Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 19.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 December 2026 (15 October, 6:06 a.m. ET).

Still open Whether Ethiopia and Eritrea fight a full war, and who could mediate between them, is not settled.

Horn of Africa geopolitics come down to one fact: the region overlooks the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the southern gate to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Those routes carried about 12% of all oil traded by sea in the first half of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

In 2026 five conflicts overlap there at once, from Ethiopia’s clash with Eritrea to Sudan’s civil war and Houthi attacks from Yemen. Almost every major and middle power has taken a side, which makes this corner of Africa one of the most explosive places on earth.

A sailor stands watch aboard the US destroyer USS Jason Dunham in the Bab el-Mandeb strait between Djibouti and Yemen in October 2018. (Photo: US Department of Defense, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Why the Horn Matters to the World

The Horn of Africa is the wedge of land that points east into the Indian Ocean, with Yemen just across the water. At the Bab el-Mandeb, Africa and Arabia sit only a short boat ride apart, and every ship between the Suez Canal and Asia must pass.

The IMF said in March 2024 that the Suez Canal normally carries about 15% of global maritime trade by volume. The US Energy Information Administration found that the Red Sea routes carried about 8% of world trade in liquefied natural gas in the first half of 2023.

Egypt feels the cost first, because Suez Canal tolls are one of its main sources of dollars. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said in October 2026 that canal revenue fell from about US$10 billion a year to US$3.3 billion, before recovering to about US$4.4 billion.

The seabed matters too, because the data cables that link Europe, Africa and Asia run under the Red Sea. Djibouti now hopes to turn that position into a digital and computing hub, and our Djibouti explainer shows how it earns its living.

Inland lies the Nile, whose Blue Nile branch rises in Ethiopia and supplies most of the river’s water downstream in Sudan and Egypt. The four core Horn states of Ethiopia, Somalia, Eritrea and Djibouti held about 160 million people in 2025, according to World Bank estimates.

Djibouti, a country of about 1.2 million people, hosts military bases for China, France, Italy, Japan and the United States, according to the World Bank. Few places on earth pack so many foreign armies into so small a territory.

The Bab el-Mandeb strait seen from mid-channel, with Yemen in the distance and Djibouti behind. (Photo: Richard Weil, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Why It Is So Explosive Now

Several local wars have always simmered in the Horn, but in 2026 they have begun to touch each other. Five fault lines now run through the region, each with outside backers, and our Horn of Africa hub follows all of them.

The first runs between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with Tigray in the middle. Federal troops retook Mekelle in early October 2026 and reached the border town of Zalambessa, as our report on the Zalambessa advance and our Tigray guide explain.

The second pits Somalia against Somaliland, the northwestern region that declared independence in 1991 and runs its own state. Israel recognised it on 26 December 2025, and our Somaliland recognition explainer sets out the stakes for Somalia.

The third is Sudan’s war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. It began on 15 April 2023, and our Sudan war explainer and our guide to Sudan in the Horn map the fronts and the backers.

The fourth is the Red Sea itself, where Yemen’s Houthi movement, an Iran-backed armed group, has attacked shipping since late 2023. It also struck Saudi Arabia in 2026, and our Houthis and Red Sea explainer and our Bab el-Mandeb analysis follow the shipping risk.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned a Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport in October 2026, which reportedly killed 12 people. Saudi Arabia, which leads the coalition backing Yemen’s government, is now itself a front line.

The fifth is the Nile, where Egypt sees Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a threat to its water. Our Nile dam explainer covers the dispute, which pushes Cairo towards Ethiopia’s rivals.

The Region at a Glance

Seven countries and territories shape the Horn’s politics, including Yemen across the strait. Population figures below are World Bank estimates for 2025 unless stated otherwise.

Ethiopia Population: About 135.5 million (World Bank, 2025) Capital: Addis Ababa, seat of the African Union Leader: Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, in office since 2018, sworn in for a new five-year term on 5 October 2026 Ports: None; landlocked since Eritrea’s independence in 1993, it trades mainly through Djibouti and wants its own access to the sea Main conflict: Renewed war in Tigray and a standoff with Eritrea; see our Ethiopia explainer Eritrea Population: About 3.6 million (World Bank, 2025) Capital: Asmara Leader: President Isaias Afwerki, in power since independence in 1993, with no national election held Ports: Massawa and Assab on the Red Sea Main conflict: Fears an Ethiopian push for Assab; cut ties with Addis Ababa on 1 October 2026; see our Eritrea explainer Djibouti Population: About 1.2 million (World Bank, 2025) Capital: Djibouti City Leader: President Ismail Omar Guelleh, in office since 1999 Ports: Djibouti, Doraleh and Tadjourah, the main gateway for Ethiopia’s trade Main conflict: None at home; it rents land to foreign armies, as our military bases explainer shows Somalia Population: About 19.7 million (World Bank, 2025) Capital: Mogadishu Leader: President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who says his mandate runs to May 2027; the opposition says it expired in May 2026 Ports: Mogadishu, Kismayo and Bosaso, and it claims Berbera in Somaliland Main conflict: The al-Shabaab insurgency, an election dispute and the Somaliland question Somaliland Population: Not known; no reliable census figure exists Capital: Hargeisa Leader: President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Irro, elected in November 2024 Ports: Berbera, run by the Dubai port operator DP World Main conflict: Seeks recognition as a state; Somalia says it is Somali territory Sudan Population: About 51.7 million (World Bank, 2025) Capital: Khartoum; the army-backed government ran the war from Port Sudan Leader: General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, army chief and head of the Transitional Sovereignty Council Ports: Port Sudan, the country’s only major seaport Main conflict: War between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023 Yemen Population: About 41.8 million (World Bank, 2025) Capital: Sanaa, held by the Houthis; the recognised government sits in Aden Leader: Split: Abdul-Malik al-Houthi leads the Houthis, and a Presidential Leadership Council leads the recognised government Ports: Hodeidah under the Houthis, Aden under the government Main conflict: Civil war since 2014 and Houthi attacks on shipping and on Saudi Arabia

Djiboutian marines practise boarding a ship at the Port of Djibouti during the Cutlass Express exercise in 2013. (Photo: SSgt Chad Warren, US Air Force, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Great-Power Contest

Horn of Africa geopolitics drew in the great powers long before the current wars. Each now has troops, ships, loans or ports in the region, and each reads the crisis through its own rivalries.

United States

Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti is the anchor of American power in the region and hosts the Combined Joint Task Force-Horn of Africa, according to US Africa Command. The command logged 86 airstrikes in Somalia in 2026 through September, against al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda affiliate, and the Islamic State’s Somali branch.

At sea, the United States set up a naval coalition to protect shipping in December 2023 and has struck Houthi targets since January 2024. Washington has not recognised Somaliland, which has offered minerals and a base in return for recognition.

China

China keeps a military base in Djibouti, one of the five national bases the World Bank lists there, not far from Camp Lemonnier. Chinese firms also built the railway from Addis Ababa to Djibouti, the main rail link between Ethiopia and the sea.

Ethiopian officials fear that the railway and other routes to Djibouti are vulnerable to attack or sabotage, Crisis Group reported in February 2026. The same group listed China among the powers that should warn Ethiopia that military action against Eritrea is unacceptable.

Russia

Russia has long sought a naval logistics centre at Port Sudan, under a 2020 agreement with Khartoum that has yet to produce a working base. Moscow courts both Sudan’s army-led government and Eritrea, one of only five countries that voted against the UN General Assembly’s March 2022 resolution on Ukraine.

At the UN Security Council, Russia has opposed extending Sudan sanctions beyond Darfur, noted Security Council Report, an independent research group, in September 2026. A Red Sea foothold would let its navy refuel and repair ships far from home waters.

France, the EU and Japan

France keeps a garrison in Djibouti, its former colony, and Japan’s Self-Defense Forces also keep a base there. Italy keeps a base as well, according to the World Bank, and our report on Djibouti and the EU mission covers Europe’s naval role.

The EU runs two naval operations nearby: Atalanta, launched in 2008 against Somali piracy, and Aspides, which protects merchant ships in the Red Sea. The EU’s foreign service describes the mandate of Aspides as defensive, so unlike the US Navy it does not strike targets on land.

The US carrier USS Enterprise and the cruiser USS Vicksburg transit the Bab el-Mandeb strait in April 2012. (Photo: MC3 Daniel J. Meshel, US Navy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Middle Powers and Who Backs Whom

The Gulf states, Turkey, Egypt, Iran and Israel are often more decisive than the great powers, because they bring money, drones and ports. Their rivalries in the Horn date back years, and Crisis Group described a new quarrel between Saudi Arabia and the UAE beginning in late December 2025.

The United Arab Emirates is the most active of them, and Crisis Group wrote in February 2026 that Abiy Ahmed is close to it. Crisis Group also called the UAE the RSF’s chief sponsor, which Abu Dhabi contests, and the Emirati firm DP World operates Berbera port in Somaliland.

Saudi Arabia, across the Red Sea from Eritrea, backs Yemen’s recognised government against the Houthis and, according to Crisis Group, favours Sudan’s army. It mediated the 2018 Jeddah Agreement between Ethiopia and Eritrea and has kept friendly ties with both since.

Turkey has long been one of Somalia’s main partners, and Turkish companies run Mogadishu’s airport and seaport, according to Turkey’s foreign ministry. In late 2024 Ankara brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia, which Crisis Group said ended Abiy’s hopes of a naval base in Somaliland.

Egypt is Ethiopia’s main regional rival because of the Nile dam, and Crisis Group calls it a close wartime ally of Sudan’s army. On 4 October 2026 Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan adopted the El Alamein Joint Declaration on the Red Sea, as our report on Cairo describes.

Qatar works mostly through money and mediation, and Crisis Group reported in 2019 that it planned to expand the Somali port of Hobyo. The same report found that Qatar and the UAE had paid rival Somali allies to undermine each other’s interests.

Iran backs the Houthis, Security Council Report noted in September 2026, and Israel has accused Tehran of shipping them weapons through the port of Hodeidah. The UN Security Council has kept a targeted arms embargo on the Houthis since resolution 2216 of April 2015.

Israel became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland on 26 December 2025. Israeli forces have also struck Houthi targets in Yemen in response to missile and drone attacks on Israel.

Who Backs Whom

The cards below list each local actor’s outside backers. Documented means an official statement or agreement, reported means credible specialist reporting, and alleged means an accusation that is disputed.

Ethiopia’s federal government UAE: Close partner, reported by Crisis Group (2026) Turkey: Brokered its Ankara Declaration with Somalia, documented (2024) Rivals: Egypt and Eritrea, documented in official statements Eritrea Egypt: Partner in the El Alamein Joint Declaration, documented (October 2026) Russia: Diplomatic partner; voted with Moscow at the UN, documented (2022) Saudi Arabia: Friendly ties and quiet diplomacy, reported by Crisis Group (2026) Somalia’s federal government Turkey: Turkish firms run Mogadishu’s airport and seaport, documented by Turkey’s foreign ministry Egypt: Partner in the El Alamein Joint Declaration, documented (2026) Eritrea: Part of a loose alliance with Egypt and Somalia, reported by Crisis Group (2026) Somaliland Israel: Recognition on 26 December 2025, documented UAE: DP World runs Berbera port, documented United States: No recognition so far, documented Sudan’s army (SAF) Egypt: Close wartime ally, reported by Crisis Group (2026) Saudi Arabia: Favours the army, reported by Crisis Group (2026) Eritrea: Sided with the army and trains allied militias, reported by Crisis Group (2026) Iran: Iranian-made drones bought for the army, documented by the US Treasury (2025) Rapid Support Forces (RSF) UAE: Called the RSF’s chief sponsor by Crisis Group (2026); alleged, the UAE contests it Ethiopia: An RSF training camp in Benishangul-Gumuz, alleged (Crisis Group, 2026) The Houthis Iran: Backing reported by Security Council Report (2026); weapons shipments through Hodeidah alleged by Israel (2024) Al-Shabaab (partner): Over 100 fighters trained in Yemen, reported by Garowe Online citing US and regional officials (2026); see our report

How the Rivalries Feed Each Other

The Nile dispute drives Egypt towards Ethiopia’s neighbours, because Cairo wants allies around the country it blames for its water risk. Crisis Group wrote in February 2026 that Egypt, Somalia and Eritrea had formed a loose alliance to counter what they saw as Ethiopia’s ambitions.

Analysts at the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute in Washington, read the El Alamein summit of October 2026 the same way. They wrote that most of its aims involve countering Ethiopia’s actions and objectives in the Nile valley and the Red Sea.

Gulf rivalries then play out on the ground in Sudan and Somaliland. When Saudi Arabia and the UAE quarrel, the army and the RSF in Sudan, and Mogadishu and Hargeisa in Somalia, each find a patron.

At sea, the Houthis and their Iranian backers face a naval presence led by the United States, Europe and Saudi Arabia. In September 2026 the UN Security Council held an emergency briefing on Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, requested by Bahrain and the UK.

On land, Ethiopia’s drive for a port collides with Eritrean and Somali sovereignty, and Abiy repeated the demand when he was sworn in on 5 October 2026. In a letter to the UN Security Council, Eritrea’s foreign minister accused Ethiopia of seeking to acquire sovereign access to the sea by force.

Three Scenarios for 2027

No one can say where Horn of Africa geopolitics will lead in 2027, but specialist analysts have sketched the main risks. Crisis Group, the conflict-prevention organisation based in Brussels, has written most closely about the Ethiopia and Eritrea front.

The first scenario is a contained standoff, in which armies face each other along the border without a full war. Crisis Group wrote in February 2026 that the huge costs of another conflict were helping hold the sides back.

In that case Saudi Arabia, Turkey and the African Union gain as mediators, and shipping keeps a risk premium without a new shock. Insurers would keep charging war-risk premiums, but more ships could return to the Suez route.

The second scenario is a regional war that starts between Ethiopia and Eritrea and spreads. Crisis Group warned that a slide toward hostilities would be easy to start but much more difficult to stop.

It added that such a war would overlap with Sudan’s, drag in powers from outside the Horn and further roil the Red Sea. Egypt, the UAE and Saudi Arabia would face pressure to choose sides openly, and our comparison of the two armies sets out what each could field.

The third scenario is a negotiated Red Sea settlement that trades secure Ethiopian access to a port for guarantees of Eritrean and Somali sovereignty. Crisis Group urged exactly that kind of quiet diplomacy, addressing Ethiopia’s desire for reliable sea access and Eritrea’s fears of an attack.

Such a deal would reward the mediators and calm shipping insurance on the Suez route. It would also need the Houthis to stop attacking ships, which no regional deal can guarantee.

What It All Means

For global trade, every flare-up near the strait raises freight rates and insurance costs, because ships must either pay more or sail around Africa. Egypt’s lost canal revenue shows how quickly one chokepoint can drain a national budget.

For energy, the Red Sea route matters more when the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, because Saudi Arabia can export oil from its Red Sea coast. That makes the Houthi threat to Saudi ports a risk for oil prices worldwide.

For Europe, war in Sudan and Ethiopia pushes more people to flee, first to neighbouring countries and then north. UN data on 5 October 2026 counted about 11.3 million people forcibly displaced by Sudan’s war, including 4.6 million who reached neighbouring countries.

Horn of Africa geopolitics also mirror the contest between the United States and China, whose bases sit close together in Djibouti. Above all, the region’s people pay the price in hunger, displacement and death, as in the 2020 to 2022 Tigray war.

Security Council Report, an independent research group, notes that estimates put the death toll of that war at about 600,000. Another war on the same ground would hit a population that has barely recovered.

What the Markets Say

On Polymarket, bets priced a 14.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 October and 19.5% by 31 December (15 October, 6:06 a.m. ET). That market had drawn about US$97,000 in bets, and the chance that Donald Trump recognises Somaliland before 2027 stood at 5%.

Bets on the market “Perim Island no longer under Houthi control”, an island in the strait, stood at 17.3% for 31 October and 34% for 31 December. A market on Somali pirates seizing a vessel by 31 October traded at 24.5% (all 15 October, 6:06 a.m. ET).

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

For American shippers and consumers, trouble at the Bab el-Mandeb means longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope and higher freight costs. Those costs feed into the price of goods from Asia and fuel bound for Europe.

For the US military, Camp Lemonnier puts American forces close to any fighting in the region, from Somalia to Yemen. A wider war could expose them to drone and missile attacks, as the Houthis have shown at sea.

For US policy, the open questions are whether to recognise Somaliland and how hard to press Ethiopia and Eritrea to stand down. The United States requested the UN Security Council session on the Horn of Africa held on 13 October 2026.

For investors, the region touches shipping stocks, oil prices and Egypt’s bonds, which depend on canal revenue. The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Tigray or to Ethiopia’s border with Eritrea.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Eritrean troops remain inside Ethiopia, or whether either army will cross the border in force. Both governments have given the UN Security Council opposite accounts of who attacked whom.

The size of outside arms supplies to Sudan’s army and the RSF is not publicly documented in full. The UAE contests UN experts’ assertions linking it to the war, and their 2026 report had not been published by September 2026.

It is also not known whether Russia will ever open its planned base at Port Sudan, or whether Washington will recognise Somaliland. The death toll and displacement since fighting escalated in Tigray in September 2026 have not been counted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the Horn of Africa so important?

It overlooks the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the gate between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean on the Suez route between Asia and Europe. The Red Sea routes carried about 12% of seaborne oil in the first half of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Which countries have military bases in Djibouti?

The World Bank lists military bases for China, France, Italy, Japan, the United States and NATO, plus forces of other countries fighting piracy. The US base, Camp Lemonnier, hosts the Combined Joint Task Force-Horn of Africa.

Who backs whom in the Horn of Africa?

Crisis Group says the UAE is close to Ethiopia and sponsors Sudan’s RSF, which Abu Dhabi contests. Egypt, Eritrea and Saudi Arabia lean towards Sudan’s army, while Turkey and Egypt back Somalia’s government.

Could Ethiopia and Eritrea go to war in 2026?

The risk is real, since the two cut diplomatic ties on 1 October 2026 and Ethiopian troops reached the border by 13 October. Crisis Group has warned that such a war would be easy to start but hard to stop.

CHILE · BUSINESS

Key Facts The country Chile is the world’s largest copper producer and one of Latin America’s most open economies, with a US free trade agreement since 2004.

What happened Fitch Ratings raised Chile’s retail giant Falabella to BBB from BBB- on its international scale, made public on Wednesday 14 October.

The company Falabella runs department stores and falabella.com, Sodimac home-improvement stores, Tottus supermarkets, Banco Falabella and the Mallplaza shopping malls.

Chile’s own scale Falabella and its Sodimac unit rose to AA(cl) from AA-(cl), and the shares kept the top grade, Primera Clase Nivel 1(cl).

The numbers Net profit was US$897 million in 2025, before a fair-value accounting effect, and US$497 million in the first half of 2026, up 17.9%.

Why it matters BBB sits two steps above junk, leaving more room above the BBB- floor that many US and European bond funds require.

Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

Fitch Ratings has raised Chile retail giant Falabella to BBB from BBB-, one notch higher on its international scale, with a stable outlook. For US and European bond investors, the owner of stores, a bank and shopping malls now sits two steps above junk instead of one.

The decision became public on Wednesday 14 October in Santiago, Chile’s capital. Fitch, one of the three big global credit rating agencies, pointed to lower debt, stronger margins and more cash.

What Fitch Changed

Grupo Falabella is a Chilean group that sells clothes, home goods, building materials and groceries, and lends through its own bank. Its Company Intelligence profile sets out its units, its markets and its listing on the Santiago stock exchange.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

On Fitch’s international scale, the rating moved to BBB from BBB-, Diario Financiero, a Chilean business daily, reported on Wednesday evening. La Tercera, a leading Santiago newspaper, reported the same move in its business section Pulso.

On Chile’s national scale, Fitch raised Falabella and Sodimac, its home-improvement chain, to AA(cl) from AA-(cl). The suffix marks a grade that compares Chilean borrowers with each other, not with companies abroad.

Fitch also kept Falabella’s shares at Primera Clase Nivel 1(cl), the top grade on Chile’s scale for listed shares. Both newspapers said the outlook on the international rating is stable, a signal that no further change is expected soon.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Chile markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Fitch Moved Now

According to Diario Financiero, Fitch said the decision reflects a stronger financial and business profile for the group. The agency credited Falabella’s market position and the spread of its businesses.

Better margins let the group build up cash, pay down debt and lower its borrowing relative to earnings, the newspaper reported. That is the core of Fitch’s case for the retail giant Falabella.

Both outlets cite the company’s recent results as the backdrop. Falabella earned a record US$897 million in 2025, excluding a fair-value accounting effect, and US$497 million in the first half of 2026.

That first-half figure was 17.9% higher than a year earlier, according to the company figures reported by both papers. La Tercera added that Falabella called the April to June quarter its best second quarter ever at the operating level.

A Long Road Back to Investment Grade

The upgrade caps a three-year climb for the retail giant Falabella. The group lost its investment-grade rating from Fitch in November 2023, Diario Financiero recalled.

Fitch restored that status on 29 October 2025, lifting the group to BBB- from BB+. S&P Global Ratings, another of the big three agencies, followed in April 2026 with a BBB- grade and a stable outlook.

Fitch now places Falabella one step above S&P’s grade. Its mall arm Mallplaza also gained, after the Chilean rating agency Feller Rate lifted its parent’s bonds to AAA in late September.

On 30 September, Falabella and Mallplaza signed two non-binding deals to reorganise part of their property, a step meant to boost growth. Fitch said the group’s cash and debt maturities leave room to fund its US$900 million investment plan in stores, malls and technology.

What the Managers Said

General manager Alejandro González Dale, who runs the group, called the upgrade a recognition of the progress the company has made, La Tercera reported. Diario Financiero quoted him as saying Falabella is now in a favourable position to deepen the synergies across its businesses.

Juan Pablo Harrison, the corporate manager for administration and finance, credited stronger cash generation and a steady cut in debt. He also cited disciplined management of resources, both newspapers reported.

What It Means for You

If you hold an emerging-market bond fund, BBB gives the retail giant Falabella more room before any cut could push it into junk. Many US pension funds and insurers may only own debt rated investment grade by the main agencies.

For shoppers and visitors, Falabella is the name on department stores and Sodimac stores in Chile, Peru and Colombia. Banco Falabella, its consumer bank, offers credit cards and everyday accounts in Chile.

A stronger rating usually lowers what a company pays to borrow, which can free money for stores, online sales and the bank. Thursday’s trading in Santiago will show whether investors had already priced in the move (Chile market report, 14 October).

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether S&P will follow with an upgrade of its own, or when. It is also open how much less the retail giant Falabella will pay on its next bond sale.

It is also unclear whether the margin gains will hold in what the company called a tougher climate for consumer spending. Its third-quarter results, the next scheduled report, will give the first answer.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Falabella?

Falabella is a Chilean retail group that runs department stores, Sodimac home-improvement stores, Tottus supermarkets, Banco Falabella and Mallplaza malls. Its shares trade on the Santiago stock exchange under the ticker FALABELLA.

What rating did Fitch give Falabella?

Fitch raised the retail giant Falabella to BBB from BBB- on its international scale, with a stable outlook. On Chile’s national scale, Falabella and Sodimac rose to AA(cl) from AA-(cl).

Why did Fitch upgrade Falabella?

Fitch cited stronger margins, more cash, lower debt and less borrowing relative to earnings. It also pointed to the group’s market position and the spread of its businesses.

Is Falabella investment grade?

Yes, Fitch restored Falabella to investment grade in October 2025 and has now lifted it one more step. S&P Global Ratings also rates the group investment grade, at BBB-.

JAMAICA · CRIME

Key Facts The country Jamaica is an English-speaking Caribbean island nation led by Prime Minister Andrew Holness.

What happened US federal prison records now list 28 January 2029 as the release date for Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke, one year later than before.

Who he is Coke, 57, is a Jamaican drug lord who once led the Shower Posse gang of West Kingston and is serving 23 years.

Where Federal Correctional Institution Fort Dix in New Jersey, where music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs is also held.

The reported fight Coke and Combs reportedly fought inside the prison, and Combs was reportedly taken to an outside hospital.

Previous date 29 January 2028, the release date the prison records showed earlier this year.

Still open The reason for the change, and any link to the alleged fight, remains unexplained.

The US Bureau of Prisons lists 28 January 2029 as the release date for Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke, the Jamaican drug lord held in New Jersey. That is one year later than the date its public records showed earlier this year.

The change surfaced on Wednesday 14 October, as reports spread that Coke had fought fellow inmate Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs at Fort Dix federal prison. For American readers, the story links a gang boss extradited by Washington in 2010 to the music mogul known worldwide as Diddy.

What the Prison Records Show

The Bureau of Prisons inmate locator, a free public database, lists the Jamaican drug lord, 57, as inmate 02257-748 at the Fort Dix prison. His projected release date there now reads 28 January 2029.

Radio Jamaica and the Jamaica Observer both reported that the same database showed 29 January 2028 earlier this year. Nationwide News, a Kingston radio network, said that was the date it saw when it checked the site in July.

Radio Jamaica, a national broadcaster based in Kingston, recalled reports in May that Coke was in line for an early release. The station said US prison authorities had not publicly confirmed that the reported fight caused the new date.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Jamaica Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Reported Fight With Diddy

The US entertainment site TMZ reported on Wednesday that the Jamaican drug lord and Combs had a physical fight inside the prison. The Jamaica Observer, citing that report, said Combs suffered a head injury and was taken to an outside medical facility.

Nationwide News, also citing TMZ, said Coke confronted Combs over prison sweeps that seized contraband, including mobile phones, from several inmates. The Observer said the clash followed disciplinary action against fellow inmates that was blamed on Combs.

US prison authorities have not publicly linked the fight to Coke’s new release date. The Observer said the circumstances of the incident had not been independently verified.

Who Christopher Coke Is

The Jamaican drug lord is the former leader of the Shower Posse, a criminal network rooted in West Kingston, the western side of Jamaica’s capital. Nationwide News calls him a West Kingston strongman, meaning a boss who held sway over a whole district.

The United States sought him on drug charges, and he was extradited in June 2010 after a month-long manhunt in Jamaica. The Observer reports that more than 70 people died during that operation.

In 2012 a US court sentenced him to 23 years in prison after he pleaded guilty. The charges included conspiring to traffic large amounts of marijuana and cocaine into the United States and conspiring to commit assault in aid of racketeering.

Why Diddy Is at Fort Dix

Sean Combs, the American music mogul known as Diddy, was sentenced last year to just over four years in federal prison. The Observer said he was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving two of his former girlfriends.

The Bureau of Prisons locator lists Combs, 56, at Fort Dix under register number 37452-054. His projected release date is 2 March 2028, almost 11 months before Coke’s new date.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the Jamaican drug lord’s case shows that a federal prisoner’s release date is a projection that can change while the sentence runs. Anyone can check a prisoner’s current date on the Bureau of Prisons inmate locator by name or register number.

For followers of the Combs case, the same public database lists his projected release as 2 March 2028. The record shows only dates and places, not disciplinary findings or the reasons behind a change.

In Jamaica, Coke’s name still recalls the deadly 2010 manhunt for him, and his case remains national news. The Observer, Radio Jamaica and Nationwide News all reported the new date on Wednesday.

Deportations from the United States were already news in Kingston after Jamaica received 22 third-country nationals on Tuesday 13 October under a deal with Washington. A guide to Jamaica and its neighbours in the Caribbean explains the island’s place in the region.

What Is Not Known

It is not known why the Bureau of Prisons moved the Jamaican drug lord’s date, or exactly when it changed. US prison authorities have not publicly linked it to the reported fight.

Nationwide News, citing TMZ, dated the fight to Friday 9 October, while the Observer said Combs went to hospital on Wednesday. The extent of any injury to Combs has not been officially confirmed.

It is also not known whether either man faces new charges or prison discipline over the incident. Nationwide News said it had asked the Bureau of Prisons for an explanation.

More: Jamaica news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke?

Christopher Coke is a Jamaican drug lord and the former leader of the Shower Posse, a gang based in West Kingston. He was extradited to the United States in 2010 and sentenced in 2012 to 23 years in prison.

When will Dudus Coke be released?

The US Bureau of Prisons inmate locator lists his release date as 28 January 2029. Earlier this year the same record showed 29 January 2028.

Did Diddy fight Dudus in prison?

TMZ reported on Wednesday 14 October that Coke and Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs had a physical fight at Fort Dix, and Jamaican outlets relayed the report. The Jamaica Observer said the circumstances had not been independently verified.

When is Diddy due out of prison?

The Bureau of Prisons lists Sean Combs’s projected release date as 2 March 2028. He is held at Federal Correctional Institution Fort Dix in New Jersey.

World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PERU · POLITICS

Key Facts The country Peru, a US free-trade partner and major copper exporter, is led by conservative President Keiko Fujimori, in office since July 2026.

What happened A survey published on Wednesday 14 October puts the Fujimori approval rating at 28.3%, down from 42.8% a month earlier.

Disapproval Disapproval rose to 53.6% from 40.3%, while 18.1% of Peruvians gave no opinion.

US operations 50.3% oppose joint US military operations on Peruvian soil against organised crime, and 28.1% support them.

Top worries Corruption, named by 58.8%, and crime and drug trafficking, named by 42.2%, are the problems Peruvians cite most.

The survey AtlasIntel polled 2,024 adults online from 2 to 7 October, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2 points.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Approval of Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori fell to 28.3% in a survey published on Wednesday 14 October, down from 42.8% a month earlier. The survey by pollster AtlasIntel, which tracks the Fujimori approval rating monthly, also found half of Peruvians oppose joint military operations with the US.

That matters in Washington, whose military commander for South and Central America was in Peru on Wednesday to widen cooperation against gangs and illegal mining. Peru’s new ambassador to the US said in an interview reported the same day that rejecting such cooperation would be “suicidal”.

A Sharp Fall in One Month

Disapproval of the way Fujimori runs the government rose to 53.6%, up from 40.3% in August, according to the full AtlasIntel report. Another 18.1% said they did not know, up slightly from 16.9%.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Asked to rate the government as a whole, 50.2% called it bad or very bad and 30.6% called it fair. Only 19.1% rated it excellent or good.

Fujimori, the daughter of former president Alberto Fujimori, won a runoff in June on her fourth bid for the presidency. The candidate of the conservative Fuerza Popular (Popular Force) party took office in July, so the series on her presidency starts in August.

La República, a Lima daily, reported the 14.5-point drop in the Fujimori approval rating on Wednesday afternoon. AtlasIntel runs the monthly survey with Bloomberg in seven countries, from Mexico to Argentina.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Peru Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Half of Peruvians Oppose Joint US Operations

AtlasIntel asked how far people agree that the United States should carry out joint military operations on Peruvian soil to fight organised crime. In total, 29.8% strongly disagreed and 20.5% disagreed, so 50.3% are against.

On the other side, 15.1% strongly agreed and 13.0% agreed, a combined 28.1%. Another 13.7% were neutral and 8.1% did not know.

Half of respondents, 50.0%, said US security policies limit Peru’s freedom to make its own decisions on organised crime. Only 21.4% said those policies strengthen that freedom.

Asked what a bigger US presence would most likely bring, 29.1% chose a lasting loss of sovereignty. Almost as many, 27.5%, expected the effective break-up of the main cartels and criminal gangs.

Corruption, Crime and a Gloomy Economy

Corruption is the problem Peruvians mention most, named by 58.8% of respondents, who could pick up to three issues. Insecurity, crime and drug trafficking follow at 42.2%, ahead of education at 26.1%.

Some 21.1% named the weakening of democracy, and 15.9% named high prices and inflation. Only 9.3% listed the economy itself among the main problems.

The mood on the economy is gloomy too, with 62% calling Peru’s economic situation bad and 22% calling it good. Some 64% gave the job market a negative rating, and only 15% a positive one.

Washington’s Security Push Meets Doubts

On Wednesday, Defence Minister Rafael Belaúnde met US Ambassador Bernie Navarro and General Francis Donovan, head of US Southern Command, in Iquitos. The Peruvian broadcaster Exitosa reported the talks in the Amazon city, citing the Defence Ministry.

They discussed transnational organised crime, illegal mining and Peru’s recent move to join the Shield of the Americas, a US-led security coalition against drug cartels. Belaúnde said the alliance would give Peru intelligence to fight organised crime.

Álvaro Vargas Llosa, the writer who is Peru’s new ambassador in Washington, told the TV channel Latina that rejecting that opportunity would be “absolutely suicidal”. He added that “nobody here is going to endanger Peru’s sovereignty”, the news site Infobae reported.

Beyond the Fujimori approval slump, the survey suggests Washington still has to win over much of the Peruvian public. About as many Peruvians fear a lasting loss of sovereignty from a bigger US presence as expect it to dismantle the gangs.

What It Means for You

For investors, a falling Fujimori approval rating in her first months may make it harder to steer laws through Congress. Peru is a major copper and gold exporter, so political turbulence there matters to mining companies and bondholders.

For US policy, the numbers show the limits of public support for American military action in Peru. Any plan for joint operations there would face a sceptical public, with opponents outnumbering supporters almost two to one.

For visitors, the survey changes nothing on the ground, but it shows what Peruvians themselves worry about. Crime and drug trafficking rank second among their concerns, behind only corruption.

What Is Not Known

The survey does not say what drove the 14.5-point fall in the Fujimori approval rating. It also cannot show yet whether the drop is a one-month dip or the start of a longer slide.

AtlasIntel publishes its Latam Pulse every month, so the next Peru edition will show whether the trend holds. It is also not known whether Lima and Washington plan any joint military operation on Peruvian soil.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Keiko Fujimori?

Keiko Fujimori is Peru’s president, elected in a June runoff as the candidate of the conservative Fuerza Popular (Popular Force) party. She is the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, who governed Peru in the 1990s.

How was the AtlasIntel poll carried out?

AtlasIntel surveyed 2,024 Peruvian adults through random online recruitment from 2 to 7 October 2026. It reports a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points at 95% confidence.

Do Peruvians want US troops to fight crime in Peru?

Most do not: 50.3% oppose joint US military operations against organised crime on Peruvian soil. Some 28.1% support them, and the rest are neutral or undecided.

Why is the poll called September if it ran in October?

AtlasIntel labels it its September 2026 edition, although the fieldwork ran from 2 to 7 October. The previous edition, labelled August, put the Fujimori approval rating at 42.8%.

COLOMBIA · MARKETS

Key Facts The country Colombia, a key US security partner in South America, has been led by conservative President Abelardo De La Espriella since 7 August 2026.

What happened Bogotá Energy Group (Grupo Energía Bogotá) auctions up to 400,000 million pesos (about US$126 million) of short-term notes on Thursday 15 October 2026.

The company A power and natural gas group operating in Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala, 65.68% owned by the city of Bogotá.

The notes Fixed-rate peso notes maturing in 180 or 364 days, sold by Dutch auction on the Colombian Securities Exchange.

Who can buy Investors in general, from 1 million pesos (about US$314), through a Colombian broker; payment is due Friday 16 October.

Rating F1+(col) from Fitch Ratings Colombia, its highest short-term grade on the Colombian national scale.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Bogotá Energy Group (GEB), controlled by Colombia’s capital city, is auctioning up to 400,000 million pesos (about US$126 million) in short-term notes on Thursday. The company, known locally as Grupo Energía Bogotá, has opened the sale to investors in general, from 1 million pesos (about US$314).

The company has already begun the process of listing its shares in the United States, the Colombian financial news site Valora Analitik reported. Thursday’s auction is the first sale under a program of up to 2.5 trillion pesos (about US$785 million) in local bonds and notes.

What Bogotá Energy Group Is Selling

The base offer is 250,000 million pesos (about US$79 million) in notes maturing in 180 or 364 days, the offer notice says. If demand is higher, Bogotá Energy Group may add 150,000 million pesos (about US$47 million) for a ceiling of 400,000 million pesos (about US$126 million).

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Both maturities pay a fixed annual rate, and interest and principal are paid in full when the notes mature. The rate comes from a Dutch auction, in which all winning bidders for each maturity receive the same cut-off rate.

Colombia’s Finance Ministry sets a maximum rate for each maturity, and that ceiling stays hidden from bidders. Bids below the cut-off are filled in full, bids at the cut-off may be cut back pro rata, and higher bids are rejected.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Can Buy the Notes and How

The notes are aimed at investors in general and are listed on the Colombian Securities Exchange (BVC), the country’s stock exchange. The minimum purchase is one note of 1 million pesos (about US$314), and notes cannot be split.

Valores Bancolombia, a Colombian brokerage, leads the sale alongside the brokers BBVA Valores, BTG Pactual and Corredores Davivienda. Brokers take orders from 8:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Bogotá time on Thursday, and exchange members can bid directly until 12:30 p.m.

Payment for the notes is due on Friday 16 October, settled through Deceval, Colombia’s central securities depository. Bogotá Energy Group must then publish the repayment terms of each series it places in a regulatory filing.

Who Owns Bogotá Energy Group

Bogotá Energy Group has a 130-year history and works across electricity generation, transmission and distribution, and natural gas transport and distribution. It operates in Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala, its September 2026 corporate presentation says.

The city of Bogotá held 65.68% of the shares on 30 September 2026, according to its shareholder list. Colombian pension funds Porvenir and Protección are the next largest holders, and an iShares fund tracking Colombia’s COLCAP stock index holds 1.94%.

Its holdings include TGI, Colombia’s largest natural gas transporter, Peruvian gas distributor Cálidda and a stake in the power company Enel Colombia. Readers can follow the group on its Rio Times Company Intelligence profile.

What the Money Is For

The company will use all the proceeds for general corporate purposes, the offer notice says. Until the cash is spent, it may sit in low-risk, highly liquid financial instruments.

None of the money may repay debts owed to affiliated companies or shareholders, the notice adds. Colombian rules also bar proceeds of such notes from funding lending activities or buying shares or convertible bonds.

The Finance Ministry authorised the program on 31 December 2024, and the market regulator, the Financial Superintendency (SFC), registered it in 2025. After this sale, 2.1 trillion pesos (about US$660 million) will remain available for future bonds or notes.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the auction is an early look at demand for a company that is preparing a share listing in the United States. Portafolio, the Colombian business daily, described the sale as debt open to every type of investor.

The notes are in Colombian pesos, at about 3,183 to the US dollar on 15 October, so dollar-based buyers take on currency risk. Buyers must be clients of an authorised Colombian broker and pass its anti-money-laundering checks.

Fitch Ratings Colombia rates the program’s long-term bonds AAA(col), its top national grade, and affirmed that rating in May and August 2026. On the global scale, Fitch rates the group BBB- and Moody’s rates it Baa3, the lowest investment-grade step at each agency.

What Is Not Known

The cut-off rates for the 180-day and 364-day notes will only be known after bidding closes on Thursday. The maximum rate allowed by the Finance Ministry is kept confidential.

It is also not known how much of the extra 150,000 million pesos (about US$47 million) Bogotá Energy Group will take up. That depends on demand and on whether rates and maturities suit the company.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Bogotá Energy Group?

Bogotá Energy Group, or Grupo Energía Bogotá (GEB), is a power and natural gas group with operations in Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala. The city of Bogotá owns 65.68% of its shares.

How much debt is GEB selling?

GEB offers 250,000 million pesos (about US$79 million) in notes and may raise that to 400,000 million pesos (about US$126 million). The notes mature in 180 or 364 days.

Can anyone buy the notes?

The offer is open to investors in general, with a minimum of 1 million pesos (about US$314). Orders go through a Colombian broker or directly through members of the exchange’s trading system.

When will the results be known?

Bidding closes on Thursday 15 October, and buyers pay on Friday 16 October. Bogotá Energy Group must publish the repayment terms of each series it places on the next business day.

World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa
