CHILE · BUSINESS

Key Facts The country Chile is a copper-rich South American economy whose largest business groups trade on the Santiago stock exchange.

What happened Chile’s environmental regulator charged fuel giant Copec over wastewater sent into Quintero Bay above its permitted limits.

The worst month In August 2025, the terminal’s load of volatile hydrocarbons, fuel-related pollutants, ran up to 382% above the authorized limit.

The possible penalty The charge is classed as minor and carries anything from a written warning to a fine of about US$882,000.

The company Copec runs Chile’s largest network of filling stations; its listed parent, Empresas Copec, also owns US fuel retailer Mapco.

Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

Next step Copec has 15 working days from notification to offer a compliance plan, or 22 working days to file a defense.

Chile’s environmental regulator has charged Copec, the fuel giant behind the country’s largest filling-station chain, over excess wastewater sent into a bay near Valparaíso. Its Santiago-listed parent, Empresas Copec, also owns Mapco, a fuel retailer in the United States.

The Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente (SMA), Chile’s environmental enforcement agency, announced the charge on Wednesday 14 October. At the worst point, in August 2025, a fuel-related pollutant from Copec’s Quintero terminal ran 382% above its limit, the agency said.

What the Regulator Found

The charge targets the fuel giant’s Terminal Marítimo de Quintero, run by Copec S.A. in the El Bato area of Quintero, on Chile’s Pacific coast. The site treats liquid waste from the terminal and a lubricants plant, then releases it into the bay through a sea outfall.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Chile’s 2000 emission rule for industrial wastewater, known as DS 90, governs discharges into the sea, rivers and lakes. A 2019 SMA monitoring order set the maximum volume of treated waste the terminal may release each day.

According to the SMA, the terminal exceeded that daily maximum in November 2023 and then without a break from April to September 2025. In August 2025, the extra volume pushed its load of volatile hydrocarbons up to 382% over the permitted level.

The agency opened the case on Thursday 8 October and made it public on Wednesday 14 October. It rests on inspections in 2024 and 2026 and on the company’s own monitoring reports.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Chile Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Big the Fine Could Be

The SMA classed the breach as minor, the lowest of the three levels in Chilean environmental law. Minor breaches can bring a written warning or a fine of up to 1,000 annual tax units (about US$882,000).

The annual tax unit, or UTA, is an inflation-linked accounting unit that Chile’s tax service updates each month. In October 2026 one unit equals CLP 865,812 (about US$882), at about 981.8 pesos per US dollar on 15 October 2026.

That puts the ceiling at about CLP 866 million (about US$882,000). The fuel giant’s parent also controls forestry company Arauco and fuel and gas distributors in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, so the sum is small.

Why Quintero Bay Matters

Quintero and neighboring Puchuncaví share a bay north of the port city of Valparaíso, lined with fuel and gas terminals and heavy industry. The SMA calls the bay a highly sensitive area with its own environmental quality standard.

The government runs a special air pollution plan for the towns of Concón, Quintero and Puchuncaví. During past episodes of mass poisoning in the area, the SMA ordered emergency measures on local plants.

In December 2024 the SMA fined the same terminal 277.4 annual tax units, more than CLP 224 million (about US$228,000), BioBioChile reported. The agency found that the terminal failed to cut operations during an air pollution alert and broke emergency orders issued during mass poisoning episodes.

On 23 June 2026, Chile’s Second Environmental Court, a specialist tribunal, struck down one of the three penalties and ordered a new ruling on it. Families from Quintero and Puchuncaví have also filed criminal complaints against former bosses of state oil firm ENAP over pollution data.

What Copec and the Regulator Say

Emanuel Ibarra, appointed head of the SMA in August, said that “the requirements set in liquid-waste monitoring programs are fundamental.” He stressed the need to protect the bay’s sensitive marine ecosystem.

The fuel giant told BioBioChile it had been notified and was reviewing the case file to decide its next steps. The company said it “reaffirms its permanent commitment to protecting the environment” and would cooperate with the proceedings.

What It Means for You

For investors, the maximum fine is small next to the business of Empresas Copec, profiled in our Company Intelligence page on Empresas Copec. The bigger cost is reputational, because the SMA already fined the same terminal in December 2024.

Americans may know the fuel giant’s parent without realizing it, because it owns the US fuel retailer Mapco. For visitors to the beaches north of Valparaíso, nothing changes for now, since the SMA imposed no emergency measures on the terminal.

What Is Not Known

The fuel giant has not yet said whether it will offer a compliance plan or contest the charge. A plan approved by the SMA would suspend the case, while a defense would lead to a ruling and a possible fine.

Whether the extra discharges harmed marine life in the bay has not been established. The final penalty, anywhere from a warning to about US$882,000, is also still open.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Copec?

Copec is the Chilean fuel giant behind the country’s largest network of filling stations. It belongs to Empresas Copec, a conglomerate listed on the Santiago stock exchange.

What is Copec charged with?

Chile’s environmental regulator says Copec’s Quintero terminal repeatedly sent more industrial wastewater into the bay than allowed. In August 2025, its volatile hydrocarbon load ran 382% over the limit.

How much could Copec be fined?

The breach is classed as minor, so the penalty ranges from a written warning to 1,000 annual tax units. That ceiling is about CLP 866 million (about US$882,000).

What happens next?

Copec has 15 working days from notification to offer a compliance plan to fix the problem. Otherwise it has 22 working days to file a defense before the regulator rules.

World.title: Why Ethiopia Cannot Win by Force Alone
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

The Tigray escarpment in northern Ethiopia, pictured in 2013. Mountain terrain like this has shaped the region’s wars. (Photo: Rod Waddington, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ANALYSIS · ETHIOPIA

Key Facts — The question Ethiopia is Africa’s second most populous country, and Crisis Group put its army at around 600,000 ground troops in 2026, against below 200,000 for Eritrea. Why has that edge never ended the Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea war by force?

— The record Imperial and Derg armies fought Eritrean rebels from 1961 to 1991 and lost. The 1982 Red Star offensive used 84,537 troops and failed (Gebru Tareke via Alex de Waal, 2009).

— The human cost Civilian deaths in the 2020 to 2022 Tigray war are estimated at 162,000 to 378,000 (Ghent University team, 2023). Nearly 353,000 people faced catastrophic hunger in mid-2021 (IPC, 2021).

— The economic bill Duty-free US market access ended on 1 January 2022 (USTR, 2022). Ethiopia missed a US$33 million Eurobond coupon and defaulted in December 2023.

— The front today Federal troops retook Mekelle, Adigrat, Adwa and Axum from Tigrayan forces and reached Zalambessa, on the Eritrean border, by 13 October 2026.

— The legal line Article 2(4) of the UN Charter bars force against another state’s territory. Ethiopia invokes self-defence under Article 51 (UN letter S/2026/797, 2026).

— What could end it The Pretoria agreement of 2 November 2022, the 2002 border ruling and a negotiated deal on sea access are the documented paths.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 19.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 December (15 October, 5:25 a.m. ET).

Ethiopia fielded one of Africa’s largest armies in 1961–91 and still lost Eritrea. The 2020–22 Tigray war ended at the negotiating table in Pretoria, after enormous loss of life, a famine and economic damage that still weigh on the country.

As federal troops reach the Eritrean border, a common question is why the Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea war cannot simply be won outright. The record shows that overwhelming force has repeatedly won battles in the north without ending the conflicts behind them.

For American readers, a new war would sit beside the Red Sea, a main shipping route between Asia and Europe. The latest advance is set out in Ethiopian Troops Reach Zalambessa by 13 Oct.

What Overwhelming Force Achieved Before

Ethiopia annexed Eritrea in 1962, dissolving a UN-backed federation, and fought Eritrean rebels until 1991. From 1974 the war was run by the Derg, the military junta led by Mengistu Haile Mariam.

Historian Gebru Tareke counts 84,537 government troops against 22,184 guerrillas in the 1982 Red Star offensive, as summarised by Alex de Waal. After four months the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) had driven it back, with about 43,000 combatants killed or wounded.

Ethiopia ended the 1998–2000 border war in the stronger military position, but the Algiers Agreement of 12 December 2000 sent the border to a commission. Its unanimous 2002 ruling left Badme, where the war began, in Eritrea, and Ethiopia accepted it only in June 2018.

The Tigray war began in November 2020, when Tigrayan troops seized the army’s Northern Command in Mekelle, and ended after a decisive federal advance in late 2022. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that long ruled Tigray, signed a peace deal in Pretoria on 2 November 2022.

That win did not settle Tigray, where federal and TPLF forces fight again, as Why Ethiopia’s Tigray Region Is at War Again in 2026 explains. Both campaigns were ordered by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, in power since 2018.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Horn of Africa (Ethiopia) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Human Cost

No full count of the 2020–22 war’s dead exists, so every figure is an estimate. A Ghent University team, including geographer Jan Nyssen, put civilian deaths at 162,000 to 378,000 in an update by researcher Emnet Negash in May 2023.

Crisis Group, the conflict-prevention organisation, describes the toll more cautiously as tens of thousands killed and hundreds of thousands displaced. In June 2021 the IPC, the UN-backed hunger scale, found nearly 353,000 people in Tigray in Catastrophe, its most severe phase.

A joint inquiry by the UN human rights office (OHCHR) and the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission in 2021 found reasonable grounds to believe all parties committed violations. It said some may amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The UN-mandated International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (ICHREE) found that the federal government’s blocking of aid to Tigray violated the ban on starving civilians. Its 2023 report said Eritrean troops kept committing atrocities in Tigray after the Pretoria deal.

The Economic Bill

Washington ended Ethiopia’s duty-free access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on 1 January 2022, citing gross human rights violations. The IMF had already paused payouts from a 2019 programme after the war began, Crisis Group notes.

AGOA 1 Jan 2022 US duty-free access withdrawn (USTR) Eurobond Dec 2023 US$33 million coupon missed on a US$1 billion bond IMF loan US$3.4 billion Four-year facility approved 29 July 2024 (IMF) Inflation 26.6% to 11.7% Average in 2023/24; 12-month rate in April 2026 (IMF)

Ethiopia then missed a US$33 million coupon on its only Eurobond, defaulting in December 2023. A US$3.4 billion IMF facility followed in July 2024, tied to a market-determined exchange rate to ease foreign currency shortages.

Average inflation fell from 26.6% in 2023/24 to 16.0% in 2024/25, the Fund’s July 2026 review shows. The next review has slipped to talks in November, as reported in Ethiopia IMF Review Talks Slip to November.

Why Insurgencies Outlast Offensives

De Waal described the Derg’s strategy as overwhelming force, and by 1989 its army listed 374,000 regular soldiers. Yet the EPLF overran the army’s largest garrison in Eritrea at Afabet in 1988, and the Derg fell in 1991.

Tigray repeats the lesson. Crisis Group wrote in February 2026 that fighting the TPLF again in its mountainous home terrain is “a forbidding prospect, no matter how depleted the Tigrayan forces.”

The Amhara region shows how one campaign can start another. The Fano, Amhara militias that fought the TPLF, rebelled in August 2023 after Abiy ordered regional special forces disbanded.

Why Eritrea Is a Harder Target Than Its Size Suggests

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Crisis Group put Ethiopia’s army at around 600,000 ground troops in 2026 and Eritrea’s below 200,000, while IISS data for 2020 published by the World Bank listed 138,000 and 202,000. Eritrea relies on mass conscription, and a UN human rights report in May 2025 said its national service remains indefinite, as Eritrea Explained 2026 sets out.

The 1998–2000 war was fought largely from trenches along the same frontier, as Part 1 of this series, Ethiopia vs Eritrea: Who Would Win a War?, shows. Its death toll has been estimated at up to 100,000, a figure cited by journalist Martin Plaut in 2005.

Crisis Group says Eritrea is “ensuring that its military is entrenched in strategic border areas.” It adds that Ethiopian commanders fear becoming “bogged down in an exhausting conflict against a dogged opponent.”

A push to Assab, Eritrea’s southern port near the Bab el-Mandeb strait, would leave Ethiopia exposed on other fronts, the group warns. It points to Eritrea’s ties with the TPLF and the Fano, which could open fighting behind federal lines.

The Legal and Diplomatic Walls

Article 2(4) of the UN Charter bars any state from using force against another’s territorial integrity. Eritrea, ruled by President Isaias Afwerki since 1993, wants Security Council action under Chapter VII, as Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia at UN on 14 October.

Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos invoked Article 51, the right of self-defence, telling the Council that Eritrean units had entered Ethiopian territory. Whatever the claim, the Geneva Conventions bind every armed force in the conflict to protect civilians.

The African Union Commission urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt on 1 October to show “maximum restraint,” as reported in AU Urges Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to Show Restraint. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Abiy that Horn of Africa states must respect their neighbours’ sovereignty and warned against cross-border incursions.

Egypt, at odds with Ethiopia over Nile waters, signed a joint Red Sea declaration with Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia on 4 October. Crisis Group warns a war could drag in Egypt and Gulf states, and urges Western powers to tie IMF support to restraint.

The Case Made for Decisive Force

Supporters of a hard line in Addis Ababa start from security. The government told the Security Council that Eritrea sent mechanised and infantry units into Ethiopia, and it accuses Asmara of channelling support to the Fano.

Officials also accuse TPLF leaders of forging a clandestine alliance with Eritrea, Crisis Group records. Eritrea denies sending troops into Ethiopia, and Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel calls the campaign “an unprovoked war of aggression.”

The second argument is the sea, and in October 2023 Abiy said “a population of 150 million can’t live in a geographic prison.” In September 2025 he said the loss of the Red Sea “will be corrected,” as Ethiopia Red Sea Access Push Risks a Wider Horn Crisis explains.

Eritrea quotes Deputy Army Chief of Staff General Abebaw Tadesse as declaring on 27 September that “our ultimate destination is Assab.” Abiy has denied plans to seize a port by force, Crisis Group notes, and Addis Ababa frames its current operations as self-defence.

What Could End It Instead

The first tool for ending the Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea war already exists. The Pretoria agreement promised federal authority and services in Tigray in return for TPLF demobilisation, but Crisis Group says full demobilisation never took place.

The deal created the Tigray Interim Administration, a federally funded regional government first led by former TPLF spokesman Getachew Reda. Crisis Group urges Kenya, South Africa and Nigeria to broker talks through the AU, which asked envoy Olusegun Obasanjo on 23 September to help.

Between the two states, the 2002 boundary ruling offers a settled line, and the 2018 Jeddah Agreement, mediated by Saudi Arabia, ended the state of war. Washington cites that 2018 framework as the basis for talks, and Crisis Group urges candid talks on reliable sea access for Ethiopia.

What the Markets Say

Polymarket gave a 16.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 October and 19.5% by 31 December (15 October, 5:25 a.m. ET). About US$97,000 has been traded, and the bet counts only an Eritrean operation holding Ethiopian ground for 48 hours or more.

A companion bet that Ethiopia targets Eritrea priced 24% by 31 October and 60% by 31 December, but only about US$470 has changed hands. That market is thin, and it counts only air or missile strikes on Eritrea, not artillery or ground incursions.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

The main exposure is shipping, because Assab lies near the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. A wider Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea war on that coast could raise insurance costs on a main route to and from the Suez Canal.

Holders of Ethiopia’s defaulted Eurobond depend on an IMF programme that a new war could put at risk. The US Embassy in Addis Ababa tells Americans not to travel to the Tigray, Amhara or Afar regions for any reason.

What Is Not Known

There is no confirmed death toll for the fighting since early October, and no census-based count of the 2020–22 war’s dead. It is not confirmed whether all Eritrean troops have left Ethiopian territory.

It is not known whether the Security Council will act on Eritrea’s request, or whether either army will cross the border. Nor is it clear whether the IMF’s November talks will go ahead on schedule if fighting spreads.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why doesn’t Ethiopia just invade Eritrea?

Ethiopia’s army is larger on recent estimates, but Eritrea defends entrenched highland positions, and the 1998–2000 war killed tens of thousands without moving the border in Ethiopia’s favour. An invasion would also breach the UN Charter, could cost Ethiopia IMF support and risks drawing in Egypt.

How many people died in the Tigray war?

No official count exists, so every figure is an estimate. Ghent University researchers put civilian deaths at 162,000 to 378,000, while Crisis Group describes tens of thousands killed.

Why did Ethiopia lose Eritrea?

Imperial and Derg armies fought Eritrean rebels from 1961 to 1991 but could not defeat them, even with offensives such as Red Star in 1982. After the Derg fell in 1991, Eritreans voted for independence in a UN-observed referendum in 1993.

What is the Pretoria agreement?

It is the deal the Ethiopian government and the TPLF signed in Pretoria, South Africa, on 2 November 2022 to end the Tigray war. It promised federal authority and services in Tigray in return for demobilising Tigrayan forces, a step never completed.

Sources: Crisis Group, Briefing 210 (18 Feb 2026) · ICHREE report A/HRC/54/55 · EHRC–OHCHR joint report · OHCHR report on Eritrea A/HRC/59/24 · USTR, AGOA termination · IMF, ECF approval · IMF Country Report 26/174 · The Reporter, Eurobond coupon · PCA, Boundary Commission · USG Tigray fact sheet (IPC data) · Ghent team estimate · Alex de Waal on Gebru Tareke · ASC Leiden seminar · World Bank, armed forces personnel (IISS data)

World.title: Does Ethiopia Have a Right to a Sea Port?
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Fuel tankers on the road through Awash in Ethiopia's Afar region, on the corridor linking Addis Ababa with the port of Djibouti. (Photo: Ji-Elle, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ANALYSIS · ETHIOPIA · ERITREA

Key Facts — Population Ethiopia has about 132 million people (World Bank, 2024), the most of any landlocked country. The next largest, Uganda, has about 50 million (World Bank, 2024).

— Coastline None since Eritrea became independent in May 1993. Ethiopian cargo used the Eritrean port of Assab until the border war of 1998 to 2000.

— Main gateway Djibouti carries about 95% of Ethiopia’s foreign trade (Institute of Foreign Affairs, 2026). Ethiopian cargo through Djibouti reached 9.5 million tonnes (2025).

— Port bill Ethiopian estimates put port-related fees at US$1.5 billion to US$2 billion a year (2026). Djibouti’s port authority puts its combined port revenue at about US$400 million (2025).

— The law The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea gives landlocked states access to the sea through transit agreements (Article 125, 1982). Ethiopia signed it in 1982 but never ratified it, and Eritrea has not signed it (UN Treaty Collection, 2026).

— The limit The UN Charter bans the threat or use of force against any state’s territorial integrity (Article 2(4), 1945). African states pledged to respect the borders they had at independence (OAU, Cairo, 1964).

— Current front Ethiopian federal troops reached Zalambessa on the Eritrean border by 13 October. On the same day Eritrea told Security Council members that Ethiopia plans to seize Assab by force.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 17.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 October (15 October, 3:57 a.m. ET). A thin market on Ethiopian strikes on Eritrea prices 24% for October.

Ethiopia is the world’s most populous landlocked country, and it routes almost all of its trade through neighbouring Djibouti. The Ethiopia sea access question is explosive because the law grants a right of access to the sea, not to another country’s territory.

This analysis sets out what the law allows and what each side has offered. It comes as Ethiopian troops stand at the border, as reported in Ethiopian Troops Reach Zalambessa by 13 Oct.

How Ethiopia Lost Its Coast

Eritrea, a former Italian colony annexed by Ethiopia in 1962, voted for independence in an April 1993 referendum observed by the United Nations. Ethiopia’s transitional government accepted the result, and Eritrea joined the United Nations on 28 May 1993.

With it went Ethiopia’s whole coastline, including Assab, Eritrea’s southern port near the Bab el-Mandeb strait. That strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, between the Horn of Africa and Yemen.

Ethiopian cargo kept using Assab until May 1998, when a border dispute became a war that ended with the Algiers Agreement of December 2000. Since then about 95% of Ethiopia’s foreign trade has gone through Djibouti, according to its Institute of Foreign Affairs.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Horn of Africa (Ethiopia) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What It Costs Ethiopia Today

Djibouti is a small coastal state whose Doraleh terminal and rail link to Addis Ababa carry most Ethiopian cargo. Ethiopian foreign trade cargo through Djibouti reached 9.5 million tonnes in 2025, Addis Standard reported in February 2026.

The same report put Ethiopia’s port-related fees at an estimated US$1.5 billion to US$2 billion a year. That is close to a third of Ethiopia’s projected 2025 export earnings of US$5.3 billion.

Djibouti disputes the size of the bill. In December 2025 Aboubaker Omar Hadi, chairman of the Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority, said combined port revenue was about US$400 million.

He said the widely cited US$1.4 billion figure includes about US$1.2 billion in inland transport costs. Those costs, he added, are earned mostly by Ethiopian trucking companies rather than by Djibouti’s ports.

The UN office for landlocked developing countries says such states face trade costs nearly double those of coastal countries. The 32 of them held just 1.2% of world merchandise trade in 2024, despite more than 7% of the world’s population.

What International Law Says

The main treaty is the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, known as UNCLOS. Its Article 125 gives landlocked states “the right of access to and from the sea” and “freedom of transit” through neighbouring transit states.

The same article says the terms must be agreed with the transit state through bilateral, subregional or regional agreements. It also confirms that transit states keep “full sovereignty over their territory” and may protect their legitimate interests.

The treaty promises a passage, not a port or a coastline, which is the core of the Ethiopia sea access debate. Ethiopia signed UNCLOS on 10 December 1982 but has never ratified it, the UN Treaty Collection shows, so it is not a party.

The UN Charter sets the outer limit. Article 2(4) requires all members to refrain from “the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.”

In Cairo in July 1964, the Organisation of African Unity pledged to respect borders “existing on their achievement of national independence.” The African Union, the OAU’s successor, wrote the same principle into its Constitutive Act in 2000.

Eritrea became independent within the borders of the former Italian colony, which an international boundary commission delimited in 2002. Under these rules, an economic need for the sea does not create a legal claim to another state’s land.

Abiy Ahmed’s Red Sea Claim

The current dispute dates from a speech by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, in office since 2018, aired on 13 October 2023. He said “a population of 150 million can’t live in a geographic prison,” Addis Standard reported.

In late 2023 he offered neighbours shares in the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Ethiopian Airlines and Ethio Telecom in return for port access. On 26 October 2023 he said, “Ethiopia is not going to invade any country for a port.”

On 1 January 2024 Abiy signed a memorandum with Muse Bihi Abdi, then president of Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Somaliland said it would lease 20 km of coastline to Ethiopia for 50 years.

Ethiopia’s national security adviser, Redwan Hussien, said the deal secured commercial sea access and a leased military base. In return Ethiopia agreed to an “in-depth assessment” of recognising Somaliland, which Somalia considers part of its territory.

Somalia rejected the deal as a breach of its sovereignty, and Turkey mediated. On 11 December 2024 Abiy and Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud signed the Ankara Declaration in the Turkish capital.

The declaration welcomed the benefits of Ethiopia’s “assured access to and from the sea” while respecting Somalia’s territorial integrity. Access was to come through commercial deals “under the sovereign authority of the Federal Republic of Somalia,” with technical talks due by February 2025.

Since then the focus has moved to Eritrea and Assab. On 28 October 2025 Abiy told parliament that sea access was “a question of national existence,” while adding that “we have no desire for war.”

Eritrea’s government says senior Ethiopian officers have since named Assab as a military objective. Its note to the United Nations quotes the deputy army chief, General Abebaw Tadesse, as saying on 27 September that “our ultimate destination is Assab.”

The Options Short of War

Ethiopia sea access could also come through routes that change no border. Their documented status varies widely, as the cards below show.

Djibouti, Doraleh

Carries about 95% of trade. A port stake agreed in May 2018 has not been shown to be completed. Tadjourah, Djibouti

Offered in September 2024 with “100 percent management” by Djibouti’s then foreign minister. No deal announced. Berbera, Somaliland

A 19% stake with DP World. Somaliland said in June 2022 that Ethiopia lost it after missing the conditions. Assab, Eritrea

Used until 1998. Abiy says Eritrea refused cranes and generators sent to revive it; Asmara rejects any Ethiopian claim. Lamu, Kenya

Kenya agreed in 2018 to lease Ethiopia space for logistics. Land was allocated, but the title deed was still pending in 2019. Port Sudan

Ethiopia agreed in May 2018 to become a shareholder. Sudan has been at war since April 2023. Somalia

Ankara Declaration, December 2024: commercial access under Somali sovereignty. No final agreement has been made public.

The share swaps Abiy floated in 2023 have not produced a published agreement with any coastal state. Only Somaliland signed a document, and its full text has not been released.

Eritrea’s Position

Eritrea, led by President Isaias Afwerki since independence in 1993, treats any claim on Assab as an attack on its sovereignty. A profile of the country is in Eritrea Explained 2026, a Red Sea Country Guide.

On 13 October its government circulated an information note to Security Council members, published on 14 October by the Ministry of Information. The note accuses Ethiopia of seeking “sovereign access to the sea, through negotiations if possible and force if necessary.”

It calls this a breach of Article 2(4) of the UN Charter and of the 2018 peace agreement between the two countries. Eritrea says the Ethiopia sea access campaign now includes a naval force with claimed reach into its southern coast.

It asks the Council to condemn a “declaration of war” and act under Chapter VII, which allows sanctions or force. The note ends by saying there is “no good faith dispute between Eritrea and Ethiopia.”

In Asmara’s reading, the problem is Ethiopian policy, not a legal dispute. The note is covered in full in Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia at UN on 14 October.

What the Markets Say

Polymarket gives a 17.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 October, and 21.5% by 31 December (15 October, 3:57 a.m. ET). The two contracts have drawn bets worth about US$96,000 in total.

Under the rules, an invasion means Eritrean forces entering Ethiopia in an operation that takes control of territory for at least 48 hours. A mere presence of Eritrean troops inside Ethiopia does not count.

A separate market on whether Ethiopia strikes Eritrea from the air or with missiles prices 24% for October and 59% for December. These are bets, not polls, and this market is thin, with only about US$470 traded.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

The Bab el-Mandeb strait, beside Assab and Djibouti, is the southern gateway for ships sailing between the Indian Ocean and the Suez Canal. Fighting on that coast could raise insurance costs and delay cargo for US importers.

Djibouti also hosts Camp Lemonnier, described by The EastAfrican as the only long-term US military installation in sub-Saharan Africa. The United States has not ratified UNCLOS, but said in 1983 that it would act in line with the treaty’s rules on navigation and overflight.

For investors, Ethiopia sea access is a question of cost and risk in Africa’s second most populous country. Reliance on one corridor raises import costs, and any conflict would add political risk to Ethiopian assets.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the Ankara talks with Somalia produced a signed commercial agreement. Neither government has published one.

The quotes from Ethiopian generals rest on Eritrea’s note and could not be checked against Ethiopian recordings. Ethiopia’s own note of 11 October, which Eritrea was answering, has not been made public.

Whether the Security Council will act on Eritrea’s request is unclear. It is also not known whether Ethiopian troops at Zalambessa will cross into Eritrea.

The background to the demand is in Ethiopia Red Sea Access Push Risks a Wider Horn Crisis. The African Union’s appeal for calm is in AU Urges Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to Show Restraint.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Ethiopia have a legal right to a sea port?

Not to a port on another country’s territory. On Ethiopia sea access, UNCLOS Article 125 grants landlocked states transit to the sea by agreement, and Ethiopia has not ratified that treaty.

Why does Ethiopia not have a coastline?

Ethiopia lost its coast when Eritrea became independent in May 1993 after a referendum observed by the United Nations. Ethiopian trade used the port of Assab until the 1998 to 2000 border war, then moved to Djibouti.

How much does Ethiopia pay Djibouti for port access?

Ethiopian estimates put port-related fees at US$1.5 billion to US$2 billion a year. Djibouti’s port authority says its combined port revenue is about US$400 million, with much of the larger figure spent on inland trucking.

Will Ethiopia go to war with Eritrea over Assab?

Abiy says Ethiopia wants sea access through talks and has no desire for war, while Eritrea accuses Ethiopia of planning to seize Assab by force. Polymarket gives a 17.5% chance that Eritrea invades Ethiopia by 31 October, which shows how uncertain the outlook is.

Sources: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, Article 125; UN Treaty Collection, UNCLOS status; OAU resolution AHG/Res 16(I), Cairo 1964; Eritrea Ministry of Information, information note, 14 October 2026; Addis Standard, 27 February 2026; Addis Standard, 28 October 2025; Capital Ethiopia, 7 December 2025; Turkish Foreign Ministry, Ankara Declaration; UN-OHRLLS, landlocked developing countries; The Reporter Ethiopia, February 2024; The EastAfrican, June 2022; The EastAfrican, May 2014; Reagan Library, Statement on United States Oceans Policy, 10 March 1983; World Bank population data, 2024.
