World.title: Belize City man fined $200 for crack pipe but ends up with 3 years in jail over unpaid $10,000 drug trafficking fine
World.content:
Belize City man fined $200 for crack pipe but ends up with 3 years in jail over unpaid $10,000 drug trafficking fine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man arrested with a crack pipe has found himself serving a three-year prison sentence after two unpaid fines from previous drug convictions caught up with him, including one dating back nearly a decade.

Erin Dillon Yacab, 28, a construction worker of West Street, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 on Tuesday, October 13, charged with possession of utensils used for smoking a controlled drug.

Police say Yacab was found with a metal pipe on Tigris Street on Sunday, October 11. He pleaded guilty and was fined $200 plus $5 court costs, payable immediately, or face one month in prison.

However, a review of his court records revealed two outstanding fines from previous drug convictions. The first, dating back to 2016, was a $10,005 fine for possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply, carrying a default sentence of three years. A second unpaid fine of $1,505 from 2018 carried an eight-month default sentence.

With the fines remaining unpaid, the Senior Magistrate ordered Yacab to serve three years in prison, with the shorter default sentences not adding to the three-year term.

Yacab was escorted to the Belize Central Prison on October 13, nearly ten years after the conviction responsible for his lengthy prison sentence.

World.title: Ruben Flores free after almost a year in prison unable to post bail on assault charge
World.content:
Ruben Flores free after almost a year in prison unable to post bail on assault charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who spent almost a year behind bars because he could not post bail has finally regained his freedom after the complainant in his common assault case failed to appear in court.

Ruben Flores was brought from the Belize Central Prison to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 14, where his trial was scheduled to begin before a Magistrate in Court #5.

However, the prosecution informed the court that the male complainant could not be located despite attempts by a process server to serve him with the necessary court documents.

With the complainant unavailable to testify, the prosecution was unable to proceed, prompting the Magistrate to dismiss the charge for want of prosecution.

Flores had been charged in connection with an alleged common assault dating back to October 2025. Although he had been granted bail, he remained incarcerated for almost a year because he was unable to meet the bail requirements.

The Magistrate informed Flores that his case had been dismissed and, with no other matters pending against him, he was free to leave.

The dismissal brings an end to nearly a year of incarceration for Flores without a conviction in the case.

World.title: Seasoned thief escapes jail time after stealing two cases of empties worth $22
World.content:
Seasoned thief escapes jail time after stealing two cases of empties worth $22

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Ladyville man with a lengthy history of theft convictions has avoided another prison sentence after pleading guilty to stealing two crates of empty bottles valued at just $22.

Eckert Anthony Fitzgibbon, 53, of Partridge Street, Ladyville, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Belize City on Tuesday, October 13, where he admitted stealing the bottles belonging to a woman.

The theft occurred on October 7, 2026, and involved one crate of empty Belikin bottles and another containing empty Guinness bottles, each valued at $11.

Despite his extensive criminal record, Fitzgibbon was fined $500 plus $5 court costs, payable by December 14, 2026, or face three months in prison.

The court heard that Fitzgibbon had numerous previous theft convictions dating back to 2007. The Senior Magistrate considered the age of his previous convictions in deciding to impose a fine rather than an immediate custodial sentence.

Fitzgibbon is no stranger to the courts. In November 2024, he was sentenced to one year in prison after pleading guilty to stealing $250 from a woman’s purse at a Ladyville gas station. That conviction was described at the time as his eighth for theft.

This latest case adds another conviction to his criminal record, although the exact total was inconsistently reported in the latest court account.

World.title: ‘Happy F*****g Birthday’: Four young men charged following birthday brawl in La Democracia
World.content:
‘Happy F*****g Birthday’: Four young men charged following birthday brawl in La Democracia

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A birthday celebration in La Democracia Village ended in violence, leaving a villager injured, a two-year-old boy reportedly struck by a bottle, and four young men facing criminal charges.

Michael Brandon, Malike Coote, Corey Jones, and a 16-year-old minor appeared before a Magistrate in Belize City on Wednesday, October 14, charged with wounding and disorderly conduct following a fight near Angie’s Store on Saturday, October 10.

Police say 25-year-old fisherman Tyrone Gillett was attacked by several young men who allegedly punched him repeatedly and struck him in the head with a pint bottle. Gillett was transported to the Western Regional Hospital, where his injuries were classified as wounding.

During their arraignment, Coote and Jones pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct, while Brandon and the minor pleaded not guilty.

Jones also attempted to plead guilty to wounding but told the court that Gillett had threatened him with a pint bottle and that he took the bottle away before striking him. He further claimed that the confrontation followed earlier threats and that his two-year-old brother had been struck by a bottle thrown during the altercation.

The Magistrate rejected Jones’ guilty plea after determining that his explanation raised a possible defence, and entered a plea of not guilty on his behalf.

Coote admitted punching Gillett but denied striking him with a bottle.

Coote and Jones were each fined $100 plus $5 court costs for disorderly conduct, payable by November 30, 2026, or face one week in prison.

The wounding charges remain pending against all four defendants, while Brandon and the minor must also answer to the disorderly conduct charge. The minor was additionally taken to the Belize City Family Court to face a separate aggravated assault charge.

All four are scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on December 9, 2026.

World.title: Two Belize City teenagers remanded to prison on firearm and ammunition charges
World.content:
Two Belize City teenagers remanded to prison on firearm and ammunition charges

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two 19-year-old Belize City men have been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after police linked them to an unlicensed 9mm handgun and 12 live rounds of ammunition.

Elijah Willoughby and Aaron Smith were jointly charged with keeping a firearm without a gun licence and keeping ammunition without a gun licence following a police discovery on Saturday, October 10, 2026.

According to court reports, police recovered a black Jericho 9mm pistol bearing a serial number, along with 12 live rounds of ammunition.

The two appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 at the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, October 13, where they both pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Due to the nature of the offences under the Firearms Act, both teenagers were remanded to the Belize Central Prison until their next court appearance on December 14, 2026.

World.title: International News: Pacific breaks record for powerful, long-lasting hurricanes
World.content:
International News: Pacific breaks record for powerful, long-lasting hurricanes

By Zoila Palma: The eastern and central Pacific has broken a record for accumulated cyclone energy, as powerful hurricanes continue to develop and last longer than usual.

Scientists say a strong El Niño, warmer ocean temperatures and favorable atmospheric conditions are contributing to the unusually active hurricane season.

Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach said the activity has intensified since Hurricane Odalys formed on September 20.

The region surpassed its previous accumulated cyclone energy record, set in 2018, on Sunday, while Hurricane Simon continued affecting the area off Mexico’s western coast. Klotzbach said the Pacific was also approaching a record for the number of days with a hurricane spinning.

Scientists attribute much of the activity to El Niño, which weakens wind shear in the Pacific, allowing storms to strengthen and survive longer. Ocean temperatures are also several degrees Fahrenheit above normal in parts of the Pacific, providing additional energy for storm development. Atmospheric scientist Kim Wood said both the eastern and central Pacific have been unusually active simultaneously this year.

The last five Pacific hurricanes—Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel and Simon—have all reached major hurricane status, with winds of at least 111 miles per hour.

Meanwhile, the Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet, with accumulated cyclone energy below 18 percent of normal for this time of year.

World.title: Soil Doctors train 20 farmers in practical soil management in Hopkins
World.content:
Soil Doctors train 20 farmers in practical soil management in Hopkins

By Zoila Palma: Certified Soil Doctors Sedella and Augustine of the Stann Creek District conducted their first farmer-to-farmer training at the Hopkins Cooperative, reaching 20 farmers as part of the rollout of the National Soil Doctor Training Programme.

The programme is implemented by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) under the Global Soil Partnership, in collaboration with the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise (MAFSE).

Building on their Training of Trainers at Central Farm, the Soil Doctors used hands-on demonstrations and Soil Doctor kits to teach farmers practical soil diagnostic techniques.

The training covered soil texture, pH and organic matter, along with sustainable soil management and climate-smart agricultural practices.

World.title: Ben apologizes following weekend incident; expresses gratitude to family and friends for encouragement
World.content:
Ben apologizes following weekend incident; expresses gratitude to family and friends for encouragement

By Zoila Palma: Social media influencer Benjamin Garcia has issued a statement following the incident that occurred over the weekend.

Garcia says that this incident has given him time “to reflect, not only on the events themselves, but also on the people who matter most to me, the responsibilities I carry, and the importance of the trust others have placed in me.

I recognize the seriousness of any incident involving a firearm and understand the concern and public discussion that the circumstances have generated.”

Ben says that beyond the headlines, he is a son, a family man, a friend, a colleague, and someone who has dedicated all of his life to building something meaningful through hard work and perseverance.

“Like anyone else, I have people who love me, believe in me, and depend on me. Knowing the worry and disappointment that the past few days have brought to some of those closest to me has weighed heavily on my heart.

To my family, friends, colleagues and clients, I sincerely regret the concern, uncertainty, and disappointment that this situation has caused,” he said.

Ben added that he has worked hard to build meaningful relationships, create opportunities, contribute to his community, and earn the confidence of those around him.

He further reassured his clients of his commitment to honoring his obligations, delivering the quality of work they expect, and maintaining the professional relationships they have built together.

Ben thanked everyone who reached out and offered words of encouragement and said that this incident served as a reminder of what really matters, his faith and family.

“I cannot change the attention or circumstances of the past few days, but I can determine how I carry myself moving forward.

With faith in God, humility in my heart, and a renewed appreciation for the people and responsibilities in my life, I intend to move forward with dignity and purpose,” he expressed.

World.title: Guilty by report?
World.content:
CHUCK... questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck has questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s (IC’s) practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption, even when those matters do not result in findings of wrongdoing.

Speaking at Wednesday’s meeting of Parliament’s Integrity Commission Oversight Committee, Chuck argued that reporting such figures could create an impression of widespread corruption even when investigations might not lead to charges.

“You must say how many investigations you have started and so on, but when you start, if you see in your report that you’re investigating permanent secretaries, you have… 18 or so permanent secretaries, even if you have three where you’re investigating, all of them come under scrutiny, and so when you say you’re investigating six, nine parliamentarians, every single one of us come under scrutiny,” he expressed.

The minister questioned whether the commission’s reporting approach was helping or hurting Jamaica’s efforts to fight corruption, arguing that the public needed to see clear results from investigations, rather than repeated references to matters still being examined.

He also questioned whether the country was getting value for money from the anti-corruption body, given the resources spent on its work and the need to demonstrate progress in tackling corruption.

“Because all I’m really saying is, yes, if there is corruption, expose it, find it, but… far too many of your reports are actually saying you are investigating, and at the end of the day nothing comes of it, or you don’t hear about it, and I am concerned, because when people speak about corruption, they should at least be able to say we have investigated these, we have charged so many for failing to report,” Chuck said.

However, Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson rejected the suggestion that the commission should be blamed for the effects of its reporting, arguing that public accountability required it to explain the work it was doing and the progress of its investigations.

Robinson said the commission had to report on the nature of matters referred to it, while the public should also question why so many matters were being brought to its attention.

“As far as I know, you get to an investigation, having gone through a process, and you have met a particular threshold to determine that somebody

should be investigated. Part of your accountability mandate must be to report where you are in a process, which means whether it is public officials, parliamentarians, you must indicate of the number, how many have reached so-and-so, so I don’t share the view that the issue is with the Integrity Commission. If there are a lot of people under investigation, then the issue must be why are there so many people under investigation?” Robinson questioned.

The debate prompted director of investigation at the Integrity Commission Kevon Stephenson to explain the distinction between matters referred to the commission and cases that proceed to a formal investigation.

Stephenson said not every complaint or referral led to an investigation, as each matter had to be assessed before a decision was made. He told the committee that only a small fraction of matters referred to the commission proceeded to investigation.

“I think the public could appreciate that when matters are reported to the commission as under [Section] One of the Second Schedule, there is no guarantee that those complaints will be investigated, because an assessment has to be done on each of those complaints for a decision to be made under Section 47 of the legislation as to whether an investigation will be conducted,” Stephenson said.

He added that investigations could also be discontinued if the evidence did not provide a sufficient basis to continue. In those circumstances, the director of investigation was required to issue findings to the commission, but those findings were not made public.

Stephenson said reports reached Parliament when a completed investigation found a breach of a code, policy or law. He also explained that the annual report’s description of matters referred to the commission should not be interpreted as a list of cases actively under investigation.

Stephenson suggested that if Parliament is dissatisfied with what the law required the commission to include in its annual report, any change in policy would need to be reflected in legislation.

In the meantime, committee Chairman Pearnel Charles Jr said the concerns about reputational damage had to be considered without restricting the commission’s work.

“The commission must fearlessly carry out its work. But fear perhaps can be spelled in two ways, F-E-A-R and F-A-I-R. So as you fearlessly carry it out, it must be fair to the persons who you may have thoughts of, but not established evidence about,” Charles Jr said.

Furthermore, director of information and complaints at the commission Joeth Jones also criticised the media for what she described as a failure to give sufficient attention to positive compliance findings in the commission’s reports.

Jones said parliamentarians had performed relatively well in meeting their statutory obligations, but argued that this aspect of the commission’s work was not receiving adequate coverage.

“The media does not pick up that,” Jones told the committee, referring to the group’s compliance performance.

World.title: Secret location
World.content:
CHANG... we handed them over to The International Organisation for Migration and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

THE location of the first batch of 22 third-country nationals (TCNs) that arrived in the island on Monday will remain concealed says National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang.

Responding to questions posed by journalists at a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, Chang maintained that though he is aware of where the TCNs are being housed, it’s not his “privilege” to announce where they are.

“I cannot give you their housing. We handed them over to International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay. The officers were in Jamaica and they looked at a number of hotels; they now have the responsibility of where they are to stay. In fact, they can move them at anytime,” said Chang.

The group, which arrived under an agreement signed between the Jamaican and United States (US) governments in June this year, comprises of 15 males and seven females, representing seven nationalities.

According to the Government, under the agreement, up to 25 asylum seekers who have unresolved migration cases in the US will temporarily transit through Jamaica en route to their home countries every two weeks.

But Chang on Tuesday shared that he is unaware of when the next batch of TCNs will arrive.

“I cannot tell you when others will arrive. We have a 14-day gap. As I’ve indicated, we can get another trip after 14 days, but there’s no guarantee. It’s not like these are designated numbers as we have with the involuntary returned migrants that we receive — our own citizens. Every two weeks, we know we get a batch, a flight, anywhere from 50 to 75 individuals. The TCNs depend on the number which might penetrate the barrier getting into the United States, as well as where they are from and what the State Department will decide or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will decide where they’re sending them and to which country,” he said.

According to Chang, no limitations will be placed on the TCNs during their stay in the country.

“They are individuals from different cultures, and what they do is up to them. They are here as visitors and they are working closely with the IOM in terms of conveying relevant information. The IOM will extract the information they require to prepare them for transit to their home country. They are free to do as they wish, like any visitor to Jamaica.

“They are individuals, who just like you in this room are regular working people who have sought to migrate, but done so illegally to the United States. The ones we accept, there are no criminals in there. They’re just families looking for a better life and we are accommodating their transition back home,” Chang reiterated.

Responding to concerns about the number of people who may want to seek asylum, Chang told journalists that the issue is not one of the Government but that of the institution which deals with the applications.

“The commissioner that deals with asylum or refugee status is a public body. It’s like a court. The documents are available. And I’m not saying we’ll not say how many…It’s their right to do so. And if they do so, it will be established. The asylum committee will sit, and the public will have access to it,” he said adding that the process can be lengthy, but the Government will notify the public as the numbers are available.

“They may ask to stay without going to asylum. It’s their freedom to do so. They are here as visitors, and if they have a skill set that is in high demand, they may. Doesn’t mean we have to accept it, but they can apply for that as well as apply for refugee status. They have a number of options,” he said.

According to Chang, their options will be discussed with them by the IOM.

“The IOM will interrogate and not only make arrangements for their movement, if they seek other alternative arrangements, then the IOM will inform us and we take it from there. But that is an important part of the nature of the IOM. As indicated, the United Nations body, they do this kind of activity globally as a trusted organisation in humanitarian relief activity. And, therefore, we allow them to proceed without any interference,” he said.

World.title: Sizzla, Chronic Law among acts for Smooth Thoughts rhythm
World.content:
Chronic Law.

After two years of planning and production, eastern entertainment Promotions is gearing up for the release of its latest musical project, Smooth Thoughts rhythm, on Friday, October 16.

The project features an impressive line-up of established and emerging dancehall acts, including Sizzla, Chronic Law, Skippa, Nation Boss, Silk Boss, Shawn Storm, Karnage, Hot Turbine, Lisa Hyper, and Krish Fullforce.

According to Judah Nugent, of Eastern Entertainment Promotions, the rhythm represents another milestone for the entertainment company, which has spent the past 14 years contributing to Jamaica’s music and entertainment landscape.

“It took us approximately two years to complete the project. One of the main factors was the availability of some of the artistes, as everyone has their own schedules and professional commitments,” Nugent explained.

“Coordinating the different artistes and ensuring that everything came together took time, but we remained committed to seeing the project through. We believe good things take time, and we are excited to finally share Smooth Thoughts rhythm with the world,” he added.

Eastern Entertainment Promotions serves as executive producer of the project, overseeing its development, artiste coordination, and overall production. Nugent said the decision to assemble such a diverse line-up was deliberate, as the team wanted to capture different musical styles and perspectives while maintaining a cohesive sound.

“We wanted to bring together a diverse group of artistes, each with their own style, personality and musical identity. Every artiste brings something different to the rhythm, and that variety allows listeners to experience different perspectives and expressions within one cohesive project,” he said.

While dancehall rhythms are often associated with Chronic Law high-energy entertainment, Nugent explained that Smooth Thoughts rhythm was conceptualised to offer listeners a more reflective musical experience.

“The name Smooth Thoughts really speaks for itself. This is the type of project you can sit back with, relax, spend time with your thoughts, and genuinely resonate with each track,” he shared. “Music is not always just about dancing and having a good time; it can also be about personal experiences, reflection, and connecting with something that speaks to you.”

Adding to the excitement surrounding Friday’s release will be the world première of Chronic Law’s official music video for Streets, which will debut on the same day.

Nugent explained that the coordinated releases form part of a wider promotional strategy aimed at generating greater visibility for the project and encouraging listeners to explore the contributions of the other artistes.

“Chronic Law has a strong connection with dancehall audiences, and we believe the video première will generate excitement and help draw attention to the wider rhythm project,” he said. “Pairing the two releases gives fans more than one reason to engage with the music on the day. Our intention is to create a coordinated release moment that encourages people to watch the video, discover the rhythm, explore the other tracks, and support all the artistes involved.”

Founded in 2012, Eastern Entertainment Promotions has established a presence in Jamaica’s entertainment industry through event staging and music production. Its previous musical projects include Heaven Gates rhythm.

For Nugent, the latest release underscores the company’s commitment to creating opportunities for Jamaican entertainers while expanding its reach beyond the island.

He is particularly hopeful that Smooth Thoughts rhythm will attract international attention and enjoy longevity in an increasingly competitive music industry. “We want the project to receive strong support from fans, DJs, radio personalities, streaming audiences and the wider music industry.

We also hope it creates greater exposure for the artistes involved and opens doors to new opportunities for everyone who contributed to making it happen,” he said. “Ultimately, we want the rhythm to have longevity. We do not want it to be something people listen to only on release day. We want listeners to keep returning to it, discovering their favourite tracks and sharing the music with others.”

The project is expected to be available across major digital streaming platforms, subject to final distribution arrangements.

Meanwhile, Eastern Entertainment Promotions is also preparing for the 12th staging of its signature event, Eastern Extravaganza, scheduled for New Year’s Day, January 1, 2027.

Nugent said the event remains an important part of the company’s journey, with further announcements expected in the coming months.

World.title: Chilling confession
World.content:
Ruddock was heard on video telling detectives that he was instructed by his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, pictured here, to carry out the gruesome, human-sacrifice killing of Taneka Gardner.

A seven-member jury in the Andre Ruddock murder trial in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston on Wednesday watched video recording of the accused appearing composed as he admitted to detectives that he cut the throat of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner on October 17, 2021 at Pathways International Restoration Kingdom Ministries in Albion, St James.

Ruddock was heard in the video telling the detectives at a police station in St James, in the presence of two justices of the peace, that he was instructed by his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, to carry out the gruesome, human-sacrifice killing of Gardner at the church.

In the video, Ruddock was seen calmly answering the 42 questions posed to him by detectives as he gave them a picture of what led up to him cutting Gardner’s throat.

Ruddock was even seen sipping what appeared to be water from a 1.5 litre bottle as he sat with his back against a wall.

The detectives did not appear to be aggressive towards him, and neither did it appear that he was forced or threatened in any way to say what he told them and the justices of the peace.

Ruddock was asked questions and he provided the responses. After the questions and answers were read out to him, Ruddock was invited to sign the document, which he stood up and completed on the table that was before him and the detectives.

One of the detectives thanked Ruddock for cooperating with them and expressed that he wished everything worked out well for him.

After the playing of the video in court, prosecutor LaToya Bernard continued her examination-in-chief of a detective corporal who was one of the two detectives present inside the room with Ruddock and the two justices of the peace. She invited him to tell the court what he did after Ruddock signed the question-and-answer document.

The detective said he packed up the video recording equipment and created two DVDs which contained all that Ruddock told them.

The prosecutor then went on to ask the witness where he was on October 21, 2021 and what activities he carried out in relation to the case.

The detective, who is now at the rank of corporal, asked to see his written statement which he gave in the matter in order to refresh his memory.

He was shown the statement and then he began to explain that he and another detective were given certain instructions by a superior.

He explained that electronic items taken from the murder scene were transported to the police’s cybercrime division where they were handed over to an analyst.

“Items included cell phones, cameras, a digital video recorder and memory cards. The analyst gave me a receipt in return and I subsequently handed over the receipt to Detective Inspector McLeod on my return to the Falmouth Police Station,” he said.

He explained that he saw the body of Taneka Gardner more than once after it was removed from the church.

“After making arrangements with the father of Taneka Gardner, I met with him at the Archer’s Funeral Home located in Spanish Town, St Catherine. We were there for the post-mortem of Taneka Gardner,” he said, explaining that a pathologist confirmed to him that Gardner’s death was as a result of a slash to the throat.

World.title: THERE’S HOPE!
World.content:
West Indies’ Captain Shai Hope plays a shot during their fourth T20 international cricket match against India at the Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium in Hyderabad, India, on Wednesday. (Photo: AFP)

HYDERABAD, India (CMC) — West Indies Captain Shai Hope produced another scintillating knock while Keemo Paul came up trumps with the ball as the regional side carved out a 24-run win over host India here in the fourth T20I on Wednesday.

Shai Hope’s latest century, his fourth of the trip, helped to propel the men in maroon to 247 for three while Paul’s five-wicket haul, supported by Gudakesh Motie’s restrictive spell, sent the series into a decider in Bengaluru as India could only manage to get 223 on the newly laid Hyderabad pitch.

Put in to bat, Hope combined with Jewel Andrew to get things going quickly against an unchanged India side. The teenager immediately set the tone, crunching a clean six off Arshdeep Singh’s second ball.

A 17-run over gave West Indies momentum, and Hope quickly tapped into his red-hot form.

Mayank Yadav attempted to rattle the visitors with early pace but occasionally overdid it, including a bouncer that flew over Samson’s head. On a patchy outfield, West Indies relied on clearing the ropes, racing to 79 for one, their highest T20I Powerplay score against India.

Axar Patel’s introduction in the Powerplay gave India a breakthrough when he removed Andrew for 21, but Shimron Hetmyer wasted little time, targeting Arshdeep’s slot offerings.

Naman Dhir, who had been among the wickets, ran into a negative matchup against Hope and conceded 19 in his only over.

West Indies’ incoming batters maintained the tempo. Prince Yadav surprised Hetmyer with a crafty bouncer to get him out for 33, but Rovman Powell capitalised in a 22-run Axar over.

By the time Sherfane Rutherford arrived, Hope had raced to 75. The left-hander tore into Mayank’s final spell, taking 22 runs as West Indies moved past 200.

India’s fielding also faltered: Mayank botched a Rutherford catch, and Tilak could not sight a straight hit off the final ball as Hope completed his century.

Hope’s unbeaten 102, which included four fours and nine sixes, saw the right-hander become the first West Indies player to three T20I hundreds.

India’s reply began brightly. Samson launched a straight hit over Roston Chase’s head and almost single-handedly controlled the Powerplay as Abhishek Sharma struggled for strike.

Chase conceded 25 in his second over, and by the third over India had raced to 50 without loss.

But on a dry surface with no dew, West Indies’ seamers adapted better, mixing their pace to restrain India. Paul struck with his first ball, using a short delivery and smart field placement to hand India their first setback as Sanju Samson held out in the deep for 56.

Three balls later, Ishan Kishan fell attempting to repeat a six.

Abhishek, starved of strike, scratched his way to 29 off 24. Shreyas Iyer made 16 off 11, ball bowled by Motie, stagnating India in the middle.

Unlike West Indies, India could not capitalise on the short balls from the pacers, managing just 32 off 31 at that length.

Tilak Varma (43) and Nitish Reddy (41) adjusted well to forge a 70-run recovery in 5.2 overs, but the late surge collapsed when both departed, leaving the tail with a mountain to climb.

Paul, who claimed the last three wickets, ended with five for 41 while Motie claimed two for 13.

The result marked the first time West Indies defeated India in India while defending a total in T20Is, after six failed attempts. The series is now tied at 2-2 with the final game set for Saturday at 8:30 am Jamaica time.

World.title: Diddy rushed to hospital after prison fight with Dudus — report
World.content:
American rapper P Diddy and Jamaican drug lord Christopher 'Dudus' Coke a

American music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs was reportedly rushed to hospital on Wednesday after allegedly getting into a physical altercation with convicted Jamaican drug lord Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke.

According to a TMZ report, the confrontation reportedly erupted after Combs allegedly caused trouble that resulted in disciplinary action against fellow inmates.

During the alleged scuffle, Combs reportedly sustained a head injury and was subsequently transported to an outside medical facility for treatment.

The circumstances surrounding the incident have not been independently verified.

Combs was sentenced last year to just over four years in federal prison after being convicted on prostitution-related charges involving two of his former girlfriends.

World.title: IC WANTS SPENDING CHECK
World.content:
The scene in Black River after the town took a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa last October.

THE Integrity Commission (IC) has called for full documentation and independent review of 476 Government contracts valued at $5 billion that public bodies identified as related to Hurricane Melissa recovery, raising questions about how the spending will be reviewed as Jamaica rebuilds after the disaster.

The contracts were awarded in the final quarter of 2025, with most using emergency or single-source procurement methods.

In its special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, tabled in the House on Tuesday, the commission said 182 of the recovery-related contracts, valued at $3.9 billion, were awarded through emergency procurement.

Another 262 were awarded through single- source procurement, while 32 were awarded through restricted bidding. “These awards warrant full documentation and independent review by the relevant authorities, and will be examined further in the commission’s report on its special monitoring programme, which is ongoing,” Director of Investigation Kevon Stephenson wrote in the report.

The findings come against the background of a sharp rise in emergency contracting last year, as public bodies responded to urgent needs, including those arising from the hurricane. The commission reported that emergency contracts for the year totalled $16.3 billion across 588 contracts, a 63 per cent increase in value over 2024.

Of that amount, $10.5 billion, covering 331 contracts, was awarded in the final quarter of 2025. The report said $9.7 billion of that fourth-quarter spending, across 278 contracts, was awarded on or after October 28, 2025, when Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica.

Stephenson acknowledged in the report the necessity for emergency procurement, but said the circumstances created heightened risks that required scrutiny. “The DI (director of investigations) recognises that emergency procurement was necessary to preserve life and to restore essential services.

However, the period following the hurricane was one of heightened procurement risk, by reason of the scale of emergency contracting, the size of certain individual awards, the use of emergency methods for contracts other than those identified as related to recovery, and the exemption of emergency procurement from the ordinary rules,” he wrote.

The report also raised concerns about how some hurricane-related contracts were recorded. It identified 360 single-source awards in 2025, valued at $840 million, whose descriptions referred to a hurricane but which were recorded as ordinary single-source contracts.

Of those, 337 were made in the final quarter of the year. The commission cautioned that some of these awards might already be included among the 262 single-source contracts identified as related to recovery. However, the report said the records indicated that emergency spending may have been understated and that the identification of disaster-related contracts was incomplete.

The findings do not establish that the recovery contracts were improperly awarded or that the spending involved wrongdoing. Rather, the commission is calling for the relevant authorities to examine the awards and the records supporting them. The report also recommends stronger checks after emergency spending.

These include requiring public bodies to report on their procurement activities following a declared disaster and improving oversight of emergency contracts, including checks on whether the Government received value for money.

The commission’s special monitoring programme remains under way, with further examination of procurement connected to the hurricane response and recovery expected to be addressed separately.

World.title: ‘A wish list’
World.content:
Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes responding to an announcement in Parliament on Tuesday by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes has described as a “wish list” an announcement by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals which will nearly double the bed capacity of the facilities they are replacing.

The facilities to be constructed are a new 250-bed Black River Hospital in St Elizabeth, a 250-bed Falmouth General Hospital in Trelawny, a 150-bed Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover, and a 720-bed Kingston Public Hospital Campus at Orange Street, downtown Kingston.

“I must tell the honourable minister, that is indeed a very well put-together wish list,” Dawes said sarcastically as he rose to respond to Tufton’s 20-minute-long statement in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in which the minister told his fellow parliamentarians of the plans to construct the new facilities.

“We can rarely call it anything more than such because the weight of Cabinet approval is not a budget item,” Dawes added.

Tufton told the House that Cabinet had approved a partnership between his ministry and the National Reconstruction and Resilient Authority (NaRRA) for the works to be carried out.

It is being done in collaboration with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB).

Dawes, the Member of Parliament (MP) for St Catherine South Eastern, told the Parliament that all Jamaicans want better, safer, and more resilient hospitals.

“The challenge we have consistently had is that whenever this Government is tasked with delivering, we don’t know the cost, we don’t know the completion time, and we don’t know who is going to staff it.

And we have seen that happen over and over again, Dawes said.

He reminded the legislature that in the early 1990s under an IDB-funded project to improve hospitals, there was a special implementation unit in the Ministry of Health.

“This project to rehabilitate and construct major hospitals is going to be lumped with the Montego Bay Hip Strip development, the Vernamfield development, and any other NaRRA project that they deem fit,” he said.

The first-term MP pointed to the continued rising costs associated with the Cornwall Regional Hospital redevelopment project and argued that patients in western Jamaica continue to suffer.

“In fact, patients all across Jamaica are suffering [and] the staff, they’re protesting almost weekly at this point.

And every time there is a protest or concern on social media we’re treated to tours of hospitals to come,” he said.

“This cannot be the status quo; we cannot continue to suffer while we hear about what is to come.

This Government has had 10 years to deliver and now they are delivering promises to come,” Dawes argued.

He said that the Opposition accepts that money must be spent on the hospitals that are being rebuilt, but said, “We would like to know how much money is going to be spent on the abandoned Black River Hospital, how much money are we sinking into these buildings that the minister has, quite honestly, said are unfit for inhabitation and occupation.” Dawes also argued that a hospital is not just a building and a bed, not [just] something to lie on.

“A hospital is service.

A bed without a nurse is a mattress,” he declared.

He lamented that there was nothing in Tufton’s presentation about a staffing plan and pointed out that by the health ministry’s own numbers Jamaica was experiencing an attrition rate of 500 nurses each year.

Dawes said the 47 nurses who arrived from Ghana recently are a welcome addition but that is a mere drop in the bucket.

In his statement, Tufton repeated that the climate-resilient facilities will be reconstructed and modernised by NaRRA.

He did not give a cost or timeline for construction.

“Together these projects will deliver some 1,370 beds inside modern, climate-resilient hospitals.

The three rural hospitals alone will raise beds from 260 today, to 650 beds, more than doubling the facility,” said the minister.

World.title: Croatia pumps the brakes on Montenegro’s EU membership bid
World.content:
“Some have been on the agenda for the last two years [with] no progress whatsoever,” he said, urging Montenegro to make headway. “We will ask our colleagues to help them to make progress, if there’s an objective to conclude the negotiations.”

Croatia’s concerns are laid out in an orientation paper, obtained by POLITICO, in which Zagreb insists it supports Montenegro’s EU membership ambitions while identifying several outstanding disputes that need to be resolved.

“Croatia seeks to facilitate Montenegro’s accession, not obstruct it,” the paper reads. Several of the unresolved issues stem from Montenegro’s involvement in the military aggression against Croatia in the 1990s, including attacks on Dubrovnik and the occupation of parts of Croatian territory, according to the document.

Among Zagreb’s demands is compensation for Croatian nationals detained at the Morinj camp, where more than 300 Croatians were held between October 1991 and August 1992, following the occupation of part of the Dubrovnik region by Serbian and Montenegrin forces.

Croatia is also calling for the preservation and permanent display of a memorial plaque at the former detention camp, as well as the renaming of a municipal swimming pool in Kotor dedicated to Zoran Gopčević, a former international water polo player who, according to the document, served as a guard at Morinj in 1991 and 1992.

Other outstanding demands include the prosecution of war crimes committed during Croatia’s War of Independence and further talks on the delimitation of the border between the two countries.

Despite those disputes, Croatia has so far consented to Montenegro’s progress in accession negotiations. The country has provisionally closed 21 of its 33 negotiating chapters, making it the frontrunner in the EU’s enlargement process.

World.title: The extremes of Reform: What will Farage do?
World.content:
Is Reform facing another growing crisis over alleged racist, sexist and violent language within its ranks?

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy assess what the latest claims within an ITV News undercover investigation mean for Nigel Farage and whether more damaging revelations are still to come.

Reform says there is “no room for racism” within the party.

Elsewhere, Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Donald Trump is putting lives at risk by cutting Ukraine’s access to Starlink, a vital satellite technology. If the US can switch off critical military technology, how safe is Britain’s growing reliance on Elon Musk’s satellite networks?

Plus, is the cabinet office heading for a historic rebrand, and who will hold the power at the heart of government?

World.title: EU leaders face off over the budget
World.content:
EU leaders meet today for their first chance to beef about the budget face to face.

On the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton dive deeper into why leaders look increasingly unlikely to reach an agreement on the EU’s next money pot by December. Plus, Zoya obtained a document revealing deepening relations between Russia and Slovakia. Will that be a cause for concern around the Council table?

Next up, Zoya spoke with Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius on stage yesterday. His main message? Europe should boost its defense capabilities and stop relying so heavily on U.S. military support.

World.title: Das Rot-Grün-Rot-Dilemma in der Hauptstadt
World.content:
Die Berliner Landespolitik manövriert sich erst in eine Sackgasse und will nun doch daraus rausfinden. Wegen des Streits um antisemitische Strömungen in der Linkspartei stehen die Sondierungsgespräche mit SPD und Grünen auf der Kippe, werden aber heute fortgesetzt. Wie sich das rot-grün-rote Bündnis gegen den Widerstand von SPD und Grünen im Bund retten will, zeigt Maximilian Stascheit auf.

Auch die Bundes-SPD kämpft mit schlechten Umfragewerten und internem Frust vor dem anstehenden Parteitag im Dezember. Im 200-Sekunden-Interview erklärt der nordrhein-westfälische SPD-Fraktionschef Jochen Ott, warum seine Partei eine neue Vision braucht und wie der Weg aus der Krise aussehen soll.

Beim EU-Gipfel in Brüssel steht Europa derweil vor einem massiven Realitätscheck in der Ukraine-Politik. Die US-Unterstützung bröckelt spürbar. POLITICO-Experte Hans von der Burchard ordnet ein, welche Forderungen Wolodymyr Selenskyj morgen mitbringt und warum der Streit um den EU-Haushalt weitere Hilfen zu blockieren droht.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

Für alle Hauptstadt-Profis: Der Berlin Playbook-Newsletter bietet jeden Morgen die wichtigsten Themen und Einordnungen. Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren.
