World.title: UK polling watchdog faces reckoning after Farage sting
World.content:
The polls had in fact been paid for by two undercover reporters posing as a wealthy American benefactor and his son. The pair had offered their support to Reform via Farage’s advisers Dan Jukes and James Orr.

At the time, the BPC said in a statement it was “clear there have been breaches” of the body’s rules and that it would seek further information from JL Partners. The BPC’s own rulebook states that polling companies must disclose who has commissioned their research and that those who fail to do so can be kicked out.

Three people familiar with internal BPC discussions — granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter — said members had since urged the industry body to dismiss JL Partners, arguing the pollster, which declined to comment for this piece, had committed a cut-and-dried violation of the rules.

However, the firm has not been expelled more than a month later — prompting concern among some members that the BPC is ill-equipped to deal with any serious misconduct.

One of the people cited above, from a rival pollster to JL Partners, said: “If the BPC isn’t able to kick someone out who’s so brazenly ignoring the spirit of the rules, it does beg the question: what’s the point of it?”

Crisis meeting

Jane Green, the president of the organization, laid bare the scale of the challenge facing the industry body at the behind-closed-doors meeting last week, according to a transcript reviewed by POLITICO.

World.title: Frontex suspends reintegration program after blowing through its budget
World.content:
The suspension comes as the EU seeks to step up deportations from the bloc — a leading pillar of EU migration policy, and the object of new legislation adopted earlier this month — and weeks before the European Commission is expected to propose expanding the mandate of the border agency, including its role in returns and reintegration.

Frontex cannot resume the program without additional cash. The agency asked the Commission for more funds, but is waiting for clarity on the EU budget for 2027, and the next seven-year budget starting in 2028, the emails said.

“There is no point in talking about a more ambitious European return policy without also talking about the resources needed to deliver it,” Frontex spokesperson Chris Borowski told POLITICO. “Ambition and funding have to go hand in hand.”

Borowski confirmed that the agency had suspended new cases, but stressed that individuals already been accepted into the program wouldn’t be affected and that Frontex would also continue to offer EU countries “other forms of assistance” on returns, such as operational and technical support.

“Returns do not end when a plane lands. Helping people rebuild their lives after returning to their home countries is an important part of making migration management work. It takes planning, people and money,” he said.

With 2,368 new cases per month on average, the agency took on significantly more migrants seeking reintegration support than it expected. Cases in September were 63% higher than Frontex’s target, according to Leijtens’ email to staff. In the first half of this year, the agency took on around 75% more cases than it did in the same period last year.

World.title: How Russia plans to revive its ties with Slovakia
World.content:
The IGC, which covers economic, scientific and technical cooperation, has been dormant since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The last meeting was the commission’s 21st session, held in Bratislava on Nov. 12, 2021.

The meeting comes as Moscow finds openings in other international arenas. The U.S. has invited Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, while the International Olympic Committee has provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and urged sports bodies to ease restrictions on Russian athletes.

Asked about the purported agenda for the IGC, the Slovak foreign ministry directed POLITICO to Blanár’s public statements after the Aug. 20 call. “We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár said at the time.

The Russian foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The renewed push for warmer Slovak-Russian relations follows Fico’s May 9 visit to Moscow, where he met Russia's President Vladimir Putin during Victory Day commemorations. It comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election, which cost Putin one of his closest partners in Europe and forced him to look elsewhere for EU allies.

Months before losing the election to Péter Magyar, Orbán rebooted the Russian-Hungarian Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, which had been suspended for several years after the 2022 invasion. Magyar's government did not confirm to POLITICO whether the commission would go ahead next year.

World.title: How Putin’s favorite sport reopened the door to international contests
World.content:
“It’s clear that, considering how Vizer promoted the Russians and kept saying they were ‘good for us,’ [he has] definitely interests and connections in Russia. Russia’s ideas are everywhere,” the Ukrainian Judo Federation’s head coach Vitalii Dubrova said in an interview.

The International Judo Federation did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment on Vizer’s ties to Russia. The IJF also did not make Vizer available to reply to requests for comment.

While the IJF offered solidarity funding for Ukrainian judo in 2022 and instituted background checks on Russian and Belarusian athletes in 2023, in November 2025 it became the first major sports organization to fully reinstate Russian athletes — allowing them to compete under their national flag for the first time since the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022.

It was part of Moscow’s use of sports as a route back onto the global stage, from comebacks in major tournaments to broader Olympic rehabilitation — and a potential return at the 2028 Games, tacitly backed by Kirsty Coventry, president of the International Olympic Committee.

That has triggered alarm in Brussels, where top EU foreign policy officials are currently circulating ideas — from sanctioning athletes to cutting EU funds for sports federations that welcome Russia back — in a bid to slam the door on Russian reintegration, according to a European External Action Service document, dated Sept. 16 and seen by POLITICO.

While the Kremlin’s aggression against Ukraine continues unabated, Russia has nonetheless managed to retain influence at the top of international sports federations, including in chess, fencing and boxing. Moscow has found platforms to advance its soft-power agenda that have rankled Kyiv and European officials, who described how sport has “increasingly become a tool of political instrumentalisation by Russia and Belarus,” in the EEAS memo.

World.title: Russia detains Swedish citizen as Moscow eyes future prisoner swaps
World.content:
Russia detained a Swedish national and a Japanese journalist within days of one another as former president Dmitry Medvedev called on Moscow to replenish its "exchange pool" of Western citizens to trade for Russians held abroad.

 

Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Wednesday it arrested the Swedish citizen in the Sebezh district of Pskov region, near the borders with Belarus and Latvia.

He is accused of entering Russia under cover of joining the Russian military while intending to carry out "sabotage and terrorist attacks" on military sites.

The FSB said it established that from February to June the detainee served as commander of a drone section in the 24th separate assault battalion of Ukraine's Aidar unit — a volunteer formation that emerged during Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 which the Kremlin has designated a "terrorist organisation," a common domestic classification aimed at Ukrainian units.

He had allegedly admitted to serving in the unit. The FSB said it holds documents confirming his participation in combat against Russian forces, and that he faces charges of illegal border crossing, organising the activities of a terrorist organisation and serving as a mercenary. His name has not been disclosed.

Sweden's government has not commented. Moscow's claims could not be independently verified.

'You have to howl like a wolf'

The second arrest — that of Yuki Imai, a journalist for Japan's Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper — took place on Sakhalin Island as he was preparing to leave the country, the FSB said.

He is accused of gathering information on Russia's defence capabilities at the direction of Japanese intelligence services.

Japan summoned Russia's ambassador in Tokyo Nikolai Nozdrev on Wednesday. Kimitake Nakamura, head of the foreign ministry's European affairs department, lodged a protest both over the arrest and Moscow's decision to announce it without first informing the Japanese government.

Tokyo has demanded consular access to Imai and assurances of humane treatment.

The Committee to Protect Journalists called for his immediate release, warning that journalists "must not be used as a bargaining chip in broader geopolitical disputes."

The organisation estimates that at least 30 journalists are currently held in Russia in connection with their work.

ARCHIVE - FSB special forces inspect a house in Nalchik, the capital of Kabardino-Balkaria (NAK video dated 11 April 2024). AP/Russian National Antiterrorism Committee

The arrests followed Medvedev's post on Telegram on 9 October calling for Russia to increase its "exchange pool" of foreign nationals it uses to negotiate the release of its citizens deemed useful to the regime.

Writing after the arrest in Montenegro of Mikhail Zvinchuk, a Kremlin propagandist and founder of Rybar — a Telegram channel close to Russia's military and security services — Medvedev said Moscow might need to detain more Western nationals to secure the release of Russians held abroad.

"Now, quite likely, we will have to fill up the exchange pool with European and American idiots in order to pull our own people out," he wrote.

"There is no other way: if you live with wolves, you have to howl like a wolf." Zvinchuk has since been returned to Russia.

Using people as bargaining chips

Russia has for years detained foreign nationals on charges including espionage and drug smuggling, a practice its critics describe as the taking of hostages for exchange.

The most recent large-scale swap took place in August 2024, when 26 people were freed in a multinational exchange: Russia released 16 detainees, and Western countries handed back 10.

Among those Russia released were Wall Street Journal journalist Evan Gershkovich, sentenced to 16 years in a high-security prison on espionage charges, and former US Marine Paul Whelan, convicted on the same charges and given the same sentence.

Brittney Griner sits in a plane on her way to Abu Dhabi, where she is to be exchanged for Russian national Viktor Bout, in Russia, Friday 9 December 2022. AP/AP

Germany obtained the release of Rico Krieger, who had been sentenced to death in Belarus, and Patrick Schabel, detained at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport over cannabis-infused gummy sweets.

Russia received back, among others, Vadim Krasikov, who was serving a life sentence in Germany for the assassination of Georgian national Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in a Berlin park in 2019, Artem and Anna Dulcev, accused of spying in Slovenia under the guise of South American art dealers, and Pablo González aka Pavel Rubtsov, a Russian-born Spanish journalist who had been held in Poland on espionage charges since February 2022.

World.title: Bulgarian PM breaks ranks with EU leaders to back Trump-Putin diesel deal
World.content:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev stunned Brussels on Thursday morning by backing the controversial diesel supply deal agreed between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in defiance of Western sanctions.

 

"You know what is our problem right now in Europe? High fuel prices," Radev said in English as he arrived at a two-day summit of leaders.

"Any step in reducing fuel prices and to guarantee our competitiveness, we appreciate."

His comments put him at odds with his fellow EU leaders, who have strongly condemned the deal as risky, dangerous and misguided. To make it happen, the US has eased sanctions on imports of Russian diesel until April 2027.

"We very much regret this agreement on diesel. It's obviously not a very big part, but still it's in the wrong direction," Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said. "Every step now to help the Russians to increase their financing of the war is a bad sign."

Earlier on Thursday, High Representative Kaja Kallas told Euronews that the diesel deal was a gift to Putin at a time when Russia is escalating its bombardment.

"The question is: what has he (Putin) given in return? What we see is that he's actually increasing the attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure. The ceasefire that was also announced is not really working on the Russian side," Kallas said.

In another sign of his split from the EU consensus, Radev criticised Ukraine's strikes against Russia's oil refineries, which Trump has asked President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt immediately. Zelenskyy has since said his campaign will continue.

"I don't support strikes on any refineries," Radev said.

"I don't support strikes on any energy power plants, like Russian attacks on energy power plants in Ukraine, because this hits us back. The prices in Europe are (skyrocketing)."

European leaders have largely rallied behind Zelenskyy, arguing the strikes on Russia's oil refineries give Kyiv a powerful leverage over Moscow.

They see Trump's request as a desperate attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, where Republicans risk losing both chambers to Democrats.

Since his election victory early this year, Radev has positioned himself as a contrarian voice in the European debate over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The prime minister recently told Euronews that the bloc's strategy of "peace by force" had failed and urged his fellow leaders to engage in diplomacy with the Kremlin.

World.title: What you need to know about Germany’s planned tax on sugary drinks
World.content:
The German cabinet has approved draft legislation to tax sugary drinks in Europe’s biggest economy. If passed by the German Bundestag, the tax will take effect on 1 July 2027. The coalition aims to raise revenue for the federal budget while encouraging manufacturers to reduce sugar content and offer healthier products.

 

The levy is intended to ease pressure on the healthcare system, which faces costs of more than €2 billion every year linked to the high consumption of sugary drinks, which contributes to obesity, diabetes and tooth decay.

According to the federal government, Berlin is using the tax to implement “what associations from the fields of health, science, child protection, and consumer protection have long been demanding.”

The tax is expected to generate additional revenue for the federal government of €690 million in 2027 and €925 million in 2028.

According to the federal government, the revenue would help limit planned cuts to its subsidy to the central health fund, potentially easing pressure to raise people’s health insurance contributions.

Which drinks are subject to the tax, and who is going to pay more?

According to the draft legislation, drinks that would be subject to this tax include those with a total sugar content of 5g per 100ml or more. For drinks containing at least 5g but less than 8g per 100ml, the duty would be €0.26 per litre. At 8g per 100ml or more, it would rise to €0.32 per litre.

The list therefore includes soft drinks, such as Coca-Cola, iced teas, energy drinks, fruit nectars and juice concentrates with added sugar.

Alcoholic drinks and their non-alcoholic versions are not included in the plans. Milk, oat, and rice drinks, as well as pure fruit and vegetable juices, would also be exempt from the tax. Drinks containing sweeteners instead of sugar would also be excluded.

Although manufacturers or wholesalers would pay the tax, the federal government expects shoppers to face price increases of tens of cents for sugary drinks.

Small, independent manufacturers with an annual production volume of up to 70,000 litres would be exempt from this duty. A further exemption for businesses producing up to 1 million litres a year would require European Commission approval under state aid rules.

The tax faced criticism both before and after the coalition reached an agreement. According to German public broadcaster ARD's Tagesschau news service, Hessian Minister-President Boris Rhein (CDU) said the tax would make drinks more expensive and could threaten jobs in the beverage industry.

The US-based Tax Foundation also questioned the health benefits of sugary drink taxes in a report published in 2025. They argued that, "While taxes on sugary drinks do seem to increase their prices, there is no evidence for significant improvement in health outcomes as a result of higher sugary drink prices."

Germany would join several EU countries that already tax sugary drinks, including France, Portugal and Hungary, where a broader public health tax has been in place since 2011.

World.title: Domestic violence in France: 111 women killed by a partner or ex in 2025, up 4%
World.content:
In France, police and gendarmerie services recorded 136 violent deaths within couples in 2025, a slight 1% decrease compared with 2024 (138 deaths). On average, one person dies like this every three days.

 

That is the finding of the National Study on violent deaths within couples, published by the Interior Ministry.

Looking at the breakdown by gender, women remain the main victims of this violence. In 2025, 111 women were killed by their partner or ex-partner, compared with 107 in 2024, a 4% rise. Women account for 82% of all victims.

Conversely, the number of men killed fell by 19% in a year, from 31 in 2024 to 25 in 2025. They make up 18% of the victims.

The report, seen by Euronews, also records 445 attempted homicides, a figure up on 2024, highlighting the scale of the violence suffered daily in people's private lives.

Break-ups and arguments often behind the tragedies

Perpetrators of fatal domestic violence remain overwhelmingly male, representing 82% of those implicated. Among the main triggering factors are arguments, which led to 36 cases and break-ups that were not accepted, involved in 30 cases. Taken together, these two situations account for almost half of the cases studied.

The violence most often takes place in the home, in 76% of cases. Knives and other bladed weapons are the most frequently used (58%), ahead of firearms (34%).

The consequences of this violence also affect children. In 2025, 106 minors lost their father, their mother or both parents as a result of these tragedies. Nine infanticides were also committed in the context of relationship conflict.

One tragic example came in February 2025 in Franconville, in the Val-d'Oise department, when a one-year-old girl was killed by her father, who then took his own life. The couple had a history of domestic violence and were already subject to judicial monitoring.

The consequences of this violence also affect children. In 2025, 106 minors lost their father, their mother or both parents as a result of these tragedies. In addition, nine children were victims of infanticide in the context of marital conflict.

Previous violence before the killings often known to the authorities

The report notes that 37% of women killed had already suffered violence. Of these, 61% had reported the abuse to the police or gendarmerie and, within this group, 88% had already filed a complaint.

Despite these reports, protective measures were very rarely in place at the time of the killings: only one victim had a "grave danger" emergency phone (TGD) and another had an alarm button.

Finally, in 36% of cases, investigators found at least one substance likely to impair judgement, such as alcohol, narcotics or psychotropic medicines, present in the perpetrator or the victim at the time of the events.

Comprehensive law against sexual violence reaches Senate

The fight against sexist and sexual violence was declared a national cause during Emmanuel Macron's first five-year term (2017-2022). Yet it took until this year, following the abduction, rape and murder of 11-year-old Lyhanna and the mobilisation that followed, for a wide-ranging cross-party bill to emerge: the comprehensive bill against sexist and sexual violence.

Backed by eight political groups in the National Assembly, the bill notably provides for a minimum investigative framework to prevent complaints from being closed too quickly, the creation of specialised police units and judicial bodies, as well as an annual compulsory interview at school to better detect violence, from 2032. It also provides for a care pathway for child victims.

On Tuesday, the bill was adopted unanimously by the National Assembly, with 503 votes in favour and none against. It must now be examined by the Senate.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 15th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: IMF warns attacks on Saudi Arabia could hurt global economy after strike on Aramco headquarters
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund warned on Wednesday that attacks on Saudi Arabia could hurt economies worldwide, after a strike damaged oil giant Aramco's headquarters.

 

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva pointed to Saudi Arabia’s economic importance.

“In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere,” she said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.

Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an administrative building at Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran was hit on Tuesday evening, causing a limited fire. It said there were no deaths or injuries.

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility. The group has also attacked Saudi airports during renewed fighting with a Saudi-led coalition.

The building's top three floors, including chief executive Amin Nasser's office, were badly damaged, a person with direct knowledge told Reuters.

Two sources said operations at the complex were continuing as normal, although some employees had been told to work from home. Another said some work had moved to offices abroad.

Aramco oversees its oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and pipelines from a centre at its headquarters. The company had not responded to the news agency's request for comment.

Oil prices rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude trading above $106 a barrel. Aramco's shares fell 0.5% in early trading.

Air travel has also been disrupted. Lufthansa has suspended flights to Riyadh up to and including 18 November, according to its latest advisory.

Saudi Arabia plans to let executives join its Future Investment Initiative conference online after attacks on Riyadh airport, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the plans. The event is due to take place later this month.

Recovery depends on shipping

Saudi Arabia's economy was already under pressure from the Iran war and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The IMF expects it to shrink by 3.3% this year, before growing by 7.9% in 2027.

The fund published those forecasts on Tuesday, but had prepared them before Saturday's deadly attack on Riyadh airport.

The recovery forecast assumes the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen from March 2027, with shipping returning to pre-war conditions by October.

Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline carries oil to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. The IMF said this had reduced the economic damage compared with some neighbouring countries.

Georgieva said the kingdom’s efforts to develop businesses outside oil had also helped protect its economy from the war’s impact.

She warned that poorer countries that depend on imported energy were among the hardest hit by rising costs. She urged governments to help people facing higher food and energy bills.

World.title: UK's hard-right Reform party hit by fresh scandal as racist views caught on camera
World.content:
Britain's hard-right anti-immigration Reform UK party was hit by a fresh scandal on Thursday after party councillors and candidates were filmed in an undercover investigation using racist language.

 

In one excerpt from the 90-minute programme "Undercover: A Year in Reform" by ITV News, black children were referred to as "animals".

In another, a Reform member said his area had become "infested" with Asian families, calling them "absolute parasites".

The broadcast followed Reform UK candidates and councillors during local elections in May and at four by-election campaigns in 2025 and 2026.

Reacting to the release of the excerpts, a Reform spokesperson said that "where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced."

Election signs for Britain's Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage are seen in gardens in Thorpe-Le-Soken, 13 August, 2026 AP Photo

"In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed."

It said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".

"There is no room for racism in Reform UK."

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson called the comments examples of "extreme racism".

"Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples," she said party leader Nigel Farage.

Last month Farage's long-term aide, Dan Jukes, and Reform head of policy James Orr stepped down after the party was reported to police over allegations it flouted donation rules following an undercover investigation by Channel 4 News.

Nigel Farage, Leader of Britain's Reform UK party, speaks during a press conference in London, 3 August, 2026 AP Photo

Farage has faced months of intense scrutiny over his party's financial arrangements, as well as a separate £5.0-million (€5.9 million) personal gift to him from Thai-based British businessman, Christopher Harborne.

Last year, Reform soared ahead in opinion polls but YouGov's latest survey this week put the party third behind the ruling Labour Party in first place and the Conservatives in second.

The ITV investigation is due to be broadcast on Sunday.

World.title: El Niño vs climate change: Which had more influence over the powerful Hurricane Polo?
World.content:
A new study finds that climate change and El Niño combined to rev up last month's explosively intensifying Hurricane Polo, which was the longest-lasting Category 5 storm ever to churn in the Pacific.

 

Global warming caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas was the bigger of the two culprits, adding nearly 10 kph to its already monstrous strength, according to a joint study published on 14 October by scientists from World Weather Attribution and Climate Central. El Niño contributed a bit less, about 8 kph, a study co-author said.

Climate change made the conditions that fuelled the hurricane 23 times more likely, while El Niño – the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific – made it 14 times more likely, the study found. It all has to do with the 31.2°C waters that were as much as 2°C warmer than normal, the study said.

This year, with a super strong El Niño, has set records for strength and longevity of Pacific storms. Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 in the Pacific at two-and-a-half days.

'El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse'

“El Niño and climate change both made this hurricane stronger than it would have otherwise been, but the effect of climate change is even bigger than the one of El Niño,” says climate scientist and study co-author Friederike Otto, who coordinates the international science team behind World Weather Attribution.

“El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse. That means that now every hurricane that will occur in the East Pacific has at least this climate change signal making it stronger. And as long as we keep burning fossil fuels, that will only get bigger,” Otto adds.

Researchers found that without climate change and El Niño, Polo would have been a monster storm anyway. But every bit of additional wind speed can dramatically increase the damage.

People evacuate their homes as Hurricane Polo approaches Puerto San Carlos, Baja California Sur state, Mexico, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. AP Photo/Eduardo Verdugo

Decoding Polo's rapid strengthening

While Hurricane Polo ultimately weakened considerably before it hit a sparsely populated part of Mexico, scientists remain fascinated by how it turbocharged from a tropical storm to a top-of-the-chart Category 5 hurricane in about 24 hours.

The study puts the different atmospheric dangers in perspective, says Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist and vice president of science at Climate Central, a science and journalism nonprofit out of New Jersey.

“It’s a powerful reminder that even though El Niño right now is shifting hazards around the globe and changing where it’s flooding and getting dry, the really dominant signal behind all of this remains climate change,” she says.

The study looked at the warm water that fuels storms, using a measure of how strong they can get. But the study didn't focus on the upper level wind shear where El Niño has a huge footprint. El Niño usually increases those storm-decapitating high altitude winds in the Atlantic. However, in the Pacific because of changes in wind patterns, El Niño decreases the winds that weaken storms.

The two sets of researchers measured conditions slightly differently and used different techniques but came to the same general conclusion, making them more confident in the result. However, the rapid study has not had time to be peer-reviewed, which is the gold standard of science.

To calculate the impact of climate change on Polo, both teams used the scientifically accepted method of comparing what happened in our warmer real world to a hypothetical world that hasn't warmed by 1.4°C since pre-industrial times.

How El Niño and climate change interact

Study co-author Daniel Gilford, a Climate Central scientist, says the process they looked at was similar to cars on a road. Wind shear from El Niño can be a red light, as it is in the Atlantic, or a green light, as it is in the Pacific. In the Pacific that green light says go, and then the water warmed by both climate change and El Niño acts like a driver flooring the accelerator.

University at Albany atmospheric scientist Brian Tang, who wasn't part of the study, says he was initially surprised that the research found climate change to be the bigger influence on Polo, “given how extreme this El Niño is, but from a long-term standpoint, perhaps the result isn’t as surprising as it might seem.”

But three other outside scientists – Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections, University of Pennsylvania's Michael Mann and North Carolina State University's Carl Schreck – say they believe the study underestimates how much climate change has added to Polo's strength. Masters points to Gilford's own 2024 study that found climate change added 30 kph to hurricanes in the Atlantic from 2019 to 2023.

Gilford acknowledges that Thursday's report could be underestimating climate change's impact a bit, but says he was factoring in other conditions and being conservative.

World.title: School roof collapse in Pakistan's Peshawar kills dozens of students and one teacher
World.content:
Local authorities said more than 50 other people were injured in the disaster. Roof collapses have become increasingly common in Pakistan.

Officials in Peshawar, Pakistan, confirmed on Thursday that at least 32 pupils under the age of 13 died when an elementary school roof collapsed in the Afridi Abad area of the city.

One teacher has also died, they said. The deceased, along with more than 50 other injured people, were brought to Lady Reading Hospital as rescue workers rushed to clear the rubble and search for more survivors.

"We have taken out ​at ‌least 45 children," said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan, but added that more children were thought to still be under the rubble.

From her hospital bed, a teacher told reporters that the school had three floors and more than 1,200 pupils and staff.

The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear.

Roof collapses becoming more regular

Local media in Pakistan noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly routine across the country, due to poor building standards and maintenance.

In July, three young girls were killed near Umerkot when the outer wall of a government school gave way. That same month, one child died and five were injured in Lahore when the roof of an under-construction private school collapsed.

One month earlier, 14 children were killed in a similar manner at a private tutoring facility in Lahore, which came shortly after yet another such incident in Dera Ghazi Khan.

World.title: Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force
World.content:
A few dozen stations, including Cologne's main station, imposed the ban much earlier as part of a test phase [FILE: July 23, 2026] Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

Alcohol bans came into force at all German train stations when the clock struck midnight and Thursday began.

All the roughly 5,700 stations across Germany, including the train platforms themselves, are now booze-free zones.

Pubs, restaurants and other such hospitality businesses at train stations are exceptions to the rule, though, and can still serve alcohol. Consumption of alcohol will also remain legal on many trains, with long distance ones still serving beers and other tipples at their on-board bistros.

Rail operator Deutsche Bahn says the change aims to make train stations safer and cleaner, and more pleasant places to spend time waiting for a (who knows, perhaps delayed) train.

Various misdemeanors and incidents had prompted discussions on alcohol at stations over the years, but two this year in particular brought the issues into sharp focus.

A 26-year-old security staff member for Deutsche Bahn was beaten and kicked by a drunken passenger when trying to check their ticket. During the struggle the train door buckled and opened, and the Bahn employee fell from the train, suffering severe injuries. Earlier in the year, a train conductor was killed when attacked by a man without a valid ticket.

The new rules are part of DB's house rules, rather than being criminal law — meaning that at least in the first instance it is a matter for Bahn security staff to enforce rather than police.

"The alcohol consumption ban applies at stations every day, also on days with major events," Bahn spokeswoman Anja Bröder said when asked about often beer-fueled train usage days, like when football fans flock to Bundesliga games.

Around 40 stations piloted the project for some time prior to its implementation, including some of the largest like Cologne, Munich, Hamburg and Berlin. DB says it has had positive experiences with the early experiments, reporting more peaceful stations with less litter and travelers and employees saying they preferred the atmosphere.

A federal group dedicated to helping the homeless has criticized the measure, however, saying that for homeless people with addiction illnesses, train stations often served as "important, weatherproof and comparatively safe places" to shelter. A spokeswoman also told the Rheinische Post newspaper that if they were driven from sites like train stations, it would be harder for social workers to locate them.

World.title: Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why
World.content:
Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.

Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.

"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.

"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."

Amazon rainforest: One of nature's most powerful defenses

The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

Parts of the Amazon rainforest have been burned down to make way for cattle farms. Image: Andre Penner/AP Photo/picture alliance

For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.

During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.

Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.

Pitting environment against the economy

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.

"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.

"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

Thousands of students have marched in Rio de Janiero protesting against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro as president following the first round of elections Image: Mariana Greif/JNA PRESS/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.

"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.

More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.

In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.

No straightforward climate success story for Brazil

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

Storing vast amounts of CO2, the Amazon rainforest is often referred to as the lung of the Earth Image: AP

Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".

"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians, climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.

"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: India news: Supreme Court hears Rahul Gandhi's Election Commission plea
World.content:
Published 10/15/2026 Published October 15, 2026 Rahul Gandhi's key petition on mass voter deletions listed in Supreme Court today

The Supreme Court is slated to hear a petition filed by India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition lawmakers over a sweeping exercise which has so far purged over 130 million names from the country's electoral rolls.

A list of cases to be taken up on Thursday by a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant shows the petition named "Rahul Gandhi and others versus Election Commission of India and others."

The plea was filed on Monday at the end of a protest march to the Supreme Court that saw Congress' Gandhi rallying thousands, including members of the opposition INDIA bloc, student leaders, activists and civil society, through a heavily barricaded part of the capital.

The protest was the latest in a series of demonstrations calling for India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The poll body, whose neutrality has come under scrutiny, rejects the allegations and says the exercise, called Special Intensive Revision (SIR), removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Modi's party has also dismissed the accusations and deems the protests as attempts to "create anarchy."

Meanwhile, neither Modi nor Kumar have publicly addressed the issue.

Gandhi's petition seeks an interim suspension of the nationwide revision of voter rolls, along with an audit of voter deletions and safeguards against deletions without prior notice.

World.title: Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums
World.content:
From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up?

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

The main culprit? Chinese competition.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

GoPro was saved from bankruptcy in September after failed product bets and competition from smartphones have contributed to its decline Image: Christian Ohde/imageBROKER/picture alliance

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

China's growing tech lead

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, founder of Prolo Ring, which makes rings that let consumers control remotes and other devices with only their thumbs Image: Benjamin Bathke/DW

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Privacy and security concerns persist

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Xreal, a Chinese smart glasses maker, recently entered the European market through retailers like the UK's Currys in an attempt to grow consumer trust Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs.

Is a new trade war brewing?

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

China's robot revolution leaves Hong Kong playing catch-up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can Western companies compete?

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's OM in a political tangle
World.content:
Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

Players like Erling Haaland may be forced to leave if City's punishment is sever Image: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/REUTERS

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in non-league, so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

Tarnished trophies?

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

UAE links have Burnham on back foot

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

Andy Burnham has faced increasing scrutiny over his relationship with the UAE Image: Phil Noble/REUTERS

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

UAE build where others can't

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

Sheikh Mansour is Manchester City's owner but is rarely seen at games Image: Martin Rickett/PA Images/picture alliance

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

State-owned clubs starting to think smart despite concerns

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

Paris Saint-Germain have become the team to beat in Europe Image: Franck Fife/AFP

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: North Korea, China open border bridge after 12-year delay
World.content:
Twelve years after it was constructed, the New Yalu River Bridge between China and North Korea is finally operational. It is the latest sign of warming ties between the two nations.

China and North Korea on Thursday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aimed at rejuvenating trade and commerce after years of strained ties and disruptions.

A ceremony was held to launch the New Yalu River Bridge, Chinese state media Xinhua News reported.

Meanwhile, China News Service showed visuals of trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea on the bridge, which itself was decorated in flags.

The bridge is expected to boost trade and people exchanges between the two nations Image: Pan Yulong/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

Spectators crowded on a road on the Chinese side, in Dandong city, overlooking the ceremony. In Sinuiju city on the North Korean side, work on the approaching road and compound remained unfinished.

'A new chapter'

The cable-stayed bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused until now due to lack of connecting roads on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap News agency reported.

The opening was further delayed by the COVID pandemic which prompted North Korea to close its borders. Train journeys between the East Asian neighbors only restarted in March after six years, but Pyongyang is yet to resume issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, which once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.

The bridge's opening marks the latest sign of warning ties between Beijing and Pyongyang which have conducted two summits between their leaders in the past year.

"(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in ​a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency said.

He added that the border crossing would "strongly promote" economic and trade cooperation and strengthen exchanges between their people.

A ceremony was held to mark the bridge's opening more than a decade after it was constructed Image: Pan Yulong/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

A conduit for trade

Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told the AFP news agency he expected hundreds of vehicles to cross every day.

"The bridge could become a conduit for China's abundant goods and resources to flow into North Korea and give its economy a significant boost," he said.

At the same time, experts believe North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.

"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return ‌to pre-sanctions ​trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies. But it will help move heavy equipment and raw material North Korea needs for development, he said.

China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner despite a series of UN sanctions banning the flow of goods and workers to North Korea over its missile and nuclear weapons program.

World.title: EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
World.content:
EU leaders meeting in Brussels will examine measures to curb the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. But they will also be looking to further agreement on the next EU budget ahead of some major elections next year.

European Union leaders are to meet in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.

The meeting is also likely to see some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.

On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.

Here are the main topics on the agenda:

Chinese competition in focus

The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.

The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.

The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.

Divisive EU budget

The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.

Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.

The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.

Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.

Ukraine support

The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.

He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.

European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.

Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.
