World.title: Kraków’s new mayor withdraws patronage of LGBT+ equality march
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march. Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall. His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city. Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026 Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people. In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”. However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did. "I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024 The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”. “I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.” Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments. Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch). During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed. When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would. However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków. In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union. The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries. Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue. Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46). The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”. Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”. World.title: Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year. Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8 — Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks. While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast. Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028. Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia. The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president. Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions. PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M — Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026 Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in. The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so. Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge. Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present. The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK. The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present. The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding. 1294/2026 Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo — Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026 Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him. However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government). Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions. Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal. Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK. Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026 Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry. Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”. However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”. This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force. ❗️Policja szarpie posłów oraz zgromadzonych obywateli pod TK ❗️ pic.twitter.com/eGPRFQJnAX — Oskar Szafarowicz (@Szafarowicz2001) October 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Man charged with plotting attack on Polish PM

We cannot do what we do without your support. A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot. The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist. Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026 On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”. On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences. “The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years. Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns. Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect. Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force. At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026 Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts. On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”. "Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026 In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty. A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison. “He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland and Norway sign declaration on deepening security ties
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine. “In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre. 🇵🇱🤝🇳🇴 Strategiczne partnerstwo Polski i Królestwa Norwegii oficjalnie przypieczętowane. ✍️ Podpisano deklarację o strategicznym partnerstwie między obu państwami, stanowiącą efekt wieloletniej współpracy oraz wspólnoty interesów biznesowych, geopolitycznych i moralnych. 🛡️ W… pic.twitter.com/vBrWrdC8oT — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 12, 2026 The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries. Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries. Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation. “The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.” The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”. Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors. Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe. “Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. It will be followed by two more new frigates as part of a €3.5bn programme to modernise the ageing Polish fleet https://t.co/093Fx2WSM7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Poland has in recent years also moved to strengthen its ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. This year, Polish and Norwegian companies announced plans to develop a new anti-drone system for Poland in the wake of incursions of Russian drones into Polish airspace. Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic. Poland will manufacture the missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is buying from South Korea. The Norwegian government says that Polish production "will strengthen security of supply for Norway and other European customers of the system" https://t.co/NIJj7owK45 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 29, 2026 Poland has also moved closer in recent years to Sweden, with which it signed a strategic partnership in 2024. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Last year, at Poland’s suggestion, NATO launched a new military mission to protect critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: Germany detains Turks suspected of sabotaging Starlink station in Poland on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia. On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”. He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”. Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026 Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA). He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life. Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”. The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion. Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military. A fire last night at a Starlink ground station in Poland that is used to provide internet services to Ukraine was caused deliberately and "the modus operandi is clearly Russian", says digital affairs minister @KGawkowski https://t.co/p2DEn7XexF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not. He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects. Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation. “We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.” Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 On Tuesday morning, German newspaper Handelsblatt reported confirmation from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Baden-Württemberg that two Turkish men had been detained on Monday in the town of Nürtingen at the request of the Polish authorities. The office did not provide further details, but Handelsblatt reports that the two suspects are due to be brought before a judge today. World.title: Four go on trial in Warsaw over arson attacks carried out on Russian orders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons. Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024. Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga. W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026 According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks. The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life. Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services. However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement. Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack. Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw. Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years. Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted. Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism. That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025 In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory. A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe. Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland. Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region. World.title: Brno Burger Brand Pickle Plans Up to Seven Locations in Prague
World.content:
A burger brand recently launched in Brno is preparing to expand into Prague, where it plans to open up to seven restaurants.

Pickle also has ambitions to enter other Czech and Slovak cities before expanding across Europe and eventually Asia.

The first Pickle restaurant opened in Brno in June 2026.



Co-founder Peter Szamuhel now plans to establish the brand in Prague and Bratislava before launching a franchise network. If preparations proceed as planned, the first franchise locations could open in early 2027.

The company is considering six or seven restaurants in Prague and two or three in Bratislava. Other potential locations include Ostrava, Olomouc, Hradec Králové, Liberec, Nitra and Trnava.

Pickle aims to have its franchise model ready by the end of 2026. Although prospective partners have already expressed interest, the company is not yet signing agreements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pickle Brno (@pickledoublecheese)

The same burgers at every location

Maintaining consistent quality will be a major challenge as Pickle expands. The company plans to use regular inspections, mystery shopping, regional managers and ongoing staff training to ensure that customers receive the same food and service at every restaurant.

Ingredient supplies are another priority. Meat, buns and other key products must match those used at the original Brno location.

The restaurant currently prepares approximately 1,000 to 1,300 burgers a day, according to Szamuhel. Expanding the chain will require a supply network capable of supporting substantially greater demand.

Global ambitions within ten years

Pickle aims to establish ten locations across Czechia and Slovakia within three years, followed by another ten restaurants in other European countries over the next five to six years.

Its longer-term goal is to operate hundreds of locations worldwide within a decade, with Asia among its eventual targets.

World.title: Do You Really Need 10,000 Steps a Day? A Doctor’s Guide to Walking in Prague
World.content:
Walking is part of daily life in Prague, but how much is enough to benefit your health?

A doctor at Charles University explains why 7,000 steps a day may be a more realistic target.

Living in Prague often means walking to the tram, crossing the city centre on foot or taking a stroll through one of its parks. But does this add up to enough physical activity to improve your health? And is reaching 10,000 steps a day really necessary?

According to research published in The Lancet Public Health in 2025, walking around 7,000 steps a day may be enough to deliver significant health benefits.



The study found that people taking approximately 7,000 steps daily had a 47% lower risk of premature death and a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease compared with those walking around 2,000 steps a day.

These figures represent associations rather than guarantees, but they suggest that the widely promoted 10,000-step target is not a requirement for better health.

Why walking matters

Regular walking can help strengthen the heart, improve circulation, regulate blood pressure and blood sugar levels, and support muscle and joint health.

Its benefits are not limited to physical fitness. Spending time outdoors and walking regularly can also help reduce stress, improve mood and support better sleep.

The World Health Organization recommends that adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week. This can include brisk walking for around 30 minutes a day, five days a week, to meet the minimum recommendation.

The pace matters, too. Brisk walking should make you breathe slightly harder while still allowing you to hold a conversation comfortably.

Where to walk in Prague

Prague offers plenty of opportunities to incorporate more walking into daily life without joining a gym or travelling outside the city.

Stromovka is a good option for beginners and those looking for longer walks on relatively flat paths. The extensive park provides a break from traffic and the busy streets of the city.

For a more demanding route, Divoká Šárka offers hills and woodland trails that provide a more strenuous workout while remaining within Prague.

Vyšehrad is suitable for a shorter walk, combining gentle climbs with views of the city and the Vltava River. Its location also makes it a practical option for those who have limited time.

For a longer weekend outing, Prokopské údolí offers walking routes through valleys and green spaces away from the city centre.

How to keep walking during winter

Shorter days, cold temperatures and icy pavements can make walking less appealing during the winter months. However, the arrival of colder weather does not mean abandoning a regular routine.

Dressing in layers, wearing shoes with good grip and choosing well-lit, cleared paths can make outdoor walks safer and more comfortable.

Even a 10- to 15-minute walk during a lunch break can be worthwhile. When pavements become icy, slowing down or choosing a safer indoor alternative is advisable.

Small changes can make a difference

Building more walking into everyday life does not require a major change in routine. Getting off the tram one stop earlier, taking a walk during lunch or using the stairs when practical can all help increase daily activity.

Those who currently walk relatively little can start with 10 to 15 minutes a day and gradually increase the duration as their fitness improves.

Rather than focusing on a fixed target, people who track their steps can aim to increase their usual daily total over time.

About the author

Darren Andrew Noronha, MD, is a medical doctor and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, with a research focus on cardiovascular health and disease prevention.

World.title: Czech Republic to See Sharp Weekend Cooldown and Possible Snowfall
World.content:
The Czech Republic is set for a change in weather this weekend, with temperatures expected to fall and snow possible in mountain areas, according to the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute (CHMI).

The colder conditions will follow several relatively mild autumn days, when daytime temperatures are forecast to reach 17 to 18 degrees Celsius.



By the weekend, however, increased cloud cover and precipitation could bring the first signs of winter to higher elevations.

The transition will come after a frosty start to the week. Meteorologists expect the coldest night of the week to have already passed, meaning temperatures should remain more moderate over the coming days.

Sunshine is forecast across much of the country during the remainder of the working week, although mornings will stay chilly. Local fog and showers may develop in eastern parts of the Czech Republic.

The outlook for the weekend remains uncertain, but forecasters expect a general cooling trend, accompanied by extensive cloud cover and periods of rain.

Mountain regions are most likely to see wintry conditions. As temperatures fall, rain could turn to snow at higher elevations, particularly in the mountains. Some locations may also experience temperatures below freezing.

However, significant or lasting snowfall is not currently expected. Any snow that falls is likely to be limited to light dustings or scattered flakes, with accumulations unlikely to persist for long.

World.title: David Duchovny Brings New Album to Prague This Thursday
World.content:
David Duchovny, best known for his acting career, will perform in Prague on October 15, 2026, presenting songs from his upcoming album Prince of Pieces at Archa+.

Tickets are on sale through GoOut.

Duchovny has spent the past decade developing his career as a songwriter and recording artist, releasing music that combines melodic rock with introspective lyrics.

Prince of Pieces is his fourth album and brings together a small group of musicians and longtime collaborators.

The new record follows Hell or Highwater, Every Third Thought, released in 2017, and Gestureland, released in 2021. According to the album’s press release, the latest project is his most cohesive and collaborative work to date, reflecting the relationships he has built with fellow musicians over the years.

Duchovny’s music has received positive reviews from critics.

AllMusic described his sound as “eloquent, alt-rock-kissed country-folk in the vein of Wilco and the Wallflowers,” while The Boston Globe praised his voice for its “parched resonance and just a hint of rasp,” adding that he sings with feeling.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by David Duchovny (@davidduchovny)

The actor has said that the arrangements on his records are shaped by the mood and rhythm of each song, rather than following a single formula.

“The arrangements of the songs have always been in service of either the groove or the emotion,” Duchovny said. He added that he looks for sounds that complement the melody, including horns, bells and harmonies, while also experimenting with rhythms and beats.

World.title: Czech Doctors May Soon Prescribe Museum Visits to Prevent Depression
World.content:
Doctors in the Czech Republic could soon recommend museum visits, dance classes, singing and creative workshops to people at risk of depression, anxiety or social isolation.

The program, known as Art on Prescription, aims to connect healthcare providers with museums, galleries, libraries and other cultural institutions.

Rather than replacing medication or psychotherapy, these activities would complement existing treatment and help prevent mental health problems.



The National Institute of Mental Health (NUDZ) is preparing a National Platform for Prevention through Culture to bring together cultural organizations, healthcare providers, social services and schools. The goal is to make existing cultural activities more accessible to people who could benefit from them.

The initiative is not intended to turn cultural institutions into medical facilities. Instead, it seeks to use local resources to support mental well-being and strengthen social connections.

Research highlights benefits of cultural activities

International research suggests that participating in cultural and artistic activities can improve well-being, strengthen social ties and reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety.

According to Dominika Grygarová, a researcher at NUDZ, an analysis combining studies from more than 20 countries found significant reductions in symptoms of both depression and anxiety.

The benefits depend not only on exposure to art but also on active participation, Grygarová said. Creating something, learning a new skill, sharing experiences and interacting with others can help people focus on something beyond their difficulties and develop a sense of belonging.

However, the programs are intended primarily as a preventive and supportive measure, not a substitute for professional treatment. Researchers also want to assess their effectiveness and economic value, with preliminary analyses suggesting that some initiatives could be cost-effective.

Czech project looks to Northern Europe

NUDZ plans to build on similar programs already operating in several countries, particularly the United Kingdom and Northern Europe.

The Czech initiative intends to follow the so-called Baltic model, with researchers planning to work with Danish colleagues next year on a European project to introduce the approach more widely.

World.title: Who Is Petr Hlaváček? The Architect Set to Become Prague’s Next Mayor
World.content:
Petr Hlaváček is seeking to become the Czech capital’s next mayor after his political movement, STAN, won the municipal elections.

STAN received 23.16 percent of the vote, securing 17 seats in the Prague City Assembly and putting the movement in a strong position to negotiate the next governing coalition.



Hlaváček, currently deputy mayor for territorial and strategic development, has indicated that he wants to take the top job at City Hall.

His priorities include expanding housing construction, redeveloping former industrial sites and improving transport infrastructure.

A key role in Prague’s new zoning plan

Hlaváček’s main achievement as deputy mayor has been his involvement in preparing Prague’s new Metropolitan Plan, which replaced the previous zoning document from 1999 when it came into effect in September 2026.

The plan sets out where construction can take place and establishes rules for future development. It identifies capacity for up to 350,000 new homes, primarily through the redevelopment of brownfield sites.

One of the main projects is the transformation of Bubny-Zátory, an underused area expected to provide housing for around 20,000 people.

Hlaváček has also backed the Prague Development Company, which manages municipal land and aims to increase housing construction. According to him, the company could facilitate the development of up to 70,000 homes while helping prevent city-owned land from being sold off.

Transport and housing at the top of his agenda

If appointed mayor, Hlaváček wants to continue work on major transport projects, including Prague’s inner ring road and the Prague Ring Road. He also supports expanding public transport and reforming parking policy, arguing that parking in the city is often too cheap.

Before the elections, he said STAN would welcome continuing the existing coalition at City Hall but wanted a more prominent role, depending on its electoral support.

From architect to deputy mayor

Born in Zlín on July 31, 1961, Hlaváček graduated from the Faculty of Architecture at the Czech Technical University in Prague. He later established his own architectural studio, taught as a visiting professor at the University of Michigan and served as vice-dean at his alma mater.

His professional work includes the renovation of the Czech Embassy in Brasília, Brazil.

In 2015, he became director of the Prague Institute of Planning and Development. He was dismissed the following year amid criticism over delays to the Metropolitan Plan, a decision that prompted protests from institute employees.

Hlaváček entered Prague politics after the 2018 municipal elections and became first deputy mayor for territorial development and spatial planning in November 2021. He remained in the city leadership after the 2022 elections and took responsibility for territorial and strategic development in February 2023.

World.title: Sinatra Tribute Pairs Frank Sinatra Classics With 1930s Dining at Prague’s Mánes
World.content:
Prague’s Art Restaurant Mánes combines live performances of Frank Sinatra’s best-known songs with a three-course dinner inspired by traditional Czech cuisine of the 1930s.

The functionalist building offers views of the Vltava River and nearby Žofín Island, providing the setting for an evening dedicated to the music and style of Sinatra’s era.



The Sinatra’s Tribute musical programme features acclaimed soloists, including baritone Daniel Klánský and jazz singer Sophie Lamoš. They perform some of Sinatra’s best-known songs, including *My Way* and *Fly Me to the Moon*, accompanied by a group of musicians.

Rather than simply imitating the legendary American singer, the Sinatra Tribute offers its own interpretation of his musical legacy.

One of the programme’s highlights is a restored 1897 Steinway & Sons grand piano, an instrument once played by Czech composer and pianist Jaroslav Ježek.

The music is complemented by a three-course dinner served before the concert.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sinatra Tribute Koncert & Večeře / Sinatra Tribute Show & Dinner (@sinatratributeprague)

Created exclusively for the programme by Mánes Restaurant head chef Jaroslav Zahálka, the menu draws inspiration from Prague’s culinary traditions of the 1930s, reflecting the period associated with the evening’s musical theme.

Visitors can contact the venue for current dates, ticket prices and reservations.

World.title: From Lisbon to Hanoi, New Flight Options From Prague This Autumn
World.content:
The autumn school break is approaching, and travelers departing from Prague still have options for trips abroad.

However, those hoping to find cheap flights may struggle to secure a good deal, as fares tend to rise closer to departure and fewer seats remain available at lower prices.

Families face an additional challenge. When booking four tickets together, they may discover that the cheapest fare is available for only one or two passengers, forcing them to pay more for the remaining seats.



Airlines are also dealing with high fuel costs and strong competition, making it important to fill as many seats as possible.

A search conducted on Wednesday, October 7, found that Kraków and Gdańsk were among the cheapest destinations available for the autumn break week.

New flights from Prague and postponed routes

Prague Airport has announced several new connections for the autumn and winter seasons, although some airlines have postponed their planned launches until spring.

Smartwings, for example, has delayed the introduction of flights to Venice, Italy, and Bergen, Norway. Both routes were originally scheduled to begin before the autumn break but are now expected to launch in March.

Despite the changes, Prague Airport continues to list the destinations among its new routes, with their original launch dates still displayed. According to the current schedule, Smartwings’ next new connection is to Lisbon, with flights due to begin on October 23.

Travelers heading farther afield have another option. Vietjet Air launched its Prague–Hanoi service on Saturday, October 10. The route includes a stopover in Kazakhstan, rather than offering a nonstop connection to Vietnam.

Closer to home, easyJet’s new route from Prague to Hamburg provides another option for the break. Return fares were available for around CZK 4,000.

Marrakech joins the network as winter routes target skiers

EasyJet is also scheduled to launch flights from Prague to Marrakech, Morocco, on October 25. The new connection will increase competition on the route, although fares during the autumn break are relatively high.

A return ticket can cost as much as CZK 16,000, excluding baggage. Prices can be considerably lower outside the peak travel period.

Wizz Air is adding flights to Poprad, Slovakia, while Sky Alps is expected to begin services to Bolzano, Italy, in early December. Both destinations provide access to mountain regions popular with winter sports enthusiasts.

Another seasonal option is Eurowings’ planned route to Rovaniemi, Finland, which is scheduled to launch on December 20. Located on the Arctic Circle, the city is closely associated with Santa Claus and attracts visitors during the Christmas season.

World.title: Bomb threats force two Budapest schools to be evacuated
World.content:
Two schools in Budapest’s 15th district received threatening letters on Wednesday evening, prompting police to search the buildings on Thursday morning. Pupils have been moved to other locations while the situation is being investigated.

Two schools receive bomb threats

Two schools in Budapest’s 15th district have received bomb threats, prompting police searches and precautionary measures to ensure the safety of pupils and staff.

Kontyfa Primary School and Secondary School and Pestújhelyi Primary School received threatening letters on the evening of 14 October, district mayor Angéla Cserdiné Németh announced on Thursday. The letters were also sent to the local police station.

Police began searching the affected school buildings on the morning of 15 October.

Where have the children been taken?

According to the mayor, arrangements have been made to ensure that the children are safely accommodated while the situation is being dealt with. Where necessary, pupils have been moved to the Pestújhely Community Centre and Hartyán Primary School.

“The safety of the children and school staff is our primary concern,” Cserdiné Németh said in her announcement, adding that residents would be kept informed of further developments.

If you missed it: Underage Ukrainian boy threatened to blow up Hungarian and Russian schools

School urges parents to keep children at home

Kontyfa Primary School and Secondary School has asked parents not to bring or send their children to school on Thursday, if possible. The school also urged parents to collect any children who were already attending its supervised care service. It said it would make arrangements for pupils whose parents were unable to collect them.

The threatening letters have also been reported to the police, and searches of the affected buildings began on Thursday morning. No further details about the threats or the outcome of the police searches were provided in the announcements.

World.title: Strasbourg court rules against Orbán: His government unlawfully restricted Hungarian teachers’ right to strike
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Hungary’s former government unlawfully restricted teachers’ right to strike, with Education and Child Affairs Minister Judit Lannert welcoming the decision and pointing to reforms introduced by the new government.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled on Wednesday that the government led by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán unlawfully restricted Hungarian teachers’ right to strike. The court found that the restrictions imposed on teachers and their trade unions were disproportionate and were not necessary in a democratic society.

The case was brought by the Teachers’ Trade Union (PSZ) and the Democratic Trade Union of Teachers (PDSZ), which turned to the Strasbourg court in 2022. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union (TASZ) represented them in the proceedings, which were subsequently joined with cases brought by two affected teachers.

The judgment is not yet final. The Hungarian government has until 6 January to request that the case be referred to the court’s Grand Chamber for reconsideration.

Why did the court rule against the Orbán government?

The dispute dates back to February 2022, when the Orbán government introduced a decree restricting teachers’ right to strike, citing the pandemic situation. The rules established minimum services that schools and kindergartens had to maintain during strikes. These included providing childcare and holding certain lessons even when teachers were taking industrial action.

The measures came shortly after teachers’ unions organised a nationwide strike in late January 2022. More than 20,000 teachers took part in the two-hour protest. The unions challenged the restrictions before Hungary’s Constitutional Court, but their complaint was rejected on procedural grounds. They subsequently took their case to Strasbourg in September 2022.

In its latest judgment, the ECHR found that the restrictions placed a disproportionate burden on both teachers and their trade unions. The state had exceeded its margin of appreciation, the court concluded, and the limitations on the right to strike were not necessary in a democratic society.

Education minister welcomes the judgment

Education and Child Affairs Minister Judit Lannert welcomed the ruling on Thursday, saying it vindicated the new ministry’s approach to teachers’ rights.

“I firmly believe that teachers should be valued, not humiliated, and that their professional opinion should carry weight,” Lannert wrote on Facebook. “One of my first decisions as minister was to change this practice.”

She criticised the previous Fidesz-Christian Democrat government for reducing schools’ autonomy, restricting teachers’ right to strike and dismissing several teachers who had taken part in protests.

Lannert also pointed to amendments to the public education law adopted in August, which she said had restored schools’ autonomy, expanded headteachers’ powers and reinstated teaching staffs’ decision-making and consultation rights. The changes also strengthened employee representation and clarified the conditions under which teachers can exercise their right to strike.

What changes for teachers?

The ruling concerns the legality of restrictions imposed under the previous government, while the new government has already introduced changes to the legal framework governing public education and industrial action. Lannert said teachers’ opinions and criticism would be important in renewing Hungarian education.

World.title: New direct Railjet train to connect Munich and Miskolc!
World.content:
Miskolc is set to gain a direct rail connection to Munich this winter, with Austrian Federal Railways (ÖBB) planning to introduce daily Railjet services between the two cities from 13 December 2026. The new route will also serve Vienna and Budapest.

According to information published by ÖBB on Wednesday, the new connection is part of the railway operator’s timetable change for December. As reported by the Facebook page PTF – Public Transport Fan, the direct service has already appeared in the timetable search, although the final schedule could still change before its launch.

The new service will give passengers in north-eastern Hungary a direct train connection to the Bavarian capital without needing to change trains along the way.

When will the trains depart?

The timetable currently lists the following departure times for the service, although these are subject to change.

Munich to Miskolc: Railjet service RJX 67 is scheduled to leave Munich Central Station at 1.28 PM and arrive at Miskolc-Tiszai railway station at 10.51 PM.

Railjet service RJX 67 is scheduled to leave Munich Central Station at 1.28 PM and arrive at Miskolc-Tiszai railway station at 10.51 PM. Miskolc to Munich: The first train in the opposite direction is scheduled to depart Miskolc at 7.03 AM on 14 December, arriving in Munich at 4.34 PM.

The new service is expected to operate daily in both directions, adding a further international rail option for travellers between Hungary, Austria and Germany.

If you missed it: Ryanair announces 29 new summer 2027 routes, including Budapest connection to UK

Where will the train stop in Hungary?

The train will call at several major stations across Hungary, including:

Hegyeshalom

Mosonmagyaróvár

Győr

Tatabánya

Budapest-Kelenföld

Budapest-Keleti

Hatvan

Füzesabony

Beyond Hungary, the route will serve Freilassing, Salzburg, Linz, St. Pölten, Vienna Meidling and Vienna Central Station.

The precise stops differ slightly depending on the direction of travel. According to the currently published timetable, the train heading towards Munich will stop at Hegyeshalom but will not call at Freilassing.

ÖBB RailJet at Keleti Railway Station in Budapest, Hungary. Photo: Daily News Hungary

A new international rail option for Miskolc

The connection would provide Miskolc, one of Hungary’s largest cities, with a direct Railjet link to Munich, potentially making international travel more convenient for residents, students and visitors.

Railjet trains are ÖBB’s long-distance services connecting major cities in Austria and neighbouring countries. The new route would extend the network further into north-eastern Hungary.

However, passengers should check the official timetable before planning their journeys, as departure times and stops may change before the new service launches on 13 December 2026.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán: Hungarian students to regain access to Erasmus+
World.content:
Hungarian university students will once again be able to apply for Erasmus programmes from the 2026/27 academic year, while Hungarian researchers and universities will regain access to Horizon Europe opportunities, the Minister of Foreign Affairs announced on Facebook on Wednesday.

Hungarian students now can apply for Erasmus+ again

In her post, Anita Orbán recalled that on Tuesday the Council of the European Union had adopted the European Commission’s proposal, bringing the rule-of-law conditionality procedure to a close and restoring full access to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes for Hungarian students and researchers.

“When we reached an agreement in May on the path towards securing the return of EU funding, it was particularly important to me that Hungarian young people and researchers should no longer have to bear the consequences of previous disputes,” the minister said.

The European Commission decided

At the end of September, the European Commission announced that, in its assessment, the reforms introduced by Hungary’s new government had delivered results: “Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the EU’s financial interests.”

At the time, the Commission recommended that the Council of the European Union enable the release of EUR 4.2 billion in cohesion funding for Hungary and restore access to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes for Hungarian students and researchers.

World.title: PM Magyar seeks EU funds for Hungary’s border fence as he vows to recover billions lost under Orbán
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in Brussels on Wednesday that the Tisza government would work in the negotiations on the European Union’s next seven-year budget to secure dedicated EU funds for strengthening the country’s border fence and border protection.

Speaking to Hungarian journalists ahead of a two-day European Council summit opening on Thursday, Magyar said the government took a firm position on migration and would continue to strengthen the protection of Hungary’s borders and hence Europe’s external borders.

He vowed that what had happened under the Orbán government, when thousands of people convicted in final judgements of people smuggling were released from Hungarian prisons, would not happen again.

He said his government is in talks with the European Commission and member states to close the procedure launched against Hungary under the Orbán government — which carries a daily 1 million euro migration fine — as soon as possible.

“Hungary has so far lost roughly one billion euros so far”, he said, blaming the Orbán government for failing to create regulations that complied with EU law “to protect Europe’s external borders and the Hungarian border”.

Concerning the summit’s planned debate on Ukraine, Magyar said Ukraine’s adoption on Monday of its law on education in minority languages was a historic breakthrough that may open the way to putting Hungary-Ukraine relations “on a new footing”.

If you missed it: Breaking: Hungary to receive EUR 250 million in Norwegian funding after years of disputes

“After long, long years of inaction and frozen relations”, he said, the Tisza government’s negotiations had achieved a breakthrough, and the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia could at last regain its educational rights, and in the future also its language-use rights, its rights before the authorities and its political rights.

Magyar said the meeting he is to hold with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels on Friday could lead to a further meeting between them in Berehove (Beregszász) this autumn.

The aim of the meeting will be to review the current state of bilateral ties and discuss further cooperation, he said, noting they are expected to hold a short one-on-one discussion.

Magyar said he wanted to confirm at the highest political level a ten-point political agreement reached with Ukraine at expert and lower political levels.

He said he expects Zelensky to reaffirm that the obligations undertaken in the agreement will be met on schedule, particularly regarding national minorities’ language-use rights, educational rights and rights before the authorities.

If Hungarian political, cultural, or church organisations in Transcarpathia reported problems, he said, he expected the Ukrainian authorities to be ready to resolve them, adding this was especially important for a country seeking EU membership, as national minority rights must be guaranteed to a European standard.

He said the agreement benefited not only Hungarians but also the other national minorities living in Ukraine, including Romanians and Poles, as it contributed to restoring their rights.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The prime minister emphasised that the agreement was backed by every Transcarpathian Hungarian political organisation, church, cultural organisation, and the university. Community representatives, he noted, had long called for an improvement in Hungary-Ukraine relations, since it served the security and peaceful life of Hungarians in Transcarpathia. “[Former PM] Viktor Orbán didn’t hear this; he didn’t want to hear it,” Magyar added.

He noted that in 2024 he visited the bombed children’s hospital in Kyiv and then travelled to Transcarpathia, where he met many local Hungarians. The government has kept in contact with the Transcarpathian Hungarian organisations, which took part in preparing the present agreement, ever since, he added.

As regards the EU’s next post-2027 budget, Magyar welcomed that under the proposal drafted by the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, the amount recommended for Hungary has not been cut and member states’ contribution obligations have not risen. The EU budget’s total may decrease, he explained, but not in areas of importance to Hungary, such as cohesion policy and the common agricultural policy.

Concerning the planned council debate on European competitiveness, he said Europe’s competitiveness had so far been “declining in a straight line”. He said the trend would hopefully reverse, adding that given the energy crisis and soaring energy prices across Europe, member states wanted concrete steps from the EC on “reining in price rises” and helping businesses and households.

On EU enlargement, Magyar said talks with Montenegro were expected to conclude, and there was “light at the end of the tunnel” for other candidate countries, including North Macedonia, Albania and Serbia. This did not mean that Serbia, for example, was very close to accession, he said, but progress could be expected, which was in Hungary’s interest given the ethnic Hungarian minority living in the country.

Magyar welcomed the EU Council decision closing the conditionality procedure launched against Hungary in 2022, saying the document was “worth 4.2 billion euros to the Hungarian people and Hungarian companies”. A further portion of the funds frozen over rule-of-law problems and corruption under the Orbán government could now reach Hungary and the Hungarian people, he said.

“Both the sums released earlier and this amount, as well as sums to be released in the future, will provide enormous help in the coming years to restart the Hungarian economy, to boost Hungary’s competitiveness and, ultimately, to deliver a significant rise in the living standards of the Hungarian people,” he said.

Magyar said Hungary had twice lost one billion euros in EU funds because of the previous government’s failures. The Hungarian people and businesses could not be blamed for the Orbán government’s failure to meet the necessary conditions, he said: it had instead spent public money on hate-mongering posters. The prime minister said he stood by his position that Hungary must be compensated for the lost support.

In the negotiations on the seven-year EU budget, he said, the aim was for Hungary to secure additional resources equal or close in value to the sum lost earlier, and there was a realistic opportunity to do so. This could be achieved through financing various projects or by increasing the EU allocations earmarked for Hungary, he said.

The prime minister recalled that many had also considered the release of some 6 trillion forints in EU support impossible, but a summer-long round of negotiations and thorough preparation had ultimately made the funds accessible.

He said he expected similar efforts from the Hungarian government, the state’s representatives and the diplomats to secure compensation for the two billion euros lost earlier.

The negotiations had already produced progress, he said: compared with the proposal of the previous, Cypriot, EU presidency, the funds earmarked for Hungary had risen by around one billion euros. He called this a significant result at the current, early stage of the negotiations, while stressing that further efforts were needed.

On the Hungarian budget, Magyar said the government had earlier made its economic policy goals clear, citing a stable and sustainable budget, a reduction of the budget deficit, a lowering of the state debt where possible, and restarting economic growth. “In the Orbán government’s last four years there was no economic growth, but there was a soaring budget deficit, a badly planned budget and rising state debt. We will now do exactly the opposite,” he said.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary to receive EUR 250 million in Norwegian funding after years of disputes
World.content:
Hungary is set to receive EUR 254.1 million (more than HUF 92 billion) in Norwegian and EEA funding after negotiations between Budapest and the donor countries were concluded. The agreement marks a major step towards restoring a funding programme that was suspended in Hungary in 2021.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced the breakthrough on Facebook, saying negotiations on the Norwegian and EEA Financial Mechanisms had been completed. The parties are expected to sign a cooperation agreement on implementing the 2021–2028 funding period soon.

Norway provides around 97% of the financing for the overall scheme, which supports projects in participating countries. The funding is intended to help Hungary access resources that were unavailable during the previous period.

Why did Hungary miss out on the previous funding?

Hungary received none of the nearly HUF 78 billion allocated to it during the previous funding period, following a dispute over who should decide how part of the money was distributed.

The disagreement centred on the Norwegian Civil Fund, which is only one component of the larger funding scheme. The previous Hungarian government wanted a state body to oversee the allocation of the funds, but the EEA donor countries refused to accept this arrangement.

The dispute ultimately prevented Hungary from accessing the funding intended for the country, while negotiations over the programme’s return continued for years.

The Norwegian and EEA Financial Mechanisms are separate from the EU’s regular funding programmes. They are designed to reduce economic and social disparities in Europe and strengthen cooperation between Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and beneficiary countries.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Talks resumed under Hungary’s new government

The Hungarian government restarted bilateral negotiations in 2024, but progress remained slow. According to Telex, in April 2026, Norwegian Foreign Ministry State Secretary Astrid Bergmål said discussions with Hungary had been under way since the previous spring and would continue with the new Hungarian government. At the time, she expressed hope that the talks could conclude by the summer.

That deadline passed without an agreement. Anita Orbán resumed negotiations on behalf of the new government in September, eventually bringing the process to a close. The forthcoming cooperation agreement will formally set out how the 2021–2028 funding period is to be implemented.

Civil society funding has already returned

Some support for Hungarian civil society has already been restored through a separate part of the Norwegian funding system. In July 2025, the Ökotárs Foundation announced the return of the Norwegian Civil Fund to Hungary. The programme is set to provide EUR 20 million in support for Hungarian civil society through 2031.

World.title: Second World War Soviet bomb found in Budapest, 200-metre exclusion zone to be imposed
World.content:
A Second World War-era Soviet bomb discovered at a construction site in Budapest’s 18th district will be defused in place on Sunday, 18 October, prompting the evacuation and closure of an area within a radius of approximately 200 metres.

Soviet bomb from the Second World War has been found

The FAB-100 demolition bomb was found at Üllői út 404 during construction work. According to the Hungarian Defence Forces’ bomb disposal service, police reported the suspected explosive device on 8 October. Bomb disposal experts who attended the site identified it as a Soviet FAB-100 bomb dating from the Second World War. Its current condition means it cannot be transported safely, making on-site neutralisation necessary.

The size and condition of the device, together with the amount of explosive it contains and its potential destructive force, mean that the surrounding area must be cleared before work can begin. Other explosive devices have previously been discovered at the same site, the bomb disposal service said. Those devices were safely removed by specialists for subsequent destruction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Roads, homes and public transport affected

Police will begin closing and evacuating the area at 8.30 AM on Sunday, 18 October, while military bomb disposal experts carry out the operation. The restrictions will affect pedestrians, road traffic and public transport. The exclusion zone will cover properties and streets around the discovery site, including the area between the market at 2–10 Balassa Bálint Street and Haladás Street. Residential buildings at 4–6 Szent Lőrinc Promenade, as well as a beauty salon at the rear of the building, will also be affected.

The restrictions will additionally cover the detached house at 424 Üllői Road and properties on the odd-numbered side of the road, from number 497 to the junction with Városház Street. The junction of Üllői Road and Vasvári Pál Street will also be affected, along with the intersection of Üllői Road, Városház Street and Thököly Road.

The operation has been scheduled for Sunday morning to allow the authorities to coordinate the necessary safety measures and give residents sufficient advance notice. Residents and travellers in the area should expect disruption from 8.30 AM while the exclusion zone remains in force. The supplied information does not specify when the restrictions are expected to end.
