According to him, exceeding the fixed limit does not mean that the transaction is automatically illegal. In such cases, the bank may review the customer’s transactions and assess their nature.

“When a customer contacts the bank and explains the nature of the transactions, the bank can make a decision based on its own assessment. In this case, the key is to correctly identify risks and ensure oversight of suspicious transactions,” he noted.

Mahmudzade added that imposing limits on financial transactions can, in certain cases, cause inconvenience for customers. However, the effectiveness of such restrictions should be evaluated by considering both the difficulties they create and their potential benefit to society.

“Any regulation imposes certain restrictions. However, it is necessary to weigh the overall benefit against the potential harm. We believe that the benefits to society from the limits set by banks outweigh the associated inconveniences. After all, as a result of illegal gambling and similar activities, many families may face serious financial problems,” the CBA’s executive director emphasized.

He noted that banks’ responsibility for risk management is not limited to setting limits. Financial institutions must continuously monitor transactions, promptly identify suspicious activity, and take appropriate control measures.

World.title: Mirziyoyev proposes AI, climate resilience initiatives at CICA Summit
World.content:
Photo: The Press service of the President of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has proposed an Asian initiative on technological trust and the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI), as well as the establishment of a climate resilience partnership, to strengthen cooperation among member states of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA). He made the proposals at the 7th CICA Summit in Baku on Thursday.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.

“Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing our daily lives. It opens up unlimited opportunities, but at the same time creates significant risks. We must do everything possible to ensure that digital progress benefits all countries and that gaps in technological development are reduced,” Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said.

To advance the initiative, Uzbekistan proposed establishing an expert platform within CICA where specialists could develop common recommendations and coordinate practical measures on the responsible use of AI.

Additionally, the country proposed creating a Partnership for Climate Resilience to coordinate efforts among CICA member states to adapt to climate change.

As Uzbekistan coordinates CICA’s human dimension activities, Mirziyoyev expressed readiness to host a Human Development Forum next year. He also emphasized the need to develop a CICA Action Plan through 2028.

In connection with Uzbekistan’s upcoming assumption of the chairmanship of the Non-Aligned Movement, the president invited member states to participate in the organization’s 20th summit, scheduled to take place in Tashkent next year.

Concluding his remarks, Mirziyoyev supported further strengthening CICA’s institutional framework and endorsed Azerbaijan’s candidate for the position of CICA secretary-general. He also welcomed Azerbaijan’s intention to continue chairing the organization.

Other leaders, heads of delegations and representatives of international organizations also addressed the summit.

World.title: Azerbaijan's central bank explains purpose of consumer loan rules
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The key aim of the regulatory measures introduced by the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA) for consumer loans is to prevent excessive indebtedness and ensure that borrowers take on loans commensurate with their income, CBA Executive Director Shahin Mahmudzade said at a news conference in Baku on Thursday dedicated to the presentation of the Financial Stability Report, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He noted that the consumer lending requirements are designed to protect citizens' financial interests and prevent them from taking out loans without adequately assessing their ability to repay them.

"Our goal is to ensure that people do not borrow more than they need. The requirements we have implemented, such as restricting lending when the debt-to-income ratio exceeds 70%, limiting the issuance of consumer loans in foreign currency, imposing additional capital requirements for credit cards, and other measures, all serve this same purpose. People shouldn’t take out loans they don’t need. Furthermore, when a loan is taken, the amount should be commensurate with the borrower's income," he mentioned.

According to the CBA executive, the new regulatory measures, including a mechanism that allows individuals to restrict their own ability to take out loans, as well as new rules governing online lending, are also aimed at reducing financial risks for citizens.

Mahmudzade pointed out that the tightening of requirements for bank lending could create a risk that some individuals seeking to borrow might turn to alternative sources of financing, such as pawnshops or informal credit channels.

"If a person is unable to obtain a loan from a bank, he/she may turn to other sources of financing, including pawnshops. Subsequently, there is a possibility that he/she might resort to informal channels. This could be a consequence of tightening requirements within the banking sector. Therefore, it is essential to assess the overall impact of regulatory measures," he explained.

He added that when drafting regulations for the consumer credit market, the CBA considers not only the situation within the banking sector but also the potential impact these requirements may have on the borrowing behavior of citizens.

According to the executive, the objective of the regulation is not to make consumer credit entirely inaccessible, but rather to protect citizens from making ill-considered financial decisions. At the same time, fostering a culture of responsible borrowing within society is of great importance.

"We are implementing these rules to encourage people to refrain from non-essential expenditures and to avoid increasing their consumption through additional debt. Some expenses generate no added value, yet they increase an individual's debt burden. Our goal is for people to understand the essence of these changes and to realize that excessive borrowing primarily harms them," emphasized Mahmudzade.

He noted that while regulatory measures help mitigate financial risks for citizens, the development of responsible financial behavior also requires individuals to properly assess their own expenses and borrowing needs. "We can protect people to a certain extent through our own regulations. However, individuals must also safeguard their own financial standing by avoiding unnecessary expenses and additional indebtedness," added the CBA executive.

Touching upon statistics regarding informal borrowing, Mahmudzade noted that it’s difficult to assert definitively whether there has been a growth in this area due to the absence of official statistics or relevant reporting for such transactions. Therefore, it’s impossible to confirm whether the volume of informal lending is rising or falling.

World.title: Azerbaijan drafts changes to expand funding options for microfinance firms
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Legislative amendments are being drafted in Azerbaijan aimed at expanding financing opportunities for microfinance organizations, particularly those that provide loans to small and medium-sized businesses, the Executive Director of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan, Shahin Mahmudzade, said at a press conference on Thursday dedicated to the presentation of the Financial Stability Report, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

According to him, the proposed changes are intended to create additional opportunities for certain microfinance organizations that prioritize business lending to attract funding and conduct their operations.

Mahmudzade noted that there are certain challenges in the microfinance sector, particularly in the area of financing small and medium-sized enterprises. The proposed changes are aimed at addressing these issues, increasing the volume of business lending, and enhancing competition in the financial services market.

As Mahmudzade noted, the sources of funding for microfinance organizations primarily fall into three categories: the issuance of securities, borrowing from banks and other financial institutions, and raising funds from foreign sources.

He emphasized that the hedging mechanisms introduced last summer for foreign-currency borrowings were primarily aimed at improving financing opportunities for microfinance organizations.

“Hedging the currency risks of microfinance organizations that raise funds in foreign currency helps reduce their financing costs. It also contributes to increased competition in the financial market,” he said.

A representative of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan emphasized that microfinance institutions’ access to alternative sources of financing also intensifies competition among banks. Thus, as microfinance institutions gain greater opportunities to raise funds from other sources on more favorable terms, banks may also be interested in offering them loans on more attractive terms.

“If microfinance organizations lack alternative sources of financing, their options are limited. In such cases, banks may offer loans at higher interest rates. However, expanding opportunities to attract foreign financing and implementing mechanisms to manage currency risks can reduce financing costs and encourage banks to offer more competitive terms,” Mahmudzade noted.

According to him, the planned legislative changes will also affect the ability of microfinance organizations to raise funds through the issuance of securities. In particular, consideration is being given to creating additional conditions for organizations that focus more on business lending, self-employment projects, and financing small and medium-sized enterprises, rather than consumer lending.

Shahin Mahmudzade reported that drafting the amendments and adopting the relevant regulatory acts will take some time.

"Therefore, the new opportunities will be implemented only after the legislative process is completed. He noted that work on implementing the main changes is scheduled to be completed in phases next year," he added.

The Executive Director also clarified the issue of the Central Bank providing financial resources to banks. He stated that the Central Bank’s financing of banks is not intended to create a permanent and general source of funds for lending to the economy.

“We do not provide funds to banks so that they can channel this money directly into the economy. The financial instruments provided by the Central Bank to banks are primarily related to liquidity management and, when necessary, to fulfilling the role of lender of last resort. The allocation of credit resources in the economy is determined by market forces and demand,” he added.

World.title: Azerbaijan's banking system remains financially resilient - CBA executive
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The banking system in Azerbaijan is financially resilient, Executive Director of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), Shahin Mahmudzade, said at a press conference dedicated to the presentation of the Financial Stability Report in Baku on Thursday, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

According to him, the application of an additional capital buffer requirement for systemically important banks in Azerbaijan serves to strengthen the resilience of these banks against financial shocks, but this requirement doesn’t imply that small and medium-sized banks are riskier or more vulnerable.

He noted that the establishment of an additional capital buffer for systemically important banks is part of the regulatory framework, aimed at ensuring the creation of extra financial reserves to cover risks these banks might face.

"The purpose of the additional capital buffer is to reflect the specific needs of systemically important banks. The existence of this requirement helps make these banks less vulnerable. However, this doesn’t imply that smaller banks are more vulnerable or prone to problems," Mahmudzade pointed out.

According to him, stress tests are conducted to assess the financial condition of banks and their resilience to potential shocks. These analyses allow determine the potential impact on the financial indicators of individual banks, as well as the overall resilience of the banking system.

The CBA executive also noted that the results of the stress tests are expected to be released early next year. These results will allow for an assessment of how the banks' capital indicators might change under various scenarios.

"Our previous reports also highlighted that the average capital adequacy ratio of the banking system stands at around 17–18%, while under stress scenarios, it falls to approximately 14%. These indicators are significant for assessing the overall resilience of the banking system," he remarked.

Mahmudzade emphasized that the emergence of financial difficulties in individual banks does not automatically mean a threat to financial stability as a whole.

"Certain problems may arise in individual banks. This may be caused by factors related to various business decisions, shareholder activities and risk management. Our main goal is to prevent systemic problems and maintain financial stability rather than problems that may arise in individual banks," the executive noted.

He added that the introduction of an additional capital buffer for systemically important banks corresponds to the role of those financial institutions in the system and the scale of potential risks. The existence of this requirement doesn’t give reason to conclude that small and medium-sized banks are more problematic.

According to Mahmudzade, CBA regularly monitors possible risks in the banking sector and continues appropriate regulatory and control measures to protect financial stability.

World.title: China backs Azerbaijan's CICA chairmanship for another two years – Wang Yi
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Azerbaijan has carried out successful work regarding climate change during its two-year chairmanship of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), and therefore China supports Azerbaijan's chairmanship for another two years, Foreign Minister of China, Wang Yi, said at the 7th Summit of CICA in Baku on Thursday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

According to him, CICA is a cooperation platform for the development of Asian countries.

He noted that CICA is a platform that supports peace in Asia.

"We are currently going through a period of rapid change. We must foster our solidarity so that we can easily overcome crisis situations. The Asian continent is home to the most dynamic and diverse civilizations. We must respect the governance models of each state," he added.

The 7th CICA Summit is being held in Baku under Azerbaijan's chairmanship.

The meeting will review progress since the launch of CICA's transformation in 2022, as well as the achievements of Azerbaijan's chairmanship in strengthening the organization and advancing practical cooperation among member states.

Under the theme “Stronger CICA: Connectivity, Digitalization and Sustainable Growth in Asia,” Azerbaijan has promoted dialogue and results-oriented cooperation during its 2024–2026 chairmanship.

World.title: Azerbaijan nears final stage of mandatory property insurance law revision
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Work on improving legislation regarding mandatory real estate insurance in Azerbaijan is in its final stages, the Executive Director of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), Vusal Gurbanov, said at a press conference on Thursday dedicated to the presentation of the Financial Stability Report, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He noted that the main goal of the proposed changes is to increase the transparency of insurance payouts and ensure a more appropriate determination of insurance coverage amounts.

In addition, the Executive Director emphasized that the decline in the number of compulsory insurance policies is due to several factors.

"These include changes in indicators related to the terms of insurance contracts, an increase in coverage amounts for certain types of insurance, and the government’s implementation of insurance programs for certain categories," he added.

He noted that there has been a decline in the number of compulsory insurance policies.

“One of the reasons for this is the timing of insurance policy issuance. On the other hand, an increase in insured amounts has been recorded for certain types of compulsory insurance. These figures were also influenced by the fact that, for some categories, insurance is provided by the state,” Gurbanov noted.

A representative of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA) reported that draft legislation on mandatory real estate insurance has been under review with the relevant government agencies for some time and is currently in its final stages.

"In addition, the Central Bank continues to work on other conceptual issues arising from the legislation," he emphasized.



According to him, the changes are aimed at ensuring greater transparency in insurance payouts, as well as a more accurate determination of insurance coverage amounts in accordance with the value of the property.

“The main goal of the new version of the legislation is to make insurance payouts more transparent and ensure a more appropriate determination of insurance coverage amounts. It is important that the insurance coverage amount be set taking into account the value of the property,” he stated.

Gurbanov emphasized that the proposed changes are not intended to increase the number of mandatory insurance policies. The main focus of the bill is to improve the quality of insurance services, streamline insurance processes, and ensure a more accurate assessment of the actual value of property for insurance purposes.

“We do not intend to increase the number of insurance policies. The goal of the bill is to improve the level of service, increase the transparency of insurance payouts, and ensure that coverage is provided in accordance with the value of the property,” the CBA’s Executive Director added.

World.title: Uzbekistan, IFAD set agricultural project priorities for 2026–2028
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Uzbekistan and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) have discussed expanding cooperation in agricultural mechanization, artificial intelligence (AI) and drone technologies, with new joint initiatives planned under grant projects for 2026–2028 during a meeting in Italy on October 14.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan's Ministry of Agriculture, following a meeting between Uzbekistan’s Minister of Agriculture Ibrokhim Abdurakhmonov, IFAD Vice President Donal Brown and the organization’s representative in Uzbekistan, T. A. Monem, during Abdurakhmonov’s visit to Italy from October 11 to 14 to attend the World Food Forum.

The parties reviewed Uzbekistan’s ongoing agricultural reforms and the implementation and future prospects of the project “Effective Solutions for Agribusiness: Higher Income, Investment and Sustainability.”

During the meeting, the IFAD vice president recognized Uzbekistan’s role in advancing food security and agricultural development in the region. Brown also highlighted that Tashkent hosts IFAD’s only office in Central Asia.

The discussions focused on opportunities to introduce AI technologies into agriculture, expand mechanization and increase the use of drones in farming under grant-funded initiatives planned for 2026–2028.

Moreover, the parties agreed to continue joint projects and explore further opportunities to strengthen cooperation in the agricultural sector.

The planned initiatives are aimed at supporting agricultural modernization, improving productivity and promoting more sustainable farming practices in Uzbekistan.

IFAD is an international financial institution and specialized United Nations agency that works to reduce rural poverty and improve food security by investing in rural communities and agricultural development.

World.title: Review ordered after man dies waiting two hours for ambulance
World.content:
Reviews are underway after two Queensland patients died in separate incidents while waiting for medical care.

A 53-year-old man who was experiencing chest pains called Triple Zero (000) to his property in the Brisbane suburb of Annerley on Saturday night.

Paramedics arrived two hours later and found the man dead inside the residence.

The Queensland Ambulance Service has confirmed a review into the matter has been launched.

"The death of a patient is a tragedy, and we extend our condolences to their family and loved ones," a QAS spokesperson said.

On Tuesday afternoon a man in his 80s was under the care of paramedics while waiting for a bed at Mater Private Hospital for approximately three hours.

Upon being admitted he went into cardiac arrest.

The man had a "do not resuscitate order" and died shortly afterwards.

In a statement addressing both matters, Health Minister Tim Nicholls extended his condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased.

He said the cases would be reviewed "as will always happen when these types of tragic events occur — to ensure all procedures and protocols were followed".

The latest Queensland Health performance data shows ambulance ramping is sitting at 42 per cent across the state's 26 top public hospital emergency departments.

World.title: Story of young woman accused of witchcraft wins $100,000 book award
World.content:
Margaret River-based author Bernice Barry has won the $100,000 ARA Historical Novel Prize for her book about a woman being pursued by a witch-hunter, The Names of a Hare.

It is the story of an unnamed woman living in Cornwall in the 17th century, a time when witches could be burned at the stake.

Barry's protagonist is the daughter of a priest, taught by her housekeeper from a young age about natural cures and magic. She also learns she has a special power of her own where she can float above her body and travel great distances.

When someone shares her secret, she is accused of witchcraft and forced to flee.

Barry, 73, was born in Cornwall and moved to Australia 25 years ago. She says winning the Historical Novel Prize is validating after 15 years writing for a mostly Western Australian audience.

"My books have been bestsellers in WA, but I don't sell a lot of books," she says. "It's a fairly niche area I've been writing in: the stories of forgotten women, history, botany.

" To be acknowledged in this way means the world to me. "

The judges, chaired by publisher and editor Linda Funnell, described Barry's writing as "work[ing] like a spell, building slowly and imperceptibly, attentively describing the natural world and the lives of rural folk in a time of great historical turmoil".

"This is a novel of quiet power that lingers in the mind," the judges said.

Bernice Barry describes The Names of a Hare as about love, home and hope. (Supplied: Fremantle Press)

The ARA Historical Novel Prize, awarded by the Historical Novel Society Australasia to novels set more than 50 years ago, is one of Australia's richest literary prizes.

The prize also awards $30,000 to a book for younger readers. Meg Caddy won this year for their young adult novel A Flash in the Dust about two young people escaping from Fremantle Asylum.

Wayne Marshall won the $5,000 Readers' Choice Award for his novel Henry Goes Bush, which turns the story of Henry Lawson's banishment to Bourke in 1892 into a surreal odyssey.

Barry says the most important thing about winning the top prize is the opportunity for "my little book to get to more readers".

"That is the reason I write," she says.

"It feels like a magical connection [with the reader]. It's the magic of words; the magic of sharing a story."

Writing a neurodivergent protagonist

In The Names of a Hare, the unnamed narrator is at the end of her life, looking back and sharing her story and what she has learned.

Writing the book was an opportunity for Barry to do the same.

The Names of a Hare is the product of meticulous research into C17 recipe books and languages. (Supplied)

"I wanted to convey some of the things that have been on my mind for many years," she says.

When living in England's Midlands and feeling homesick for Cornwall, Barry started to write a short story. More than 30 years later, those pages became the prologue of The Names of a Hare.

But the inspiration for her protagonist goes back even further, to being nine years old and reading RD Blackmore's historical novel Lorna Doone.

She recalls being fascinated by a minor character, who was based on a real woman and dubbed Mother Meldrum.

"I wondered about this old woman who was a healer from Cornwall," Barry says. "Nobody knew her name, and they were afraid of her, but they needed her."

Barry's protagonist, also unnamed, is a neurodivergent woman who avoids eye contact, flinches from touch and is averse to loud noises.

September's best books The latest new releases from some of the world's biggest literary stars, including Emily St John Mandel, RF Kuang and Kate Atkinson, are among this month's best books.

They are qualities borrowed from her own experiences.

"Life was difficult for me as a young woman because I knew I was different," she says.

"I was strange, I was weird, and I spent a lot of time masking. I spent a lot of time thinking it was all my fault.

"I would never have talked about those things until probably two or three years ago, and I wouldn't want anyone else to go through life hiding something that is so discomforting."

It was not something Barry initially set out to include, but when she was about 10,000 words into the manuscript, she realised what she was doing.

"I was thinking, 'There must have been women like me in the 17th century,'" she says.

"It must have been very hard, where people would just look at her and say, 'She's different; she must be a witch.'"

Why witches?

Barry's novel is one of a spate of recent books exploring ideas around magic and witchcraft, including Lucianne Tonti's Good Witch and Kaz Cooke's Spooky Ladies.

They are being released as more young women try out "witchy" things like manifestation, crystal-collecting and solstice rituals.

Barry suggests this interest may stem from young women feeling confident to speak out about misogyny — the same social ill that fuelled the witch trials that form the backdrop of The Names of a Hare.

"I wonder if we'll ever be free of it; of that way of viewing women that makes some people feel women take away their power," she says.

That way of viewing women is something she describes in the novel.

"Having the skill to remove pain and restore good health, that's power, and power in the hands of a woman is not a thing men can swallow easy like a slippery syllabub," she writes.

Barry sees that renewed sense of confidence, paired with "witchy" rituals, as part of a cycle she also recalls from her early adulthood, when she was a student in London.

"The late 1960s and early 1970s was a time when there was a similar wave of confidence and a united feeling of women being able to speak out and do something about [misogyny]," she says.

Barry also wrote the novel Sarah Evans, about an 18th-century convict, and two books about botanist Georgiana Molloy. (Supplied: Fremantle Press)

That united feeling is also in the novel.

"It's about the steadfastness of women and friendship; the way we always turn up for one another," Barry says.

Still, the author would prefer for the reader to decide for themselves if her unnamed protagonist is a witch or not.

"Was this woman a witch or was she someone who had a natural ability for healing?"

World.title: Inquest hears missing schoolgirl's skull used as ashtray at pub
World.content:
The man who found part of missing Mackay schoolgirl Marilyn Wallman's skull took it to a pub where it was used as an ashtray, an inquest has heard.

Greven Breadsell told police he had found the skull in 1974 at McGregor Creek near Mirani, about 40 kilometres from where Marilyn went missing two years earlier.

A 2015 video re-enactment of his discovery was played in a coronial investigation that is seeking to determine who is responsible for the 14-year-old's death.

During the re-enactment, Mr Breadsell said police questioned him about the skull in 1974 after he had taken it to a pub.

"I don't like to say this, but we took it over to the pub and used it as an ashtray one night," he said.

" Made me feel a bit shitty when we found out it was hers and we were mucking around with it. "

In the video played to the court, Mr Breadsell showed police where he saw the top part of a skull lying on grass in a cattle paddock, near an illegal dump site.

He told police he had gone to the property to collect palm fronds to shelter his mother's orchid house.

Greven Breadsell leaves the Mackay Court House. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

He said he initially thought what he found was an Aboriginal person's remains.

"Who else's skull would it be?" Mr Breadsell said.

"I had it at the shed there [at my home] for at least a fortnight or three weeks."

A 2015 video recording of Greven Breadsell showing police where he found the skull. (Supplied: Department ofJustice )

A pre-inquest hearing in August had heard that in 2006, updated DNA testing methods confirmed the skull was Marilyn's remains.

The court heard that in the past decade, Mr Breadsell had become close friends with person of interest Noel Morris, who was married to Marilyn's cousin at the time of her disappearance.

Marilyn 'scared' before disappearance

Trudy Voltz, a friend of Marilyn Wallman, told the inquest Marilyn looked "scared" the day before she disappeared.

Ms Voltz said Marilyn argued with another friend that day and had been quiet during a lunch break at North Mackay State High School.

Marilyn Wallman's family have been notified of the development in the case. (Supplied)

The 68-year-old recalled that, at one stage, Marilyn had left to walk towards a school gate but did not say why.

Ms Voltz told the court Marilyn sat near a window looking out at the same entrance in maths class.

"I said to her, 'Who's out there?' And she answered me," she said.

"I think she said the word 'uncle.'"

The court heard Marilyn sat alone near the tuck shop after school and told Ms Voltz she did not want to catch the bus.

It also heard Ms Wallman declined to go home with her friend.

Marilyn Wallman's siblings Lenore, Rex and David. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Earlier 'incident' with man after school

Council assisting the coroner, John Aberdeen, asked Ms Voltz to recall an "incident" on March 17, 1972, the Friday afternoon before Marilyn disappeared, involving Marilyn and a man.

Ms Voltz said she noticed her friend walking on the other side of the road outside the North Mackay State High School.

"A man approached her, and when she saw him, she took a couple of steps back," she said.

"He started talking to her … Marilyn had a very defensive pose.

" She was not happy to see him at all. "

Ms Voltz told the court the man was aged 19 to 20 and was about a "head height" taller than Marilyn.

She said she had assumed at the time it was someone Marilyn knew through her hockey club.

The inquest will continue Friday.

World.title: Man faces court after 'frightening, costly' truck collision with train
World.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to two charges over a crash that derailed a train in the Northern Territory and seriously injured at least two other people.

Christopher Berto, now 37, was driving a prime mover on June 14, 2023, in the Katherine region when the vehicle collided with a locomotive.

The court heard he was on his fourth run of the morning, moving tonnes of gravel from a quarry.

The truck caused the freight train to derail, injuring two workers on board.

The train was derailed in Cossack, outside Katherine, in June 2023. (Supplied: NTPFES)

Mr Berto pleaded guilty to two counts of careless driving causing serious harm, a plea the defence said he took at the earliest opportunity, in Darwin Local Court today.

Marty Aust SC said his client could not explain why he did not see the crossing lights when they started flashing and that there was no speeding, drug or alcohol use involved.

"At that point in time he has about 70 seconds to slow the vehicle before he started skidding … the prime mover was not capable of being stopped so he had to make a split-second decision to try and get it across," Mr Aust said.

" Ultimately he wasn't able to get the trailers across. He narrowly escaped serious, serious injury, but the consequences were serious to two persons in the locomotive. "

Mr Berto conceded people had been seriously harmed and that the derailment was "frightening and costly".

"[Mr Berto] has been experiencing flashbacks, he has had to undergo counselling sessions himself … he understands that is exactly what [the injured people] would be going through, and in addition they have physical complications," Mr Aust said.

Marty Aust says his client has experienced flashbacks of the accident. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

He argued that the two workers suffered serious harm but their injuries were towards the lower end of the spectrum.

Mr Berto, a Katherine resident, was supported in court by his family, including two of his children.

Mr Aust argued his client should not be disqualified from driving because he was a father of four and the family's sole provider, and had "never had an issue" driving before or since the offending.

Crown seeks imprisonment

Prosecutor Rhiannon McGlinn said the Crown would not ask the court to disqualify Mr Berto from driving, but sought a term of imprisonment. She said the Crown would be open to such a sentence being wholly suspended.

Ms McGlinn said one of the men who was injured required surgery to his wrist and had suffered psychological injuries.

The derailment occurred on June 14, 2023. (Supplied: Simone Siedel)

"He could not return to work for three and a half months after this event," she said.

Ms McGlinn said the other worker suffered a back injury that required ongoing physiotherapy.

"He can't even hold his children up for too long due to his ongoing back pain," she said.

Ms McGlinn said the man also suffered financial strain and had to change careers.

Mr Berto's matter will return to court next month for sentencing.

World.title: Chickens euthanased in NSW egg farm 'emergency situation'
World.content:
Chickens at an egg farm on the NSW Central Coast are being euthanased as the business is investigated over claims of animal cruelty.

Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty today told the upper house of NSW Parliament that the Department of Primary Industries was aware of concerns about Mountain Pride Farms.

She said an enforcement agency was investigating and "live chickens are currently being euthanised at that site".

She described it as an "emergency situation".

"The department has commenced an investigation to determine if there are food safety or biosecurity concerns at the property," Ms Moriarty said.

Mountain Pride Farms declined to comment to the ABC on the investigation. (Supplied)

"That is a desperately sad situation, but ... these things need to be done in order to spare animals that might otherwise be in a very difficult situation."

Video was released by advocacy group Animal Liberation earlier this week depicting dead and dying chickens allegedly filmed at Mountain Pride Farms.

An egg business on the NSW Central Coast has been accused of animal cruelty. (ABC News: Shauna Foley)

Greens MLC Abigail Boyd said concerns about Mountain Pride Farms were first raised in September 2025.

She said those concerns were allegedly brought to the attention of the RSPCA, the NSW Department of Primary Industries, NSW Police and the Central Coast Council.

"It's deeply concerning that they've known about this, they've had footage and yet there's not been an urgent response," Ms Boyd said.

Blocking eggs from sale

Ms Moriarty said action had been taken to ensure eggs from the farm could not enter the food supply chain.

"The department will continue to monitor to ensure biosecurity controls are dealt with and maintained," she said.

But Animal Liberation spokesperson Lisa Ryan said eggs from the farm were observed for sale in generic packaging at the Central Coast fresh food markets on Saturday.

The owner of Mountain Pride Farms in Peats Ridge has declined to comment on the investigation. (ABC News: Shauna Foley)

She also said the eggs were being sold at a Peats Ridge petrol station on Wednesday night.

The ABC has contacted the operator of the farm who declined to comment.

The farm's website includes information that it aims to produce "the best quality eggs", which are "high welfare and free range".

Delayed response

Ms Boyd said she had lost faith in the food authority's capability to ensure products were what they were purported to be.

"These were supposed to be free range, ultra-healthy eggs with the highest welfare standards … and what it appears we've discovered is something very, very different," she said.

"I think the public have a real right to be concerned about who is protecting their food sources."

World.title: ACT walks back pledge for ankle bracelets on DV perpetrators
World.content:
The ACT government has scrapped its pledge to subject domestic and family violence perpetrators to electronic monitoring bracelets despite its corrections minister saying it was a "good idea".

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr had announced the scheme in 2024 after a national summit aimed at addressing the domestic and family violence crisis.

But two years later it has been parked.

The Justice and Community Safety (JACS) directorate said it had explored the use of ankle bracelets for the monitoring of domestic and family violence perpetrators, as well as offenders on intensive correction orders, parole, bail, and other conditions.

But in a statement, a JACS spokesperson said monitoring a "relatively small number" of offenders in the community could cost more than $4 million a year, increasing to $18 million annually for DFV monitoring.

"The ACT government has made the decision not to proceed with the implementation of an electronic monitoring scheme in this term of government," the JACS spokesperson said.

'Horrendous what's happening'

Corrections Minister Caitlin Tough says the scheme was too costly for the ACT government to implement right now. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

When asked how the cost of the abandoned scheme compared with incarcerating people who could otherwise be monitored in the community, ACT Corrections Minister Caitlin Tough said she did not have costs on hand, but it was being examined.

"Look, it is definitely one way that we could free up space in the [Alexander Maconochie Centre] and allow people to transition into the community," Ms Tough said.

"It's just the size of the ACT; the cost of operating a system at this time is just not a feasible way of monitoring.

"I know the whole ACT government and ACT community are so appalled at the continuing escalation in family domestic violence across our country.

"It's horrendous what's been happening recently," she said.

Safety versus illusion of safety

DVCS ACT chief executive Sue Webeck is unconvinced electronic monitoring can protect victim-survivors. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Domestic Violence Crisis Service (DVCS) ACT chief executive Sue Webeck said her organisation had not been consulted and had no "line of sight" about any early scoping the government might have done before it walked back its promise.

"In many ways, we are part of the service system and we hold the least amount of power in that service system," Ms Webeck said.

But she said she expected that if the scheme had progressed, DVCS's expertise eventually would have been sought, in which case Ms Webeck would have shared her reservations about the technology.

"Electronic monitoring can never and will never replace the responsiveness of the services and systems that are built of people to respond in the moment when risk is evident," Ms Webeck said.

An electronic GPS monitoring bracelet used on interstate offenders. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

She said she was aware of interstate victim-survivors who "still struggled to get the system to respond to their safety needs" despite their perpetrators being electronically monitored.

Ms Webeck said she feared the technology might merely provide an illusion of safety.

Police disappointed

Troy Roberts says electronic monitoring would have helped ACT police. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The Australian Federal Police Association's Troy Roberts said ACT police were "quite disappointed" the scheme had been parked.

"It's something that we were looking forward to seeing introduced," Mr Roberts said.

"The electronic monitoring would assist ACT Policing to monitor serious offenders, domestic violence offenders, but also people out on bail.

"So, this initiative could've actually stopped people being on remand and in custody and it could've helped with rehabilitation," Mr Roberts said.

He said there was evidence recidivism was low among offenders subject to electronic monitoring in NSW and South Australia.

Mr Roberts said the GPS technology in the bracelets would have been helpful in cases where perpetrators' bail conditions sought to prevent them from leaving the house at night.

World.title: Man to serve more than five years over fatal crash
World.content:
A drug-affected driver who killed a Nathalia mother of four in Northern Victoria last year will serve at least five years in prison.



Lance O'Brien, 31, pleaded guilty in September to culpable driving causing death and contravening bail conditions.

O'Brien was on bail at the time of the crash awaiting an appeal of a jail sentence for other offences including burglary and intentionally causing injury.



O'Brien's Toyota was heading north on the Barmah-Shepparton Road at Kaarimba at 4:40pm on October 2, 2025, when it veered into the lane that Vilia Sutherland was driving in.

Ms Sutherland died at the scene.

O'Brien appeared via video link from Loddon Precinct Prison where Judge Carolene Gwynn handed down her sentence.

He was sentenced to eight years and two months for the charge of culpable driving.

He has already served 26 days of that sentence and will be able to apply for parole in December 2031.

The court was told that at the time of the Kaarimba crash, O'Brien was on his way to report to police as part of his bail conditions.

Profound impact on the victim's family

Judge Gwynn addressed the victim impact statements made by members of Ms Sutherland's family.

She said the statement from her daughter Tammy Woods showed the enormous impact the loss of her mother had on her, which was both heartbreaking and life-altering.

Ms Woods was in Darwin when she learnt of her mother's death and had an agonising return to Victoria feeling helpless.



"On her return, the necessary drive to the coroner's office saw her exposed to remnants of her mother's car and her mother's glasses on the roadside," Judge Gwynn told the court.

"She feels that her life and that of other family members will never return to what they once were and that she will spend the rest of her life missing her mother."

Judge Gwynn also said the impact of Ms Sutherland's death would last longer than the sentence she imposed.

Troubled upbringing

Defence lawyer Aggy Kapitaniak submitted a letter to the court from O'Brien's brother Myles that said his life had spiralled out of control because of drug use.

O'Brien had a difficult upbringing, which included family violence and his mother was dependent on alcohol.

She had also introduced her teenage son to methamphetamine as early as 13 years old.

The court heard that Myles once found his mother and brother "hiding in a wardrobe … holding an ice pipe and smoking ice".

The court heard O'Brien's mother had regretted her actions and admitted her son did not have a fair start in life.

Lance O'Brien attended the court hearing via a link from Loddon Prison. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)



O'Brien had managed some employment as a fencing contractor and abstained from drugs for some time until two years ago. O'Brien had managed some employment as a fencing contractor and abstained from drugs for some time until two years ago.

He relapsed after the death of his nephew and his cousin's wife in a car accident.

His criminal history since 2014 included 13 court appearances for several offences including breaches of court orders, drug possession, violence and weapons possession.

Ms Kapitaniak said that O'Brien, a Yorta Yorta man, had shown remorse for his actions and that he had prospects of rehabilitation where he has been working as a peer listener with an Aboriginal welfare officer in prison.

Judge Gwynn also fined O'Brien $1,200 for committing an offence while on bail and disqualified him from driving for five years.

Family of Ms Sutherland observed proceedings via court video link while O'Brien's relatives attended court in person.

World.title: Indonesia to deploy dry ice to reduce thick haze from fires
World.content:
Indonesian authorities will deploy dry ice to reduce a thick haze blanketing the country and other parts of South-East Asia, caused by large fires.

Indonesia experiences forest fires during its dry season, but this year the blazes have been especially severe due to strong El Niño droughts.

The fires began burning in August. (Reuters: Arief Rahman Septian Prathama)

Authorities have recorded more than 280,000 respiratory problems in haze-affected regions since August 18, as fires burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares in Borneo and Sumatra islands.

Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Dudung Abdurachma said the first dry-ice trial would take place on Thursday, local time, and would focus on the haze in South Sumatra.

"This dry-ice deployment trial is a direct instruction from the president to help address the haze in South Sumatra," he said.

Loading Instagram content

"We will first assess the results and, if effective, this method could potentially be implemented in other areas."

A total of 1.5 tons of dry ice is being prepared for distribution by Cessna aircraft in the Palembang area.

On Tuesday, a fire razed nearly 300 homes on Sumatra, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, according to an official.

The trial will be focused on the area of Palembang. (Reuters: Abriansyah Liberto)

Singapore issues highest pollution warning

The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, and as far afield as the Philippines.

According to Singapore's National Environment Agency, air pollution in western Singapore was "very high" — the country's top level — on Wednesday.

Haze shrouds a luxury condominium at Keppel Bay in Singapore. (Reuters: Suhaimi Abdullah)

It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, exceeding the World Health Organization's recommended average annual exposure.

Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.

Singapore's west has been given the country's highest warning level for air pollution. (Reuters: Suhaimi Abdullah)

The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.

Schools close in East Timor

East Timor began a three-day school closure on Thursday, local time, due to the haze.

The government said it was necessary to close schools "to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions".

It urged families to keep children indoors and advised citizens to wear masks if venturing out.

AFP/ABC

World.title: The new Bluey video game has one big advantage: it’s made in Brisbane
World.content:
NationalQueenslandVideo games The new Bluey video game has one big advantage: it’s made in Brisbane Nick Dent October 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Quite late in the process of developing Bluey’s Happy Snaps, the Gameloft Brisbane team realised that something was missing. Enter: the grannies. “The grannies level is just about creating mayhem,” Gameloft head of studio Manea Castet says. “The more chaos you create, the more points you win.” Bluey’s Happy Snaps has been designed end-to-end by Gameloft Brisbane. Gameloft/Ludo Studio/BBC Studio To demonstrate, Castet uses a PlayStation game pad to steer Bluey as the granny “Janet” in her toy car as she knocks over plants and toys in the Heelers’ backyard and tries to locate hidden cans of baked beans.



“The grannies have actually become everyone’s favourite part of the game,” marketing manager Mark Fordham adds. Cantet suddenly puts the console down and covers his ears. “I don’t want to hear this [bit],” he says. “I want to discover this with my daughter.” Manea Castet, head of studio, Gameloft Australia, said making Bluey’s Happy Snaps in Brisbane was critical to the game’s success. Gameloft Brisbane We’re at the CBD offices of Gameloft Brisbane, the developers tasked by BBC Studios with the designing and marketing of Bluey’s Happy Snaps, the new video game for PC and console, on sale worldwide from October 15. The Gameloft building is just a 10-minute walk from Ludo Studios in Fortitude Valley, where the 154 episodes of Bluey were made.



I’m amused to note it’s across the road from the old Hotel Orient, where Custard, the band of Dave McCormack, the voice of Bandit, regularly played in their early days. (McCormack, Melanie Zanetti and other cast members contribute their voices to the new game.) Gameloft originated in France, and has branches in 10 cities spanning Europe, Canada, Vietnam and Indonesia. The Brisbane business is the fastest growing. In 2014 it had just 15 employees; now it has 130, and plans to have 200 by 2030. Added value comes in the form of colouring in and other mini-games. Gameloft/Ludo Studio/BBC Studio Meanwhile, over in Red Hill, close to where Bluey’s fictional Queenslander house is said to be, is the headquarters of Halfbrick Studios, makers of the previous Bluey game, Bluey’s Quest for the Gold Pen. Halfbrick put Brisbane on the gaming map with the billion-download Fruit Ninja back in 2010. For Gold Pen, which was released in December 2025, chief executive Shainiel Deo collaborated directly with Bluey creator Joe Brumm on a game based on the characters’ fantasy drawings, tapping into the show’s imaginative ethos.



Ron Curry, chief executive of Interactive Games and Entertainment Association for Australia and New Zealand, says the two Bluey games from two different studios are a reflection of the talent and creativity of Queensland games design. Related Article Opinion

CBD ABC Bluey it: Hit Aussie show makes millions … for BBC John Buckley CBD columnist “Around 27 per cent of all [Australian games] employees are in Queensland, and 17 per cent of the studios,” Curry says. “Those are last year’s figures, and that will maybe even go up for the current year, because we know how successful, for example, the expansion of the team at Gameloft has been.” Queensland is second only to Victoria for digital game production, bolstered by Screen Queensland and the federal government offering a combined 40 per cent tax offset.



The IGEA estimates that Queensland-developed games supported by the state government’s Digital Games Incentive have generated nearly $120 million in consumer revenue. But it wasn’t just smart accounting that brought Bluey back to Brisbane. Bluey: The Videogame, developed by Spanish company Artax in 2023, received something the world’s favourite blue heeler dog is not used to getting: negative reviews. Bluey: The Videogame received something the world’s favourite blue heeler dog is not used to getting: negative reviews. “It feels like a merchandising attempt, rather than a proper extension of the show,” Leigh Stark’s assessment on Pickr.com said, opining that “it’s a total missed opportunity to not employ Australian game developers”. Luke Reilly’s review for IGN.com said the game looked like the show but was “rife with annoying bugs, frustrating controls, and a bafflingly brief runtime of a little over an hour”.



“I cannot speak for what happened for [that] game,” Castet says, “but what I do know is that from the beginning both Ludo and BBC said that for Bluey ’s Happy Snaps we really want a high rating, a positive reception. “Some people care a bit less about the quality for kids’ games, and I think that’s wrong, I think that’s almost the opposite. I am a father of a six-year-old daughter, I want her to have the best game possible.” Brisbane locations seen in the show such as South Bank are fleshed out for in-game exploration. Gameloft/Ludo Studio/BBC Studio The new game’s premise is that Bluey and Bingo have found their dad’s old Polaroid camera and must use it to take snaps of objects hidden around the house, receiving a “sticker” for each successful find. Subsequent missions take them around Brisbane locations familiar from episodes of the show: New Farm Park, Mount Coot-tha Lookout, and South Bank, as well as the camp site (from the episode Camping), and Hammerbarn (aka Bunnings).



But the game isn’t simply a treasure hunt. Players can mess around with objects they find along the way: kicking and rolling balls, drawing with chalk, jumping on a trampoline and such, with popular supporting characters from the show popping up throughout. “It’s an open sandbox where we give them a tonne of toys to play with, exactly like in real life,” Castet says. Gameloft worked with QUT’s Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child to ensure the game fosters creativity, safety, identity and collaboration. Unusually for a video game, Bluey’s Happy Snaps has frequent touchpoints encouraging off-screen play, including a packet of cards in every box with ideas of “Things to Find” and “Family Fun”. “We really want you to turn the console off and go outside,” Fordham says.



Being based in Brisbane, Castet says, was “critical” to making a game that’s as much a love letter to the city as the show is. Game artists spent weeks visiting the locations – “to create them as faithfully as we can. You will see many things that you don’t see in the TV show, but that are here in real life in Brisbane.” Related Article Tourism and Events Queensland Bluey’s World pulls in half a million visitors Castet indicates a pink cockatoo in the New Farm Park setting. “You hear the bird? It’s the real bird that our audio team spent time recording in the Currumbin Sanctuary, which again could have been done only here.” So is the new game worth the $69-$85 price tag? My focus group of two played it for two solid hours before bedtime and only got through two levels. The ability to take photos of anything within the world of the game, and to play mini-games on the way towards achieving goals, kept them enthralled.



A reminder from Bingo between levels to go and take a “tactical wee” caused much hilarity. Castet wants the launch of Bluey’s Happy Snaps to spotlight the importance of the industry in Queensland. “Last year, if you take all the revenue generated by cinema box office, music, books, and combine all that together, multiply by four, you get the revenue of the video game industry. And this year it looks like it’s going to be times six. “It’s a really big industry, and it’s an industry where Australia is well positioned.” The game was launched at Queensland’s Parliament House on Thursday night, which Screen Queensland head of games Jed Dawson says “feels like a real milestone”.



Future Bluey games made in Brisbane are a distinct possibility, Dawson says. “I think the BBC were very impressed by the game studios that they came out here to do a recce on. So keep your eyes open, there might be more on the way.” Bluey’s Happy Snaps is released on all platforms on October 15. Millionaire businessman Antony Catalano has received planning approval to expand his family’s luxury Byron Bay compound as he prepares to return to court on Friday over allegations he violently assaulted his wife. The fallen media mogul plans to build a third expansive home in the exclusive Wategos Bay enclave, creating a sprawling estate worth more than $67 million. Stefanie and Antony Catalano. Instagram Whether he will be there to watch it come to fruition remains up in the air, as he faces Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on eight criminal charges, accused of threatening to kill and breaking the tailbone of Stefanie Catalano in a late-night incident at their luxury St Kilda penthouse in March. The couple, who share four children alongside Antony’s further five children from previous marriages, have reconciled since the incident, with Stefanie making two statements of no complaint to police, saying she does not support the case going ahead and does not want to provide evidence against her husband – although she could still be subpoenaed to do so.



As well as the “statements of no complaint” Stefanie has also lodged a police ethical standards complaint about her treatment in the months since her husband’s arrest, alleging authorities were seeking to “destroy” him. Related Article Exclusive

Antony Catalano Casa Catalano: Media mogul seeks approval for $67 million mega-compound in Byron Bay Police claim Catalano swung a clothes iron at his wife’s head, unlawfully imprisoned her in the apartment, threatened to stab her to death, and choked or strangled her. Stefanie was admitted to hospital with a fractured tailbone. CCTV footage showing common areas adjacent to the Catalano’s apartment is part of the police case against him, with Stefanie also providing a statement shortly after the incident. The $30 million penthouse apartment in the Saint Moritz building on the St Kilda foreshore is currently being rented to Hollywood actor Jamie Foxx, who is in Melbourne working on a film project. The apartment is rented at a peak short-term nightly rate of about $9,000.



Catalano has been on bail since March, when he entered a residential rehabilitation facility in Melbourne. At the time, he said he was “struggling with significant mental health and substance abuse issues”. He was stood aside from his role as executive chair of Australian Community Media, which he owns 50-50 with billionaire Alex Waislitz. Two of Catalano’s oldest sons, Jordan and Luca, took over as directors of their father’s myriad business interests. These include a large portfolio of property and businesses in Byron Bay, including luxury boutique hotel Raes on Wategos. The media proprietor has been quietly progressing plans for what has been a controversial development of the family compound in the exclusive precinct of the glamorous resort town. Plans for the original two-home family estate were first rejected by Byron Shire Council. After an 18-month battle, Catalano successfully appealed the decision to the NSW Land and Environment Court, which conditionally approved his plans in June.



In August, this masthead exclusively revealed that Catalano had submitted more plans to build a third home on an adjacent block, which is held in Stefanie’s name and would also form part of the family complex. Related Article Property development Antony Catalano expands Byron Bay hospitality empire with $17.35m deal The total cost of the development is in the order of $67 million based on land acquisition and stated building costs, but could be expected to run to a higher total spend as construction unfolds. The project would make it one of Byron’s most expensive residential estates. Council documentation reveals the third, recently approved, residence would cost an estimated $4.1 million to build and be three levels including basement storage, underground parking and an upper-level swimming pool. It would be similar in style and materials to the neighbouring larger, two-home development. Separate lawyers for both Stefanie and Antony Catalano were contacted for comment. World.title: Trump’s new press secretary: not quite attorney-at-law
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s new press secretary: not quite attorney-at-law Shawn McCreesh October 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: Is US President Donald Trump’s new press secretary a lawyer – or did she just play one on TV? Three days into her job, Katie Zacharia is facing questions about whether she has embroidered her credentials. She describes herself as a lawyer, and the president called her “an attorney”. When she was asked on Tuesday (Washington time) in which state she passed the bar exam, she twice replied: “When I moved to China.” Huh? Katie Zacharia standing behind Donald Trump as he spoke to reporters on Tuesday before boarding Marine One. Bloomberg The moment capped off a shaky debut for the woman who has accepted what is perhaps the most challenging public relations post in the United States. Now she was struggling to tell her own story.



On Wednesday evening, she told The New York Times that this whole mishegas over “lawyer”, “attorney” and “China” has been one big misunderstanding. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House ‘My president ... excuse me, my husband’: Trump’s new spinner gets off to a rocky start “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she said, taking a quick phone call on the tarmac in Arizona, where the president was holding a midterm rally. “That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she said. “And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.” It was only her second day on the job, she pointed out.



So here’s the truth about Katie Zacharia, not quite attorney-at-law: she graduated with a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. By some interpretations, that technically makes her a lawyer, though many legal experts said it would not. But is she an attorney, someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice? For that, she would have needed to pass the bar. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that she sat for the California bar exam after graduating law school, but didn’t pass. The Times was unable to find a law licence for her in California, or anywhere else she has lived in the US. During the brief phone call on Wednesday, the Times did not get a chance to press her again about whether she had ever passed a bar exam. But before she had to go, she did explain that when she first began appearing on cable news, she consulted with Pepperdine’s president as to how she should identify herself. She said she was warned not to use the words “attorney” or “esquire”, but that “lawyer” was OK. Loading But what about “general counsel”, would that be OK? Because, on LinkedIn, Zacharia identified herself as such for Fix California, a group led by Trump loyalist Richard Grenell. “You can’t be a general counsel to a company in the United States unless you’re admitted to the bar to practise law,” said Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the law school at the University of California, Berkeley. “A general counsel implies that you’re practising law, giving legal advice to the company. You can’t practise law without a licence.”



On Wednesday, a watchdog group filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association, calling for an investigation into whether Zacharia “repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime”. And that brings us to China. “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’ ” Katie Zacharia The White House explained this week that Zacharia moved to China with her husband, Tyler, who had a job at a US private equity firm. While there, she worked on “international transaction law”, Zacharia has claimed. On her LinkedIn profile, she listed nearly two years of employment at Zhong Lun Law Firm, which is one of China’s biggest law firms, with headquarters in Beijing and offices in Tokyo, New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Almaty, Kazakhstan.



The law firm did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Related Article Trump's White House Trump picks Fox News expert for next White House press secretary Opportunities for foreign lawyers in China are extremely narrow. Foreign nationals cannot sit for China’s bar exam, hold a Chinese lawyer’s licence or advise on Chinese law. They can, however, be hired by Chinese law firms to work on cross-border deals and to advise on foreign or international law. Gary Gao, a partner at Zhong Lun who is based in Shanghai, said the firm often hired foreigners for language assistance and to help Chinese staff understand foreign business culture. “They are not practising Chinese law at any time,” he said, adding that Zacharia’s role at the firm would have likely been similar to a paid internship.



Sida Liu, a law professor at the University of Hong Kong who specialises in mainland law, said it was misleading for Zacharia to describe herself as a former associate at Zhong Lun, because it implied that she was a licensed lawyer in China. “Chinese law firms can hire foreign nationals to work in their mainland offices, but such individuals are not classified as PRC lawyers because PRC lawyer qualification requires PRC citizenship,” Liu said, referring to the People’s Republic of China. “The title ‘associate’ may therefore be somewhat controversial.” So what are we to make of all this? It was Trump who called Zacharia an “attorney”, and she certainly never corrected the record. She called herself “general counsel”, which was misleading at best. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

Mark Nawaqanitawase might have made himself unavailable for November’s Nations Championship, but Les Kiss is confident the dual international will declare his allegiance to the Wallabies, and not Fiji, for next year’s World Cup. “I think there’s no doubt that he wants to be back in the game for us, that’s for sure,” Kiss said on Thursday at Sydney’s Accor Stadium. Loading While Nawaqanitawase was enjoying some time away from the paddock earlier this week before moving to Japan to join League One heavyweights Saitama Wild Knights next month, the try-scoring machine’s name was back in the headlines. It came after one of his agents, Milan Volavola-Shankar, left the door open for Nawaqanitawase to jump ship and play for another nation other than Australia. The winger will qualify for Fiji and Italy in August, having served his mandatory three-year break from international rugby.



The 26-year-old, who was one of the shining lights for the Wallabies during their terrible 2023 World Cup campaign, shapes as one of the poster boys for next year’s tournament. Already, sponsors are lining up to make him the face of the World Cup, having emerged as a household name in Australian sport after leaving the NRL with a premiership ring on his finger after starring in the Sydney Roosters’ recent grand final triumph. Mark Nawaqanitawase playing for the Wallabies in 2023. Getty Images Now, a tug of war looms for his services, with new Fiji coach Jake White likely to leap at the chance to have the athletic freak represent the island nation. On Thursday, Kiss confirmed Nawaqanitawase would be unavailable for the Wallabies’ three-Test tour in November.



“Yes, that’s no issue,” said Kiss, who spoke to the 190cm star recently. “For us, we’ve got plenty of good options, and we’re going to focus on those.” Most would consider Nawaqanitawase a walk-up starter for the Wallabies next year, but Kiss stopped short of guaranteeing the code-hopper a place at the World Cup. Mark Nawaqanitawase won his first NRL title with the Roosters. George Chan “Everyone will earn their way, but if he’s playing good footy, he’ll be in the mix, that’s for sure,” Kiss said. “There’s no doubt he’s a quality player that we’ll keep an eye on. We’ll have some opportunities going forward, definitely, and he’ll have some opportunities.



“But first and foremost, get his rest, get himself together and get into some rugby back in Japan. It’s a different game in terms of height and how you attack the game, how you move in the game, how you defend, the aerial game is different, so he’s got a lot of things just to relearn. It won’t take him long, but there’s been some positive dialogue between myself and him.” Zac Lomax received a late call-up for the Australia A team. Getty Images Meanwhile, fellow former Origin star Zac Lomax was a late inclusion in the Australia A squad for their two-match tour of the USA. Despite not being named on Monday, Lomax was included in a 28-man touring party, which includes Wallabies halves Kalani Thomas and Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, for matches against the Eagles in Nashville and New Jersey. It comes after Wallaby Tom Lynagh was ruled out with a knee complaint. With Nawaqanitawase out of the November Tests, the two matches will give Kiss something to think about, especially with Lomax one of the best in the air in Australian rugby after joining the Western Force earlier in the year.



Related Article Wallabies Debutant set for Bledisloe baptism as Wallabies suffer cruel setback “Zac had a baby recently, and it’s been a new experience and [he’s] had an interesting couple of weeks,” Kiss said. “We just asked would he like to come in there, and it’s eventuated in that way. He’s really happy to go on and be part of that. We’ll get a good chance to see him, and he’ll see us in that next level. So looking forward to that.” Angus Crichton, who has joined the Waratahs after bowing out with another NRL premiership, will stay in Sydney to help recover from a lingering foot issue.

This year’s season of reality renovation TV show The Block is almost at the finish line, but potential buyers of the five homes could find other luxurious homes nearby for a similar budget or less. Homes from the show are for sale with a $3.6 million to $3.9 million price guide, but the contestants trying to sell will face competition from other vendors within the same suburb of Mount Eliza and across the wider Mornington Peninsula. The Block’s contestants worked on homes in Mount Eliza this year. With the housing market in a downturn, questions remain over whether The Block homes will all sell on auction day. The Block airs on Nine, owner of this masthead. On last year’s season of the show, two houses failed to find a buyer at auction. They sold months later at a discount, and one settled on Thursday for $2.15 million to a corporate entity of which serial Block bidder Danny Wallis is the director. That price is $840,000 less than its auction reserve.



McEwing Partners’ Quentin McEwing is selling a number of properties on the Mornington Peninsula, and is also selling Chantel and Wyatt’s home at 3 Mackillop Place on The Block. He’s also selling a five-bedroom home a minute’s drive away, at 112 Old Mornington Road, Mount Eliza with a price guide of $3.2 million to $3.5 million. The home is set on a 3553-square-metre block and has a tennis court and a swimming pool. “I am competing against myself,” McEwing joked. “This property has a pool and tennis pavilion and land you could subdivide. Dollar for dollar it’s offering a great buy for families.”



In a strong market, properties like Old Mornington Road would sell for at least $4 million. But in the weaker market vendors were being more realistic about prices, McEwing said. Related Article Auctions ‘Can’t help but feel like you’re losers’: The Block’s homes fail to sell While there had been interest in The Block houses, he admitted it would be a tough market to sell in. “I think we’ve all got our challenges in terms of buyer depth,” McEwing said. “Lots of people would like to be a buyer, but they don’t have the [financial] depth to do it.” Even so, The Block homes were also offering great value – with the land worth about $1.8 million and build costs of about $3 million.



“It would be an over $5 million replacement. It is a ripper buy,” McEwing said. Mount Eliza’s median house price was $1.64 million in the June quarter on Domain data, rising 3.8 per cent over a year and bucking Melbourne’s downturn. 112 Old Mornington Road, Mount Eliza is one of the houses competing with The Block for buyers. McEwing Partners However, agents say there are few buyers at the $3 million-plus price bracket, as interest rate rises and the cost-of-living squeeze budgets and change plans. Buyers have also been looking at nearby Mount Martha and Mornington as prices fall.



A six-bedroom property at 8 Birdwood Avenue is up for sale in Mornington, with a $3,495,000 to $3,844,500 guide. The property has ocean views, a swimming pool and an al fresco terrace. It includes a two-bedroom unit built into the roofline, and comes with an option to buy a beach box. Belle Property’s Mark Logue said the property had been chasing north of $4 million, but the price changed with the market. “Sub-$1 million the market is pretty active and buoyant,” Logie said. “North of that buyers have a lot more choice and options. It’s pretty tough.”



Vendors were becoming more accustomed to the current market, and were more willing to meet buyer expectations than a few months ago. “The vendors understand it’s a tough market and all of the confidence that has been eroded from the market, has eroded price,” he said. A couple of suburbs south in Safety Beach, a four-bedroom house at 2 Sovereign Point is on the market for $3.3 million to $3.6 million. The waterfront house in Martha Cove comes with its own boat berth and a swimming pool.



“A house like 2 Sovereign Point is more likely to be something a buyer would have as a holiday home,” Marshall White Mornington Peninsula’s Brad Pearce said. Many properties were transacting off-market as prices softened, with buyers in the $3 million plus price range looking for homes that don’t need a renovation. “A lot of buyers have car collections, and they want somewhere for their cars or boats or jet-skis - something for the toys,” Pearce said. “So that really is a huge focus for them.” Property alerts are now available in The Age app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

The guerilla editing that resulted in the removal of a Ben Roberts-Smith image by persons unknown from Sue Lyall’s Herald (C8) could’ve been worse, reckons Peter Miniutti of Ashbury: “Instead of opening your paper and finding something removed, you could’ve found an inserted centrefold of Barnaby Joyce. Talk about a page being re(a)d.”

“Like Peter Hayes (C8) I’m tired of the ubiquitous use of ‘influencers’,” says John Lees of Castlecrag. “My suggestion for an alternative description is ‘inflatulancers’ bearing in mind that all we hear from them is a load of hot air!” Paul Koff of Glenhaven finds himself on a similar path: “Because of the trite garbage most of them peddle, we’ve taken to calling them ‘effluencers’.”

“Our Irish chums have a very accurate way to describe influencers,” advises John Elder of South Brisbane (Qld). “Gobshites.”

“Stand aside ‘shevelled’ and ‘gruntled’ (C8),” declares Greg Phillipson of Aranda (ACT). “My wife sends me out in search of ‘gorm’ whenever I accompany her to the shops.”

Philip Aspden of Miranda is currently conducting “experimental English classes at the Dawu Experimental School in Hubei Province, China, with the Herald for company and reading about all the strife in the world, I’m happy to remain ‘mented’.”

A man was found dead in his Brisbane home two hours after he called for an ambulance and was told to make his own way to the hospital.

The 53-year-old Annerley man died on Saturday night, having called Triple Zero complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath.

A man has died after waiting more than two hours for an ambulance in Brisbane. Dominique Tassell

He was categorised as a code IC, which 90 per cent of the time is seen to within 27.2 minutes.

However, the Queensland Ambulance Service called the man back and asked him if he could make his own way to the Princess Alexandra Hospital, as he lived three streets away.
