Photo: Matt Davidson HEALTH The action of One Nation, the Coalition and the Greens to defeat the government’s changes to private health insurance rebates for over-65s in the Senate destroys our confidence that they have the nation’s best interest at heart (“Coalition, Greens sink $3 billion aged care plan”, 15/10). The changes in the private health insurance rebates for over-65s was intended to provide $3 billion for aged care services. The action of the three parties is another example of why the community is frustrated, angry and disillusioned at the party politics that appear more important than wellbeing and the social cohesion of our nation.

Ray Cleary, Camberwell Labor’s aged care plan foolish

Millions of Australians over 65, this writer included, rely on being able to claim a rebate against soaring medical expenses. The government must have realised it was playing with fire to even think of bringing in such legislation. Thankfully, the Coalition, the Greens and One Nation have shut that down. What was the government thinking? One could say it was an obvious case of what the Butler didn’t see.

Chris Burgess, Port Melbourne



Are taxpayers getting value for money?

It appears that any changes to the private health insurance legislation are an attack on the pensioners and the elderly.

Medibank was created by Gough Whitlam, and privatised by the Fraser government. Medicare was introduced by the Hawke government. The Howard government then instituted the Medicare levy surcharge and forced people to contribute to private health insurance whether they wished to or not through the health insurance rebate.

Between 24 and 32 per cent of private health contributions are paid for by the taxpayer, now to the tune of about $6.9 billion, along with about $8 billion to private hospitals. Is this value for money? These amounts are in a large part funded by those who choose not to have private health insurance and believe strongly in a universal healthcare system as planned with Medibank and Medicare.

I wonder how many public medical centres, accessible to pensioners and the elderly, could be funded by $14.9 billion?

David Raymond, Doncaster East Access denied for rural Australians

Health Minister Mark Butler defends the government’s record in providing rural health (“‘Appalling’: Rural health funding gap blows out to $9.2b”, 15/10) and points to a $617 million training package for doctors and nurses. But last November, the government restricted access to nurse practitioners, requiring patients to have an annual face-to-face visit in order to claim a Medicare rebate. This effectively prevents rural Australians’ access to the highest-qualified nurses who can practise autonomously, and provide prescriptions, pathology and referral to specialists.

The article states that death from diabetes is four-fold in remote areas. Diabetes is one example of healthcare that can be effective via telehealth. Yet, there are geographically isolated Australians who cannot access any nurse practitioners under Medicare due to an easily reversible ruling ... no extra training required.

Eli Kinnersly, diabetes nurse practitioner, Richmond Warning on medical procedures overseas

I write to warn others about having medical procedures overseas. They may be less expensive than in Australia but may also cost you your life. My beautiful daughter, Jacky, had a severe hypoxic brain injury while undergoing dental implants in a Vietnam dental clinic. Some companies offer insurance for travel to Asia for medical or dental procedures. These practices should be investigated, and I have written to the federal minister for health regarding this matter. However, nothing will mend the hole in our hearts. On October 10, 2026, all life-maintaining procedures were discontinued, and we let our beautiful girl go.

Noel Norris, Casterton THE FORUM Brethren control

The Exclusive Brethren possibly once was a mainstream Christian church, but is no longer (“Ex-members claim their church leader directed political push”, 15/10).

When my parents were excommunicated from the Exclusive Brethren (the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church) in 1956, I was six years old. I remember the serious men in black suits; the fear in our home; being cut off from communication with all our relatives who were still “in”; the sense of being adrift from the certainties of childhood. My dad never completely recovered from the way he was treated.

In the 1820s, the Brethren started as a reform movement within the church in England. Under the leadership of John Nelson Darby who held extreme and coercive doctrines, the “Plymouth” group separated from the much more “Open” group in 1848. Since then, the Plymouth Brethren later known as the Exclusive Brethren have become ever more controlling.

My own journey has taken me to the Anglican Church of Australia in which I serve as a bishop. Here, there is – as there should be in religion – freedom to explore faith within a non-coercive Biblical framework, and to live that faith with a grateful love for God, filled with excitement to serve the whole of humanity in the world God loves.

No political involvement happens without Bruce Hales knowing, and the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church defiles both “Christian” and “Church”.

Bishop Ian Palmer, Mt Duneed



Facts of the matter

Ross Gittins’ article (“Immigration is too easy a scapegoat”, 14/10) demonstrates the disconnect between our commentariat and the one-third of Australians intending to vote for One Nation.

It’s not that Gittins gets it wrong – his facts are on the money – it’s that he, and many of our opinion-makers, don’t quite grasp that One Nation’s popularity has nothing to do with these “facts”. These voters are told, as if they are naughty children who won’t eat their veggies, that immigration is good for them. But One Nation supporters have their own “facts”, which are equally real: the decline or lack of infrastructure, services, jobs and opportunities; a political class out of touch with, and dismissive of, a broad swath of the electorate; and a mainstream culture that appears to exalt difference over commonality. For these folk, immigration is the most visible aspect of a system that they believe discriminates against them.

Shouting “facts” at this group is a waste of breath. But one fact borne out by history is not in dispute: a society with ever-widening inequalities will ultimately get a new politics, and it won’t be pretty.

Greg Gardiner Brunswick Grievance gravy train

Shaun Carney (“We get one letdown after another”, 15/10) is right in noting that many people are angry, and he correctly identifies some of the sources of that anger, but he misses some important points.

Many people are doing just fine. Ironically, the populist grifters, such as Donald Trump, Nigel Farage and Pauline Hanson, are wealthier and more powerful than they have ever been. They are driving the grievance gravy train for all it’s worth.

They have no idea where it’s going, but they know that there is money and power to be collected on the way. There is a cost-of-living crisis being felt by many ordinary people, but this is not the crisis identified by the billionaire backers of the grievance grifters.

Their concern is that ordinary people might realise that the solutions to our problems might reduce the wealth and power enjoyed by the billionaires themselves. The strategy employed by the populist agitators is to divide and inflame misplaced anger to distract from what is really going on. It seems that many genuine people are keen to jump onto the grievance express, even though we can see clearly the train wreck that Donald Trump is delivering in the United States.

Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen Related Article Note From The Editor How The Age chooses which letters to publish Climate awareness key

Shaun Carney’s opinion piece is a nice read about the confluence of economic and political challenges nationally and globally. However, he makes no mention of the existing and future devastation of climate change. Our beloved country faces floods and fires, and famine is faced in parts of the world where climate is reducing food production.

Surely, these factors are a cause for anger.

We can change this trajectory but personal and political commitment to reduce carbon emissions is increasingly essential.

In coming elections, we have the chance to scrutinise candidates’ climate awareness and policies. For all of our sakes, let’s do this.

Carmel McNaught, Balwyn North

Sustainable can be cheap

Unfortunately, the beautiful property featured in The Age (“Toorak mansion sets standard for sustainable living”, 15/10) sets an unrealistic bar for most of us seeking sustainable living.

Forty-five years ago, my neighbours, with the help of family and friends, built a passive solar house using State Electricity Commission plans for an energy-saving prototype. It was inspirational at the time and still is. Now, back in the city, we have retrofitted our very modest two-bedroom dwelling to save energy and adapt to a warming climate.

Sustainable living can be achieved without spending millions of dollars.

An optimistic but urgent step to achieving sustainable living in the inner city would be for Victoria’s planning minister to adopt an approach of “adapt and re-use” instead of “knock down and rebuild”. Demolition of city buildings is a major contributor to green house gases and therefore totally unsustainable.

Susan Mahar, Fitzroy North



Staggering step backward

The state government’s directive forcing the City of Greater Geelong to remove light-coloured roof requirements from its Creamery Road Precinct Structure Plan is a staggering step backward for climate resilience.

Local councils are trying to innovate and protect their communities from the urban heat island effect, yet they are being actively handcuffed by state planning authorities.

Research shows that widespread dark roofs can increase household cooling bills by up to $700 annually while significantly raising ambient neighbourhood temperatures.

’The state government’s refusal to close the policy gap between federal building codes and state planning policy is incredibly short-sighted. By stripping away local mandates for lighter roofs, the state is effectively locking future generations of suburban residents into decades of higher energy costs and dangerous localised heat.

If the government insists on overriding local planning authorities, it must take responsibility for enforcing climate-ready housing standards.

Jennie Epstein, Little River Plenty of potholes

In a small lane near us, developers somehow are allowed to build two huge “mansions”, making huge profits and necessitating the use of huge heavy cranes, trucks and tradies’ utes. Potholes galore!

This is true all over Melbourne. Road repair surely should be on those developers.

Kay Moulton, Surrey Hills Lesson in respect

As a keen teenage photographer, travelling in central Australia in the 1970s, I attempted to photograph a group of Aborigines sitting in the dry Todd River in Alice Springs. I grew up in “white” Melbourne, and it was my first experience seeing Indigenous people. I was immediately howled down and put in my place by these people who felt victimised and exploited. It taught me a lesson, there and then.

As a 15-year-old white male, I had crossed a line I didn’t even know existed. I spent the rest of my life learning to respect and appreciate the incredible history and culture of the First Australians.

Fifty years later when the Voice to parliament did not succeed, I was crushed. The thought that Liberal leader Jess Wilson would remove Victoria’s Treaty really pours salt on that wound.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson Treaty question

Your correspondent (Letters, 15/10) suggests that getting rid of Treaty is essential and claims that “there are better means of addressing Indigenous disadvantage”. Perhaps he could tell us what those “better means” are?

Jo Bond, South Melbourne Two sides to the story

Re the article, “Firefighters shocked at receiving debt recovery letters from union” (14/10): To be upfront, I’m a firefighter and a rank-and-file United Firefighters Union member. These views are my own.

When someone signs up to join an organisation, they agree to abide by the conditions and pay their dues. Members joining a union are no different. They need to pay dues and levies for the union to fulfil its functions.

I’m sure if my Age subscription was $644 in arrears, I’d be receiving correspondence.

The article fails to highlight the huge amount of litigation brought upon the UFU by the Victorian government, and rather focuses on the Operation Richmond action. That report failed to find corruption but brought to attention the “extraordinary influence” the union secretary had.

Umm, yeah. That’s his job. Like any industrial lobbyist – union, corporate or industry – he seeks to meet with and establish working relationships with government ministers. He does his job well, and rightly so.

Greg Abramovitch, Portarlington



Just don’t do it

I see that the latest proclamation from Dario Amodei’s Anthropic predicts their AI agents are on the verge of being self-replicating, having the ability to embed themselves in everything from fridges to robo-Hoovers, and use the devices’ power to operate independently.

He and other AI company CEOs have been calling for legislation to limit or slow AI development. But they seem to forget they are the ones who, for now, have control of where this technology goes.

If Amodei really thinks it is that dangerous, he and his colleagues should just stop development now.

Mick Cahill, Fitzroy North AND ANOTHER THING ... Frydenberg

So Josh Frydenberg may be coming back. Wonderful. I’ll dust off my “Back in Black” mug — the perfect souvenir of that brief period when announcing a surplus was apparently considered an acceptable substitute for having one.

Catherine Ross, Sandringham Photo: Matt Golding If Josh Frydenberg decides to be a candidate at the next election, will the Liberals bring out the “Back in Black” mugs?

Barry Kranz, Mount Clear



If Josh Frydenberg is the answer, what is the question?

Kevin Rugg, Beaumaris Politics

Will Jess Wilson demand the 9000 businesses repay the $285 million they rorted during the pandemic?

George Reed, Wheelers Hill About time politicians looked at the happiest people in the world. Yes, I’m referring to Finland and Norway. They pay higher taxes yet their countries are ranked as one of the best places in the world to start and run a business. Go figure.

Ian Anderson, Surrey Hills America

Donald Trump has made America grate again.

Paul Drakeford, Kew The saying goes, “God works in mysterious ways”. A perfect example of this is the Pope getting lung cancer and Donald Trump getting richer and richer.

Randall Bradshaw, Fitzroy

World.title: The new Bluey video game has one big advantage: it’s made in Brisbane
World.content:
NationalQueenslandVideo games The new Bluey video game has one big advantage: it’s made in Brisbane Nick Dent October 15, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Quite late in the process of developing Bluey’s Happy Snaps, the Gameloft Brisbane team realised that something was missing. Enter: the grannies. “The grannies level is just about creating mayhem,” Gameloft head of studio Manea Castet says. “The more chaos you create, the more points you win.” Bluey’s Happy Snaps has been designed end-to-end by Gameloft Brisbane. Gameloft/Ludo Studio/BBC Studio To demonstrate, Castet uses a PlayStation game pad to steer Bluey as the granny “Janet” in her toy car as she knocks over plants and toys in the Heelers’ backyard and tries to locate hidden cans of baked beans.



“The grannies have actually become everyone’s favourite part of the game,” marketing manager Mark Fordham adds. Cantet suddenly puts the console down and covers his ears. “I don’t want to hear this [bit],” he says. “I want to discover this with my daughter.” Manea Castet, head of studio, Gameloft Australia, said making Bluey’s Happy Snaps in Brisbane was critical to the game’s success. Gameloft Brisbane We’re at the CBD offices of Gameloft Brisbane, the developers tasked by BBC Studios with the designing and marketing of Bluey’s Happy Snaps, the new video game for PC and console, on sale worldwide from October 15. The Gameloft building is just a 10-minute walk from Ludo Studios in Fortitude Valley, where the 154 episodes of Bluey were made.



I’m amused to note it’s across the road from the old Hotel Orient, where Custard, the band of Dave McCormack, the voice of Bandit, regularly played in their early days. (McCormack, Melanie Zanetti and other cast members contribute their voices to the new game.) Gameloft originated in France, and has branches in 10 cities spanning Europe, Canada, Vietnam and Indonesia. The Brisbane business is the fastest growing. In 2014 it had just 15 employees; now it has 130, and plans to have 200 by 2030. Added value comes in the form of colouring in and other mini-games. Gameloft/Ludo Studio/BBC Studio Meanwhile, over in Red Hill, close to where Bluey’s fictional Queenslander house is said to be, is the headquarters of Halfbrick Studios, makers of the previous Bluey game, Bluey’s Quest for the Gold Pen. Halfbrick put Brisbane on the gaming map with the billion-download Fruit Ninja back in 2010. For Gold Pen, which was released in December 2025, chief executive Shainiel Deo collaborated directly with Bluey creator Joe Brumm on a game based on the characters’ fantasy drawings, tapping into the show’s imaginative ethos.



Ron Curry, chief executive of Interactive Games and Entertainment Association for Australia and New Zealand, says the two Bluey games from two different studios are a reflection of the talent and creativity of Queensland games design. Related Article Opinion

CBD ABC Bluey it: Hit Aussie show makes millions … for BBC John Buckley CBD columnist “Around 27 per cent of all [Australian games] employees are in Queensland, and 17 per cent of the studios,” Curry says. “Those are last year’s figures, and that will maybe even go up for the current year, because we know how successful, for example, the expansion of the team at Gameloft has been.” Queensland is second only to Victoria for digital game production, bolstered by Screen Queensland and the federal government offering a combined 40 per cent tax offset.



The IGEA estimates that Queensland-developed games supported by the state government’s Digital Games Incentive have generated nearly $120 million in consumer revenue. But it wasn’t just smart accounting that brought Bluey back to Brisbane. Bluey: The Videogame, developed by Spanish company Artax in 2023, received something the world’s favourite blue heeler dog is not used to getting: negative reviews. Bluey: The Videogame received something the world’s favourite blue heeler dog is not used to getting: negative reviews. “It feels like a merchandising attempt, rather than a proper extension of the show,” Leigh Stark’s assessment on Pickr.com said, opining that “it’s a total missed opportunity to not employ Australian game developers”. Luke Reilly’s review for IGN.com said the game looked like the show but was “rife with annoying bugs, frustrating controls, and a bafflingly brief runtime of a little over an hour”.



“I cannot speak for what happened for [that] game,” Castet says, “but what I do know is that from the beginning both Ludo and BBC said that for Bluey ’s Happy Snaps we really want a high rating, a positive reception. “Some people care a bit less about the quality for kids’ games, and I think that’s wrong, I think that’s almost the opposite. I am a father of a six-year-old daughter, I want her to have the best game possible.” Brisbane locations seen in the show such as South Bank are fleshed out for in-game exploration. Gameloft/Ludo Studio/BBC Studio The new game’s premise is that Bluey and Bingo have found their dad’s old Polaroid camera and must use it to take snaps of objects hidden around the house, receiving a “sticker” for each successful find. Subsequent missions take them around Brisbane locations familiar from episodes of the show: New Farm Park, Mount Coot-tha Lookout, and South Bank, as well as the camp site (from the episode Camping), and Hammerbarn (aka Bunnings).



But the game isn’t simply a treasure hunt. Players can mess around with objects they find along the way: kicking and rolling balls, drawing with chalk, jumping on a trampoline and such, with popular supporting characters from the show popping up throughout. “It’s an open sandbox where we give them a tonne of toys to play with, exactly like in real life,” Castet says. Gameloft worked with QUT’s Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child to ensure the game fosters creativity, safety, identity and collaboration. Unusually for a video game, Bluey’s Happy Snaps has frequent touchpoints encouraging off-screen play, including a packet of cards in every box with ideas of “Things to Find” and “Family Fun”. “We really want you to turn the console off and go outside,” Fordham says.



Being based in Brisbane, Castet says, was “critical” to making a game that’s as much a love letter to the city as the show is. Game artists spent weeks visiting the locations – “to create them as faithfully as we can. You will see many things that you don’t see in the TV show, but that are here in real life in Brisbane.” Related Article Tourism and Events Queensland Bluey’s World pulls in half a million visitors Castet indicates a pink cockatoo in the New Farm Park setting. “You hear the bird? It’s the real bird that our audio team spent time recording in the Currumbin Sanctuary, which again could have been done only here.” So is the new game worth the $69-$85 price tag? My focus group of two played it for two solid hours before bedtime and only got through two levels. The ability to take photos of anything within the world of the game, and to play mini-games on the way towards achieving goals, kept them enthralled.



A reminder from Bingo between levels to go and take a “tactical wee” caused much hilarity. Castet wants the launch of Bluey’s Happy Snaps to spotlight the importance of the industry in Queensland. “Last year, if you take all the revenue generated by cinema box office, music, books, and combine all that together, multiply by four, you get the revenue of the video game industry. And this year it looks like it’s going to be times six. “It’s a really big industry, and it’s an industry where Australia is well positioned.” The game was launched at Queensland’s Parliament House on Thursday night, which Screen Queensland head of games Jed Dawson says “feels like a real milestone”.



Future Bluey games made in Brisbane are a distinct possibility, Dawson says. “I think the BBC were very impressed by the game studios that they came out here to do a recce on. So keep your eyes open, there might be more on the way.” Bluey’s Happy Snaps is released on all platforms on October 15. World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAntony Catalano Catalano back in court as expanded $67m Byron compound gets green light Christine Lacy October 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Millionaire businessman Antony Catalano has received planning approval to expand his family’s luxury Byron Bay compound as he prepares to return to court on Friday over allegations he violently assaulted his wife. The fallen media mogul plans to build a third expansive home in the exclusive Wategos Bay enclave, creating a sprawling estate worth more than $67 million. Stefanie and Antony Catalano. Instagram Whether he will be there to watch it come to fruition remains up in the air, as he faces Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on eight criminal charges, accused of threatening to kill and breaking the tailbone of Stefanie Catalano in a late-night incident at their luxury St Kilda penthouse in March. The couple, who share four children alongside Antony’s further five children from previous marriages, have reconciled since the incident, with Stefanie making two statements of no complaint to police, saying she does not support the case going ahead and does not want to provide evidence against her husband – although she could still be subpoenaed to do so.



As well as the “statements of no complaint” Stefanie has also lodged a police ethical standards complaint about her treatment in the months since her husband’s arrest, alleging authorities were seeking to “destroy” him. Related Article Exclusive

Antony Catalano Casa Catalano: Media mogul seeks approval for $67 million mega-compound in Byron Bay Police claim Catalano swung a clothes iron at his wife’s head, unlawfully imprisoned her in the apartment, threatened to stab her to death, and choked or strangled her. Stefanie was admitted to hospital with a fractured tailbone. CCTV footage showing common areas adjacent to the Catalano’s apartment is part of the police case against him, with Stefanie also providing a statement shortly after the incident. The $30 million penthouse apartment in the Saint Moritz building on the St Kilda foreshore is currently being rented to Hollywood actor Jamie Foxx, who is in Melbourne working on a film project. The apartment is rented at a peak short-term nightly rate of about $9,000.



Catalano has been on bail since March, when he entered a residential rehabilitation facility in Melbourne. At the time, he said he was “struggling with significant mental health and substance abuse issues”. He was stood aside from his role as executive chair of Australian Community Media, which he owns 50-50 with billionaire Alex Waislitz. Two of Catalano’s oldest sons, Jordan and Luca, took over as directors of their father’s myriad business interests. These include a large portfolio of property and businesses in Byron Bay, including luxury boutique hotel Raes on Wategos. The media proprietor has been quietly progressing plans for what has been a controversial development of the family compound in the exclusive precinct of the glamorous resort town. Plans for the original two-home family estate were first rejected by Byron Shire Council. After an 18-month battle, Catalano successfully appealed the decision to the NSW Land and Environment Court, which conditionally approved his plans in June.



In August, this masthead exclusively revealed that Catalano had submitted more plans to build a third home on an adjacent block, which is held in Stefanie’s name and would also form part of the family complex. Related Article Property development Antony Catalano expands Byron Bay hospitality empire with $17.35m deal The total cost of the development is in the order of $67 million based on land acquisition and stated building costs, but could be expected to run to a higher total spend as construction unfolds. The project would make it one of Byron’s most expensive residential estates. Council documentation reveals the third, recently approved, residence would cost an estimated $4.1 million to build and be three levels including basement storage, underground parking and an upper-level swimming pool. It would be similar in style and materials to the neighbouring larger, two-home development. Separate lawyers for both Stefanie and Antony Catalano were contacted for comment. World.title: ‘Which treaty?’: Liberal candidate drops ball on core policy and earns party rebuke
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD ‘Which treaty?’: Liberal candidate drops ball on core policy and earns party rebuke Fiona Byrne October 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria’s treaty has been the subject of years of passionate political debate, but one Liberal candidate appears to have completely missed the memo. Appearing at a candidates forum hosted by Yarra City Council on Wednesday evening, Charles Aponso, 19, who is running for the seat of Richmond in November’s state election, totally dropped the ball. Loading Asked by an audience member, “Why doesn’t the Liberal Party support treaty in Victoria?” Aponso replied, “So, the treaty, um, which treaty are you talking about?” Cue awkward silence. MC Mary Gearin and the woman who asked the original question filled in the gaps, explaining to Aponso what Victoria’s treaty – a legal agreement between Victoria and the First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria which came into effect in December 2025 – was. The Liberals have pledged to scrap the treaty within 100 days if elected.



Liberal candidate for Richmond, Charles Aponso. Details about treaty may not be the only thing Aponso, arguably an underprepared candidate, may have missed. He seems to have overlooked a memo from the Liberals’ state director, Alyson Hannam, that any debate or forum appearance by candidates must be approved by her. Aponso’s gaffe prompted a terse message sent via WhatsApp on Thursday from Hannam to all MPs and Liberal candidates which CBD has seen. “Team, I continue to get both members and candidates agreeing to debates without my approval,” the message read.



“The instruction that all debates must be approved by me has gone out each week for months. There is NO EXCUSE. “I attach this clip as an example of why we must know. Not being across your brief puts not only you, but the team at risk and risks others getting a question about your mistakes. “This candidate was not approved to do this, and we were not informed. This is unacceptable. Alyson.” We reached out to Hannam and Aponso to find out if they had caught up for a chat, but are yet to hear back from either. Richmond is held by Greens MP Gabrielle de Vietri, who won the seat off Labor in the 2022 election.



Family sporting twist ahead for Michelle Payne Michelle Payne has become an Australian sporting great thanks to her efforts in the saddle as the first female jockey to win the Melbourne Cup, but there is no guarantee her child will follow her into the racing game. Michelle Payne at the Women of the MCC Business Breakfast at the MCG on Thursday. Getty Images Payne, 40, who is expecting her first child, a boy, in early January, said her partner Gabriel Ribeiro’s sporting interests may well take precedence over the thoroughbreds. “Gabriel, my partner, is Brazilian. He loves surfing and motorbikes,” Payne said.



“I am sure he will have him out in the ocean before I have him on a horse. “It will be up to them [her son]. Whatever they want to do, I’ll be supportive.” Payne, who was the guest speaker at a Women of the MCC business breakfast at the MCG on Thursday, has seen the highs and lows of the racing game. She retired as a jockey in July 2024, but continues to train a small team of racehorses. “Some riders have a very trouble-free career and some have bad luck along the way, and unfortunately, for me, that [bad luck] started pretty young,” Payne said.



At 18, she suffered a fractured skull in a race fall from which she took seven months to recover, and during her career had another five or six serious falls – which involved several concussions. Related Article CBD The next big change coming for pregnant Michelle Payne “Probably the worst one [fall] was after I won the [2015] Melbourne Cup. I had a very simple fall at Mildura, and the horse stood on my stomach and tore off three-quarters of my pancreas,” she said. “It was unbelievable to go through that, but what was amazing was how incredible your body is. To recover from that and now to be able to carry a child without too much trouble is incredible.” Payne, who will be part of the Melbourne Cup Carnival TV broadcast next month, recalled her life changing the minute she won the Cup on Prince of Penzance.



“Somebody passed the phone to me at the press conference after the Cup and said, ‘Oh, it is the prime minister’. It was such a whirlwind, all I could think of was ‘who is the prime minister?’” It was Malcolm Turnbull on the line. You never know who is going to get your number! SPOTTED David Southwick was a man in a hurry on Thursday afternoon when CBD spotted him doing almost a semi jog in a suit through the Crown complex on the way to a meeting. Must have been an important meeting because he was moving with intent. While in this instance CBD was sitting down and finishing a phone call when the state’s deputy opposition leader hot-footed it past us, we are all too familiar with the “Crown dash”. It is a particular type of power-walk cum trot, usually from the West End car park to the Palladium. Always good to get your steps up.

World.title: Trump’s new press secretary: not quite attorney-at-law
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s new press secretary: not quite attorney-at-law Shawn McCreesh October 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: Is US President Donald Trump’s new press secretary a lawyer – or did she just play one on TV? Three days into her job, Katie Zacharia is facing questions about whether she has embroidered her credentials. She describes herself as a lawyer, and the president called her “an attorney”. When she was asked on Tuesday (Washington time) in which state she passed the bar exam, she twice replied: “When I moved to China.” Huh? Katie Zacharia standing behind Donald Trump as he spoke to reporters on Tuesday before boarding Marine One. Bloomberg The moment capped off a shaky debut for the woman who has accepted what is perhaps the most challenging public relations post in the United States. Now she was struggling to tell her own story.



On Wednesday evening, she told The New York Times that this whole mishegas over “lawyer”, “attorney” and “China” has been one big misunderstanding. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House ‘My president ... excuse me, my husband’: Trump’s new spinner gets off to a rocky start “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she said, taking a quick phone call on the tarmac in Arizona, where the president was holding a midterm rally. “That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she said. “And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.” It was only her second day on the job, she pointed out.



So here’s the truth about Katie Zacharia, not quite attorney-at-law: she graduated with a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. By some interpretations, that technically makes her a lawyer, though many legal experts said it would not. But is she an attorney, someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice? For that, she would have needed to pass the bar. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that she sat for the California bar exam after graduating law school, but didn’t pass. The Times was unable to find a law licence for her in California, or anywhere else she has lived in the US. During the brief phone call on Wednesday, the Times did not get a chance to press her again about whether she had ever passed a bar exam. But before she had to go, she did explain that when she first began appearing on cable news, she consulted with Pepperdine’s president as to how she should identify herself. She said she was warned not to use the words “attorney” or “esquire”, but that “lawyer” was OK. Loading But what about “general counsel”, would that be OK? Because, on LinkedIn, Zacharia identified herself as such for Fix California, a group led by Trump loyalist Richard Grenell. “You can’t be a general counsel to a company in the United States unless you’re admitted to the bar to practise law,” said Erwin Chemerinsky, dean of the law school at the University of California, Berkeley. “A general counsel implies that you’re practising law, giving legal advice to the company. You can’t practise law without a licence.”



On Wednesday, a watchdog group filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association, calling for an investigation into whether Zacharia “repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime”. And that brings us to China. “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’ ” Katie Zacharia The White House explained this week that Zacharia moved to China with her husband, Tyler, who had a job at a US private equity firm. While there, she worked on “international transaction law”, Zacharia has claimed. On her LinkedIn profile, she listed nearly two years of employment at Zhong Lun Law Firm, which is one of China’s biggest law firms, with headquarters in Beijing and offices in Tokyo, New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Almaty, Kazakhstan.



The law firm did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Related Article Trump's White House Trump picks Fox News expert for next White House press secretary Opportunities for foreign lawyers in China are extremely narrow. Foreign nationals cannot sit for China’s bar exam, hold a Chinese lawyer’s licence or advise on Chinese law. They can, however, be hired by Chinese law firms to work on cross-border deals and to advise on foreign or international law. Gary Gao, a partner at Zhong Lun who is based in Shanghai, said the firm often hired foreigners for language assistance and to help Chinese staff understand foreign business culture. “They are not practising Chinese law at any time,” he said, adding that Zacharia’s role at the firm would have likely been similar to a paid internship.



Sida Liu, a law professor at the University of Hong Kong who specialises in mainland law, said it was misleading for Zacharia to describe herself as a former associate at Zhong Lun, because it implied that she was a licensed lawyer in China. “Chinese law firms can hire foreign nationals to work in their mainland offices, but such individuals are not classified as PRC lawyers because PRC lawyer qualification requires PRC citizenship,” Liu said, referring to the People’s Republic of China. “The title ‘associate’ may therefore be somewhat controversial.” So what are we to make of all this? It was Trump who called Zacharia an “attorney”, and she certainly never corrected the record. She called herself “general counsel”, which was misleading at best. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Three hospitalised after chemical exposure in Christchurch
World.content:
A commercial building in Christchurch has been made safe after a chemical spill left three people in hospital.

Emergency services were called to a building in Coleridge Street in the suburb of Sydenham about 3.50pm on Thursday.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said seven crews attended and firefighters had to rescue two people from the building.

St John said one person was in a critical condition and two others were in moderate conditions.

FENZ assistant district commander Michael Balmer said crews found a person unconscious.

"On arrival they discovered there were chemicals involved, they made a very snap rescue. The crews did a great job in getting the patient out of the danger area and into fresh air," he said.

"It was a liquid product but it gave off vapours, I believe, that affected the individual and they collapsed inside the building."

Three people were taken to hospital after being exposed to the chemicals. Nathan Mckinnon

The affected business recycles paints, cleaning and waste products, and other solvents.

"We were able to isolate the systems involved so that it wouldn't escalate any further, once the chemicals were isolated power was isolated to that section of the factory," Balmer said.

"We were able to determine that the product wasn't a huge amount but it was safe enough to then hand back to the property representative."

Balmer said the firefighters responded to a difficult situation well.

"You turn up to incidents like that, chemical incidents, and you're going into the unknown really so it's quite a high risk environment. I was very proud of the way the crews responded to that."

World.title: 'Four-headed beast': ACT leader David Seymour hints at potential for coalition with Opportunity
World.content:
ACT leader David Seymour says he could be open to a "four-headed beast" coalition with Opportunity to stop a left-wing coalition taking power.

Speaking to a crowd of supporters in Wānaka, he admitted that if Opportunity crossed the 5 percent threshold, a coalition with them to keep the Greens and Te Pāti Māori from running the country "would be a good outcome".

However, Seymour said he felt Opportunity may not be the kingmaker, "despite the best efforts of the media".

National has ruled out working with the Opportunity on multiple occasions.

Leader Christopher Luxon initially stated he would not do business with a party that wants to raise taxes at the end of July.

Following the TVNZ leaders' debate last week, Luxon reiterated he would not work with Opportunity.

"I have been crystal clear with who we could or couldn't work with. I've laid that out from the very beginning of the year. I've been clear about Opportunity," he said at the time.

Last week, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong dismissed the comments.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong is continuing to keep the door open to coalition negotiations with National. RNZ / Blessen Tom

"I don't believe him. Because he would rather be in government than in opposition, I assume," she said at the time.

"There are many things we could work with National on, I think the five bottom lines are realistic for them to commit to."

At the end of September, Opportunity set out its five minimum requirements a potential coalition partner would have to agree to.

The party's bottom lines are giving the Commerce Commission more teeth, regulating lobbying and capping political donations to "clean up politics", developing a 10-year plan to "fix the health system" alongside health professionals, phasing out bottom trawling, and recommitting to Paris Agreement emissions reduction obligations and protecting the Climate Change Commission's independence.

Multiple polls have shown Opportunity poised to decide who will lead the next government.

The latest 1News Verian Poll, released earlier this week, showed Opportunity winning a potential 10 seats in the election.

If that poll's results were replicated at the election, National would get 34 MPs and New Zealand First and ACT would each get 12 - a coalition bloc of 58.

On the left, Labour would get 34 MPs, the Greens 18, Te Pāti Māori four - depending on how the Māori seats were calculated - and Te Tai Tokerau Party one seat - for a total of 57.

World.title: The Helicopter Line ordered to pay $17,740 over the unjustified dismissal of Mount Cook cafe employee
World.content:
Just two weeks after being ordered to forfeit two of its $1 million helicopters to the Crown for illegal crayfish gathering, The Helicopter Line has found itself in turbulence again.

The Queenstown company has now been rapped by the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) over its unjustified dismissal of former cafe employee Jonathan Lovatt following the closure of its Delta Tasman Cafe near Mount Cook in 2024.

In an ERA decision, authority member Antoinette Baker said The Helicopter Line (THL) "fell well short" of treating Lovatt fairly, and found the company effectively blamed him for the cafe's closure after he allegedly refused to train new staff and take on other duties.

"It ended his employment suddenly for reasons of fault without any evidence of a process addressing those things beforehand."

Lovatt worked as a cafe assistant for THL for eight months in 2024.

His employment was ended in a December 2, 2024, letter from THL director Mark Quickfall.

The letter stated that during Quickfall's previous visit to Mount Cook, he and Lovatt had discussed changing the cafe business model to ensure it could continue operating.

They agreed to wind back the menu and serve coffee, cabinet food and other self-serve items. The model required the support of all managers and staff.

But Quickfall wrote that the acting cafe manager had since told him Lovatt was unwilling to help order food, support the cafe while replacement staff were recruited after two employees left, or train new staff.

"Unfortunately, the situation at the cafe is out of our control and despite extensive advertising it will take time to find and induct staff. We will close the cafe from 5 December," the letter read.

"As per your contract we will pay you two weeks' notice from today. We will also require you to vacate the staff accommodation. We are unable to meet your requirements and are now forced to close the cafe."

The cafe has since reopened.

Quickfall told the authority that Lovatt had been made redundant and said THL had consulted with him through a series of meetings and discussions before the decision was made.

However, Baker rejected THL's claim that Lovatt's dismissal was a genuine redundancy.

She said Quickfall had communicated in the letter that the cafe had to close because Lovatt would not perform certain tasks while the business recruited more staff or help train the new employees.

Quickfall also confirmed in evidence that Lovatt's employment was terminated because he had refused to operate the cafe under the proposed self-service cabinet model and instead wanted to continue serving a menu with food cooked to order.

"Again, this supports that THL was effectively blaming Mr Lovatt for the closure of the cafe rather than perhaps addressing in a more transparent way its concerns that he was not allegedly prepared to change and behaved in a manner now claimed to be problematic about this," Baker said.

There was no evidence there had ever been a "sensible discussion" about those issues between the parties or that a fair process had been followed, she said.

The authority heard Lovatt had told his then acting manager three days before receiving the termination letter that he was "burnt out" and needed to take a sick day, which Baker said was a catalyst for his dismissal.

Baker found that, because the dismissal was not a genuine redundancy, THL was not justified in ending Lovatt's employment. The company was ordered to pay him $17,740, comprising $16,000 compensation and $1740 in lost wages.

In a written statement, a spokesperson for THL said it had operated at Aoraki Mount Cook for 40 years and valued the people who had worked with the company.

"We take our obligations as an employer seriously and are carefully considering the determination and our options. As this involves employment and privacy matters, we are unable to comment further."

The decision comes just two weeks after THL was fined $12,000 and ordered to forfeit two Airbus AS350 helicopters after it was sentenced in the Queenstown District Court for its part in an illegal crayfish gathering operation in 2022.

THL provided flights as part of its collaborative heli-crayfish experience with The Rees Hotel.

A crayfish diver would fly with tourists to a remote South Island location and gather crayfish, which were then given to The Rees Hotel for its dining service.

Under the Fisheries Act 1996, any seafood used as part of a commercial business must be sourced under a valid commercial permit, which neither party had.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: NZ apple sector helps Indian growers to expand orchards under FTA commitment
World.content:
New Zealand's apple industry is sharing the secrets of its productive pipfruit success with growers in India, but assures the efforts will not hurt competition exporting there.

Sector leaders and diplomats have returned from a week in India, where they met with state officials and apple growers in key growing region Himachal Pradesh, known as the apple bowl of India in the western Himalayas.

Here, New Zealand was setting up a centre of excellence, as part of a co-operation commitment under the new free trade agreement (FTA) with India coming into effect on Tuesday next week.

Audio player for " Midday rural news for 15 October 2026 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/country/1925779%2Fnz-apple-sector-helps-indian-growers-to-expand-orchards-under-fta-commitment

Midday rural news for 15 October 2026 Rural News Download MP3 3m

In addition to bolstering online data and resources, the centre will feature an apple orchard with different apple varieties, a research centre and foster collaboration with New Zealand experts to expand India's domestic production.

The project built on earlier efforts of sending scientists from Plant and Food Research (now under the Bioeconomy Science Institute) to the region again to help growers improve production.

New centres will be established in India for kiwifruit development too.

What's your experience? Let us know by emailing monique.steele@rnz.co.nz

Danielle Adsett, chief executive of industry group New Zealand Apples and Pears, was accompanied by the country's special agricultural trade envoy Nathan Guy on the trip in late September, early October.

New Zealand apple exports will face smaller import tariffs and new quota concessions under the NZ-India FTA coming into effect soon. www.alphapix.co.nz

Adsett said the project was a result of new FTA provisions.

"India should absolutely benefit. For New Zealand, we have been provided with tariff concessions and a quota.

"So that's what we managed to get on the table, and the co-operation plan is what we offered up to get that result."

Adsett said India deeply trusted New Zealand and its expertise, and there was good opportunity to help Indian farmers increase productivity on their orchards.

AFP

She said Indian apples sat in a different market segment to more premium New Zealand apples, that would also be counter-seasonal.

"India relies on imported apples and they've got 1.4 billion people to feed," she said. "And India fundamentally cannot produce enough apples for the demand that they have.

"There are hundreds of thousands of growers in India farming on very, very difficult terrain with very difficult access and fundamentally growing a different variety mix to what we can offer the Indian consumer.

"So I do not see a world of which New Zealand apples would compete directly with Indian apples."

But she said it would not be without its challenges, including access to nursery stock and cold chain issues.

"Very, very old orchards. Very, very big trees that are not producing much at all. So there's a real opportunity to help that shift, but the opportunity obviously will have a lot of challenges alongside."

A bite into the apple

India was New Zealand's fourth largest export market for apples and pears in the year to June, worth around $100 million, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

https://www.mfat.govt.nz/en/trade/free-trade-agreements/free-trade-agreements-concluded-but-not-in-force/new-zealand-india-free-trade-agreement/key-facts-on-new-zealand-india-trade

A recent Ministry for Primary Industries report showed apple exports reached more than 38,564 tonnes in the year to December, according to its Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries report.

But Adsett said they would be close to 50,000 tonnes this year, mostly Royal Gala, which faced the current 50 percent import tariff on top of the sales price.

"So a very, very difficult market to make any margin on. In fact, most of our product struggles to be competitive in that market, due to the nature of the other markets that they import from."

Himachal Pradesh in northern India in the western Himalayas. Susan Murray

The FTA will see new quotas for apples from year one during India's off-season, in the window of April to the end of August.

The first 32,500 tonnes will be subject to 25 percent tariffs, and the current 50 percent tariff would apply for volumes in excess of that.

Adsett said apple exporters would likely exceed that volume next season.

India's import quota concessions would reduce for Aotearoa over the next six years, expanding to 45,000 tonnes at the remaining 25 percent tariff.

Tariffs on pears into India will drop to 16.5 percent over the next decade, with no quota limit.

For kiwifruit, New Zealand exporters would face duty-free access for 6,250 tonnes each year, widening to up to 15,000 tonnes by year six. Out-of-tariff quotas will halve to 16.5 percent.

The FTA will come into effect on 20 October, Tuesday next week.
