World.title: Employment Court rules five Calendar Girls dancers were employees, not contractors
World.content:
Five former dancers who worked at a Wellington strip club have won their case, after arguing they were treated as employees despite being employed as contractors.

The former dancers told the Employment Court that because the club considered them to be contractors, they missed out on entitlements such as annual and sick leave, had to pay their own taxes and were not able to work for other clubs or agencies.

During the hearing in June, one of the dancers described the lack of autonomy the workers had over the services being sold.

She said there was an illusion staff could refuse clients, but if they did, there were consequences.

She said she had to perform a lap dance with a client she was not comfortable with and was reprimanded when she refused to remove her g-string.

Another described having to dance on the main stage and rely on tips for payment. The worker said dancers were not allowed to refuse to strip nude and several said the club had set hours that they expected dancers to be there, regardless of whether paying clients were present.

The workers said in practice, they were treated as employees and Judge MS King agreed.

"When the plaintiffs commenced work with Calendar Girls, there was a clear common intention to do so as independent contractors. However, the evidence demonstrates an inequality of bargaining power between the parties, which points away from the plaintiffs being in business on their own account and requires consideration of how the relationship operated in practice."

World.title: The busy little berm garden helping feed a community
World.content:
Page told Checkpoint the garden was a way to give back to the community and use an otherwise wasted space.



"[I was] thinking, it's dead space. I have to get out there with a lawnmower, I don't have to do that now.



"A lot of people have been curious and stop and chat about it... they help themselves, sometimes they even bring a number of seedlings for me to plant and keep going, so it's really sweet.



"Probably three or four days a week we'll see people there.



"Everyone now is talking, and [have] been for some years, about the increasing price of vegetables and the fact that they're actually probably better for you if you've got them fresh."



While the garden takes time and attention, Page finds it quite therapeutic.



"[It's that] feeling at the end of it that you've helped create something to help other people."



Page said his parents and grandparents were keen gardeners.



"I've always been brought up doing a bit of gardening, I would certainly not view myself as a professional gardener, I just do it because I like it."



Brocolli and rhubarb were currentyl flourishing in the garden, with lettuce due to go in soon.



"There's a lemon tree that's going to have tonnes shortly, the blossom has gone bonkers."



He also puts out boxes of passionfruit, figs and feijoas from his own garden, which he said he simply can't get through.



While Page didn't initially ask council for permission to plant on the berm, he said after making sure he was complying with rules, the garden has been welcomed with open arms.

World.title: A-League star in fiery exchange with reporter over suspension loophole
World.content:
Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has blown up over questions about using a "loophole" to serve out a suspension before the A-League Men season.

Cosgrove was handed a two-game ban after being sent off in the closing stages of Auckland's 1-0 FIFA Intercontinental Cup loss to Saudi side Al-Ahli in August.

Auckland are allowed to play A-League professionals in their reserves side under New Zealand Football's participation agreement and competition regulations.

That includes up to two 23-year-old non-citizens for each match-day squad.

The clause opened the door for the 29-year-old Englishman to serve out his ban in Auckland's recent New Zealand National League fixtures against Wellington Olympic and Miramar Rangers.

In a fiery exchange on Thursday, Cosgrove could not recall the two matches and was bemused when asked if he had any unease or embarrassment over using the "loophole".

Loading Instagram content

"Embarrassment?" he shot back at a reporter.

"Why would the club not push to have a player available and use every power that they have?"

Cosgrove bagged 11 goals in his debut season with Auckland, securing the men's competition golden boot along the way to the club's first championship.

"It doesn't matter, does it? I have technically [served my ban]. I've missed two NPL matches," Cosgrove said.

"If you pick up a suspension in the A-League, you have to serve it in the A-League.

"So technically, in that case, I should be missing the next few Intercontinental Cups, but I'm not."

Auckland FC are the reigning A-League Men champions. (Getty Images: New Zealand Herald/Alyse Wright)

The media conference ended abruptly before the reporter repeated his claim that Cosgrove had not actually served the ban.

"What are you doing here then? Bugger off, if you're going to talk shit," the striker replied.

An Auckland FC minder stated that FIFA, Football Australia and Football New Zealand were "fine" with the way the ban was served.

"You know what football's like in this country, mate? We f***ing work hard to get it good. You bring it down with shit like that," Cosgrove said, prompting a chuckle from the reporter.

"What are you laughing for? We'll just f*** you off. You won't get back here again."

In a podcast episode posted on Tuesday, Cosgrove said he was relieved when news of the rule's workaround became public so he could "finally stop lying about it".

"It was a poor challenge in oppressive heat and late in the game, but the two-game suspension was a little bit harsh," he told The Unused Subs podcast.

"We were trying to get that reduced, and the power of lawyers and legal teams these days, they managed to find a way to sign me up with the Auckland reserves."

The defending champions will begin their A-League campaign at home to Melbourne City on Saturday, before an away trip to face Western Sydney Wanderers on October 24.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Live: Moses and Ponga injured, Walsh vomits as Australia win all-time classic
World.content:
Australia has won a classic World Cup clash against New Zealand, with debutant Jack Bostock scoring a match-winning hat-trick.

Bostock's third and final try won the match for the Kangaroos, who were second-best for so much of Thursday night's World Cup opener.

Both the Kangaroos and Kiwis have injury worries, with Mitchell Moses limping off and Kalyn Ponga having his arm in a sling.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: Wallabies show faith in rookie fly half for final All Blacks Test
World.content:
Declan Meredith will start at fly half against the All Blacks for just the fourth time in his young Test career, as the Wallabies make changes for Saturday's final Bledisloe Cup clash at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Meredith, who made his Test debut against France in July, replaces Ben Donaldson in the number 10 jersey.

Donaldson was ruled out with a minor upper leg injury in the wake of the 50-19 thrashing dished out by the All Blacks at Auckland's Eden Park last Saturday night.

Back-up fly half Harry McLaughlin-Phillips will make his Test debut if he comes on as a reserve in Sydney.

He is joined on the bench by reserve scrum half Kalani Thomas, who is yet to play a Bledisloe Cup Test.

Wallabies thrashed by All Blacks The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

It will be a tough initiation for Meredith, although he will be playing outside Brumbies teammate and scrum half, Ryan Lonergan.

The 27-year-old got his first taste of playing the All Blacks after coming on as a reserve at Eden Park last weekend.

Meanwhile, the Wallabies have moved Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back to the centres.

He started on the wing in the Wallabies' past two Tests, but the absence of Len Ikitau (concussion) forced Wallabies coach Les Kiss to shift the ex-NRL star back to the midfield.

He will partner Isaac Henry, who switches from outside to inside centre, while Harry Potter will start on the wing.

Ikitau is a massive loss for the Wallabies, who are also missing Hunter Paisami (suspension) from their midfield options.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted back to the centres for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Elsewhere in the Wallabies' match-day squad, former All Black Aidan Ross will start at loosehead prop, alongside hooker Josh Nasser.

Ross replaces Angus Bell, while Brandon Paenga-Amosa (rested) made way for Nasser.

Hooker Billy Pollard, lock Josh Canham, openside flanker Carlo Tizzano and utility back Filipo Daugunu have returned to the Wallabies' squad as reserves.

Wallaroos lose star for historic 'quadruple header' The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

"We got a clear picture last weekend of where we need to be better," Kiss said in a Rugby Australia statement.

"We've said all along we'll continue to work hard and grow our game, and the squad has been impressive in the way they have prepared this week."

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, who retained his place alongside Jeremy Williams in the second row, will appear in his 50th Test.

The Bledisloe Cup Test will cap off a historic "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos play Scotland earlier in the day, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams meet New Zealand and Fiji respectively.

It is the first time all four national teams have featured on the same match-day schedule.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Aidan Ross, Josh Nasser, Allan Alaalatoa, Jeremy Williams, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Declan Meredith, Harry Potter, Isaac Henry, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright

Reserves: Billy Pollard, Angus Bell, Massimo De Lutiis, Josh Canham, Carlo Tizzano, Kalani Thomas, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Filipo Daugunu

World.title: Wallaroos lose star but regain experience for historic 'quadruple header'
World.content:
The Wallaroos have been forced to leave out star fullback Caitlyn Halse for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Halse is unavailable for the WXV Global Series Test due to concussion symptoms.

The 20-year-old's withdrawal is a blow but the Wallaroos have regained experienced winger Maya Stewart, who returns to the starting XV.

Stewart, a 27-Test veteran with the Wallaroos, was named after recovering from an Achilles tendon injury.

Her inclusion sees Desiree Miller move from the wing to fullback in place of Halse.

Wallaroos 'got some work to do' Ending a run of six straight defeats was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

In the forward pack, captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona and Pia Tapsell swap positions in the back row, starting at blindside flanker and number eight respectively.

Eva Karpani and Cecilia Smith have returned to the match-day squad on the reserves bench, which also features fresh faces Allana Sikimeti and Piper Simons.

"We have maintained considerable selection consistency throughout the WXV, strategically strengthening our cohesion and combinations," Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, said in a statement.

"During the WXV we have layered specific areas of our game to build stronger performances each Test.

"We have selected a balanced 23 armed with leadership, power, strength and speed."

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona will play at blindside flanker against Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland.

In their most recent Test, the Wallaroos triumphed 30–10 in Edinburgh late last month.

The two sides meet in Sydney and Canberra (October 23) to conclude their WXV Global Series campaigns.

Saturday's match is part of a rugby "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallabies meet the All Blacks in the final Bledisloe Cup Test, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams are also appearing.

The world champion Australian women's team plays arch rivals New Zealand, while the men's squad faces two-time Olympic champions Fiji.

It is the first time all four national rugby teams will be playing on the same match-day schedule.

Wallaroos squad (1-15): Brianna Hoy, Brittany Merlo, Faliki Pohiva, Kaitlan Leaney, Michaela Leonard, Siokapesi Palu Sekona (c), Piper Duck, Pia Tapsell, Samantha Wood, Waiaria Ellis, Amelia Whitaker, Faitala Moleka, Georgina Friedrichs, Maya Stewart, Desiree Miller

Reserves: Tania Naden, Allana Sikimeti, Eva Karpani, Jemma Bemrose, Emily Chancellor, Lily Bone, Piper Simons, Cecilia Smith

World.title: Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
World.content:
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.

Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.

The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.

Australia's 2017 World Cup win was the last game before the women's game changed forever. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.

Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.

These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.

The women's World Cup will again be held alongside the men's tournament. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.

Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.

In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.

Unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign Jessica Skinner once doubted her coaching style was elite. Now she believes it's exactly what the top level needs, and her journey from rural NSW has shaped why.

The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.

They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.

State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.

The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.

Tamika Upton has won three of the last four Dally M medals. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

They are, without question, the best women's rugby league team ever, and they are so much better than everyone else that anything less than a dominant run to the final and a thumping victory at Lang Park will feel like a departure from a predestined fate.

Other teams have improved. New Zealand, which handed Australia its sole loss in recent years in 2023 and went down by just six points in one game last year, has risen highest with the tide.

As the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, they could rise higher still, and their squad for this year's tournament should put them in contention for the final.

Samoa is another side that has improved and could still get better. The Fetu have benefited from the injection of diaspora players like Taliah Fuimaono, Evania Isa'ako and Amber Hall, plus fresh faces like Queensland Origin flyer Destiny Mino-Sinapati and reigning NRLW rookie of the year Mercedez Taulelei-Siala.

Samoa will be making its World Cup debut. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

They are a vision of what is possible for the expansion of women's rugby league and beneficiaries of the improved pathways leading to the NRLW.

It will take time, because we are talking about change that can take a decade or more to become apparent, but the benefits are there for all to see in the men's game.

The women's game is on the same path; they're just not as far along. This is a brave, dangerous side with a real future, one which is easy to see unfolding before us.

One day a team like Samoa might be able to give the World Cup a real shake. But not these days.

The Samoans are currently 53.5-point underdogs against the Jillaroos in tomorrow night's match. They lost to them 60-0 in the corresponding clash last year.

Even that was nothing compared to the 90-4 belting England copped in Las Vegas last year, an eye-popping result that showed just how lopsided things had become.

England was humiliated in its last meeting with Australia. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

The English will get a chance at revenge in Perth next week, and they're a much better side than the one that travelled to Nevada.

Roosters backrower Jasmin Strange is a welcome addition, and they have a core of NRLW players, including North Queensland's Fran Goldthorp, Canberra forward Hollie-Mae Dodd and clever Newcastle playmaker Georgia Roche.

If they can keep things respectable against the Jillaroos, that will be progress.

That gap can close as more top-level talent filters through the ranks, for England and everybody else.

But it will take time to run the Jillaroos down. And because the women's game is semi-professional, it's unlikely to happen as rapidly as it has in the men's game, meaning progress could take a decade or more.

New Zealand shape up as the only side with a realistic chance of taking down Australia. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Until then, there is no choice but to keep going.

Every nation will have a moment. Some will have more than one because there will be glories outside of absolute victory. Fiji will make its World Cup debut and Papua New Guinea will look to continue its steady progress of recent years.

A semi-final berth would be a major achievement for Samoa and a place in the final would be a shot in the arm for the game in England, so their group-stage clash is the pick of the early tournament matches.

The Kiwi Ferns will fancy their chances of an ambush should they meet Australia in the final, given the Jillaroos will have had a soft run in. They will point out that they are the one in 15-1, and perhaps they will be right.

But at the end lurks Australia, the monster at the end of the dream that turns it into a nightmare. And, just under a decade since the rest of history began, the truth of the pain it is about to inflict is simple.

This is the best collection of players ever assembled in women's rugby league, and if they are at any point over the next month beaten, it will be one of the biggest upsets the game has known.

World.title: The data that shows who won and lost in this year's AFL trade period
World.content:
If footballing dreams are lived out in September, they are first shaped in October and November.

If you nail an off-season it can set you up for years to come. If you stumble it can hurt for even longer.

The 2026 off-season class was one of rare quality. Instead of list-cloggers and fringe players that sometimes monopolise trade chatter, this year's crop is full of proven stars.

Lachie Neale, Scott Pendlebury, Jesse Hogan, Toby Greene, Zak Butters, Rowan Marshall and Ben King all found new clubs, among a host of others. It would be hard to find a trade period with a better combined resume than the one we've just seen.

The 2026 trade period has seen 23 trades and seven free-agency moves take place, with 30 players finding new clubs for season 2027. The dealing isn't done yet, with more picks set to change hands before and during the draft.

While much of football — and football commentary — is about instant gratification, the trade period is often a slower burn. Most AFL grand finals are blowouts well before the final siren, and most trade periods have deals that hang in the balance until the final minutes.

This year the opposite was the case. Little suspense was left by the time the last day rolled around, while the ending to that grand final was one that will be remembered for years to come.

While winners or losers of the off-season often take years to fully work out, the direction each team is taking is usually much clearer after the final trade is called.

Dogs taking a big bite

Each trade period it seems like at least one side pushes firmly towards the present over the future. Last year the Saints were the most aggressive side, bringing in a host of players to hopefully kickstart their resurgence up the ladder.

This year it was the Bulldogs that were the busiest club in the league.

All up the Dogs brought in four new players, the most of any club this off-season. The centrepiece of the four was the move for free agent Zak Butters, but the acquisition of Jordon Butts should be equally important for an often under-siege defensive unit.

There are some slight queries about how Butters will fit alongside Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, but with the Dogs captain turning 32 next year this potentially sets the midfield group up for contention over the next half decade. The Bulldogs' best over the past three seasons has rivalled practically any other side. The time is now for them to take the next step.

But the Dogs may not be the biggest winners of the trade period for next season in isolation. Geelong's acquisition of proven talent in Toby Greene, Jordan Ridley and Rowan Marshall looks like providing the most upside next year, while Hawthorn will also be quietly confident in Zach Merrett and Ben King.

At the other end of the "win now" scale, the preliminary finalist Swans will be forced to retool without Nick Blakey and Joel Amartey, and GWS have made the call to get younger with the loss of Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Kieren Briggs and Lachie Whitfield.

Blakey's big deal

Whispers about a Nick Blakey move became increasingly loud as the off-season progressed. The chatter about his discontent in Sydney didn't abate, and quickly the defender became the focal point of an otherwise quiet second week of the period.

There's a couple of good reasons for that too. It's uncommon that a 26-year-old who is arguably the best player in a valuable role becomes available on the trade market.

In all, no club this century has traded more pick value for a single player than North has just traded for Blakey. The trade takes them out of multiple drafts. If North Melbourne was to win the 2028 premiership, the value of the picks traded would still outweigh what Adelaide traded for Wayne Carey way back in 2002.

Beyond the stated cost above, it also has deprived them of another top draft pick — the likely early 20s they would have received in compensation for Essendon's upcoming bid on Dougie Cochrane.

North Melbourne had hoped to pair Blakey with Adelaide's Nick Murray to bolster its defence, but that fell through at the deadline. It could be a bigger loss than it appears. North's defensive stocks are some of the weakest in the league, and its ability to transition the strongest part of their back half game.

Future failing

As predicted here before the trade period began, most clubs were cautious of the value of next year's draft.

One of the clearest examples was offered by Melbourne early in the trade period in its public negotiations for newly minted Demon Zane Duursma.

"We offered (pick) 47, we also offered a 2027 future two, or 2028 future two," Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb told the media.

That pick 47 is notionally a third-round selection, indicating that the drop in value increases to about a round for the next two drafts, which are compromised by the new Tasmania team being handed high picks.

This was even clearer in the trade that took place between Richmond and Port Adelaide, with the Tigers sending pick 22 this year alongside their round one, two and three picks next year for Port Adelaide's fifth pick.

This reflected the general trend of how picks traded hands. Only clubs who have clear father-son or academy talents seemed to be on the hunt for picks next year, with other clubs pushing for lower selections this year or selections in 2028 instead.

Port Adelaide was the keenest to get 2027 draft picks through the door. That's no shock, given it has up to four tied talents. In fact, every club bar possibly Sydney to invest in next year's draft have prospective father-son or academy talents likely to be selected in the upper reaches of the draft.

Most other clubs were somewhat keen to escape the oncoming chaos, or try to move picks into the (slightly) less compromised 2028 draft. The compromised drafts might also be playing into another trend that has emerged recently.

The past two trade periods have seen a re-evaluation of how clubs see the value of players against picks. Instead of the promise of youngsters, the increasingly uncertain availability of young talent has turned the attention of clubs to proven talent instead.

World.title: Aussie cyclists begin World Championships with silver medal
World.content:
Australia has claimed a silver medal in the men's team sprint on the opening night of the UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai.

The Australian trio of Leigh Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Danny Barber finished runner-up to the Netherlands in the final.

It was Australia's fifth consecutive World Championships medal in the event.

"For the final, we made a minor change in strategy," Hoffman said.

Richardson withdrawn from world champ squad British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai.

"We just tried to have a little gamble, and it almost paid off.

"We were up to the 500-metre mark, so we definitely gave the Dutch a run for their money.

"It's definitely bittersweet to miss out on the [winner's] rainbow bands, but considering last year was a bronze and this year we have silver, I think this team is on the way up."

Australia won a first-round duel against a British team missing Matt Richardson.

He was withdrawn from the British squad earlier in the week over alleged misconduct.

Richardson won three Olympic medals for Australia before switching allegiance to Great Britain after the 2024 Paris Games.

In other results in Shanghai, Australia's Kristina Clonan, Molly McGill and Alessia McCaig finished seventh in the women's team sprint.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Top gymnastics coach fined after assaulting two female teen athletes
World.content:
A gymnastics coach with more than 30 years' experience has avoided conviction and instead been ordered to pay a fine after assaulting two teenage female athletes.

Over the length of his career, Jamie Glen Cannon, 49, has trained athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, in Cairns, and at Brisbane Grammar School.

Mr Cannon was sentenced in Maroochydore District Court last week, after pleading guilty to four charges of common assault against the two teen gymnasts, each aged between 13 and 16.

Jamie Cannon has coached athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, Cairns and at Brisbane Grammar School over his 30-year career. (ABC News: Alex Papp)

Coach touched athletes

Crown prosecutor Alex Stark described Cannon's behaviour as "a breach of trust, both professional and personal" and tendered an agreed statement of facts about the offending.

The court heard Cannon was a senior coach at a Sunshine Coast club when the incidents occurred in 2022 and 2023.

The two girls were under his supervision as athletes.

One of the assault charges related to Cannon smacking the bottom of a 13-year-old as she performed handstands with other gymnasts at the club.

One athlete's victim impact statement said the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely". (Pexels: Ivan Samkov / CC licence)

Three more offences occurred at the same club, involving Cannon touching and rubbing the inner thigh of a second athlete, aged 15 at the time.

The court heard that in one interaction, Cannon asked the teenager if she wore make-up, told her she was pretty, then put his hand on her inner thigh.

In another, he asked if he could touch the teenager's leggings, and before she could respond, he put his hand on her knee.

The fourth charge involved Cannon approaching the 15-year-old as she prepared to coach a class, standing in between her legs before placing his hands on her knees and rubbing her thighs as she attempted to move away.

The court heard it was accepted that Cannon's behaviour had "no sexual intent".

Gymnast left the sport she loved

The 15-year-old athlete's victim impact statement was read to the court at his sentencing by Mr Stark.

The teenager wrote that the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely".

She described problems falling asleep and how it damaged "many friendships", particularly at the gymnastics club.

"[It] affected the development of a romantic relationship with partners due to fear and sensitivity to certain actions and situations," Mr Stark read to the court.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this story, please contact Owen Jacques at jacques.owen@abc.net.au.

Mr Stark said there was a "vulnerability" in the situation because the teenagers were under his supervision.

He said both teenagers had been clear about their boundaries to Cannon, including the request not to be touched.

"It was really that sense of breach of trust that was at the heart of the impact for both of them," he said.

Cannon declined to be interviewed by police.

The court heard he has not been involved with the sport since being charged.

Decades as a top coach

Cannon's lawyer Ambyr Cousen described how her client had been involved with the sport for 30 years both as an employee and as a volunteer, including as a committee member with Gymnastics Queensland (GQ).

"He has won a number of awards for peer service within that industry," Ms Cousen told the court.

Cannon was working with Brisbane Grammar School as a senior coach in 2019 when he received GQ's Individual Service Award for his service to gymnastics in Queensland.

He also spent more than a decade leading GQ's Men's Artistic Gymnastics Sport Committee.

Ms Cousen also supplied the court with several character references for her client.

Court accepts 'no sexual intent'

Cannon provided a written apology to the court for his actions, and offered to pay $1,000 to each of the victims as compensation.

Jamie Cannon was sentenced on four counts of common assault in the Maroochydore District Court last week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In sentencing, Judge Amanda McDonnell told Cannon he treated "these young, vulnerable girls in a way that they didn't wish to be touched".

"I have no doubt that they looked up to you for guidance," Judge McDonnell said.

" I accept that there was no sexual intent, but that you acted in an overly-familiar way. "

Cannon was ordered to pay a single fine of $2,500 for the four offences, plus the promised compensation.

No conviction was recorded.

Tech.title: McKinsey is making job applicants spar with a fake AI client
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Consulting firm McKinsey & Company is going to ask some entry-level candidates to have a 10-minute conversation with an AI simulation of a client as part of the interview process, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The AI simulation “aims to reflect 80% of the scenarios McKinsey consultants might encounter in their day-to-day work,” the WSJ says, and it isn’t designed to “mimic an unhinged client.” The AI won’t score the candidates — humans will be in the room to assess the candidates and see how well they deal with the simulated situations.

The McKinsey tool will be in testing for undergrads seeking business-analyst jobs in “some” offices in North America this fall, and the WSJ says “hundreds” may use it.

Other companies are also building tools to use AI avatars as part of the job interview process, and my colleague Hayden Field tried some of them out for a video we published in March.

Tech.title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

I’m just going to come right out and say it. I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? No. But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? Absolutely.

A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. And yes, its features replicate many of the things you already do on the devices you use all the time. But that’s kind of the point. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with.

I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. It wasn’t great. I’ll have to test HomeView, of course, but my initial impression is that this could be a much better solution for those use cases.

My iPad in the wall experiment lasted several unsuccessful years.

Most iPads are more expensive, have worse speakers, and do not like to be plugged in all the time (I present my sad, warped iPad Mini as tribute). An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching.

Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. This means it’s always where you expect it to be, which matters when you want to adjust the thermostat or can’t find your phone and want to check your calendar. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion.

And while many people are fine using their personal phones and tablets to interact with the digital world when at home, and don’t want yet another device with a screen on their countertop or wall, the millions of Echo Shows, Google Nest Hubs, Skylight Calendars, and the like in homes today are a good indicator that there’s interest in this type of interface.

The HomeView’s footprint is smaller than that of most smart displays I’ve tested.

As Apple’s uncharacteristically chaotic launch video shows, HomeView targets a new demographic for the company: busy, Apple-centric households. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. I’ve occasionally used the drop-in feature on Echo smart speakers to get her attention, further proof of the advantage of always-on home devices.

The HomeView uses Siri AI (which requires an AI-capable iPhone) to provide useful personal information. An iPhone or iPad is required for a user profile, but anyone in the home can control devices like smart lights. (But that’s one really big button … )

I see HomeView as filling the awkward space where families don’t want phones at the dinner table or on the kitchen counter, but still want to check what time Zoey’s soccer game is or look up the origin of French toast (yeah, just kidding). This inevitably ends with one person pulling out their phone, which gives everyone else implicit permission to do the same.

Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). Siri AI’s much-hyped “personal context” capabilities, in which it can scan your text messages and emails and serve up relevant information to up to six members of your household, also give it an edge here.

The HomeView has a variety of customizable faces.

I asked Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, why Apple chose now for its biggest smart home push yet. She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.

As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.” — Lilian Rincon, Apple

Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. She also pointed to its new conversational abilities. “It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”

Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. Based on the demos I saw, and my time using Siri AI on the iPhone, when you ask it to do something, it does it without peppering you with follow-up questions. Rincon confirmed this is by design. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. “For us, it isn’t about that. We’re there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way.”

The Home control widget on the HomeView can show live views of security cameras.

My first reaction to hearing about HomeView’s smart home features, which are basically just what the Apple Home app on your phone can do, was disappointment. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. I’m still waiting on that.

On reflection, I’m okay with this — for now. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights.

Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing.

HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? My family.

Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen.

HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.
